title: Titan Marching Band Advances To KMEA Semi-Finals
description: Ben Sears Contributing Writer Mercerbandmedia@gmail.com Well, for those at home who have been keeping score, they made it! The Mercer County Titans Marching Band traveled to Irvine this past weekend…
content:
Ben Sears
Contributing Writer
Mercerbandmedia@gmail.com
Well, for those at home who have been keeping score, they made it!
The Mercer County Titans Marching Band traveled to Irvine this past weekend as Estill County High School hosted the East Region of the Kentucky Music Educators Association 2024 2A East Region Regionals. To qualify for regionals, a band has to compete in two regular-season competitions. Mercer competed at three contests and was rained out for the fourth.
Mercer went on at 2 p.m., performing their show 'My Hollow Heart.' They have spent weeks practicing and perfecting their show. Their performance was fantastic. Their hearts were in it.
'Get out there and lay it all down today. Give it your best shot,' said field commander Reagan Sims. 'If you aren't doing it for yourself, do it for the seniors. Do it for the people who want to see one more Saturday,' Sims continued her pep talk with great enthusiasm before they went on the field. The words rang true in the hearts of the students. They all did their best, and in the end, it all paid off.
The judges made their tabulations, and 13 bands marched into the stadium and around the track, being announced in performance order. They all took their positions together on the field in retreat. With KMEA it is tradition to have the bands march around the track and be announced. It is special for all band kids to be recognized in such a proud way.
Drum Major Reagan Sims looks over the band before beginning the show.
The announcer named all the bands in order of place by score. Mercer just needed to make the top six to advance. They started at 13 and named the band's placements one-by-one, each field commander stepping forward to receive their trophy. They got down to seventh place… Corbin High School. We knew we were in at that point. Then sixth place… Christian Academy of Louisville. Fifth place… Mercer County. All excitement was contained until after the ceremony. They had made the top six. They advanced.
'This is when it gets fun,' said Band Director Erica Ashford. 'This is what we have worked so hard for,' she continued. The band was presented with a good show this year and has worked hard and made it what it was. It is all things familiar to so many and has turned out great.
The band performs again on Saturday, Oct. 26, at noon at the Christian Academy of Louisville. We are competing with 11 other bands in the 2A Semi-Finals. From there, the judges will tabulate and pick six bands to move on to 2A Finals at Cardinals Stadium on Saturday evening. Join us this week in supporting and cheering on the band. We will be performing the halftime show one last time at Alvis Johnson Field during the Titans Football game.
For additional information, you can visit Mercer County Band on Facebook or @mercercoband on Instagram. The band is led by Erica Ashford with assistance from Jeremy Ellis (percussion) and Alex Smith (colorguard). The drum major is Reagan Sims and the Assistant Drum Majors are Josephine Doan and Matthew Clark. title: Community Helps Zack Ison With The Harvest
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreZack Ison and family stand in the parking lot of the Mercer County Cooperative Extension Office, surrounded by the farm equipment of friends, fam
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Zack Ison and family stand in the parking lot of the Mercer County Cooperative Extension Office, surrounded by the farm equipment of friends, family and fellow farmers who came to help Ison, who has been diagnosed with a brain tumor, with his harvest. Front row (from left): Millie Arnold, Beckham Arnold and Ashlynn Ison. Back row: Elizabeth Arnold, Ella Arnold, Gary Arnold, Deanna Arnold, Robin Ison, Zack Ison, Tiffany Ison, Tanner Ison and Zane Ison.
By 10 a.m., they were raring to go. They were farmers, most of them, and used to going to work early. But on Tuesday, Nov. 5, they met up at the Mercer County Cooperative Extension Office and waited. There were combines and tractor-trailers and they were there to help Zack Ison with his harvest. On this day, they had to wait until they heard from Ison first.
In addition to their farm equipment and their labor, they also brought food and offered Ison storage space for his crops.
'Everybody has called, wanting to help,' said Ian Thomas, who was helping to organize the event. 'It's a huge community effort.'
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
'Everybody has called, wanting to help,' said Ian Thomas, who was helping to organize the effort to help farmer Zack Ison with his crops.
Ison has been diagnosed with a brain tumor. On Tuesday, he told the crowd of his friends, family and fellow farmers that he and his family were seeking a second opinion, with the hope of surgery and a complete recovery.
'It's unreal how much support there is and how much it's brought the community together,' said Ison, the son of Robin Ison and the late Charlie Ison. In addition to farming, Zack Ison has served in various leadership positions with the Mercer County Farm Bureau, among other local organizations.
'It's just remarkable how everybody came together in a time of need,' he said.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Debbie Jones, Tina Murphy, Denise Burke and Georgetta Bailey prepare a meal for everyone at the Mercer County Cooperative Extension Office Tuesday.
Ison went from one group of people to another to shake their hands and thank them.
'They're not just my friends,' he said, 'they're my family.'
Before they went to work, had lunch prepared by the Mercer County Cattleman's Association. Before they prayed, an emotional Ison addressed the crowd. By that point, the parking was packed, with vehicles overflowing into nearby fields.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Tiffany Ison, Zack Ison and Ian Thomas address the crowd at the extension office.
'I want to thank you all from the bottom of my heart,' Ison said, one arm wrapped around his wife, Tiffany, the other arm around Thomas. 'Next fall, you all are going to get Ison every day.' title: Burgin's Lynley Thacker Selected For National Office
description: Lynley Thacker Burgin's Lynley Thacker was selected as secretary of the first Future Business Leaders of America national middle school leadership council (FBLA). FBLA is a non-profit organization…
content:
Lynley Thacker
Burgin's Lynley Thacker was selected as secretary of the first Future Business Leaders of America national middle school leadership council (FBLA).
FBLA is a non-profit organization that helps students prepare for careers in business and business education. The organization works to bring business and education together through leadership development programs.
Thacker, at 8th grader at Burgin Independent, was chosen as a finalist from applications submitted from across the country. After successfully completing the interview process, she was named to the national council.
'I was very excited when I found out I was going to be on this council,' said Thacker. 'I will be able to give ideas to promote middle school FBLA as well as attend monthly meetings and travel with the organization.'
Thacker has been active in the community organizing food and clothing drives, along with her younger sister Laykyn, since they were both young. She has been active in FBLA where she has been secretary of her local chapter for the last three years; on the honor roll; cheers for her middle school and high school teams along with Kentucky Spirit; is active in 4-H and her youth group at Harrodsburg Baptist Church. She is the daughter of Jeremy and Jamie Thacker. For more great stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Darrian Baker And The Colonels Are Back In The Playoffs
description: Former Mercer County standout defensive lineman Darrian Baker and the Eastern Kentucky University football team earned an at-large bid for the Football Championship Series (FCS) Playoffs after picking…
content:
Former Mercer County standout defensive lineman Darrian Baker and the Eastern Kentucky University football team earned an at-large bid for the Football Championship Series (FCS) Playoffs after picking up their fifth straight win on Saturday, Nov. 23. The final win of the regular season was also the fifth straight victory for the Colonels, which is the longest winning streak in Baker's college career, and the longest in Head Coach Walt Wells tenure in Richmond.
Darrian Baker pictured with his parents Greg and Linda Baker, and girlfriend Jaicy Todd during senior day, Saturday, Nov. 23. (Eastern Kentucky Athletics/Corey Rush)
'It's super special, because I came in with Coach Wells during his first year taking over the program, and during this time there've been a lot of ups and downs. To get our highest win season in my senior season, with other guys from coach Wells' first recruiting class, is extremely special for us seniors who have been here five years. It has just been great to build a bond with these men over these years, and it is a testament to the hard work we have put in this year and all the years before,' said Baker.
The fifth year senior was selected to the Community Trust Bank 2024 Kentucky Collegiate All-Commonwealth Team before the season began, and in his final season, has played a key role in the Colonels' success. In the crucial part of the season, when EKU faced United Athletic Conference leaders Central Arkansas and Tarleton State, Baker earned 12 tackles, 2.5 for a loss, in the upset victories. In total, Baker has grabbed 36 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, two sacks, a forced fumble and an interception in his final season.
Darrian Baker celebrated with his teammates in the backfield after wrapping up a North Alabama runner for a loss in EKU's 21-15 win on senior day. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren)
Against North Alabama in the season finale, Baker busted through the line of scrimmage and threw down runner Jayvian Allen for a loss of a yard, ending the Lion's opening drive. Baker chased down the Lion quarterback later in the game and combined for a half sack. The Lions rallied to take a one point lead after Eastern threw an interception that shifted the momentum, but Marcus Calwise Jr. earned the lead back for the Colonels after a 67 yards touchdown reception. EKU's defense snagged interceptions on each of the last two drives to put the game away, and finished the regular season with a 21-15 win, and a 8-2 record within the FCS. This is EKU's 23rd appearance in the FCS playoffs, which is the second most in FCS history. Wells became the first coach to lead the program to multiple playoff berths since Dean Hood.
The playoff selection committee pitted two historically great FCS programs against one another for the first time in the schools histories. EKU will play 11-seed Villanova in the opening round of the 24-team tournament on Saturday, Nov. 30, in Villanova, Penn. The game is set to kickoff at 2 p.m., and can be streamed live on ESPN+.
'I have great confidence in this team, and I feel this is the closest a team I've been on has ever been. It truly feels like a family. I have great confidence in us because we are getting hot at the right time and hitting our stride in the right part of the season,' said Baker.
Baker is grateful for the opportunity to join the program back in 2020, and the last four years have been some of the most transformative of his life. Baker became a first generation graduate when he earned a Bachelor's degree in sports management, and is currently working toward a Master's degree in business administration. Eastern's FCA program has had a tremendous effect on Baker as well, and the Mercer County native has grown both in his faith, and as a person.
'Being a Colonel has been a huge privilege and honor to play at such a prestigious university and football program alongside some great players and amazing people. I'm truly thankful that Coach Wells and his staff gave me the shot to come in 2020. Being a Colonel takes a great sense of pride, being the best version of you,' said Baker. title: Earn A Free T-Shirt With Your Donation At Blood Drive On Friday, Dec. 13
description: Photo SubmittedAll donors receive a free T-shirt like the one above for donating blood at the Kentucky Blood Center's drive on Friday, Dec. 13. Earn a free T-shirt for donating blood at the Kentucky…
content:
Photo Submitted
All donors receive a free T-shirt like the one above for donating blood at the Kentucky Blood Center's drive on Friday, Dec. 13.
Earn a free T-shirt for donating blood at the Kentucky Blood Center's blood drive for Mercer County on Friday, Dec. 13, from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. at Lions Park Community Center (133 Factory Street). The blood drive will feature an 'Eat, Donate, Hibernate, Repeat' T-shirt as a nod to what's most essential in the winter months.
Winter is just around the corner, which means it's time to stock the shelves and ensure local hospitals have the lifesaving blood products they need no matter what Old Man Winter has in store.
The winter season can disrupt blood collections because of weather cancellations and an uptick in illnesses. Proactive blood donation at Kentucky Blood Center drives like this one in your community are vital to a healthy blood supply.
Donors can pass on the thank you item and the value will be donated to Greenhouse 17 to help victims of domestic violence.
Consistent blood donation is essential to maintaining a healthy blood supply for the more than 70 hospitals served by the Kentucky Blood Center. Blood is an everyday need and cannot be manufactured. To serve local patients, donors must step up.
Blood donors must be at least 17 years old (16 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, be in general good health, show a photo I.D. and meet additional requirements. Sixteen-year-old donors must have a signed parental permission slip, which can be found at kybloodcenter.org.
Appointments are preferred but walk-ins are welcome. To schedule a donation, visit kybloodcenter.org or call 800-775-2522.
Kentucky Blood Centeris the largest independent, full-service, nonprofit blood center in the commonwealth. KBC has been saving local lives since 1968. Licensed by the FDA, KBC's sole purpose is to collect, process and distribute blood for patients in Kentucky. KBC provides services in 90 Kentucky counties and has donor centers in Lexington, Louisville, Frankfort, Pikeville, Somerset and the Tri-County area (Corbin). Kentucky Blood Center
Mercer County Community Blood Drive
Friday, Dec. 13
10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Lions Park Community Center
(133 Factory Street)

title: One-Man Marvel: Solo Performance Of ‘A Christmas Carol' Brings Dickens' Classic To Life
description: Scrooge was transported through time by the Spirit of Christmas Past, Present and Future showing him what he has missed over the years. In the above scene the dying flame in the grate leapt up as if…
content:
Scrooge was transported through time by the Spirit of Christmas Past, Present and Future showing him what he has missed over the years. In the above scene the dying flame in the grate leapt up as if to say ' I know him! Marley's ghost!'
The start of the holiday season can be marked by the appearance of Christmas lights, the occasional sighting of Ol' Saint Nick and Ragged Edge Community Theatre's annual production of Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol.' This year's performances will be on Saturday, Dec. 7, at 7 p.m. and Sunday, Dec. 8, at 3 p.m. All tickets are $12 and are available through the theatre's website www.raggededgetheatre.org or at the box office on the night of show.
'It is my favorite thing that I get to do all year,' said Ragged Edge's Managing Director Allan Barlow, who has been a professional actor for 30 years.
This production is a one-man show adapted for the stage and performed by Barlow. He created his one-man version of 'A Christmas Carol' in 2003. While this is Ragged Edge's 13th production. It marks Barlow's 22nd year. His first captive audience was a class of third graders. Since then, he has performed it at theaters, churches, colleges and private events across the country to spellbound audiences.
'Here I am 20 plus years in, and it still picks me up and carries me off. It is a beautiful story, beautifully written and I never get tired of telling it.'
Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol' is a timeless novella first published in 1843. It tells the story of Ebenezer Scrooge, a miserly and cold-hearted businessman in Victorian England who undergoes a profound transformation after being visited by four spirits on Christmas Eve.
'It paints an almost photographic vision of Victorian England and it's crammed full of warm, nostalgic, incredibly vivid imagery, but I believe when all is said and done, it's remained popular and able to touch people deeply because it is a parable about redemption. I mean…what could be more fitting at Christmas time than a story about redemption?'
Tickets can be purchased by visiting raggededgetheatre.org or by calling 859-734-2389. All seats are $12. Show begins at 7 p.m. on Saturday, Dec. 7, and 3 p.m. on Sunday, Dec. 8. title: Patsy Bailey
description: Patsy Blankenship Bailey, 80, of Harrodsburg, Kentucky, died Tuesday, Nov. 26, 2024, with her family lovingly by her side. She was born on Sept. 6, 1944, in Warren County, to the late Rev. Aubrey and…
content:
Patsy Blankenship Bailey, 80, of Harrodsburg, Kentucky, died Tuesday, Nov. 26, 2024, with her family lovingly by her side.
She was born on Sept. 6, 1944, in Warren County, to the late Rev. Aubrey and Lunie (Luna) (Jones) Blankenship.
She is also preceded in death by one sister, Betty Lyles of Gallatin, Tenn.; three brothers, Murrell Blankenship of Lexington, Joe Blankenship of Harrodsburg, and Sonny Blankenship of Bowling Green.
Patsy is survived by her loving husband of 26 years, Gary Sewell Bailey; one daughter and son-in-law, Tracey and James Tennill of Taylorsville; two grandsons and their wives, Clayton and Amanda Walker of Shelbyville and Aaron and Renita Walker of Simpsonville; four great-grandchildren, Daxton, Vaeda, Gabereal and Tyrstin Walker; two sisters, Brenda Collins and Carolyn Blankenship, both of Clarksville, Tenn. and numerous nieces and nephews.
Patsy retired from Bell South Communications after 35 years of service between the Bowling Green and Louisville areas. She volunteered at Audubon Hospital NICU comforting addicted newborns. She was a member of Harrodsburg Baptist Church.
Patsy has chosen cremation with a private ceremony with her immediate family. A celebration of life will be scheduled later in the spring of 2025.
To share a memory of Patsy or leave a special message for her family, please visit www.newcomerkentuckiana.com.

The first-ever Downtown Harrodsburg Santa Shuffle happens Saturday, Dec. 14, from 4 p.m. to midnight. Visit five of the 16 participating locations to be entered into a giveaway for a gift basket valued at over $500. This winter there will be two basket giveaways. title: Burgin falls as TCA rallies late
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Bulldogs basketball team (1-4) played their first of two matchups against district rival Trinity Christian (4-1) on Friday, Dec. 13.…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Bulldogs basketball team (1-4) played their first of two matchups against district rival Trinity Christian (4-1) on Friday, Dec. 13. The Bulldogs picked up their first win of the season three days prior over Casey County. Senior JT Boswell and sophomore Micah Mayes combined for 38 points on 6-13 shooting from deep to lead Burgin to their first win against a 12th Region opponent.
Head Coach Todd Claunch was happy with the 61-30 win against the Rebels, but he was
'I was more proud of them in their performance in almost every aspect of this game than I was in the Casey County game. I told them that games like Casey are easy when you are just clicking in every way and your opponent is struggling to get one to fall,' said Claunch.
Trinity Christian Academy was determined to get back in the win column after a 59-25 loss to Mercer County three days prior, and Burgin was forced to match their physicality in the paint throughout the game. Mayes got Burgin on the scoreboard first after draining a corner three. Much like in their win over the Rebels, Burgin was lethal from behind the arc, and Landon Sexton's movement led to several open shots in the opening quarter. Sexton assisted Mayes' second three and Hudson Taylor's first, and Burgin led 9-6. Casey Dodson put his body on the line play-after-play, but TCA's duo of big men, Allen Okorley and Noah Westerfield made it difficult for Burgin to make an impact on the glass. The Titans' advantage down low was negated again and again by Burgin's sharpshooters. This time Dodson drove into the lane before kicking out to Taylor for another trey. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Edna Lister
description: Edna Mae Sparks Lister, 68, widow of Gerald Clayton Lister, died Thursday, Dec. 19, 2024, at the Ephraim McDowell James B. Haggin Hospital. Born Feb. 23, 1956, in Mercer County, she was the daughter…
content:
Edna Mae Sparks Lister, 68, widow of Gerald Clayton Lister, died Thursday, Dec. 19, 2024, at the Ephraim McDowell James B. Haggin Hospital.
Born Feb. 23, 1956, in Mercer County, she was the daughter of the late Edward and Alice Dean Sparks.
She was a homemaker and a member of the Perryville Church of God.
Survivors include: one son, Josh (Trish) Lister of Harrodsburg; five daughters, Tabby Ryan, Heather Lister, Amber (Angelica) Lister, Ashley (Timothy) Bottoms and Brittany (Hagan) Smith, all of Harrodsburg; two brothers, Ronnie Sparks of Millington, Tenn., and Connie (Joann) Sparks of Lawrenceburg; three sisters, Barbara Turpin of Harrodsburg, Elizabeth Hale of Harrodsburg and Joyce Scull of Salvisa; four grandchildren; two great-grandchildren; and several nieces and nephews.
She was preceded in death by one daughter, Tracy Lister; one granddaughter, Lillyann Maddox; two brothers, Marvin Sparks and Edward Sparks Jr.; and one niece, Amanda Watts.
Funeral services will be 1 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 28, at the Alexander & Royalty Funeral Home, Inc. and Cremation Services with Paul Stratton officiating. Burial will be in the Parksville Cemetery.
Pallbearers will be Timothy Bottoms, Marcus Walker, Michael Royalty, Dereck Whitis, Scotty Robbins and Alex Grubbs. Honorary pallbearers will be Zack Ryan, Austin Stanley, Blake Devine, Maddi Curtsinger, Westyn Curtsinger and Hagan Maddox.
Visitation 6-8 p.m. Friday and after 7 a.m. Saturday at the funeral home.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.alexanderandroyalty.com.

content:
Wayne Young Morris, 81, husband of Ivana (Eckl) Morris, of Lancaster, died Wednesday, Nov. 20, 2024, in Bad Durkheim, Germany.
Born March 7, 1943, in Harrodsburg, he was the son of the late Clarence Overstreet and Emma (Thomas) Morris.
Wayne was a Veteran of the U. S. Army and received the National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal, Combat Infantryman Badge and Sharp Shooter Badge (Rifle). A retired human resources specialist for the Department of Defense/Civil Service in the United States Army, he was of the Christian faith.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: three children; two brothers, Carroll Morris and Ralph Morris; and seven grandchildren.
He was preceded in death by five brothers, Garnett Morris, Aubrey Morris, Larry Morris, James 'J.R.' Morris and Stanley Bennett Morris, and two sisters, Mildred Irene Crum and Mary Joyce Niederlehner.
Burial was in Camp Nelson National Cemetery in Nicholasville with Military Honors.
Arrangements by Ransdell Funeral Chapel.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.ransdelfuneralchapel.com.

title: Cats Roll Into Conference Play
description: Fried Gator, anyone? Well that's exactly what was on the menu for Mark Pope and his Kentucky Wildcats when they defeated the (previously) undefeated Florida Gators on Saturday, Dec. 4, to start…
content:
Fried Gator, anyone? Well that's exactly what was on the menu for Mark Pope and his Kentucky Wildcats when they defeated the (previously) undefeated Florida Gators on Saturday, Dec. 4, to start conference play. In a year where the SEC is likely the best conference in the nation– some are saying the best in the history of college basketball– starting the campaign with a big home win was critical for the Cats, and they delivered.
Rolling into the 11 a.m. tip-off, Kentucky boasted a strong record of 11-2. With notable top-10 wins over Duke and Gonzaga, Pope was looking to be the first Kentucky coach since Adolph Rupp to start his career 3-0 against AP top-10 opponents. However, this would be no easy task, with a hungry group of Gators taking the floor.
Amari Williams blocks a shot in Kentucky's 106-100 win against Florida in the seasons SEC opener. (Image: Jordan Prather/Imagn Images)
This year's Florida team looked to be a tough matchup for the Wildcats, as they boast three of the league's top-scoring guards, an area Kentucky has consistently struggled combatting so far this season. Furthermore, Florida's strength as a team is their perimeter defending, offensive rebounding, and athletic penetration, all things that give the Wildcats a hard time. This made for a terrific litmus test for Mark Pope's coaching ability and his team's aptitude to win in different ways than they are used to.
Despite these obstacles, the Wildcats delivered an exemplary performance. Whenever the Gators landed a hard punch, the Wildcats hit back harder. Throughout the game, Kentucky even went on three different 10+ point runs. Pope's group of veteran transfers proved if you give them an inch, they will take a mile. When this team of Wildcats gets hot, watch out.
This performance led the Wildcats to take an impressive 106-100 victory, sealing their place in the top-10 rankings for another week. The biggest question moving forward is: Do we finally know what this team is? Are they a group of under-talented, un-athletic, poor-defensive shooters whose whole is greater than the sum of its parts? And if they are, is that a bad thing? Well, yes and no.
At this point, it is clear the Wildcats will be very matchup-prone. They will undoubtedly struggle against athleticism, physicality, and any team that presses the three-point line. The scary part is that the SEC is chock-full of rosters. However, at some point, we have to give Pope the benefit of the doubt. title: Colts Win Second Matchup Against Titans
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/April EllisTitan forward Trevor Ellis and West Jessamine guard Gavin Murphy waited for play to restart during Mercer's 50-48 lo
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Titan forward Trevor Ellis and West Jessamine guard Gavin Murphy waited for play to restart during Mercer's 50-48 loss to West Jessamine on Monday, Feb. 3.
After a 16-point win against West Jessamine on Jan. 24, Mercer went into their second match-up against the Colts a little too overconfident, and West made them pay for it with a 50-48 overtime loss.
Mercer took good shots, but they either rolled around the rim or popped out. The Titans didn't score until the 4-minute mark when junior Kaleb Murray drove to the basket, 5-2. Murray's second drive was the only other points the Titans scored in the first quarter, trailing 11-4.
West put up four quick points to open the second quarter before senior Trevor Ellis hit a mid-range jumper. On the defensive end of the court, Ellis blocked a shot. The Titans did a good job containing Luk Tut to eight points. Ellis took care of the front assault, Murray snuck in to strip the ball from the back and Mercer's guard were there anytime he held the ball low to the floor.

title: David Coleman Steps Down As Manager Of Old Fort Harrod
description: Photo SubmittedDavid Coleman is stepping down as manager of Old Fort Harrod State Park after 20 years of service with Kentucky State Parks-16 ye
content:
Photo Submitted
David Coleman is stepping down as manager of Old Fort Harrod State Park after 20 years of service with Kentucky State Parks-16 years at Old Fort Har­rod. Coleman is taking a job with the Mercer County government. He is pic­tured with interim director Autumn Morrison.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
David Coleman is stepping down as manager of Old Fort Harrod State Park. Coleman has worked for 20 years with the Kentucky Department of Parks, serving 16 years at Old Fort Harrod. Coleman's last day was Friday, Feb. 28. He is taking the position of building inspector with Mercer County. Autumn Morrison will serve as interim director.
'While I am very excited about this new opportunity and career path, I am just as sad to leave behind all the great people at Old Fort Harrod,' Coleman said in a Facebook post. 'I will always love this park, the best park in the nation's finest system.'
Coleman sells a mug celebrating Harrodsburg's 250th Anniversary.
Coleman is a native of Arkansas who moved to Kentucky in 1984. In his years with the park, he has become as much of a downtown figure as Pioneer Man, the coonskin-cap-wearing statue that had stood outside Old Fort Harrod since 2005 and now resides in the James Harrod Amphitheater.
Coleman gives the cast of 'James Harrod: The Battle For Kentucky' a safety lecture.
During annual events at the park—including the Settlement and Raid, which returns this year on Saturday, June 14, and Sunday, June 15—visitors could find Coleman, usually dressed as an early Kentucky pioneer. That was hardly his only role at the park. Coleman could be seen everywhere, from teaching schoolchildren about Kentucky history to picking up litter to running the beer stand to serving as the narrator of the Haunted Frontier, which returns for a week of historically terrifying fun on Friday, Oct. 24.
David Coleman participates in the 2019 Settlement and Raid.
As Coleman told the Harrodsburg Herald in 2019: 'In a park of this size, the manager does a little of everything.'
Coleman's time at the park has included a lot of history. His tenure has coincided with the return of outdoor drama—'James Harrod: The Battle for Kentucky' returns for a three weekend run starting Friday, July 10—as well as the closing of the James Harrod Conference Center in 2017 and the replacement of the stockade walls at Old Fort Harrod, which was made possible due to a $100,000 grant from the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourism Commission.
David Coleman, park manager at Old Fort Harrod State Park, takes time out from the Grand Council to snap a picture with his anachronistic smart phone.
On Friday, friends and coworkers from across the state gathered to celebrate Coleman's service.
Old Fort Harrod is one of the most unique sites in the system. The park's entire 15 acres is located in downtown Harrodsburg. In addition to the replica fort, it includes the Mansion Museum, the Lincoln Marriage Temple, the 'Pioneer Cemetery', the oldest in Kentucky, and the ancient Osage Orange tree.
David Coleman, manager of Old Fort Harrod State Park, taking aim. (File image from 2018).
Here is a list of events at Old Fort Harrod State Park (100 South College Street).
Coleman leads the crowd in a hearty 'Huzzah!' at Harrodsburg's 250th Celebration.
• Harrodsburg Kiwanis Club Easter Egg Hunt on Saturday, April 19. The free event is open to children up to the age of 12 and runs from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.
• Native Dawn Flute Gathering, from Friday, May 23, through Sunday, May 25. Three day festival celebrating Native American music as well as traditional arts and crafts runs.
• Picnic in the Park returns Friday, June 6, and happens every Friday at noon through July. Mercer County's oldest live entertainment series.
• Settlement and Raid on Saturday, June 14, and Sunday, June 15. Full scale re-enactment, with settlers, natives, traders and living history both days.
• 'James Harrod: The Battle for Kentucky' for three weekends Thursdays through Saturdays starting Thursday, July 10, through Saturday, July 26. Outdoor drama.
• 13th Annual Pioneer Days Festival from Thursday, Aug. 14, until Sunday, Aug. 17, with the Big Jack Pearson Memorial Car Show on Saturday, Aug. 16.
• Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival, three days of jazz at the fort from Friday, Oct. 10, through Sunday, Sept. 12.
• Haunted Frontier runs two weeks starting Friday, Oct. 24, and ending on Halloween, Friday, Oct. 31.
• Fifth Annual Winter Encampment and Holiday Open House and the lighting of the Christmas Tree Forest on Saturday, Nov. 22.
For more information about Old Fort Harrod, call the park at 859-734-3314, email ortharrod@ky.gov or visit them on Facebook @ fortharrod.statepark. For more great stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Pioneers Claim MidEast Region Title
description: The Campbellsville-Harrodsburg Pioneers played host to the NCCAA Division-II MidEast Regional Tournament this past weekend, taking down Welch College for a third time this season before facing Simmons…
content:
The Campbellsville-Harrodsburg Pioneers played host to the NCCAA Division-II MidEast Regional Tournament this past weekend, taking down Welch College for a third time this season before facing Simmons College of Louisville in the title game. The Pioneers are used to winning on this stage, and have won three times in the past, but never on their home court. The crowd was rocking in Harrodsburg, and Pioneer Head Coach Austin Sparrow was happy with the support.
'The community has done a great job supporting us this year and the families of our players and the staff here at CU-Harrodsburg has really bought-in to making Campbellsville-Harrodsburg basketball an absolute enjoyable time. For me personally, I'm ecstatic. It's something I've been wanting for the last six years,' said Sparrow, who was recently named MidEast Region Coach of the Year for the second season running.
Harrodsburg went on the first run and jumped to an early 6-0 lead. Both teams were playing good defense early and the intensity was palpable. Pioneer forwards Warner Bryan and Evan Frederick got into a bit of foul trouble early, but Colton Ralston answered by jumping a pass and knocking down his first triple of the game. Moments later the sophomore from Lincoln County tracked down a Simmons breakaway and swatted the shot just as it left the hands of Gavin Withrow. Withrow made some tough shots of his own though, and with 10:45 left in the first, the Pioneers called a timeout after Simmons tied the game at 15. Simmons' lead didn't last for long though as Ralston inbounded a long ball to Braden Smith, who took a deep three to break the tie. Moments later, Bryan stuck a hand out and forced a turnover, and Smith finished with a pull up jumper on the other end.
One possession later, Bryan made a move down low and finished strong off the backboard while being fouled. Withrow was causing lots of problems for the Pioneer defense. The Male High School graduate knocked down a corner three and picked the Pioneers pockets in a manner of seconds. He continued to make big shots until the buzzer sounded. At the half, Campbellsville-Harrodsburg trailed Simmons 34-30.
The beginning of the second half was much of the same. Everything the Falcons threw toward the basket dropped through. Two unfortunate foul calls kept the Pioneers from being able to rebuttal. With 17:25 remaining, Simmons knocked down a corner three in transition, taking their lead to 41-30. Frederick backed down Simmons' Phillip Richards and spun around for the Pioneers' first basket of the second half. Moments later, Chivion Ashby blew by his defender on the way to the basket and made two free throws, cutting the Falcons' lead to seven. Senior Jeremiah Williamson played some crucial minutes and made an impact defensively, swatting a Simmons' shot and forcing another turnover on the following possession. When Ralston knocked down his third three of the game the arena exploded with energy. Landon Elmore made a statement with his own three seconds later, and after back-to-back Simmons' travels, Harrodsburg had a chance to retake the lead. Senior Elijah Frye did just that with 6:48 to go in the game. The senior made two clutch free throws to put the Pioneers on top 48-46.
CU-Harrodsburg senior Warner Bryan pictured drawing a foul, eventually going to the line and sinking both shots to give the Pioneers a 56-55 lead with seconds remaining. Photo: The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren.
Bryan and Frederick only combined to feature 44 minutes, but after subbing into the game in crunch time they both made the impact needed to push the Pioneers forward. Senior Nakyir Joyce set up the offense and got the ball to Frederick with just over 2 minutes to play and the sophomore kissed the ball off the glass, claiming a 3-point lead over his former team. Smith made a cut across the basket and nailed a floater to keep the Pioneers on top, but in the closing moments, Simmons retook the lead, 55-54. Bryan, a three-year senior from Hodgenville, made a run down the baseline and received a pass from Joyce before rising up to the rim, but his shot slowly bounced out. It didn't phase him though, and he went on to make both shots, reclaiming a 56-55 lead for Harrodsburg. Winthrow's game-winning 3-point attempt from the top of the key bounced off the rim twice, and the subsequent tip, hit the inside of the rim before bouncing out. It was an agonizing final 4 seconds for the fans and Pioneer players alike, but as the ball bounced to the floor, the relief could be seen on the face of each Pioneer, as they were named back-to-back MidEast Region Champions. This is the third time the program has claimed a regional trophy, with the other coming in 2022, the year CU-Harrodsburg won the NCCAA D-II National Championship. This is the final run for five Pioneer players. Joyce, Bryan, Frye, Ethan Bailey and Sebastian Dixon, who Sparrow noted was the scout team player of the year and did a great job of preparing the Pioneers for their competition week in and week out will lead the Pioneers as they enter the NCCAA National Tournament hosted by Crown College in Minneapolis, MN, beginning on Thursday, March 13. Each of the seniors outside of Bryan have been with the program all four years of their college career, and Sparrow is proud of their accomplishments.
'It's pretty awesome. We've been talking to them about building a tradition, and these guys have finally set the tone of what we want that tradition to be about,' said Sparrow. title: Titans Repeat As 46th District Champions
description: A year ago, when the Mercer County High School boys basketball team took down Trinity Cristian by a score of 66-44 in the 46th District Championship game, it was the first district title for the…
content:
A year ago, when the Mercer County High School boys basketball team took down Trinity Cristian by a score of 66-44 in the 46th District Championship game, it was the first district title for the program in five years. The 2024-2025 Titans (21-10) entered the postseason battle-tested and eager to repeat as the area champions, but West Jessamine (17-9) stood in the Titans' way. The Colts shocked Mercer a month prior, knocking off the Titans in Harrodsburg in an overtime thriller, but Mercer never stepped off the gas on this occasion.
2025 12th Region Player of the Year Trevor Ellis made a statement in the opening moments of the game, blowing by Jessamine's 6 '9 center Luk Tut and scoring through a foul. Ellis finished past Tut three times to set the tone and earn an early 7-2 lead for the Titans. Kaleb Murray created a fast-break opportunity out of nothing, driving into the lane like a train off the tracks and colliding with two Colt defenders, but the junior fought for his own rebound, went back up, had his shot swatted, plucked it from the air and drained his third attempt from close range. Hagan Preston was in the right place at the right time, stepping in front of a lazy pass at the free throw line, and drawing a foul at the rim seconds later, making both shots. After starting 1/6 from the field and turning the ball over three times, Jessamine began to tighten up defensively, and Gavin Murphy knocked down a triple from the top of the arc. A Titan turnover in the final seconds of the first quarter allowed Tut to slam the ball down in transition, tying the score at 11.
Trevor Ellis, Hagan Preston and Kaleb Murray were each selected to the 46th District All-Tournament Team. The trio were the only scorers in Mercer's 48-43 win. Photo: The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren.
West continued their run into the second quarter and scored eight points in just over 60 seconds of play. One possession after scoring his second basket at the rim over Tut, Murray handed the ball to Ellis just outside the perimeter. No one stepped up to defend, and Ellis swished the long range jumper. On the following Titan possession, Jackson Doughty fed Ellis the ball inside, and Ellis backed down Tut again, this time crossing face and finishing off the glass. Preston was a menace defending the perimeter and came away with another steal seconds later. Preston moved the ball to Doughty, and the junior delivered a touch pass to Ellis cutting to the rim for a slam-dunk, tying the game at 19. Colt guard Murphy knocked down another three to quiet the Mercer crowd for a moment, but Murray and Ellis both got to the line in the closing moments of the first half. After two quarters, the game was tied at 22. Ellis and Murray combined for 20 points in the first half.
Murray assisted the first Titan basket of the second half when he connected with Ellis on the wing, and the big man finished with a reverse layup to reclaim a two-point lead for the Titans. Murray and Doughty met West's J.T. Messick at the rim moments later and rejected his shot. Seconds later, Preston delivered a rocket of a pass to Murray under the basket and the junior was sent to the line, making one. Murphy knocked down his third trey of the game to tie the game at 29, but Preston grabbed a missed Murray shot on the following possession and put it back up off the glass. Moments later, Murray delivered a high arching pass that traveled over the rim before falling into Ellis' hands for an easy two. Preston kept the momentum moving in the Titans' direction after a tough drive that forced his defender off of the court before he finished with ease. The Titans had opened up their first lead since the opening quarter, and led 35-31 with 8 minutes remaining.
Two minutes passed before a basket was scored, but Preston nailed a step back three from the top of the key, extending Mercer's lead. Seconds later, West fumbled the ball, Preston scooped it up and drew a foul at the rim, making one and giving Mercer its biggest lead of the game. With 5:26 remaining, the Titans led 39-31. Preston and Ellis combined for the exclamation when Preston plucked the ball out of the air, drove down the court and played a perfect bounce pass to Ellis for an easy finish at the rim.
'Our guys were ready to play,' Mercer Head Coach Keith Adkins said of the win. 'I think the loss in the last game to West Jessamine stung a little and gave us some fuel for this game. You don't ever want to lose, but I think that loss gave us the motivation and focus that we may have needed.'
The Titans went on to win their second 46th District Title in a row under Adkins, 48-43.
'I think the success over the last two seasons can be attributed to the players in this program. The ability has been there. All I have provided is some direction and motivation. My focus has been to get this group to realize what their ceiling is and work hard to reach that. The biggest challenge has been to get them to quit settling for second place or third place when first place is right there within their grasp. But, this group has bought into everything I have thrown at them and they are really close to achieving something really special,' said Adkins. The organizers are also partnering with Harrodsburg Rotary Club to sponsor the event, which honors the life of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., was an advocate for racial equality and nonviolent social change, as well as provide volunteers. title: Donation Shines A Light On Mercer County's Past
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreDavid Kirkpatrick, assistant director of the Mercer County Public Library, Jerry Sampson of J. Sampson Antiques and Robin Ison, director of the public library, hold…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
David Kirkpatrick, assistant director of the Mercer County Public Library, Jerry Sampson of J. Sampson Antiques and Robin Ison, director of the public library, hold a ledger book which contains information about the history of Mercer County. A new donation to the Mercer County Public Library shines a light on the area's history. The item is a ledger book from a wool and fur hat factory dating back to the 1820s–1830s, said Jerry Sampson of J. Sampson Antiques, Books and Appraisals on Main Street. Sampson said the book caught his attention at an estate sale. Last week, at the History Research Center, Sampson leafed through the book, which lists some of the oldest family names in the area, including Cook, McDowell, Moore, Overstreet and Speed. 'They would trap the fur and bring the fur in,' Sampson said. 'It's laid out in alphabetical order.' 'We were kind of suspecting it was part of the Thompkins and Reed Hat Factory,' he explained. The business was located in Danville, which at that time was located in Mercer County. 'These things hardly ever survive,' he said. Sampson said rather than letting the ledger languish in his collection, he donated it to the library 'where people can see it.' 'The Mercer County Public Library History Research Center is actively seeking and accepting historic donations,' Sampson said. 'We're very excited to have it here at the library,' said David Kirkpatrick, assistant director of the library and head of genealogy. 'A little bit of their life is revealed.' The ledger and other exhibits is on display at the Mercer County Public Library's History Research Center (114 Main Street). The center is open Monday through Friday and the third Saturday of each month from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. For more information, visit their website at mcplib.info or call 859-734-3680. For another glance at Mercer County's history, the library will host a table reading of 'The Trial of James Bridges' on Saturday, March 16, starting at 3:30 p.m. It will be a cold reading of the one hour play exploring one of the theories about Harrod's 1792 disappearance. It will be performed during Harrodsburg's 250th birthday celebration in June. For more great stories, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Stephen Ransdell Named Permanent Director At Anderson-Dean Community Park
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreStephen Ransdell has been named the new director of Anderson-Dean Community Park. Stephe
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Stephen Ransdell has been named the new director of Anderson-Dean Community Park. Stephen Ransdell has been named the full-time director of Anderson-Dean Community Park'
Ransdell has served as the interim director since January. He was promoted by the Anderson-Dean board of directors at their meeting on Thursday, March 14, according to a Facebook post. Ransdell served as facility maintenance planner at Essity since 1995. He has been working at the park since 2022. 'It's a great hire,' said Judge Executive Sarah Steele. 'He's done a tremendous job in the last month getting projects moving. I'm excited to see where we'll be in a year.' 'We've got a lot going on,' Ransdell said Tuesday. People have been complaining about the condition of the park for years, but issues came to a head last year, when the park was forced to shut down the pool after learning it had lost a million gallons of water in its first week. Since then, the county and city, which own the park jointly, have reorganized the board of directors and changed park directors. They hired American Leak Detection of Mount Washington to make repairs to the pool. On Monday, the Mercer County Fiscal Court voted to purchase a 60 millimeter PVC membrane for the pool at a cost of $197,880. On Tuesday, Ransdell said the liner 'will make it basically a brand new pool.' He said the pool will have all new plumbing and concrete and, thanks to the liner, a new, smooth surface. Ransdell said the current plan is to begin filling the pool on May 1. 'That's still the plan even with the lining purchase,' he said. Ransdell said he is also looking at buying new tables and chairs for the pool. Once the pool is full, they will spend a month or so making sure it doesn't leak. 'We want to make sure it's 100 percent,' Ransdell said. He said new scoreboards have been installed, although there have been some issues. He said they are looking at replacing a faulty processor in one of the scoreboards. Ransdell said they are waiting for parts. Currently, five of the seven new scoreboards are operational, he said. The City of Harrodsburg learned last week that they will receive $217,730 from the state to build a new playground and install a sprinkler system at the park. Ransdell said they are looking for additional funding to get the playground installed. He said they have ordered new volleyball nets and boundary lines, which will include the park's logo. He said they are looking to have the volleyball courts ready by summer. 'It will feel like you're playing on a professional court,' Ransdell said. The park has ordered new flooring for the Lions Pavilion. 'I will pick it up at the end of the week,' he said. They are looking to have the new flooring basically installed by Friday, March 29, Ransdell said. The new batting cages have been installed, and Rnsdell said he is looking at installing new rims for the basketball court. The park is replacing the barn that had to be torn down after last year's storm with a 60 foot by 40 foot storage building. Construction on that should start by the middle of April, Ransdell said. Resurfacing of the walking trails will begin when the weather is warm enough, he said. 'Then it's just a matter of catching up with the office work,' Ransdell said Tuesday. The office, officially known as the Thomas Long House, dates back to 1790. It too was damaged in last year's storms. Ransdell said he is working with the Harrodsburg Historical Society about possible solutions for the building. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. title: Commission Votes To Deny Rezoning For Controversial Development
description: File
content: File image. The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission voted to recommend denying a request to rezone 104.41 acres of land at the southeast corner of Garriott Lane and Robb Road from A-1 (agricultural) to A-3 (small community agricultural). Both zoning designations allow for residential development. A-1 zoning requires a building lot of 2.5 acres. A-3 zoning requires a building lot of one acre. The planning and zoning board votes to either recommend approving or denying rezoning requests, which are then sent to the Mercer County Fiscal Court. The commission voted to accept the findings of fact from the public hearing on Feb. 20, but listened to no public comments. More than 70 people showed up at the public hearing held last month to voice their opposition to AFI 001 LLC's rezoning request. Many—but not all—returned for the vote. 'You are welcome to stay,' said Bobby Upchurch, who chairs the planning and zoning commission. Few of the audience members stayed after the vote was held. The commission also voted to adopt the findings of fact from a public hearing also held in February. The commission already approved a request by Samudio Construction LLC to rezone 1.962 acres located on the northern side of Pinehurst Way from B-3 (central business) to R-2 (high density residential). The rezoning goes to the Harrodsburg City Commission next. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Harrodsburg Receives State Funding For Anderson-Dean
description: File image. The City of Harrodsburg will receive $217,730 from the state to build a new playground and install a sprinkler system at Anderson-Dean Community Park. It is one of 32 projects announced…
content:
File image. The City of Harrodsburg will receive $217,730 from the state to build a new playground and install a sprinkler system at Anderson-Dean Community Park. It is one of 32 projects announced last week by Gov. Andy Beshear that the governor said will enhance accessibility and upgrade parks and recreation spaces throughout the Commonwealth. The federally funded Land and Water Conservation Fund has allotted $3.9 million to communities across Kentucky for a wide variety of outdoor, health-related improvements, including the renovation or replacement of playground equipment, the construction of walking paths and bringing recreational facilities into compliance with Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility guidelines. 'These dollars improve parks across Kentucky and make them more accessible to all Kentuckians,' said Gov. Beshear in a press release. 'We will continue to make our parks a priority. They bring a sense of community, offer a place for our families to spend time together outdoors and are worthy of continued investment.' To receive the federal funds, which are administered at the state level by the Department for Local Government, selected applicants must undergo federal review and receive approval from the National Park Service. Pool membrane covering at Anderson-Dean Community Park
In related news, the Mercer County Fiscal Court voted Monday in a special-called meeting to pay $197,880 to purchase a 60 millimeter PVC membrane for the pool at the Anderson-Dean Aquatics Center. The fiscal court also approved making a payment of $99,375 to American Leak Detection of Mount Washington for phase II or repairs to the pool. The City of Harrodsburg will be responsible for the other half of the payment, which totals $198,750. At the special-called meeting, Stephen Ransdell, the newly hired manager at the park, went over issues with the original liner, which Ransdell said was not installed according to the original drawings. Ransdell said there was a crack that runs almost the length of the shallow end. He said the contractors have had to make cuts they didn't think they'd have to make, and that may lead to leaks. Ransdell said the membrane is guaranteed for 20 years. 'It will look like a completely new pool bottom,' Ransdell said. Magistrate Jackie Claycomb moved to go forward with the membrane, seconded by Magistrate Tim Darland. The pool was shut down in June 2023 after officials learned it had lost a million gallons of water in its first week of operations. 'We don't want to have to throw a waterhose in it every week,' Darland said. The pool liner is an add-on expense, separate from the ongoing repairs to reopen the pool. Expenses to maintain the pool and the rest of the park are split evenly between the county and city, but the city has taken no action as of press time. title: UK Basketball's March Madness Preview
content:
Photo by UK Athletics/Chet White
Wildcat freshman Rob Dillingham used the glass on this layup for two of his 15 points during the loss to Texas A&M in the SEC Tournament. It's March Madness time in the Bluegrass, and the Kentucky Wildcats are ready to prove to the world that they are no fluke. With Calipari and his team having much to prove, the Cats eagerly awaited their tournament draw on 'Selection Sunday.' Despite the team falling short in the SEC Tournament (yet again), Big Blue Nation went in with high hopes of a strong seed, a good path and a real shot at making a deep March run. Going into the SEC Tournament, all indications were that the Cats sat firmly on the 3-seed line, with a chance to move up after a couple of quality wins. However, this was not to be. Despite an extremely favorable draw, Kentucky played a poor brand of soft basketball, getting physically torched on both ends of the court. Although the Cats clearly had the most talent of any team in Nashville, their run was cut short by a Texas A&M team that needed the win. After the loss, fan morale seemed to hit a very low point. Thousands of fans from across the state made the trip down to Music City, and hundreds of thousands more sat and watched on their couch thinking the Cats were finally back and Nashville was finally going to be reclaimed. But yet again, the BBN found themselves disappointed and with nothing to do, as soon as the Saturday of the tournament rolled around. The disappointing loss caused every online 'bracketologist' to drop Kentucky as quick as a Friday night Aggie 3-point shot. In most predictions, John Calipari and the Wildcats went from a high three, to a low four borderline five, and to make matters worse, because of the circumstances around the loss and the teams right around Kentucky in the seeding, this drop in ranking gave a strong indication that Kentucky would be shipped out to the west coast, and be forced to play in a very difficult region. Or, by the account of some online BBN conspiracy theorists, in Boston with number one overall seed University of Connecticut. title: Anna Kate Drakeford Wraps Up Accomplished Career With Lady Titans
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/April EllisAnna Kate Drakeford will graduate from Mercer County this spring and was named 12th Region Player of the year and was a Miss Basketball candidate. In the 2020-21…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Anna Kate Drakeford will graduate from Mercer County this spring and was named 12th Region Player of the year and was a Miss Basketball candidate. In the 2020-21 Mercer County Senior High girls basketball season, the Lady Titans hit their stride going into tournament play. They won the district and advanced to the region championship game against Southwestern. They lost that game by six points, 62-56, after starter Anna Kate Drakeford went down in the second half with a knee injury. What could have been a career-ending injury instead was a motivator to an illustrious high school career that included achieving a 16th straight district championship title, a 12th region championship, a KHSAA Sweet 16th appearance at Rupp Arena, district and region all-tournament teams, and the 12th Region Player of the Year and Miss Kentucky Basketball candidate. 'As soon as I went down, I knew something was seriously wrong,' said Drakeford, 'But, this was the region championship. I wanted to get back out there for my team. I tried to jog along the sideline and convince them I could go back in, but we all knew it was worse than we wanted to admit. My coaches care about me. They thought it was in my best interest to sit out.' Drakeford suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) along with two tears to her meniscus, which added more time to her recovery. She headed to the University of Kentucky sports medicine clinic and Dr. Austin Stone. Stone had operated on other Mercer athletes and was optimistic he could get her back on the floor for the 21-22 season. During her work to return to the basketball court, she also had to deal with a worldwide pandemic. One of the few silver linings of dealing with COVID protocols was the Kentucky Legislature voted to allow students to reclassify and have a fifth year of eligibility. After her knee injury, Drakeford opted to repeat her sophomore year and made the most of the opportunity. The Lady Titans made a repeat appearance at the regional championship game in the 2021-2022 season but again fell to Southwestern, 58-42. There were high hopes for the 2022-23 season until leading scorer Timberlynn Yeast went down with a season-ending knee injury during a pre-season scrimmage. Sports critics wrote the Lady Titans off, but Drakeford had other plans. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Titan Boys Find Footing, Win 8 Of Last 11
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warr
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Mercer County sophomore Carter Devine has been in excellent form at the plate this season. Over 13 games, Devine has 21 hits and 14 RBIs, and leads the Titans with a .457 batting average. The Mercer County Titan baseball team (7-6) pushed their record back over .500 this weekend following two extremely tight wins over Wayne County and Scott High School. The Titans lone loss of the weekend was their final contest. The Collins High Titans (9-4) earned five walks in the top of the seventh inning to overturn a 4-0 Mercer County lead and claim a 5-4 win. Carter Devine gave his team momentum early when the sophomore singled past the shortstop on Mercer's opening at bat. Sophomore Andrew Tatum was able to reach second following an error at first base for Collins, and Devine scored the game's first run. Ayden Stephens smacked a ball deep into center field and moved Tatum to third before Noah Worthington scored Tatum on a ground out. Back-to-back doubles from Evann White and Brayden Campbell scored the Titans third run in the bottom of the fourth. Sophomore Jeran Layton pitched an amazing game, allowing only two hits and striking out eight batters over 6.1 innings. 'That's one of the best games I've seen him throw. We know he has it in him every time he steps on the mound, he needs to continue that competitive mindset he had in this game every day,' said Head Coach Cody Christopher. title: Bulldog Baseball Takes On Mercer
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenSophomore Bulldog pitcher Casey Dodson let one fly during the first game of Burgin's double header with Mercer County on Monday, Apr
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Sophomore Bulldog pitcher Casey Dodson let one fly during the first game of Burgin's double header with Mercer County on Monday, April 1.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Sophomore Bulldog pitcher Casey Dodson let one fly during the first game of Burgin's double header with Mercer County on Monday, April 1. The Burgin Bulldogs baseball team (0-9) made the short drive to Harrodsburg on Monday, April 1, where they played back-to-back games against the Mercer County Titans (9-6). The Bulldogs failed to score a run over their first three games, but have shown significant improvement over the last two weeks, scoring 19 runs over their last five contests.
Bulldog junior J.T. Boswell singled in his first at bat but no one else in the lineup could advance him.
It was a close matchup through the first two innings. Mercer's Andrew Tatum walked in the top of the third and eventually scored the game's opening run. Boswell singled again and read the high throw into first before continuing to second. He later scored Burgin's opening run on a wild throw into the infield.
After three and a half innings of stiff competition, neither team gained an edge. In the bottom of the fourth, Mercer opened up an 8-1 lead following three walks from Casey Dodson and two errors by the Bulldog defense. Next, Andrew Tatum blasted a double into right field and scored two more Titan runners.
Senior Ethan Slone and sophomore Zachary Logue singled on pitches from Davis Tyler. Tyler walked Easton Devine and Adrian Quiroz popped up to second base, scoring Slone from third.
'Our offense is really beginning to come around. Our coaching staff has been challenging our guys to work on some fundamental things at the plate and they're beginning to respond,' said Head coach of the Bulldogs, Philip Dean.
The Titans extended their lead in the fifth inning and eventually ended the first game of two, 12-2, when Tatum and Stephens took home plate following a wild pitch from Logue.

title: Lady Titans Win Five Straight
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenLady Titan sophomore Ella Davis made a diving save and throw to first during Mercer's win over Marion County. The Mercer County Lady Titans softball team (8-2) won…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Lady Titan sophomore Ella Davis made a diving save and throw to first during Mercer's win over Marion County.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Lady Titan sophomore Ella Davis made a diving save and throw to first during Mercer's win over Marion County. The Mercer County Lady Titans softball team (8-2) won four games in three days this past week, including a 16-5 route of Rockcastle County (4-7) on Thursday, March 28.
Vs Rockcastle County (3/30) The Lady Titans played a rematch with Rockcastle County two days after their 16-5 win, on Saturday afternoon, March 30. Eighth grader Ava Musick earned her fifth win of the season. She never left the mound, struck out six batters and gave up only one run in 90 pitches. Senior Peyton Boyd signed to continue her softball career with Carson-Newman University before the game began, and showed why any college would be lucky to have her. Boyd walked and scored the Lady Titans first run after Musick doubled into center field. In the bottom of the fourth, Boyd smacked a three run-bomb over the center field wall and gave Mercer a 6-0 lead. In the bottom of the sixth, Boyd popped up over second base and advanced after the Lady Rockets second baseman dropped the throw in.
'I am extremely excited for Peyton's signing,' said Head Coach Darren Ransdell. 'Carson Newman University is getting not only a great shortstop that will be the first to show up for practice and work as hard as anyone on the field, but the Eagles are getting an awesome student in the classroom.'
Mercer was propelled by its performance in the fourth and sixth innings. Izzie Carlton smacked a solo home run over the center field wall in the first at bat of the fourth inning. Mia Floro followed with a single, and senior Ashley Howard hit a line drive to left field, scoring one run. Freshman Jaley Bowman became the third Lady Titan to homer early in the sixth inning. Senior Hanna Beasley doubled into left field and scored another runner. Floro batted in Beasley later in the sixth and Jayla Sanders stole home plate after replacing Musick on the bases. Senior Haylee Ransdell waited patiently for a walk and Howard reached first on an error, loading the bases. Lily Hart struck out swinging in the first at bat of the sixth inning, but the freshman made up for it with a perfectly placed pop up that dropped just inside the foul line behind third base, scoring two runners.
In the end, Mercer County softball defeated Rockcastle County 12-3, and 28-8 over the teams two matchups last week.
'To be honest, they are ahead,' said Ransdell when asked if the Lady Titans are playing at a level above what he expected at this point in the season. 'Not that I expected less, but they bought in quicker to becoming a team and accepting their role. The Lady Titans set the bar in the offseason and they continue to raise it,' said Ransdell.

title: New Exhibit At Harrodsburg Historical Society, Bunch with the Babies And More
description: Bedtime with at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill and Battle of Perryville exhibit at Harrodsburg Historical Society. (Composite image). Check out the new exhibit exploring the aftereffects of the…
content:
Bedtime with at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill and Battle of Perryville exhibit at Harrodsburg Historical Society. (Composite image).
Bedtime with at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill and Battle of Perryville exhibit at Harrodsburg Historical Society. (Composite image). Check out the new exhibit exploring the aftereffects of the Battle of Perryville in Harrodsburg at the Harrodsburg Historical Society (220 South Chiles Street). The exhibit opened Tuesday, April 9.
Kentucky's bloodiest Civil War battle resulted in hundreds of wounded soldiers being cared for in almost all the town's homes, churches and public buildings. Artifacts on display include a surgeon's journal listing the names and military affiliations of the men he operated on, medical equipment used at the time, hand-written accounts of soldiers' appreciation for the townspeople who cared for them, and profiles of prominent local citizens with divided loyalties.
A new exhibit exploring the aftereffects of the Battle of Perryville on the town of Harrodsburg launches this week at the Harrodsburg Historical Society (Image: Wikipedia).
A new exhibit exploring the aftereffects of the Battle of Perryville on the town of Harrodsburg launches this week at the Harrodsburg Historical Society (Image: Wikipedia). 'The entire town came together as one to minister to the flood of wounded soldiers in the aftermath of the horrific battle,' said Nancy Hill, president of the Harrodsburg Historical Society. 'Visitors will learn how the repercussions of a single battle impacted the community long afterward.'
A walking tour of sites highlighted in the exhibit is featured in a companion map available onsite. The exhibit is free and open to the public. The historical society is open Tuesdays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Wednesdays through Fridays and the first and second Saturdays of the month from 1 to 4 p.m. The historical society is closed on the second and fourth Saturdays of the month, as well as Sundays and Mondays. The exhibit was made possible in part by the Friends of Perryville Battlefield with a generous Preserving America grant from Americana Corner.
To learn more, visit online at harrodsburghistorical.org or call 859-325-9028

title: Magistrate Kevin Hicks: A Closer Look
description: Photo SubmittedDistrict 5 Magistrate Kevin Hicks and his wife Deanna enjoy a sunset over the water. Kevin Hicks moved to Harrodsburg, where he liv
content:
Photo Submitted
District 5 Magistrate Kevin Hicks and his wife Deanna enjoy a sunset over the water. Kevin Hicks moved to Harrodsburg, where he lives on Perryville Street, in 2019. Soon after, Hicks decided to
run for office, and now repre­sents District 5 on the Mercer County Fiscal Couft, replacing Wayne Jackson, who served on the fiscal court for 29 years. Hicks was raised in 'a little spot on the road' named Casey Creek in Adair Coun­ty and graduated from Adair County High School in 1981. Hicks grew up in as rural an area as south central Kentucky had to offer. His dad, Loyde Hicks, drove a fuel truck and his mom, Deloris, worked at a Fruit of the Loom factory for many years. 'Growing up out in the country, it was one of those things where we didn't have a lot, but you can't miss it if you don't have it,' said Hicks. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Melvina Cheatham
description: Melvina D. Cheatham, 89, of Harrodsburg died Friday, April 12, 2024, at her home in Harrodsburg. Born March 15, 1935, in Harrodsburg, she was the daughter of the late George and Cordelia (Claunch)…
content:
Melvina D. Cheatham, 89, of Harrodsburg died Friday, April 12, 2024, at her home in Harrodsburg. Born March 15, 1935, in Harrodsburg, she was the daughter of the late George and Cordelia (Claunch) Durr. She was a member of Harrodsburg Baptist Church and a retired employee of Signet Systems. Survivors include: one daughter, Edwina (John) Tarter; two sons, Joe (Elizabeth) Cheatham and George (Donna) Cheatham; one sister, Bea Gritton; six grandchildren; eight great-grandchildren.

title: Colts Outrun The Bulldogs In First District Match-Up Of The Season
description: The
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Casey Dodson pitched one and two thirds innings during the Bulldogs loss to West Jessamine on Mon­day, April 15. The Burgin Bulldogs (0-13) had trouble keeping up with the West Jessamine Colts (13-3) in a 19-1 loss on Monday, April 15. West Jessamine wasted no time getting on the board in the top of the first inning after Aubrey Kearns singled to earn an RBI. Cooper Morton tripled and brought in three more. Three more batters earned RBIs for the Colts. Casey Dodson sta1ted on the mound for Burgin, and earned the first out when he struck out Ryan Long. Third baseman Braxton Sprinkles, connected with first baseman Ethan Slone for the second out. Andrew Hays caught a fly in the left field, but the damage had been done and the Colts lead 7-0 to end the top of the first. Dodson led off for Burgin and made his way to first base after being hit by a pitch. Burgin struggled at the plate, but Dodson was able to make it around the diamond and cross home plate after two steals and a RBI for Adrian Quiroz, 7-1. West scored five runs on four hits in the top of the second inning. Nate Hershey and Kean1s both doubled for two RBIs and Eli Nickell singled for an RBI. Dodson earned another strike out for the first out. The second out came from a short grounder back to Dodson who found Slone waiting on the bag at first. Boswell came in to relieve Dodson and closed out the top of the second with a strike out, 12-1.

The 3rd Annual Model Train Show and Sale happens at the Stable at Mercer County Fairgrounds (560 Linden Avenue) on Saturday, April 20, starting at 10 a.m. In addition to model trains, there will be door prizes every hour as well as food trucks. The cost is $5 per person and free for children aged 10 and under as well as veterans and active military. Proceeds will benefit the Harrodsburg Christian Church Youth Group.
Ready to roll up your sleeves? Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill is hosting Stewardship Saturday on April 20. You—yes, you—can help maintain the nearly 40 miles of recreational trails, as well as battle erosion and clear invasive species. Volunteers must be at least 18 years of age and willing to use hand tools including shovels and loppers, and should wear leather work gloves and sturdy, closed-toe shoes or work boots.
In return, volunteers are eligible to receive 20 percent off an overnight stay (available the Thursday—Sunday nights of stewardship weekend) and a voucher for 20 percent off one meal at the Trustees' Table.
