title: AmeriPro Health To Host Public Meet And Greets On Friday, April 26, and Saturday, April 27
description: Photo SubmittedAmeriPro Health has been hired to provide ambulance service in Mercer County. The company is accepting applications for staff at their website. st
content:
Photo Submitted
AmeriPro Health has been hired to provide ambulance service in Mercer County. The company is accepting applications for staff at their website.
Photo Submitted
AmeriPro Health has been hired to provide ambulance service in Mercer County. The company is accepting applications for staff at their website. Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com Mercer County's new ambulance service provider, AmeriPro Health, will host community meet and greets on Friday, April 26, and Saturday, April 27, from 2 to 5 p.m. at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse (207 West Lexington Street).
The events will be the public's first opportunity to meet the AmeriPro EMS Team, tour the new ambulances servicing the county and learn hands-only CPR.
AmeriPro is also hiring for both full-time and part-time positions. According to a press release, the company is offering leading salaries with generous benefits and perks. including 401K, flexible schedules, health and medical benefits and tuition reimbursement. The new ambulance provider is looking to add staff and is accepting application at their website.
The Mercer County Fiscal Court voted in a special-called meeting last Friday to terminate its agreement with Mercer County Emergency Medical Service and enter into a new agreement with AmeriPro Health to provide ambulance service. AmeriPro will receive $62,917 a month to provide ambulance service, including two ambulances staffed with a paramedic and an EMT or advanced EMT.
The magistrates voted unanimously to enter the three year agreement with AmeriPro, which will go into effect when the previous provider, Raintree Health—which was operating as Mercer EMS—closes. In a Facebook post, Raintress announced they would cease service at noon on Saturday, April 27.
According to Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, the county filed to receive a certificate of need—which would allow the county to either negotiate with a new ambulance service provider or to start providing ambulance service themselves—on Jan. 30.
'We've been working on this for months,' Steele said.
She said the county began to explore other options due to concerns with the current status of the provider, delays in coverage and relying on other agencies to provide service. The judge said an investigation is still ongoing at the state inspector general's office, with the earliest possible hearing in August. Normally, obtaining a certificate of need can take up to eight months, Steele said, and the final hearing for that is scheduled for June.
However, Steele said the county has applied for emergency hardship licensure under state law, and they have received notice that the county will get the certificate of need when Raintree closes.
The fiscal court also voted unanimously to enter into an agreement with AmeriPro Health. In a press release, AmeriPro calls itself 'a leading provider of patient logistics and last-mile healthcare delivery services.' The company began in the Metro Atlanta area in 2018 with 10 ambulances and has grown to have more than 800 employees with operations across six states, including Indiana and Kentucky.
Joe Rose, the director of operations at AmeriPro Health, was at Friday's meeting.
'We're excited to be working with Mercer County,' Rose said. 'We've already started ramping up operations on our end.'
Rose said AmeriPro can begin as soon as the county receives the certificate of need from the state.
Rose told WLEX that AmeriPro in Mercer County is hiring EMTs or paramedics. Anyone interested can visit ameriprohealth.com/ems-and-medical-transportation-careers for an application.
The current plan is for AmeriPro to operate from an open bay at the Harrodsburg Fire Department. Steele said the long term plan is to house operations within the community.
'We will work out those details when they arrive,' Steele said.
At Friday's meeting, Steele thanked Boyle and Anderson counties for providing assistance. She said Boyle County will station two trucks locally in Mercer for 24 hours during the transition.
'We are 100 percent covered in our community,' Steele said.

title: Police Find Heroin, Meth And Cash In Search; Suspect Pleads Not Guilty
description: A Harrodsburg woman has pleaded not guilty to drug trafficking charges after police discovered substances suspected of being drugs during a search. On the night of Sunday, April 28, the Harrodsburg…
content:
A Harrodsburg woman has pleaded not guilty to drug trafficking charges after police discovered substances suspected of being drugs during a search. On the night of Sunday, April 28, the Harrodsburg Police Department executed a search warrant at a residence on Azalea Street in Harrodsburg, where they located 26 grams of methamphetamine, 7.7 grams of black tar heroin, 10.62 grams of fentanyl, three suboxone, a digital scale, distribution baggies and ledgers. In addition, investigators seized a 'very large amount of currency' estimated to be between $10,000 to $25,000, according to the uniform citation.
The only resident of the apartment, Megan Rae Marlow, 34, was arrested and charged with trafficking in carfentanil or fentanyl derivatives, 1st degree trafficking in methamphetamine, trafficking in heroin and possession of drug paraphernalia.
Photo Submitted
The Harrodsburg Police Department say they located 'evidence of drug trafficking including a substantial quantity (of) black tar heroin, fentanyl, methamphetamine and $41,443 in cash,' according to a Facebook post.
Photo Submitted
The Harrodsburg Police Department say they located 'evidence of drug trafficking including a substantial quantity (of) black tar heroin, fentanyl, methamphetamine and $41,443 in cash,' according to a Facebook post. In Mercer District Court the next day, Marlow pleaded not guilty to all the charges against her. Her bond was set at $10,000. Marlow is scheduled to return to court for a pretrial hearing on Thursday, May 9.
In August 2019, Marlow was charged with 2nd degree manslaughter for what investigators said was her role in a death by suspected overdose. Marlow was also charged with tampering with physical evidence, aggravated trafficking in heroin, trafficking in marijuana and possession of drug paraphernalia.
While searching Marlow's home on Azalea Street, investigators said they found evidence of what they called a 'large narcotics sales operation,' including transaction ledgers, drug paraphernalia, cutting agents and a large amount of cash in excess of $40,000 hidden in multiple locations throughout the house.
The victim who made the purchase was found dead from a suspected overdose, according to the citation. Narcotics recovered from the victim's pockets matched the requested purchase from Marlow, according to the citation.
The charges against Marlow were 'dismissed without prejudice' on April 18, 2024, after the grand jury adjourned without either indicting her or referring the matter to the next grand jury.
Cpl. Chase Hale (HPD) is the case officer, with assistance from Patrolman Hunter Kelly and Deputy Paul Parks of the Mercer County Sheriff's Office.

title: Titans Track Competes In Central Kentucky Conference
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Marshall HartMercer County junior Jordan Piazza burst out of the blocks during the 110 meter hurdles event. Piazza placed first in the event with a time of 15.06 sec­onds.<
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Marshall Hart
Mercer County junior Jordan Piazza burst out of the blocks during the 110 meter hurdles event. Piazza placed first in the event with a time of 15.06 sec­onds.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Marshall Hart
Mercer County junior Jordan Piazza burst out of the blocks during the 110 meter hurdles event. Piazza placed first in the event with a time of 15.06 sec­onds. The Mercer County Titan track and field team traveled to Nicholasville on Friday, May 10, for the Central Kentucky Conference track meet hosted by West Jessamine.
Both the boys and girls teams had several standout performers, but neither Mercer squad was able to claim the top spot in the team rankings. Mercer was without senior Donovan Wright, who more often than not wins the long jump competition at every meet he enters.
Junior Jordan Piazza was the only Titan runner to place first in an event when he edged out Mathias Robertson of West Jessamine to claim first place in the 110 meter hurdles with a time of 15.06. Junior Marshall Hart had a fantastic performance in both the 1600 and 3200 meter runs. After running a personal record 4:30.96 time in the mile, Hart continued pushing and capped off his meet with a second personal best time of 9:48.25 in the two mile.
Between cross country and track and field, Hart had been unable to chase down Boyle County senior Max Germann for much of this year, but Hart was able to claim the top spot amongst class 2A competitors in each event.
'Max and I go back and forth on occasion, but it does feel good to get him in the two mile. Usually I am more dominant in the mile and sometimes struggle in the two mile so a win over him and a personal record in the same night was a pretty good feeling,' said Hart.
The Titan 4×800 meter relay team composed of Kyler Sallee, Liam Potts, Mason Sanders and Hart had their best run of the season so far when they finished with a time of 8:17.34, nearly 10 seconds faster than any run this season. The group finished in fourth place behind the Lafayette, Woodford County and East Jessamine teams, none of which will be competing against the Titans at the regional or state meets later this spring.
Senior Byron Collier launched the discus 141'3,' only one inch away from setting a new personal record. Collier's effort was enough to earn a second place finish behind Andrew Sparks of Garrard County.

title: Voters To Decide On Medical Cannabis In November Election
description: File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. The Mercer County Fiscal Court has approved resolution 2024-5, which allows a medical cannabis option to be…
content:
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. The Mercer County Fiscal Court has approved resolution 2024-5, which allows a medical cannabis option to be submitted to local voters. The state legislature legalized medical cannabis in 2023, but amended that law to expedite the process of licensing cannabis businesses in 2024. If the fiscal court takes no action, medical cannabis automatically becomes legal across the state on Jan. 1, 2025. According to Tim Sturgill, general counsel for the Kentucky Association of Cities, if the county took no action, medical cannabis businesses would be allowed to operate in the county once licensed by the state. County officials say the resolution will allow local voters to choose what happens in the general election on Tuesday, Nov.5.
According to Sturgill, the state can begin issuing licenses for cannabis operations effective July 1. Counties and cities can pass an ordinance by Dec. 31 to prohibit cannabis operations in their jurisdiction. If the state has already issued a business license and the local government passes an ordinance by Dec. 31 to prohibit this activity, the business would be forced to cease operations. However, if the county or city enacts its prohibition after Dec. 31 any licensed medical cannabis businesses at that time would be allowed to continue operations.
If the county ultimately prohibits the operation of cannabis businesses, cities within the county—such as Burgin and Harrodsburg—may still pass an ordinance to authorize those businesses within the city limits or they may pass a resolution to place the issue on the ballot for the voters to decide.
'This is just sales,' noted County Attorney Ted Dean at the fiscal court's meeting on Tuesday, June 11. 'This is not use.'
Depending on the vote, the court has until Dec. 31 to enact regulations. The motion passed, with Magistrate Dennis Holiday voting no.
'It really helps people on chemo,' Holiday said.
Mercer County Sheriff Ernie Kelty was asked for his opinion.
'The state passed it,' Kelty said.
'If it can be regulated and watched, I've got no problem with it,' Kelty said. 'I don't want nobody out there suffering who don't have to.'

title: Mercer School Board Approves ‘Historic' Seven Percent Pay Raise
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreStudents and staff at Mercer County Senior High School celebrated the school's report card at a rally IN November 2023. (File image). Th
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Students and staff at Mercer County Senior High School celebrated the school's report card at a rally IN November 2023. (File image).
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Students and staff at Mercer County Senior High School celebrated the school's report card at a rally IN November 2023. (File image). The Mercer County Board of Education has approved a minimum guaranteed 7-percent raise for all certified, classified and stipend positions except grant-specific stipends. At a special-called meeting on Tuesday, June 4, the board unanimously approved the 2024-25 salary schedule, which gives staff what school leaders are calling a 'historic pay raise.'
In a press release, Superintendent Jason Booher noted the Mercer School District now offers the highest starting teacher salary—$47,080 for one school year, or 185 days—in Central Kentucky and one of the highest in the state. In addition, starting bus driver pay is now $19.19 per hour. The district also offers in-house childcare for teachers and staff members. Over the past three years, Mercer Schools have provided a combined 15% raise for all certified and classified staff.
'Through this historic pay raise, our Board of Education reaffirms its commitment to excellence across all facets of education, be it academics, arts, or athletics,' Booher said in a press release. 'We believe this investment in our staff is an investment in our students and their future.'
At their last regular meeting, the board approved a $26 million tentative budget that only included step increases for current staff. Options, including breakdowns and budget impact of raises from three to nine percent, were sent to the board last week for review and were presented at the special-called meeting.
The discussion about tax rates won't come until the end of July, Finance Officer Amber Minor said.
'We have to make tough discussions when it comes to the tax rates,' Minor told the board. She said increases in tax assessments have allowed the district to not increase rates. Minor said she hopes that trend continues into next year.
'We do look at every single position, every step compared to our competitors,' Booher said, referring to surrounding school districts. Mercer gave a five percent raise two years ago and a three percent raise last year, he said.
'There's no better place for me to be in Central Kentucky than Mercer County schools,' Booher said. He said staff had responded to pay increases and the school district rating had increased, referring to the significant improvements Mercer School made in the 2023 Kentucky School Report Card, including Mercer County Senior High School, which received the blue rating, the highest rating in the state.
'We believe this investment in our staff is an investment in our students and our future,' Booher said.
'I'm proud to do this,' said Board Chairman Randy Phillips. 'You can see the improvement everywhere.'
'The fact that we can recruit and retain the best of the best,' Phillips said. 'Why would you not want to be here?'
'I feel honored to have been part of it,' said Board Member Amber Franceschi. Franceschi attributed it to not standing still.
'You all really are looking for ways to make improvements,' she said. 'We're not going to stand still.'
'Everything rises and falls with leadership,' said Board Member Cliff Prewitt. 'Over the last few years, I feel we've played catch-up for the district.'
'I will amen everything everybody said,' said Board Member Billy G. Montgomery.
'Now that we have things going in a good direction, it seems like things are continuing to go that way,' Montgomery said. 'I'm proud of everything everybody's doing.'
'I've kind of stepped into the best situation ever for a new board member,' said Board Member Amy Hart. Hart said it was a pleasure to be a part of it.
'I think it's going to be great for retention and recruiting,' she said.

title: Troy Reilly Competes In World Archery Championships In Daytona
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
King Middle School archer Trey Reilly competed at the NASP archery world championship in Daytona, Florida, this past weekend, shooting a 271 out of 300. Mercer County seventh grader Trey Reilly has had a season like no other. At only 13 years old, Reilly spent this past weekend competing with some of the best archers in the world. Reilly steadily improved throughout the winter and played an important role in helping the Titans to a second-place fin­ish at this season's regional tournament. After qualifying for state, Reilly dominated the competition and finished the tournament as the top archer in Kentucky in the seventh grade, and the third overall archer out of 1763 middle school competitors. At the National Archery in the Schools Program Nationals in Louisville, Reilly shot a 284, enough to qualify for the World Championships in Daytona, Florida, June 6–8. Reilly wrapped up an amazing season competing against the world's best and scored 271 on the big stage, enough to place him 134 out of 482 middle school boys. 'He wasn't happy, but he understood that it was the world championship and it was a good ending to his seventh grade year,' said Trey's father, Richard Reilly. Troy Reilly plans to reach the world championship again and will be focus­ing on his consistency next season as an eighth grader. Along with qualifying for NASP nationals and worlds, Reilly has set a goal of helping the Mercer County Titans win a region championship and qualify for state in 2025. 'Daytona was a cool experience, just getting to go. I plan to keep practicing and challenging myself to do better each time I shoot and continue to be coachable,' said Reilly. title: Through Corning's Gorilla Glass, Harrodsburg Connects To The World

content:
Photo Submitted
Corning's Harrodsburg facility first fired up in 1952. The plant now employs approximately 400 people and the Gorilla Glass they manufacture there is in the hands of billions of people across the world.
Photo Submitted
Corning's Harrodsburg facility first fired up in 1952. The plant now employs approximately 400 people and the Gorilla Glass they manufacture there is in the hands of billions of people across the world. Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com Harrodsburg is celebrating its 250th anniversary this month. While the oldest continuous settlement west of the Allegheny Mountains has a lot of history to celebrate, one aspect of life in Mercer County that tends to get overlooked is the role of industry. And there is no better symbol of the importance of industry than Gorilla Glass.
Corning began manufacturing Gorilla Glass here in its Harrodsburg facility in 2007. Today, the majority of the facility's manufacturing is dedicated to producing cover glass materials for mobile consumer electronics. According to Corning, the product has been used on more than 8 billion devices by more than 45 major global brands. If you're reading this story on a handheld device, your fingers are probably scrolling along on Gorilla Glass.
Corning Incorporated is one of the world's leading innovators in materials science, with total sales of $13.6 billion. Formed in 1851 and headquartered in Corning, New York, the corporation employs approximately 50,000 people across the world—approximately 400 of them here in Harrodsburg. In addition to damage-resistant cover glass for smartphones and tablets, Corning also produces precision glass for advanced displays, optical fiber, wireless technologies, connectivity solutions for high-speed communications networks and emissions-control products for cars, trucks and off-road vehicles.
Corning is one of the world's leading innovators in materials science. For over 170 years, the corporation has applied its expertise in glass science, ceramic science and optical physics to develop products that transform industries and enhance people's lives. Corning's innovations include the first glass bulbs for Thomas Edison's electric light, the first low-loss optical fiber, the cellular substrates that enable catalytic converters and the first damage-resistance cover glass for mobile devices.
Corning is one of the world's leading innovators in materials science. For over 170 years, the corporation has applied its expertise in glass science, ceramic science and optical physics to develop products that transform industries and enhance people's lives. Corning's innovations include the first glass bulbs for Thomas Edison's electric light, the first low-loss optical fiber, the cellular substrates that enable catalytic converters and the first damage-resistance cover glass for mobile devices. Corning began developing a tough, new cover glass for electronic devices in 2006. The company's scientists implemented significant compositional as well as other changes to achieve superior product characteristics including damage resistance, while making the glass compatible with Corning's proprietary fusion-draw manufacturing process. The end result is an exceptionally thin glass surface that is damage-resistant.
When Apple introduced the original iPhone, Steve Jobs was dissatisfied with how the prototype's hard plastic screen would get scratched when he carried it in his pocket. Insisting the iPhone had to have a glass screen before it went on the market in a few months, Jobs met with Wendell Weeks, Corning chairman and CEO, to devise a solution.
Apple and Corning have partnered on product development for more than 15 years, with Corning playing a key role in delivering glass solutions for iPhones, Apple Watches and iPads. With the support of Apple's Advanced Manufacturing Fund, Corning continues to innovate new manufacturing technology that not only enables next-generation mobile consumer electronics but also sustains and creates high-value manufacturing jobs.
In the years since its introduction, Gorilla Glass has helped revolutionize the way we communicate. In a sense, you could say that nearly everyone in the world possessing one of the billions of mobile devices featuring Gorilla Glass has a piece of Mercer County in their hands.
'We could have deployed this technology in any number of locations worldwide, but we chose Harrodsburg because of the legacy of this plant and the talent of our people,' Weeks said. 'With Corning's advanced leadership in U.S. manufacturing, this facility's technology not only enables next-gen mobile consumer electronics, but also sustains and creates high-value manufacturing jobs.'
One example of the importance of the Gorilla Glass coming out of Corning Harrodsburg's facility came in May 2017, when Apple invested $200 million here. Ultimately, they would invest nearly half a billion here in Harrodsburg.
At the announcement of the first investment, Wendell Weeks introduced Janice Byrge, who had worked for at the Harrodsburg facility for more than 50 years.
'We are truly blessed to have employees who are so talented, so flexible and so loyal,' Weeks said in 2017, as workers at the Harrodsburg facility watched from the catwalks.
The announcement was cheered by Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who held up his own iPhone. McConnell said the device was composed from parts manufactured in 30 different nations, 'but the part we touch comes from Harrodsburg, Kentucky.'

title: Mercer School Board Gives Raise To Superintendent
description: File image. The Mercer County Board of Education voted to give Superintendent Jason Booher an eight percent pay raise last week. On top of the seven percent pay increase previously approved by the…
content:
File image.
The Mercer County Board of Education voted to give Superintendent Jason Booher an eight percent pay raise last week. On top of the seven percent pay increase previously approved by the school board, that gives Booher a 15 percent total pay raise.
Jason Booher
The raise came after the superintendent's evaluation, in which the board ranked Booher from one to four on seven standards and three goals. Chair Randy Phillips said Booher's score on each was four.
'We're certainly blessed to have you as a leader,' Phillips said. 'We greatly appreciate everything you have done for us.'
In 2023, the school district made significant improvements in the 2023 Kentucky School Report Card, including Mercer County Senior High School, which received the blue rating, the highest rating in the state. Booher called it 'a tremendous success for our high school and our county.'
During his report to the school board, Booher shared a photo album, starting with graduation pictures and reviewing some of the projects completed during his administration, including the athletic complex with new chipping green and baseball and softball fields. Booher noted seven students had applied and been accepted as Governor's Scholars, while three students had applied and been accepted at the Governor's School for the Arts. In addition, a Mercer student had recently achieved the first perfect ACT exam in the district's history. He also noted that they'd been able to get the bids to come in a lot lower than expected for the construction of the new elementary school.
'A picture's worth about a thousand words. You had a thousand pictures,' said board member Cliff Prewitt, who said he looked forward to many years working with Booher.
'It's been a joy working with you,' said board member Billy G. Montgomery. 'Your leadership is what has rubbed off on a lot of the staff.'
Booher was hired as superintendent in 2021. Prior to that, he had served as principal at Pikeville High School. Prior to joining Pikeville in 2014, Booher served as assistant principal at Covington Holmes High School, where he coached the Bulldogs to winning the 2013 Ninth Region tournament championship.
'You're only as good as your team and your players,' Booher said at the school board's regular meeting on Tuesday, June 18, 'We've got great players. It's a great place to be right now.' title: Fiscal Court Gives First Reading To Zoning Ordinance Amendment
description: File Image. The Mercer County Fiscal Court has given first reading to text amendments to the Mercer County Zoning Ordinance that include proposed changes to minimum lot sizes in the a
content:
File Image.
The Mercer County Fiscal Court has given first reading to text amendments to the Mercer County Zoning Ordinance that include proposed changes to minimum lot sizes in the agricultural zoning districts, setbacks, the addition of accessory dwelling units, changes to conditional uses and some grammatical revisions.
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission conducted a public hearing on the proposed text amendments on June 11. And, as at that public hearing, much of the comments concerned a proposal to change agriculture lot sizes. The changes would increase the minimum lot sizes for A1 districts from 2.5 to five acres, reduce the minimum size for A2 districts from 2.5 acres to 2 acres, reduce road frontage requirements from 250 feet to 200 feet and reduce minimum front yard setbacks from 80 feet to 40 feet.
At the fiscal court's special-called meeting on Monday, July 24, Shawn Moore, executive director of planning and zoning, said the intent behind the proposal was to protect farmland.
'We ought not to be destroying our farmland to be building houses,' Moore told the magistrates. He said development should be concentrated on where sewer and water lines are currently located.
'You don't have infrastructure to support large-scale development outside the city,' Moore said. He said they didn't want to create isolated islands of development.
Moore said there would be a marked increase in housing with the development of the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park. It was noted that the city was working to extend sewer service outside the bypass, which could lead to development north and south along US 127. Land next to current development could be rezoned.
'You want to develop in the most economic form,' Moore said. He said the most economic way to develop was in locations that were already developed.
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele stressed the need to preserve Mercer County's farm land.
'You've got to preserve your farmland in some way, or it's going to be gone,' Steele said. She said the amendments would allow the county to preserve some of its best farmland.
Steele noted that drafting the amendments had been a long process, with several magistrates serving on the committee along with Steele and Moore. During the process, they contacted the Kentucky Farm Bureau as well as state and local officials.
'I've prayed on this since Thursday night,' said Magistrate Stephen 'Pete' Elliott, who said he'd farmed his whole life, but most of it was not on A1 farmland. While noting his son was a developer, Elliott called himself an 'old hillside farmer' and asked if it was right to limit what a farmer could earn for the sale of his land.
'Is it right for the government to say he could get $500,000 to sell his farm to keep on farming?' Elliott asked, noting a farmer might possibly double his money by selling to a real estate developer. 'I just hate to see the government control what the old farmer can and cannot do with his property.'
Agricultural production contributed approximately 6.7 percent of the Commonwealth's gross domestic product. That's according to a report compiled by the Community and Economic Development Initiative of Kentucky using 2019 production numbers.
Elliott said investors are 'not buying farmland to farm.'
Moore said he agreed with Elliott.
'I believe the farmer has the right to do what he wants and cut it up as he sees fit, as long as he obeys the same rules as everybody else,' Moore said.
'Eventually, you're going to run out of farmland,' Moore said. He called investment firms 'road rapers.'
'They're not doing anything to benefit us,' Moore said.
No public comment was heard at Monday's meeting. Steele advised the magistrates to talk to people over the next couple of weeks. She asked people to address their concerns to the judge or magistrates.
'This is very important,' Steele said. Want to read the rest of the story? Click to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission approved a new budget for the 2025 fiscal year. The budget is nearly $200,000 less than last year's budget.
At their regular meeting on Wednesday, June 26, the tourist commission approved a budget of $1,059,500 for the new fiscal year, down from last year's budget of $1.2 million. According to the draft budget the tourist commission provided the Harrodsburg Herald, the previous budget forecasted revenues of more than $1.2 million over the year, but the commission had only received $1.07 million.
Most of the money—$873,900—is being spent on marketing. That includes nearly $600,000 in sponsorships and grants. Some of the biggest beneficiaries include Anderson-Dean Community Park, which is set to receive $176,400 in quarterly payments as well as $7,500 for fireworks; the Harrodsburg First Main Street Program, which is set to receive $117,200, including $60,000 for Oktoberfest, $44,000 to the agency, $7,700 for the Christmas committee and $5,500 for the downtown flower project. The Mercer County Chamber of Commerce is set to receive $71,350 for events, including $27,600 for Pioneer Days, $40,000 for the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival, $1,000 for the Shop Local event and $2,750 for Small Business Saturday.

title: Anderson-Dean Pool Will Open Saturday, July 13
description: Lynlee Gowins enjoys the pool at Anderson-Dean Community Park in 2019 (File image). Good news everyone, the pool at Anderson-Dean Community Park (1501 Louisville Road) will open Saturday, July 13.…
content:
Lynlee Gowins enjoys the pool at Anderson-Dean Community Park in 2019 (File image).
Good news everyone, the pool at Anderson-Dean Community Park (1501 Louisville Road) will open Saturday, July 13. That's according to a Facebook post by the park.
Park officials had hoped to open Friday, but had to wait for a state inspection. According to their Facebook page, the cost will be $7 ages 12 and up, $5 for ages 3 to 11 and free for children two and under.
Pool hours are 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 1 to 6 p.m. on Sunday. Seating is limited. Visitors are allowed to bring in their own chairs.
Pool parties are also available nightly from 7 to 9 p.m. The cost is $450. For reservations contact: 859-734-9167
Initially, officials hoped to open the pool on Memorial Day weekend, but the date has been pushed back because of a myriad of last-minute issues. The pool was shut down June 6 of last year after the park learned the pool had lost a million gallons of water in its first week. During the one week the pool was open, officials say it drew up to 400 people a day.
'We know that it's holding water,' Park Manager Stephen Ransdell told the Mercer County Fiscal Court Tuesday.
Randell told the magistrates they were working on correcting some issues with features in the children's area. He said the slide was getting coated with wax Tuesday.
'Once that is done, all the features will work,' Ransdell said. 'Everything else is in place.'
So far, the project to repair the pool has cost $1,247,480. The county has paid $762,280. Expenses for the park are supposed to be split evenly between the county and the City of Harrodsburg. The city is obligated to pay $485,200 but has not contributed to the new liner or the return system.
Once repairs are finished, officials say the park will basically have a brand new pool, which could last another 20 years if done correctly.
The next meeting of the Anderson-Dean Community Park board of directors is scheduled for Wednesday, July 17, at noon.
Anderson-Dean Community Park is located at 1501 Louisville Road. The park hours are 6 a.m. to 11 p.m.
To learn more, call the park at 859-734-9167, email Ransdell at Stephen.andersondeanpark@gmail.com, visit their website at andersondeancommunitypark.com, or visit their Facebook page @ andersondeancommpark.

title: 197th Mercer County Fair And Horse Show Kicks Off With Dairy Show And Demolition Derby On Saturday, July 20
description: The Harrodsburg Herald (Composite Image). The Mercer County Fair and Horse Show, the nation's oldest continuously running county fair, returns for its 197th consecutive year this weekend. Th
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald (Composite Image).
The Mercer County Fair and Horse Show, the nation's oldest continuously running county fair, returns for its 197th consecutive year this weekend.
The fair kicks off this Saturday, July 20, with the dairy show at 10 a.m. and the demolition derby crash­ing and banging starts that night at 7 p.m. at the motor­sports track. 'Run what you brung minis' will be the first class, 'SS Madness' will be the second class, and built minis will be the third class. Cars should be paid and in line by 6 p.m. Admission for the demolition derby is $15 per person and 10 and under are free.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ April Ellis
Miss Mercer County Fair and Horse Show 2022 Annie Pendygraft crowned Ellie Jenkins the 2023 Miss Mercer County Fair and Horse Show last year.
The actual carnival begins on Monday, July 22, and is run by Casey Rides. The beauty pageants also begin on Mon­day. Back again this year is the Mrs. Mercer County Fair pageant for contestants aged 23 and above. The Mrs. pageants begins at 6:30 p.m. along with the teen and miss pageant. The pageants will be co-mingled.
Tuesday night will wrap up the rest of the pageants, with Tiny Miss and Mister beginning at 5 p.m., Little Miss and Mister at 6:30 p.m. and the Preteen at 8 p.m.
'We're looking for a great time as long as the weath­er holds out,' said Mercer County Fair and Horse Show Board President Dr. LeMayne Ellis. This fair marks Ellis' 20th year as fair board presi­dent. While Mercer County needs rain, organizers have their fingers crossed that it doesn't rain out events during the evening.
Fan favorites Like the Floral Hall exhibits will run throughout the week. Dirt drag racing will be on Mon­day at the motorsports track, and the truck tug event will be on Friday. Livestock shows will take place throughout the week, culminating on Mon­day after the fair with the open beef show on Monday, July 29.
The horse show contin­ues to grow and draw entries from across the country.
'Early indications look great for the number of hors­es coming to the Horse Show. We have several stables coming in from out of state and as far away as California,' said Horse Show Manager Brad Noel.
Noel has been chairman of the horse show for 23 years. He took over for the late Tom Moore, who passed away in 2001. Moore was inducted into the fair's hall of fame in 2003. This year's judge is Nelson Green from Nicholasville. Those unable to attend the horse show can pay to stream the show online at rich­fieldvideo.com.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Volunteer Kurt Buterbaugh showed off this enormous cabbage head at the 2023 Floral Hall.
There will also be classes for young, beginning riders starting at 9 a.m. on Saturday, July 27. Children are also invited to show off their best riding skills in the stick horse class or the lead line class, the two classes on Saturday night. While there is no entry fee for the class, admission has to be paid.
Also this year, three men who contributed countless hours to the motor track will be inducted into the Mercer County Fair and Horse Show Hall of Fame. Woody Holt, the late 'Big Joe' Wilson and Ricky Keller will be recognized.
The Mercer County Fairgrounds are located at 560 Linden Avenue. Admission to the fair is $8. The fair is free to children aged 5 and younger and the cost for a one-night unlimited ride bracelet is $15. For more information, visit mercercofair.com.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore

title: Meeting To Discuss Burgin Flooding Relief Effort On July 31
description: File image. While most of Mercer County is complaining about a drought, Burgin Mayor Joe Monroe
content:
File image.
While most of Mercer County is complaining about a drought, Burgin Mayor Joe Monroe said there has finally been some movement in the effort to deal with flooding in the friendly little city.
Mayor Joe Monroe said there would be a meeting Wednesday, July 31, with all the concerned parties, including engineers and scientists.
'I'm hoping that when they walk in here they say they can start testing,' Monroe said.
Sections of Burgin, particularly along Water Street, have been plagued by flooding for as long as anyone can remember, but residents say it has gotten worse over the past several years. The current plan to alleviate the flooding is to install two 30 inch pipes at least 150 feet under the city as well as pumps to control flooding. But first, they will need to conduct a geophysical survey, drilling at least two wells. It has been estimated the testing would take two or three days to perform and the city would receive the report within a couple of weeks.
The U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is providing $562,500 to pay for the flood relief effort, with the Kentucky Department for Local Government providing $317,500 from the Flood Assistance Program. The funding was announced over a year ago, but not much has happened since then.
'There's people calling me all the time,' Mayor Monroe said at the Burgin City Council meeting on Tuesday, July 9.
'I've had one woman who's threatened my life over it,' Monroe said, making a joking reference to Burgin citizen Margie Brothers, who has been a tireless advocate for Burgin flood relief. title: Elder Returns As Assistant Chief Of Harrodsburg Police Department
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
From left: Harrodsburg Police Chief Tim Hurt, newly hired Assistant Police Chief Scott Elder, his son, Drew Elder, and Commissioner Missy Banks.
Scott Elder has returned to the Harrodsburg Police Department as its newest assistant chief.
'I'm just happy to be back again,' Elder said. 'I look forward to passing on my knowledge and experience to the younger officers.'
Elder was hired at a special-called meeting of the Harrodsburg City Commission on Thursday, July 11. The commission voted unanimously—Commissioner Kerry Anness was not in attendance—to hire Scott Elder as assistant police chief at $34 per hour, pending drug, alcohol and background testing. Elder's hire goes into effect on Monday, July 22. He replaces former Assistant Police Chief Larry Wesley, who resigned at the beginning of March.
Elder began his career in law enforcement in Bell County back in 1997. He first joined the HPD back in 2001, moving to the Mercer County Sheriff's Office—where he rose to become chief deputy—in 2009. He retired from the MCSO in 2022 and served as chief of the Burgin Police Department before rejoining the HPD as a sergeant. He has recently been serving as chief of the Junction City Police Department.
'He has strong community ties,' said Commissioner Missy Banks, who referred not only to Elder's law enforcement career but also his experience as a basketball coach.
'His vision for the department is in line with mine and Chief Hurt,' said Banks, who said she wants the HPD to be a 'powerhouse' and looking for community ties and community presence.
'It's great to have an assistant chief to assist with our vision to eventually have a premier agency,' said HPD Chief Tim Hurt after the meeting. 'It's great to have a partner who will get more involved in community policing.'
'I appreciate the opportunity,' Elder said. He said he will work with the department to 'give the city something to be proud of.' Want to read the rest of the story? Click to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Weekender Aug. 1—9: 127 Yard Sale, Crafts Fair And More
description: Bluegrass Antique Boat Gathering on Herrington Lake, Crafts Fair at Shaker Village and 127 Yard Sale at Smocks Farm (Composite image). It's a very busy weekend with the 127 Yard Sale starting…
content:
Bluegrass Antique Boat Gathering on Herrington Lake, Crafts Fair at Shaker Village and 127 Yard Sale at Smocks Farm (Composite image).
It's a very busy weekend with the 127 Yard Sale starting Thursday, Aug. 1, and running through Sunday, Aug. 4. While there will be sales practically everywhere in Mercer County, the biggest will be at the Smock Farm (3580 Louisville Road) where more than 100 vendors have their wares on display. The Smock family have been participating in the 127 Yard Sale for more than two decades, and their event has grown to be the second largest in Kentucky.
More than 80 artists and artisans from all over Kentucky—and as far away as Minnesota—will display their wares at the 2024 Craft Fair this weekend at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill. The craft fair happens from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 3, and Sunday, Aug. 4. Local artisans include Keith Chambers of Woodwerks in Harrodsburg, wood turning by Bob Cairns, ceramics by Hannah Baker of Three Lick Pottery, fiber products by Deborah Bonanno Slaninka of Black Watch Alpacas, mixed media by Patrick Horn of Top Shelf Products, botanical products by Brandi Monett of the Shaker Village Farm Stand and Diane Green of Herbal Kreations and two-dimensional work by LaChrista Ellis of Live Art, Pop Art and Portraitures. In addition to arts and crafts, there will also be live music on both days and plenty to eat from the Shaker Village Grill and Bar, as well as food trucks, including Casa Grande, Captain Franks Hotdog Emporium, Gotchee Hibachi, Hogtown BBQ, the Mercer County Cattleman's Association, Mimi's Mac and Southern Style Kettle Corn.

title: Titan Soccer Looks To Build Momentum This Fall
description: The Harrodsbur
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Front row: Giovanni Ward, Cael Boyd, Zayne Cox, Billy Vaught, Brycen Jones, Ashton Butler. Middle row: Blake Votaw, Joseph Stocker, Brandon Johnson, Gabe Hopper, Dylan Coslow, Mijiah Dunn, Luis Osoy, Landon Steele, Grant Bennett, John Hopkins. Top row: Griffin Fister, Jacob Murphy, Liam Moffett, Ian Alcorn, Brantley Reed, Hayden McGuire, Jordan Piazza, Aiden Duncan, Tanner Ison, Cannon Buchanan, Grayson Guerra, Jack Gammon, Daniel Vera.
The Mercer County boys soccer team struggled to keep their offensive momentum going at any point last fall, resulting in a four-win season and a six-game losing skid to finish the regular season.
In his first season at the helm, Head Coach Mark Dunn had only three seniors available when selecting his team. Liam Potts, Kylar Sallee and Ben Waddell did all they could to maintain composure and push the Titans forward, but a lack of upperclassmen depth meant most of the starting roles were filled by fresh­men and sophomores who had never played full 80 minute games before.
Mercer County Senior High School's 2027 and 2028 graduating classes are each loaded with talented soccer players, and much like last season, most of the Titan's starting 11 will be freshman and sophomores.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Like last season, the Titans will have three seniors leading the charge: midfield maestro Luis Osoy, winger Jordan Piazza and utility player Hayden McGuire.
'Last year, the team was really young and inex­perienced, but they're still young now. However, they're becoming more competitive. They've played together enough to build trust among themselves and are showing a strong desire to win, which is evident in their practice ses­sions,' Dunn said.

title: Trilogy Health Services Adding 32 Units To The Willows At Harrodsburg
content:
Photo Submitted
Trilogy Health Services will add 32 new patio homes and a clubhouse at the Willows at Harrodsburg. The expansion is expected to begin in September. Universal Design Associates has been selected as the architecture firm for the project.
Trilogy Health Services is expanding at the Willows at Harrodsburg. According to a press release, the investment is aimed to address the growing demand for senior living accommodations and services. Trilogy said it is part of a bigger investment the company is making across the Midwest to senior living and assisted living services in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan and Ohio. The Harrodsburg Herald first reported on Trilogy's expansion plans in 2023, when they won approval from the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission.
Trilogy said they will add 32 new patio homes and a clubhouse at the Willows at Harrodsburg. Construction is expected to begin in September. Universal Design Associates has been selected as the architecture firm for the project. The new patio homes and clubhouse will reflect the aesthetic of the main health center and assisted living building, formerly the site of Eddie Montgomery's Steakhouse.
'We are thrilled for this addition to the Willows at Harrodsburg, which will enable us to support and care for so many more members of our community, providing them with the comfort and assistance they deserve,' said Rachel Dadisman, executive director of the Willows at Harrodsburg, in the press release. 'We believe this expansion will significantly impact the lives of our residents and their families, fostering a stronger, more connected community.'
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission approved the construction of 16 duplex senior housing units with a 2,200 square feet club house back in April 2023. title: Lady Bulldogs fall short in clash with Titans
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Lady Bulldogs volleyball team has been hindered this preseason by the lack of a coach. The squad was not able to resume practices…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs volleyball team has been hindered this preseason by the lack of a coach. The squad was not able to resume practices consistently until the appointment of a new head coach a couple of weeks ago. Jonesy McGregor, a former Anderson County High School volleyball player and collegiate player at Berea College, is excited to have her first opportunity coaching at the high school level.
'It has been a lot of fun, I like working with the girls. I like playing volleyball so seeing it is really cool too,' said McGregor.
In her first week leading the Lady Bulldogs program they lost 3-0 to Danville and won in three sets to Danville LIGHT two days later.
'I graduated two years ago so it's pretty fresh on my brain. I feel like I have a lot of ideas too on how to improve as well. It's a really great opportunity and I wanted to coach so it was perfect,' said McGregor.
Lady Bulldog freshman Macy Greenleaf served during Burgin's match with Mercer County on Monday, Sept. 2. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Noxious Weed Treatment On US 127 Scheduled For Tuesday, Sept. 10
description: File image. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet advises motorists of scheduled spraying operations for noxious, and nuisance weeds. The treatment aids with controlling the spread of undesi
content:
File image.
The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet advises motorists of scheduled spraying operations for noxious, and nuisance weeds. The treatment aids with controlling the spread of undesirable plants along state highway right of way. Work will begin Tuesday, Sept. 10, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
KYTC, in accordance with state law, targets Johnson grass, giant foxtail, Canada thistle, nodding thistle, common teasel, multiflora rose, amur honeysuckle, poison hemlock, marestail, Japanese knotweed and kudzu. Left uncontrolled, noxious weeds can grow so large that they interfere with a driver's line of vision on highways. They can also damage pavement and embankments and clog ditches, causing drainage problems.
Noxious weeds often invade and destroy the roadside turf grass, leaving these areas vulnerable to erosion. They can also smother native plants through rapid reproduction and long-term persistence.
Work begins Tuesday, Sept. 10, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Spraying will be focused on rock medians and barrier walls. A single lane closure will be in effect in the right/fast lane.
Mercer County Operations will begin on US 127 B between milepoints 4.483 – 0.0 (both directions)
Jessamine County Work will move to US 27 between milepoints 6.011 and 0.0 (both directions)
Garrard County Spraying will proceed to US 27 between milepoints 16.691 and 15.617 (both directions)
Noxious weed treatment is a mobile operation. Motorists are advised to be aware and use extra caution.
All work and/or closures are scheduled on a tentative basis, and subject to change depending on weather, emergencies, and other factors beyond the control of the Department of Highways
District 7 includes Anderson, Bourbon, Boyle, Clark, Fayette, Garrard, Jessamine, Madison, Mercer, Montgomery, Scott, and Woodford Counties.
For more information, visit with KYTC online.
Navigate traffic with GoKY or via Waze on your smartphone.

title: Burgin is taking strides forward
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Lady Bulldogs volleyball team (1-4) returned to the court at Jack Coleman Sr. Memorial Gymnasium on Saturday, Sept. 7, for a matchup…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs volleyball team (1-4) returned to the court at Jack Coleman Sr. Memorial Gymnasium on Saturday, Sept. 7, for a matchup with the Bath County Lady Cats (3-7).
Senior leader Ava Todd returned to the court after missing games against Mercer County and Berea last week and made an immediate impact. Both teams were evenly matched, but it was clear Todd provided a spark to the Lady Bulldogs.
Kaydance Logue started her service with an ace, and Burgin rallied to win the next five points and tie the game at seven. A clever tap over at the net into a pocket of empty space by the line by Briana Florian tied the game at 12. Burgin kept the first set within contention for a few more points, but eventually some mishits gave the Lady Cats a comfortable lead. Haleigh Wells served an ace to finish the third set 25-17 in Bath County's favor.
Logue continued her excellent service in the second set, and after back-to-back aces, the Lady Bulldogs led 6-5.

title: Shawn Moore Resigns As Planning And Zoning Executive-Director: Kylie Donnally Named Acting Director
description: Shawn Moore (file image). After 19 years, Shawn Moore is resigning his position as executive-director of planning and zoning. Moore made his announcement Tuesday, Sept. 10, at the Harrodsburg-Mercer…
content:
Shawn Moore (file image).
After 19 years, Shawn Moore is resigning his position as executive-director of planning and zoning. Moore made his announcement Tuesday, Sept. 10, at the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission meeting.
Kylie Donnally will serve as acting director starting Monday, Sept. 23.
Donnally was hired as administrative assistant—with the goal of eventually taking over Moore's position—in May. The commission made arrangements for Moore to come back on Fridays and work with Donnally. He will continue to attend meetings for the planning and zoning commission and the board of adjustments for six months. To work with Moore's schedule, board of adjustment meetings have been moved to 7 p.m.
Moore will assume the duties as executive-director for the Joint City County Planning Commission of Nelson County.
'I've been thrilled and honored to be part of Harrodsburg for the last 19 years,' Moore said. 'I'm proud of the things I've been part of. I'm grateful for all the friendships and the lessons I've learned from other officials in the government.'
Donnally, the acting director, is from Harrodsburg. She graduated from the University of Kentucky in December, where she majored in business administration and marketing.
'I'm excited about this opportunity and grateful for everything Shawn has done for me and continues to do for me,' Donnally said. 'I'm excited to serve the community I grew up in.'
The planning and zoning commission will advertise for a new administrative assistant. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Titans Fall Short As Warriors Rally For Dramatic Victory
description: Senior wideout Cameron Bottoms followed several Titan blockers toward the goal line during Mercer County's 28-10 loss to Southwestern. Bottoms finished the game with 61 yards on two touches, and six…
content:
Senior wideout Cameron Bottoms followed several Titan blockers toward the goal line during Mercer County's 28-10 loss to Southwestern. Bottoms finished the game with 61 yards on two touches, and six tackles. ( The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren)
Titan Football (1-3) played likely the toughest road game of their season on Friday, Sept. 20, when they traveled to Southwestern High School (1-3). Despite being without two of their most prolific playmakers, Braidin Baughman and Ashton Drakeford, the Titans played their most defensively sound half of football in 2024. All 11 defensive players were flying to the ball, and outside of a 21-yard pitch and catch to Parker Burton on the Warriors opening drive, Mercer County nullified every aspect of the Southwestern offensive game plan.
Junior outside linebacker Cohen Sanford forced Warrior quarterback Ryan Anderson out of the pocket and into a bad throw on fourth and two, ending the Warriors' initial drive.
The Titans coaching staff has faith in Cornelius Mapp, and gave the junior the start after allowing sophomore Michael Cox to step in behind center and lead the Titan offense in their 41-0 win over Danville. Mapp's first completion came on the third play of the game, connecting with Cox on a 5-yard curl route. The sophomore turned, made a defender miss and dove for a first down. Mapp's next drop back came three plays later, but an unblocked Southwestern rusher ended the play almost as soon as it started. The Titans' second drive stalled after Mapp was brought down again, this time for a gain of one, on third and 15.
Southwestern was able to move the ball to the Titan 32-yard line on the ensuing drive, but a holding call forced them into a second down and 23 situation they couldn't recover from.
Mapp and the Titan offense returned to the field prepared for the Southwestern rush and completed three straight passes, to Trenton Berry, Landon Yates and Cox respectively.
'He did make some smart decisions, we're still working out kinks… I'm okay with the short passing game. I'd like to take some shots down field, but I don't think we're quite where we need to be with that,' said Coach Craig Yeast.
After another sack forced the Titans into a third and long situation, Mapp stepped up in the pocket, rolled out and connected with Yates, who was uncovered in the middle of the field. title: Lady Titans Battle Hard But Fall To Lady Rebels In Straight Sets
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenAnne Whitenack (foreground) and Mia Floro look on as Addisen Shepherd digs out a Lady Rebel serve during the Titans match with Boyle County on Monday, Sept. 30.
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Anne Whitenack (foreground) and Mia Floro look on as Addisen Shepherd digs out a Lady Rebel serve during the Titans match with Boyle County on Monday, Sept. 30.
The Mercer County Lady Titans (8-8) traveled to Boyle County High School (21-8) with a chance to bolster their 8-4 record in the 12th Region against one of the regions' best programs.
The Lady Titans took an early lead in each set and earned a 7-6 lead in the first period after a blistering hit from Ralasia Piazza landed just inside the corner. A block by Izzie Carlton earned Mercer a 10-6 advantage moments later.
Just like that, a flip switched, and Boyle County went on a six-point run before Coach Lynn Flach called a time-out. The Lady Rebels were firing hit after hit, and Mercer County couldn't catch a break for the remainder of the first period, eventually dropping it after a foul serve earned Boyle their 25th point, completing a 19-5 run.
Carlton made two blocks early in the second, and back-to-back kills from Piazza, much like the first half, gave Mercer an early 6-5 lead. Piazza's fifth kill of the game tied the score at seven, and it stayed tied for most of the remaining set. Sophomore Anne Whitenack rose high up for a hit to tie the game at 11, and Austin Dean did the same on the next rally to give Mercer a one point advantage.
A killer ace from Lady Rebel Charli Grubbs couldn't be returned and opened up a 17-13 lead for Boyle, but the efforts of Piazza and Whitenack earned Mercer several points in quick succession to tie the set at 24. Eventually, Grubbs' hit was smacked in Piazza's direction and the junior couldn't get out of its path before it eventually landed out of bounds. The second set ended 26-24.
Mercer jumped out to an early 5-0 lead in the final set, but Boyle battled back behind strong play from seniors Gracee Teague and Kendra Christopher, cutting Mercer's lead to 7-5. title: State Releases Preliminary Data For School Performance In 2023-2024: Burgin, Mercer Proud Of Student Performance
description: The Kentucky Department of Education (KDE) has released assessment and accountability data for the 2023-2024 school year on as required by state statute and the federal Every Student Succeeds Act.…
content:
The Kentucky Department of Education (KDE) has released assessment and accountability data for the 2023-2024 school year on as required by state statute and the federal Every Student Succeeds Act.
According to a press release, KDE will release the assessment and accountability data in phases. The data is initially available in datasets on Open House, an online platform. Due to a vendor change, a new School Report Card dashboard will be available later this year.
Both of the school systems, Burgin Independent Schools and the Mercer County School District, have released preliminary results from the latest assessment.
File image.
Burgin Independent Schools
According to a press release from Burgin Independent, students continue to outpace other students across Kentucky. Some of the highlighted results from the 2024 Burgin Independent Schools' State Accountability Rankings in Kentucky by District:
• Burgin Independent District ranked 28th out of 172 districts in Kentucky.
• Burgin Elementary ranked 55th out of 172 districts in Kentucky.
• Burgin Middle School ranked 32nd out of 172 districts in Kentucky.
• Burgin High School ranked 22nd out of 172 districts in Kentucky.
According to Burgin's press release, Burgin Independent ranked fourth as a district out of 31 districts in the Central Kentucky Education Co-op and second as a district for elementary, middle school, and high school for proficiency and Distinguished on the Reading and Math Assessments. Boyle County Schools ranked first. In addition, Burgin Independent ranked second as a district in the area for overall combined index, again finishing behind Boyle. Finally, Burgin High School tied for first in the state for postsecondary readiness scores.
'Really proud of our students for their individual performances on our latest state assessments,' Burgin Superintendent Will Begley said in the press release. 'Finishing first in the state with post-secondary readiness and second in the area as a district is tremendous. Our state assessment data only cements the fact that the strategies and interventions by our entire staff is spot on. The district will continue to work on strategies that enable students to sustain high growth and achievement.'
'Our community is very proud of all the hard work our students and staff put forth,' said Burgin Principal Chris LeMonds. 'It also proves that our unique, small school setting provides us the opportunity to focus individually to ensure student success.'
File image.
Mercer County School System
The Mercer County School System also has a lot to be proud of this year. In a press release, they announced that all their schools continue to receive high marks in academics.
For the first time, the system scored green in every academic area at every school level—elementary, middle and high school.
Mercer officials also pointed out the district was rated as 'increased' in eight of 11 main measurable areas and 'maintained' in the other three. In addition, Mercer County Senior High School was in the top 15 percent in the state and the top high school in all of Mercer County. King Middle School finished in the top 40 percent of middle schools in the state, while the elementary schools improved for the third year in a row, up from 50.8 to 63.7, according to the press release.
Mercer officials also announced students had increased their composite score in ACT testing for the third straight year, up from 17.8 to 19.2.
'We are incredibly proud of our students and the academic results they have earned,' said Jason Booher, superintendent of Mercer County Schools, in a press release. 'Our staff has worked extremely hard to establish a culture of high achievement and continuous improvement.'
For more information, including the full data sets for every school system in Kentucky, visit education.ky.gov/Open-House. For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Woman In Custody After Allegedly Shooting A Man Saturday
description: File image. A Harrodsburg woman is in custody after shooting a man in an apparent domestic dispute Saturday. Kadesha Aundrea Burch, 30, of Harrodsburg, has been charged with attempted murder and 1st…
content:
File image.
A Harrodsburg woman is in custody after shooting a man in an apparent domestic dispute Saturday.
Kadesha Aundrea Burch, 30, of Harrodsburg, has been charged with attempted murder and 1st degree wanton endangerment.
Officers from the Harrodsburg Police Department were dispatched after a man living on Perryville Road called 911 saying he had been shot. According to the uniform citation, they found the caller lying in the driveway two with gunshot wounds to his right leg, one in the thigh and the other in the shin. The victim told police the shooter 'was still inside the residence,' according to the uniform citation.
Police applied a tourniquet to the victim's leg to control the bleeding until emergency medical services could arrive, according to the uniform citation.
Police arrested the alleged shooter, Burch. According to the uniform citation, Burch said she and the man 'had been fighting all day.' Burch told police the man had 'strangled her.' She picked up a 'gun from the ground' and admitted firing one shot towards the victim, according to the uniform citation.
While in the back of the patrol car, Burch yelled out the window to the victim, 'I didn't mean to shoot you twice, I hope you're okay,' according to the uniform citation.
Police found three .45 caliber shell casings in the driveway 'directly out the back door from the residence,' according to the uniform citation
The victim was airlifted for medical treatment. According to an HPD Facebook post, he is expected to survive.
Burch is being held at Boyle County Detention Center on a $50,000 bond. For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Pioneers rise to Eagles level in exhibition match
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Pioneers (2-6) hosted the Midway University Eagles (4-7-1) at Hilpp Family Field on Friday, Oct. 10.…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Pioneers (2-6) hosted the Midway University Eagles (4-7-1) at Hilpp Family Field on Friday, Oct. 10.
Despite playing a formidable NAIA opponent, the Pioneers immediately took control of the game. Sophomore John Harrigan delivered a pinpoint cross onto Gabe Cisneros' foot, and the senior turned to shoot just feet away from the goal, but his shot was deflected (2').
Freshman winger Buhari Kadusi was the leading scorer for Bryan Station last season in high school and was wreaking havoc on the Eagle back line Friday. Kadusi consistently beat any defender who attempted to close him down in the first half, and his speed kept the defense checking their shoulder for touchline runs all 90 minutes. He ran circles around his defender before finally laying the ball off to Pacifique Bebe. Bebe's shot fell at Cisneros' feet, and the senior turned and laid it back off to Bebe, whose second chance smacked off of the bar (8').
Harrodsburg earned another golden chance ten minutes later when they won a free kick just outside of the 18-yard box. Cisneros is usually automatic from such a short range, but his shot rolled straight to the keeper this time.
Despite the Pioneers controlling the first 20 minutes of the game, Midway got on the scoreboard first after Jacob Schultz finished his first goal of the season (30').
The Pioneers moved the ball back into the Eagles' territory almost immediately. Cisneros connected with Gomez in the middle, who played Carlos Hernandez in toward the goal, but his first touch shot was saved by Eagle goalkeeper Bryson Lynch.
Buhari Kadusi went to the ground to win the ball back during Harrodsburg's match with Midway University.
Hernandez was sent down the left side again moments later and was pulled down from behind. Harrodsburg had as good a scoring opportunity as they could on the ensuing free kick. Bebe sent a perfectly lofted cross to Cisneros two yards away from the goal line, but the senior couldn't keep the shot down (35').
Kadusi, Bebe and Harrigan have a great connection and created chance after chance in the first half, but the shots weren't decisive enough. The Pioneers put the Eagles under pressure all the way til the halftime whistle blew, but trailed 1-0.
Both teams struggled to keep possession and the start of the second half was a fight for the ball in midfield. Hernandez played a cross that beat the keeper and made it behind, but Cisneros was just inches away from reaching the ball and tying the game (63').
Bebe won the ball in midfield two minutes later and surged upfield before being brought down from behind and earning the Pioneers a free kick. The shot flew over the bar, and the Pioneers pressed and won back the ball immediately after the goal kick. Cisneros fired another shot but it sailed just inches wide (73').
'Personally, I think what was keeping us from a goal was just hanging on too long, just looking for the most perfect moment that sometimes just doesn't exist in the game. Certainly there were times we could have released a bit sooner,' said Head Coach Louis Jones.
Midway had their first breakaway of the game moments later but Mercer County Senior High graduate Ben Waddell tracked back and was there to make a goal-saving deflection. After outperforming the Eagles in almost every facet of the game, the Pioneers eventually fell 1-0. Jones is happy that his squad of just 17 players, primarily freshmen, competed with a program boasting a roster of nearly 50 players. He hopes a sound performance against a reputable team will give his squad more confidence in the weeks moving forward.
'It was one of those games that we lost, but it didn't really feel like it. It felt like a good mental edge for us. Maybe we can capitalize on some of that energy moving forward,' said Jones.
The Pioneers will be back in action in Harrodsburg on Saturday, Oct. 19, when they face Ohio Christian University. Kickoff time is still to be determined.
