title: Board Of Education Approves Changes For New Elementary School
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreContractors work at the site of the future home of the Mercer County Elementary School. The Mercer County Board of Edu
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors work at the site of the future home of the Mercer County Elementary School.
The Mercer County Board of Education received some good news about the sinkhole that had been discovered at the building site of the new Mercer County Elementary School.
At their regular meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 15, the board was informed they had saved a little more than $37,000 for sinkhole remediation. They were told the cost would be $112,000.24, less than the $149,659.84 the board approved at their September meeting.
'We've been very fortunate in the past month,' said David Milan, vice president of Trace Creek Construction, which is serving as the construction manager for the project. Milan showed the board drone footage of the construction site.
'There has been minimum settlement,' Milam said about the sinkhole. He said the contractor was doing additional checking.
'That was good news,' said Superintendent Jason Booher.
Milam said contractors were completing the footers and beginning work on walls. He said they hope to start installing plumbing and work on the foundation.
'I just like seeing walls,' said Chairman Randy Phillips.
'It's always good seeing walls,' Milam said.
The school board approved a series of other change orders, including one for the King Middle School restroom project. Chief Finance Officer Amber Minor said the original revised estimate was $754,471.43 and the actual total ended up being $731,416.59. Minor said she was still working on clearing out all construction projects. The board also approved closing out the district energy savings project, which has a remaining balance of $1,546.42 to be used on future construction projects.
The board approved a change order to install a cafeteria curtain wall sill. They agreed to pay $4,102.49 for additional angle iron to fasten three windows in place—each one 28 feet wide—in the cafeteria. Beth Bauer, the project manager for RossTarrant Design, the architectural firm that designed the elementary school, explained it had to be added for the window system.
The school board approved another change order, opting to spend $16,560.00 to install aluminum storefront windos frames in the entry hall. AF asked if they needed to match other windows in the area.
'It was tagged wrong on blueprint,' Bauer said.
'Luckily we caught it,' said Laith Ross, of RossTarrant. He said neither manufacturer picked it up during the design stages.
'The price is what they would have paid originally if it hadn't been missed,' Bauer said.
Booher recommended going with aluminum storefront window frames.
'It's a maintenance issue over time,' he said. 'To me, it's worth the extra money.'
The board approved another change order to install three-phase power for the telescoping bleachers at a cost of $3,213.58. Bauer said they realized the bleachers had no power.
'You're not paying for it twice,' she assured the board. Ross said the price is for single-phase, but the electrician is providing three-phase at no extra cost.
'Do we think we found all the things?' asked board member Amber Franceschi.
'It happens,' Bauer said.
'A lot of stuff comes up,' she told the board. 'Hopefully this is it.'
Under questioning from the board, David Milam of Trace Creek Construction said the breaker would be able to handle the power.
'It's a blessing it was missed,' Milam said. 'You're going to end up with a better product.'
Finally, the board approved spending $128,156.03 to install terrazzo flooring in the classroom corridors. Bauer noted that terrazo was going to be used for the main hall and cafeteria.
'This floor will stand up much better,' Phillips said.
'It looks like it's a pretty amazing type of floor,' board member Billy G. Montgomery said.
Booher said there were two things he wanted for the new elementary school: terrazo flooring, at least in the main entrance, and no flat roofs. He noted they'd chosen Terrazo for the cafeteria already. 'If we'd known the bid was going to come in $1.5 million under, we could have gotten terrazo in the high-traffic areas,' Booher said. He said the flooring was low maintenance and would look beautiful for decades.
'Terrazo is there for the life of the building,' Booher said.
'Let's go for the nicer flooring,' Franceschi said. She said the floor was one of the first things that could become an eyesore.
In other business, the Mercer County Board of Education received the monthly report from Superintendent Jason Booher, who discussed the constitutional amendment that would enable the General Assembly to provide financial support for the education costs of students in kindergarten through 12th grade who are outside the system of public schools. While most of Mercer County has signs encouraging people to vote no on the amendment, Booher said they were being bombarded with vote yes fliers.
'A lot of information is not correct,' Booher said. While some Republican officials—including State Rep. Kim King, who said she was voting yes for the amendment at Tuesday night's Election Forum—Booher said he's had many Republicans say they were going to vote no.
'It's not a partisan issue,' Booher said. 'It's about public schools and taxpayer money.' He said the amendment would give the Kentucky General Assembly a blank check to do whatever they wanted with money for public education. Booher said the schools have never gotten information on how the money will be spent.
He said the claim that the amendment supported school choice was 'a totally false claim.'
'You can go to any public school in Kentucky free of charge,' Booher said.
He said private schools don't have to account for their money or undergo any testing.
'You don't have to be a radical politician to vote no on this amendment,' Booher said.
The superintendent noted it was the last meeting before the general election on Tuesday, Nov. 5. He said the amendment, if enacted, would harm rural communities in Kentucky, noting Mercer County stood to lose more than $5.3 million in funding, according to some estimates.
Currently, a little over a third of funding for education comes from local taxes. If the amendment passes, Booher said the burden of educational costs such as staffing will fall on local taxpayers.
'There are a lot of repercussions,' Booher said. 'It can effect Mercer County.'
Board member Billy G. Montgomery said he'd heard a group out of Pennsylvania had donated $14 million to get the amendment passed.
'Somewhere, somebody's going to pay that back some day,' Montgomery said.
'Sounds to me like there's a lot of uncertainty,' Phillips said. 'There's a bit of a concern.' For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Despite Injuries, Lady Titans Coach Souder Is Determined To Be Courtside For Season Opener
description: File ImageAfter being injured this summer, Mercer County Lady Titans basketball coach Chris Souder has been doing all he can to make sure he can lead the 2024-25 Lady Titan basketball team from…
content:
File Image
After being injured this summer, Mercer County Lady Titans basketball coach Chris Souder has been doing all he can to make sure he can lead the 2024-25 Lady Titan basketball team from courtside.
It may not sound like much but being 'well enough to go back to work' is a significant milestone for Mercer County girls basketball coach Chris Souder.
He was seriously injured in a tubing accident on the Lake of the Ozarks in mid-June when he suffered a broken hip, broken pelvis and knee injury.
Souder had made the decision to leave South Laurel, where he had a 136-63 mark with two 13th Region championships in six seasons, to return to Mercer County where he won state championships in 2017 and 2018. He compiled a 490-214 record at Mercer from 1999-2018, and won five 12th Region titles — including four straight from 2015-18 — and 17 46th District championships. His 626 total wins place him eighth on the list of Kentucky's all-time winningest girls coaches and fourth among active coaches.
'I am a full-time sub at the high school and my original plan was not to start until after the October fall break but I decided to go back earlier even though I'm on crutches,' he said. 'I've been doing PT (physical therapy) three times a week and it is way harder than I ever imagined. I had never really done PT. I am not a crier but a couple of days I'll admit I thought I might cry because it hurt.'
His limp is not as noticeable now but he says he still has a long way to go.
'I am not crazy mobile yet,' Souder said.
That has created some limitations on his coaching during preseason workouts but he insists he will 'not miss a regular practice' because the team has too much work to do.
'I just want to get to where if we are doing a drill I can show the players what to do and not have to get an assistant to do it,' he said. 'I got to do some summer basketball with the players before I got hurt. We are kind of in a rebuilding mode and I needed to be in the gym more than I have been. I was not as visible with the middle school team as I wanted to be.
'I don't think I ever missed a day of conditioning or practice as a coach but now I have missed some due to PT. I have great assistants but that still bothers me because I know I need to be there.'
Souder brought strength coach Chuck Miller from South Laurel back to Mercer, and considers that a 'vital' move to help his young players get more accustomed to the weight room workouts.
Sean Pigman is returning home to Mercer as an assistant coach after spending the last five seasons as head coach at Whitley County. Jennifer Merchant was on the previous staff and will remain as director of basketball operations to do 'social media, stats and all the stuff' Souder does not like to do.
Souder's son, Conner, will coach the junior varsity teams and also help with the varsity.
Conner's son will be one year old in November and that was a big reason Chris Souder came back to Mercer County.
'I want to see him in the gym. I can remember days where Connor was running all over the gym as a kid,' the Mercer coach said.
He would also like to eventually have key players off his two state championship teams at Mercer helping the program.
'I have been trying to get Emma Davis and Seygan Robins (a former Miss Basketball) involved to help bring some energy back in the program. However, they are both expecting (pregnant) but I told them next spring we can get babysitters while they help,' Souder said. 'Getting them around the kids would be big.
'I have also talked to the Lake twins (Faith and Lexy) and they have done some work with our kids but the more we can get these players back around, the better off our younger kids will be.'
Souder knows he faces a major rebuilding job after Mercer lost Anna Drakeford and Sara Dunn, who combined for 37 points per game, off last year's team.
'We have more questions than I have about a team in a long time,' Souder said. 'I can talk all I want about what Mercer has been and how we can get back there, but these kids are so young.'
His centerpiece will be sophomore Izzie Carlton, who averaged 11.1 points and a team-high 8.6 rebounds per game last year while shooting 47.5 percent from the field.
'I am used to my teams being small, quick and running. This will be one of the bigger teams I have had,' Souder said. 'She is 6-3, and her sister (Kate Carlton) is 6-1 and our only senior. We are going to have size and have to figure out how to get the ball to them.
'Some of our ball handlers might be middle school kids. We have got to be creative. Izzie is a really good piece to build around. She does natural things. Both her and her sister are natural shot blockers with deceptive length.'
Mercer will open the season Dec. 3 in Louisville against Mercy Academy and Souder has set his own personal goal for that date.
'People asked if I was still going to coach when I got hurt,' he said. 'I said then if I have to crawl out there, I will coach. My goal for the first game is to be as active as always because that is what the players deserve.' title: Sara Niemann
description: Sara Sue Claiborne Niemann, 78, widow of Kenneth Joseph Niemann Jr., of Harrodsburg, died Monday, Oct. 21, 2024, at the Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center in Danville. Born on Feb. 14, 1947, in…
content:
Sara Sue Claiborne Niemann, 78, widow of Kenneth Joseph Niemann Jr., of Harrodsburg, died Monday, Oct. 21, 2024, at the Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center in Danville.
Born on Feb. 14, 1947, in Knoxville, Tenn., she was the daughter of Hollis F. and Mildred Marguerat Claiborne.
She worked at the Bingham Child Guidance center in Louisville, was involved with breeding, training and racing thoroughbreds, retired as an administrative assistant at St. Andrew Catholic Church, was a member of Pastoral Council, Laudato Si' Planning and a greeter in Catechist Information Programs, was a member of the Lions Club, James Harrod Trust, the MLK Day and Mercer Transformation boards and volunteered as a community tutor.
Survivors include: two stepdaughters, Vickie Crane (Mark) of Jeffersonville, Ind. and Michelle Wheeler (Mark) of Floyds Knobs, Ind.; 14 grandchildren; 17 great-grandchildren; and several other family members and friends.
She was preceded in death by one brother, Hal Claiborne; one daughter, Natalie Cox Watts; son-in-law, Jason Watts; and stepchildren Brenda Niemann Schroeder and Kenneth J. Niemann Ill.
Mass of Christian Burial was held Saturday, Oct. 26, at the St. Andrew Catholic Church.
Memorial contributions are suggested to the St. Andrews Catholic Church, 1125 Danville Rd., Harrodsburg, KY 40330.
Arrangements by Ransdell Funeral Chapel.

title: Titan Band Places Fourth In 2A
description: Well that's all folks! It's a wrap, the Marching Titans' season is done. They pulled off the finale to an incredible season. The Mercer Band advanced from fifth place in regionals to compete in the…
content:
Well that's all folks! It's a wrap, the Marching Titans' season is done. They pulled off the finale to an incredible season.
The Mercer Band advanced from fifth place in regionals to compete in the KMEA Class-2A Semi-Finals at the Christian Academy of Louisville this past Saturday, Oct. 26. The competition comprised 2A bands from the West and East Regions to form the top 12. The wind was wicked, the sun was out, and even though it was chilly, the band kids found a drive within them to compete.
The band took the field at CAL Stadium and played their most phenomenal show. The band parents jumped up and down on the sidelines and screamed in excitement. We were all overjoyed and filled with incredible excitement because we all watched our kids play and march their hearts out and produce a sound and visual that was better than anything we had seen in years.
When it was time for awards, the announcer named the 12th through 7th place recipients. This is where we have found ourselves in the past two seasons. We were 11th in 2023 and 8th in 2022. They named 12th place, 11th place, and so on. When they announced 7th place and they didn't call our names in any of those placings. The lump in my throat hit and I looked at my fellow media member, Mike, and I could mutter out a squeak of the words, 'They made it.'
The announcer named the top six bands in no particular order to advance to the KMEA State Finals: '…and with a distinguished rating,' the announcer said, 'Mercer County!'
Drum Major Reagan Sims (Center) along with Addison Woodward (Left) and Alexis Clark (Right) Pose with the new State Finals Plaque after winning 4th in 2A Finals Competition.
I am not going to lie, I have been humbly writing these articles to support and lift our band kids to the community for two years now. I am a big guy. I have a humble heart. When they announced those kids were going to the top six at L&N Credit Union Cardinal Stadium to perform at the state finals. I cried like a baby. I couldn't contain those crocodile tears any longer. My heart swelled with such immense pride and excitement. I have watched these kids fight for years to get there. The last time they were in the Finals was 2021.
'This is it folks,' said Band Director Erica Ashford. 'This is what you have worked for. This is what the countless hours of practice have led to. This is where you have fun. Get out there and have the time of your life. You have earned it and I am very proud of all of you.'
So there we were Cardinal Stadium. There were six bands in each class, ranging From 1A to 5A. Mercer performed in 2A. When those kids walked through that tunnel and onto the turf at Cardinal Stadium, their eyes lit up as if they were seeing Disney World. You could not have wiped the grins off of their faces. It was the same for all of us adults, too. I have done band media for eight years and have been on that field with other bands. Let me tell you…you have yet to learn how big that stadium is and the thrill you get walking out there. This time was different. I had a kid in that band. My son played percussion and drum set in the front ensemble. I am proud of him, but he is one cog in the wheel of all the band kids I have grown to love over the seasons who helped get that show over the finish line.
The sound of that show inside that massive stadium was, well, music to my ears. They outperformed themselves in every way and laid it all on the field. The flags were spot on, the horns were perfect, the percussion was rocking, and the drum major was swelling with pride. As they finished the show and walked off the field and back through the tunnel, they did so knowing their hard work had paid off and they laid it all out on the field.
The parade of bands filled the arena during the award ceremony, and they lined up on the field in what is called 'retrient' later that night. The placings were all named, starting with 1A bands and going up to 5A bands. When they got to 2A bands, we watched as they called 6th place- Christian Academy of Louisville. Fifth Place- Loyd Memorial. Fourth Place- Mercer County. The Titans earned a top four place in Class-2A in the KMEA State Finals and were ecstatic.
The town came out hugely last Thursday night to support the band in their community performance and sent them off with love and well wishes. The community has helped us raise these kids. Our kids. The kids! The Band Kids! Say it out loud one more time! The band kids got 4th place in the finals!
Each band member was awarded medals for being state finalists, and they have a huge plaque to hang in the band room. This is their championship trophy, they earned it.
'These are all my kids,' said Ashford. 'They all started with me, I helped teach them, but they all worked to get here.' Don't be fooled. The staff got choked up too. It was a day. If the words I put here didn't paint the picture, I only pray someday, those of you who never felt that can join us as we try again next year to make the 2025 finals.
Director Erica Ashford leads the Mercer Band with assistance from Alex Smith, Jeremy Ellis, Emily Curtsinger and former Assistant Director Adam McRay. The field commander was Reagan Sims, and the assistants were Josephine Doan and Matthew Clark. Visit us on Facebook at Mercer County Band and Instagram @mercercoband.
The show My Hollow Heart, was inspired and developed by Adam McRay, Erica Ashford and Alex Smith. For more stories like this one, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Will Burgin Go Wet? Voters Get To Choose Nov. 5
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreThe Van Halen cover band Completely Unchained performed to a huge crowd at Oktoberfest, which drew approximately 24,000
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
The Van Halen cover band Completely Unchained performed to a huge crowd at Oktoberfest, which drew approximately 24,000 visitors while downtown Harrodsburg drew approximately 220,000 visitors over the past year. Organizers hope Burgin will see similar success if voters choose to go wet at the upcoming election on Tuesday, Nov. 5.
Burgin voters will finally get to vote on whether to go wet or remain a dry city at the general election on Tuesday, Nov. 5.
On the ballot, Burgin voters will be able to choose yes or no on the sale of alcoholic beverages.
In April, Mayor Joe Monroe told the Burgin City Council he had filed paperwork to get a wet-dry initiative on the ballot. At the time, Monroe said they needed 85 signatures to get the question on the ballot.
Councilman Sindicat 'Sid' Dunn, who organized a previous effort to get an initiative on the ballot, said they collected 115 last time. The number of necessary signatures is based on turnout at the previous election.
Officials said the last time, a lot of people who did not live in Burgin signed the petition.
A large number of visitors come through Burgin every year on their way to Herrington Lake, and local leaders have wondered if allowing alcohol sales—as Harrodsburg voted to do in 2016—could have a similar impact in Burgin as it did in Harrodsburg. Local leaders are also looking at Lancaster in Garrard County, including a new store just across the lake.
The topic came up at the Burgin Election Forum on Tuesday, Oct. 22, at Burgin Independent School. Only three of the candidates running for the Burgin City Council—Dunn, Councilwoman Melinda Wofford and Jim Caldwell—appeared at the forum. Councilman Jamie Keebortz, Councilman Travis Irvin, candidate Sarah Moran and write-in candidates George Hensley, Timothy Dollar and Barbara Watts did not attend.
'We've got a wet-dry vote coming up,' said Caldwell, who has previously served Burgin as police chief and mayor. 'I want them spending that money here,' Caldwell said. 'That's money that's staying in this town that's going to other communities.'
'We need little mom-and-pop start-up businesses,' Dunn said. He said alcohol sales would be a way for Burgin to grow and to increase revenue for the city government without increasing taxes.
'We're of the only cities in Kentucky that don't charge an occupational tax,' Dunn said.
Dunn noted Burgin no longer has a police officer. He said the city lost their last officer to a school system.
'We can't afford to pay them what our schools can pay now,' Dunn said.
The candidates were given a chance to give opening statements and then answer six questions from Burgin High School Junior Barron Bradshaw and Mercer County Senior Sage Markham. Earl Motzer served as the moderator. The city council candidates were also asked about dilapidated properties.
'You have to lead by example,' Dunn said. He said he bought a dilapidated house and tore it down.
Dunn and Wofford noted the difficulty in finding the property owners. Wofford said she serves on other boards, including Mercer County Habitat for Humanity. She noted a property owner had sold their property to Habitat for Humanity.
'There's a home being built for a Burgin family,' Wofford said.
Caldwell said he could bring his experience from 22 years in law enforcement to deal with the issue. He said Burgin had tore down a dozen such properties during his administration.
'The houses that we did tear down were replaced with better houses,' Caldwell said.
'We're getting it done,' he said. 'We may not be getting it done as fast as you want it to.'
The candidates were asked for their top priorities.
'Number one is getting the flooding issue fixed,' Wofford said. 'We need to be more transparent with the way taxpayers' money is being spent.'
'You don't get things done in a year,' Caldwell said. He said it took three and a half years to get money for the flooding. He said the administration before his 'didn't want any transparency.'
Another priority for Dunn was the park, including building a permanent structure.
They were also asked what they would do if their personal values conflicted with those of their constituents.
'I'm out,' Caldwell said. 'I don't sell my soul.'
Caldwell and the other candidates said they would try to work with constituents.
'The main thing is to sit and listen,' said Dunn, who said he'd never been put in that position in his time on the city council.
'I'm always willing to listen,' Wofford said. 'I'm definitely not going to bend to something that's morally wrong.'
The candidates were asked about improving infrastructure, such as roads and utilities. Dunn said he's spoken with the state to deal with the bridge in front of the school.
'That's probably the main priority,' Dunn said.
He said the sewer system has encouraged construction in Burgin and wanted to make sure the roads would be able to handle it.
Wofford said some city ordinances need to be updated. She said they are limited by state law from doing some things to protect the city. Wofford said they are trying to organize a code enforcement board.
Caldwell said, under the previous administration, funding from the state and federal government had stopped because of poor financial record keeping.
'We got the books balanced,' Caldwell said. 'We brought in millions of dollars in funding.'
They were also asked about areas where the city government needs to focus.
'We need some more money,' Wofford said. She said the city could increase revenue by attracting more businesses and residents.
'Our primary focus is the flooding,' said Caldwell, who said 25 percent of the city goes underwater every time it rains.
'If we can get that flooding under control, we can develop that property and turn it into tax money,' Caldwell said.
Finally, the candidates were asked about transparency.
'We've already done it,' Caldwell said. He said there were no open records violations during his time as mayor.
'Since I've been in charge, we've been open,' Caldwell said.
'We have moved into the new era of Facebook Live,' Dunn said. He said he enjoys having conversations with constituents.
'I'm always making myself approachable,' Dunn said.
Wofford said her number one thing was to continue to learn. She said Kentucky statutes are very confusing.
'I want to make sure I'm doing what I'm supposed to do,' Wofford said. While part of that was seeking more training with the Kentucky League of Cities, part of it was 'asking questions and learning more.'
'You have to continue to ask questions,' Wofford said. 'We can get better as a council and as a city in being transparent and letting citizens know what's going on.'
At the election forum, three of the candidates for the Burgin Board of Education—current board member Ben Bradshaw, Bryan Vandiviere and Kathryn Hendershot—appeared. Board member Keith Monson did not attend.
The three candidates got a chance to introduce themselves. Bradshaw has served on the school board for eight years. He has worked for Kentucky Utilities for 20 years. He only sought election to the school board after another longtime member relocated.
'At the end of the day, it's all about the kids,' Bradshaw said.
Vandiviere, a Burgin graduate, said he has worked in education for 25 years, the last 10 years in higher education. He currently works for a web-based company and has three kids in the school system, two are currently enrolled. Vandiviere also coaches crosscountry and track.
'It's a special place and a special community,' he said.
Hendershot earned a doctorate from Asbury University, from which she retired.
'Our children are facing many challenges that their parents and grandparents never faced,' Hendershot said.
Asked about leadership opportunities for students, Bradshaw said Burgin's small class size enabled the school to focus more on the leadership capabilities of the kids.
'We're able to find the kids who may not know they're capable of that,' Bradshaw said.
'I wouldn't be where I am today,' Vandiviere said, without the opportunities he received at Burgin.
'I want to see the growth of our clubs,' Vandiviere said. 'I want to see more of those led by our students.'
'I don't have anything additional to add,' Hendershot said.
They were asked about long term goals for the school.
Vandiviere called himself a 'fiscal conservative.' He said he wants the school and the community to work together.
Hendershot said she had no long-term goals beyond saving children from agendas that would harm national pride.
'I am new here,' Hendershot said. 'I have a lot to learn.'
Bradshaw said his goal was to make sure the school is financially solvent. Sometimes that entails making unpopular decisions, he said.
'I also want to make sure we can retain the wonderful teachers we have here,' Bradshaw said. He spoke of increasing revenue by increasing the student population.
'We can attract some of the best kids around,' Bradshaw said.
The candidates were asked how they would handle budget gaps.
'I have no idea,' Hendershot said. 'I've only lived here a year and a half.'
'We're very limited in our revenue streams,' Bradshaw said. 'We have to depend primarily on the residents in Burgin.'
He said the school district is in competition with other districts for staff.
'We want to attract the best,' Bradshaw said. He said the district needs to narrow the gap in compensation.
'It's hard to overcome, but we have to work toward that year in and year out,' Bradshaw said. 'You have to make decisions that aren't popular.'
Vandiviere said they need to look at outside revenue options, including grants and working with corporations.
'I don't like taxes,' Vandiviere said. 'I want to explore outside options.'
Asked about school safety, Bradshaw said he wouldn't say there is a direct safety issue. Burgin does not have a school resource officer.
Bradshaw said the state has mandated an SRO in every school but does not provide funding. He said the board of education is working closely with the City of Burgin and the Mercer County Sheriff's Office.
'That's everybody's biggest fear,' Bradshaw said. He said the staff does a great job of keeping doors locked and monitoring the school.
'I think every building needs that,' Bradshaw said.
'That is one of the big gaps,' Vandiviere said. While the school does a great job at security, he said he wanted to pursue technological options.
'That really has jumped out at me,' Hendershot said. 'That would be something I would really want to press into.'
While she also discussed the possibility of arming the staff, Hendershot said it was a priority of hers to have a safety officer.
The candidates were asked about their opinions about amendment two.
'I personally am not for amendment two,' said Vandiviere, who said the wording opens the doors for a lot of possibilities. 'It opens up the door for potential abuse at the state level.'
'I want to continue to grow our public education system,' Vandiviere said. 'There are a lot of good possibilities, but there are a lot of possibilities for harm.'
Hendershot read from the amendment. 'To me, that's pretty clear,' she said.
'There's a lot of misconception out there,' Bradshaw said. He said students already had school choice, and state money follows the students to any public school they choose to attend.
'It's pulling funds from public schools,' Bradshaw said. He said public schools are mandated in how they handle money, including contractors.
'I am against tax dollars funding private schools,' Bradshaw said.
Finally, the candidates were asked about accessibility. Hendershot said she wanted to find out what the people wanted and act as a liaison.
'That's not why we're here,' Bradshaw said. 'We're here for the kids.'
'You have to listen to everyone's voice,' he said, 'but at the end of the day, you have to decide what's best for the kids.'
Vandiviere said the easiest way to be accessible is to be plugged into the school, being active and available.
'I've always tried to be as reachable as I can,' he said. 'We want to make sure at the end of the day that we're happy with all our decisions.'
The general election will be on Tuesday, Nov. 5. Excused in-person absentee ballots can be left at the drop box starting Wednesday, Oct. 23 through Wednesday, Oct. 30.
In-person no-excuse absentee ballots can be cast on Thursday, Oct. 31; Friday, Nov. 1; and Saturday, Nov. 2; at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse (207 West Lexington Street). The hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For more stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

content:
Elizabeth Joyce Rhorer, 90, wife of the late William Joseph Rhorer, died Thursday, Oct. 24, 2024, in Lexington.
Born Jan. 19, 1934, in Lexington, she was the daughter of the late David and Stella O'Nan.
Survivors include: one daughter, Sandra Willhoite; one son, Marc Rhorer; five grandchildren; 10 great-grandchildren; five great-great-grandchildren; and several nieces and nephews.
She was preceded in death by one son, James Joseph Hill Jr.; one daughter, Alesia Gail Rhorer; two sisters, Zella Mae Webster and Margaret Perkins; one brother, William O'Nan; and one granddaughter, Deanna Osborne.

title: Titan Cross Country wraps up season at Kentucky Horse Park
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County Senior High School cross country team has been on an outstanding run over the last two seasons. Last fall, the boys' third…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Senior High School cross country team has been on an outstanding run over the last two seasons. Last fall, the boys' third place finish at the Class-2A Region 5 meet was the highest in Titan Cross Country's history (post '06). In 2024, the Titan boys knocked 24 points off of their team score, surpassing last year's champions, Corbin, for a new program-best second place finish at the Region 5 meet held Saturday, Oct. 26, at Wayne County High School. In similar, momentous fashion the Lady Titan runners' third placed appearance in 2023 marked the first season in Titan cross country history that both teams qualified for the state meet in the same season. Even more impressively, the Lady Titans managed to claim the final qualification spot with only one repeating runner from last year's team, eighth grader Layla Nowlin.
Roxy Bogardus, Addyson Foster, L. Nowlin, Daisy Nowlin and Journee Humpert were the top five Lady Titan runners at the Region 5 meet and they finished in nearly the exact same order at the Class-2A state finals at the Kentucky Horse Park on Saturday, Nov. 2. Bogardus finished 54 out of 218 runners with a time of 22:51.56. Foster finished 116 and L. Nowlin followed close behind in the 142 spot. The pair are both still in middle school but ran times of 24:36.90 and 25:50.59 respectively. L. Nowlin was the only Lady Titan runner to run a faster time at state then in the Region 5 meet a week prior, when she ran a 26:08.45. Her time of 25:50.59 at state is also a career personal best. D. Nowlin and Julia Hart were the fourth and fifth finishers for Mercer. D. Nowlin knocked nearly two minutes off of her time since competing in the state meet last fall, and finished with a time of 26:57.35 Saturday. Hart finished 171 out of 218 with a time of 27:21.10, and Humpert followed just three spots behind with a time of 27:34.77. Abigail Woods was the seventh and final Lady Titan to cross the finish line on Saturday. The sophomore finished with a time of 28:12.05. As a team, the Lady Titans placed 21 out of 28 programs.
No one from the current squad is graduating, and three of the Lady Titans' elite runners, Foster, L. Nowlin and J. Hart are competing at a high level despite still being in middle school. It is an exciting time to be around Mercer County cross country according to coach Derek McIntyre.
'It's encouraging we have so many young runners who are dedicated to cross country. That's kind of been a change in the last few years, to have people who are truly cross country runners, versus multi-sport athletes. The future is so bright on the girls' side. Just being able to compete at the state level as a middle school student is special, and they have so much potential for growth,' said McIntyre.
Freshman runner Ashton Butler set a career personal record time of 18:48.28 at the KHSAA Class-2A state cross country meet on Saturday, Nov. 2. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

2024年8月15日〜17日にRMサザビーズがアメリカ・モントレーで開催したオークションにおいてポルシェ「911ターボ フラットノーズ」が出品されました。同車は、新車からわずかに1万3700kmを走行したのみのアメリカ仕様で、2022年発行のポルシェ・クラシックお墨付きの1台です。 ポルシェ935とよく似た外観が人気に
1975年に登場したポルシェ「911ターボ」（社内では930ターボと呼ばれていた）は、まさに世界のスーパーカーの序列を並べ替えるほどの圧倒的なパフォーマンスで、多くのファンにとって夢のクルマとなった。巨大なリアフェンダーとクジラの尾のようなリアデッキスポイラーを備え、その外観はまさに当時のスーパースポーツの頂点を誇るかのような造形。同時にそれはポルシェの作品であり、911のファミリーにあることがひと目で分かるフィニッシュだった。
ポルシェ911ターボはもちろん市場で非常に大きな成功を収めるが、1982年になるとポルシェのレース・スポンサーがある提案を、ポルシェのエクスクルーシブ・マニファクチャー部門（ゾンダーヴィージュとも、またはスペシャル・ウイッシュとも呼ばれていた）に持ち込んだ。
それはモータースポーツの世界で大成功を収めたポルシェ「935」のような外観を持つロードカーの製作であり、その結果誕生したボディワークは、よりエアロダイナミクスに富む935にとても良く似た外観となる。ルーバー上のフロントフェンダーはボンネットと面一に仕上げられ、ロードユースのために格納式ヘッドライトが装備された。
箱型のロッカーパネルや、リアフェンダー上のサイドストレーキ付きブレーキ冷却用エアインテーク、さらに追加のオイル冷却用電動ファンが採用されたことも、このニューモデルの大きな話題。ホイールとタイヤもよりワイドなサイズ設定に改められることになった。
911ターボ フラットノーズとも、あるいはスラントノーズやフラッハバウとも呼ばれたこのモデルには、多くのカスタマーが興味を示し、完成から数カ月も経たないうちに同様のカスタマイズを求める裕福なカスタマーからのオーダーが、ポルシェのもとへは多数寄せられるようになった。 TAG BRAND

title: Titans Fall In Second Round Of State Tournament
description: The Mercer County football Titans ended their season on Friday, Nov. 15, in the second round of the Class-3A KHSAA State Playoffs after Christian Academy of Louisville (9-3) scored 21 second half…
content:
The Mercer County football Titans ended their season on Friday, Nov. 15, in the second round of the Class-3A KHSAA State Playoffs after Christian Academy of Louisville (9-3) scored 21 second half points and won, 49-22.
Mercer's offense got off to as good of a start as it could, and they scored their first two touchdowns in only six plays. The Titans ran the read option with both Ashton Drakeford and Cornelius Mapp at quarterback on the first two plays of the game. Drakeford broke through the middle and picked up 22 yards, and Mapp shot outside after pulling the handoff, speeding 57 yards down the sideline, untouched, for the game's opening score.
The Centurions' offense revolved completely around quarterback Connor Hodge. The senior was CAL's leading receiver and racked just under 1500 yards last season, and after taking over the quarterback spot from his brother Cole Hodge this fall, he plays quarterback like a wide receiver. His ability to stay alive in the backfield and evade Mercer County rushers made all the difference Friday. On CAL's second play of the game Hodge ran into an open hole, bounced outside and juked two Titans on the way to the sideline. He was finally brought down by the backside cornerback, Jayden Sailor, after a gain of 51. Trenton Berry wrapped up Hodge in the backfield and forced an incompletion, but back-to-back short curl route completions moved the ball 18 yards. One play later Hodge rolled out to the left, juked two Titans to the ground, and outpaced every defender to the opposite pylon. The Centurions' first drive was indicative of how the game would play out for Mercer County. The CAL passing attack was a fraction of a second faster then the Titans secondary on nearly every play, and no matter how effective the Titans pass rush was, once Hodge built up momentum he was uncatchable.
Braidin Baughman picked up ten yards in three carries on the Titans second drive. On the following first down Baughman went in motion and Mapp faked the handoff. CAL rushed an inside linebacker, but Mapp evaded the pressure and found Baughman standing alone near the sideline. Senior Landon Yates sprinted down the sideline and picked up the final block, allowing Baughman to complete the 51-yard touchdown untouched. Daniel Butler made the extra point and Mercer County led CAL 14-7 with 4:55 left in the first quarter.
Braidin Baughman tried to find the edge during Mercer's 49-22 loss to CAL on Friday, Nov. 15. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren).
The Titans' defense seemed to be catching on to the Centurions' gameplan on the following drive. CAL earned just 11 yards in four plays, and JJ Goodman leveled Hodge on the following first down, but Darwin Cotton was unbeatable. The senior received a short pass and danced down the sideline, slipping free of four Titans before opening up his stride for the endzone, but Drakeford made a great play, punching the ball out just before Cotton crossed the goal line. Cohen Sanford recovered the fumble.
Baughman was caught in the mess at the line of scrimmage on the first two plays of the drive and Mercer couldn't recover.
Hodge led the Centurions down the field and finished the drive with a powerful run that left several Titans on the floor and tied the game at 14-14.
On the following Titan drive, Mapp was inched off the mark on a deep shot to Drakeford, and Baughman bounced a run outside, but the Centurions' pursuit was unlike any other Mercer had seen this year. Ultimately they were forced to punt.
Mercer held a 14-7 lead for over five minutes of gametime, but the momentum completely flipped after Hodge scrambled for a 38-yard touchdown and gave CAL their first lead of the game, 21-14.
Fortunately for Mercer County, despite going three and out again on offense, C. Sanford put his helmet on the ball when tackling CAL wideout Gaines Howard and forced another fumble. Despite recovering the loose ball on the Centurions' 20-yard line, and a CAL penalty moving the ball halfway to the first down marker, Mercer could only move the ball four yards in four plays.
After turning the ball over on downs with 1:21 remaining in the first half, the Titans' defense was caught a step behind in their pass coverage. By the time Stone Perkins planted his foot in the ground on a corner route, Hodge had already put the ball in the air. Seamlessly, Perkins caught the ball, found the edge and ran 84 yards down the sideline for the Centurions' fourth touchdown. At the half, Mercer trailed CAL 28-14. Outside of their two initial scoring drives, the Titans' only moved the ball an astonishing 11 yards in 17 offensive snaps.
'We're a running football team not a passing football team. They did a great job of taking away the run; they're a great football team. They're very good upfront and are very well coached, and they just didn't allow us to get started in the run game,' said Head Coach Craig Yeast.
The Titan defense looked more prepared in the second half and forced CAL into a third down situation twice. After C. Sanford set the edge and forced a bad pass from Hodge on third down, the Centurions' faced a fourth down and seven. The Centurions lined up with five wideouts and they each ran short routes, except Perkins, who executed his post route perfectly. Hodge timed the throw perfectly, and Perkins was wide-open for his second touchdown grab of the game. The Centurions took more than six minutes off of the clock on the 69-yard scoring drive, and extended their lead to 35-14.
The Titans continued to go to the air in their first drive of the second half, but Mapp's throws weren't hitting the mark. Drakeford forced another fumble, this time recovered by Cameron Bottoms, and Baughman broke several tackles and found the sideline, picking up 30 yards, but the Titans' drive stalled again after several incompletions.
Drakeford eventually stepped in at quarterback, and scrambled for 30 yards on fourth down, keeping the Titans' hopes alive. Two plays later, Drakeford placed a perfectly thrown ball on Jacob Sanford's back shoulder and the junior made the grab while falling backward into the endzone. Drakeford scrambled for a two-point conversion, but time was ticking away fast, and the Titans couldn't overcome a 20-point deficit in just over seven minutes of play remaining. The Centurions scored their seventh touchdown of the game on the ensuing drive, and the Titans lost to the top ranked Class-3A team, 49-22.
'I think our program has continued to move forward steadily each year,' said Yeast, who says the standard is still not being met.'Competitive is not good enough. We want to win, and continue to advance in the playoffs. I'm very pleased with our progress, but we still have a long way to go to get to where we need to be to play championship caliber football here in Mercer County.'
The Titans ended their 2024 campaign with a 7-5 overall record and an undefeated district record. The 2024 squad is the only group of Titans to earn back-to-back district championships. The Titans graduate eight seniors in the spring of 2025. Baughman, Berry, Gage Bennett, Bottoms, Landon Gonzalez, Ashton Pusey, Gavinn Rodriguez and Yates make up one of the more successful classes to graduate from Mercer. Yeast, who was selected as the Class-3A District 4 Coach of the Year for the second straight season, believes all but two of the eight man group will play football at the college level.
'They played extremely hard all year and I'm proud of all they accomplished… They've developed into some good leaders and they will be some very, very productive individuals when they become grown men. I expect all of them that want to go to college, will go to college, will play extremely hard for their program and earn a college degree,' said Yeast, 'because of them, our program has moved forward.'
Baughman finished the season with 1,227 total yards on 105 touches. His average of 11.7 yards per touch is unparalleled in Titan history. Yates had a historical season receiving the ball. His 503 yards and four touchdowns is the most productive season by a Titan receiver since Dillon Warren grabbed 538 yards and seven touchdowns in 2019.
Despite having next to no varsity football experience, Mapp did a great job of leading the offense this fall. His 1.289 yards and 14 touchdowns played an important role in the Titans most productive passing attack since 2017, but his speciality in ball protection sets him apart. His 6.5 touchdown to interception ratio is the highest in Mercer County's recorded history.
'Cornelius made a lot of strides this year. He played, for the most part, good football. We've still a lot of things to work on but the thing that he did was protect the ball,' said Yeast.
The Titans have two great options at quarterback next season in Mapp and Drakeford, but Drakeford is slowly climbing the ranks as one of the most productive wideouts in Titan history. His 937 career receiving yards is currently third on the all time Titan leaderboard, behind Layne Peavler (1,678) and Aaron Johnson (1,329).
'He means a lot to our program, and I'm looking forward to him being a tremendous leader for us next year,' said Yeast. For more great stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Jenkins and Thompson lead the Lady Bulldogs into new season
description: The Burgin Lady Bulldogs 2024-2025 basketball team from left to right: Leah Jenk
content:
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs 2024-2025 basketball team from left to right: Leah Jenkins, Haley Hurst, Kynlee Sexton, Ashton Lester, Gabby Thompson, Head Coach Keith Monson, Jemma Jenkins, Bristol Keith, Beth Motley, Claire Pauley and Jocelyn Stanley. (Image: Christy Lee Photography.)
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs basketball program has come a long way in ten years time. Ten seasons ago Burgin won one game, but this season Head Coach Keith Monson and the Lady Bulldogs have high hopes. The program's 33 wins over the last three seasons is the most successful period since 2011 to 2013, when they earned 38 wins in three seasons.
The 2024-2025 Lady Bulldogs will be led by seniors Jemma Jenkins and Gabby Thompson. The latter has been one of the most efficient scorers in the program for each of the last four years. Since leading the team in scoring her eighth grade season, Thompson has gone one to amass 917 points, and she hopes to check the 1,000 point milestone off of her list this season, along with the Burgin record of 83 successful 3-point attempts held by Baleigh Turner. To reach her goal, she understands the team needs to move the ball well as a unit.
'I think we just need to move the ball and I love moving the ball. It gets people open,' said Thompson.
The Lady Bulldogs main focus this winter will be on just that, ball movement and intense defensive pressure.
'We don't have any height so we're gonna have to learn to block out, play it up and down the floor and press a lot,' said Monson.
Monson says the Lady Bulldogs will struggle if they're not shooting well, but he doesn't expect that will happen often.
'They're a good shooting bunch.' For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Former Humane Society President, Two Others, Indicted On Animal Cruelty Charges
description: File image. Four people—including the former president of the Mercer County Humane Society—have been indicted in connection to police discovering animals that had been mistreated, malnourished, and…
content:
File image.
Four people—including the former president of the Mercer County Humane Society—have been indicted in connection to police discovering animals that had been mistreated, malnourished, and did not have proper living conditions at a Salvisa residence in August.
Three of the four people indicted—Gabriella A. Follmer, Amanda G. Coontz and Karen Aubrey, the former president of the Mercer County Humane Society—face multiple misdemeanor charges for intentionally or wantonly subjecting an animal to cruel treatment 'through failing to provide adequate space, health and care and by subjecting the animal to cruel neglect,' according to the indictments. In addition, Follmer and Coontz also face a felony charge for torturing a dog, for intentionally restraining the animal 'with wanton disregard for its pain, suffering and injury,' according to the indictments.
The indictments stem from a search warrant police executed at the home located at 2595 Oregon Road in Salvisa on Sunday, Aug. 25, 2024. According to the uniform citation, 'All the dogs living in the resident were badly injured and not fed properly.'
In addition, officers located drug paraphernalia and methamphetamine, according to the uniform citation.
The animals were taken to the Mercer County Animal Shelter. Director Wendy Quiggle said they were dealing with 24 dogs—three of them were in 'bad shape, Quiggle said. She said eight cats had been sent to the Mercer County Humane Society.
The Mercer Humane Society Board of Directors said they are closely following the matter related to the nine dogs from the humane society which were kept at the house in Salvisa, which they called a kennel owned by Aubrey. According to the board, Aubrey resigned as president and as a volunteer on Aug. 28.
'Throughout the year, those MHS dogs were taken to special events, including Bark in the Park, the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival, Shaker Village events, other festivals, as well as adoption events,' the board said in a statement. 'They were also made available at the MHS office for meet and greet with prospective adopters. All nine dogs were happy, clean, and in excellent condition. All nine had been vetted, neutered or spayed. Any other dogs found at the facility belonged to an outside occupant, which may have caused a temporary overcrowding situation.'
'The humane society has been providing shelter and care for neglected, abused, and abandoned animals for more than 50 years and continues to being committed to rehabilitating them and connecting them with their forever homes,' the board said in the statement.
According to the board, Aubrey has been dedicated to helping animals in need for more than three decades.
'Those who have volunteered with her or who have been helped by her know that she is a wonderful and caring person who would never do harm to any animal,' the board said. 'She has actually nursed all of the animals that came to her tortured, abused, and starving, back to good health. She has advocated for the animals and been involved in providing assistance and support to law enforcement in animal cruelty cases, such as the case in 2022 when two pit bulls were abandoned in a vacant home for weeks and were at the point of death when discovered.'
The board is referring to the case of Rocket and Titan, two dogs that were found to have been abandoned without food or water after their owners moved out of Mercer County back in 2022. The owners pleaded guilty to two counts of 2nd degree animal cruelty in 2023, and were both sentenced to 365 days to serve for each count, totalling 730 days each. Aubrey would bring one of the dogs, Titan, to the courthouse to advocate for changes in Kentucky's notoriously lax animal cruelty laws.
'As a result of Ms. Aubrey's aftercare, these dogs were in the process of being rehabilitated as the MHS reached out to the community to seek adopters or fosters,' the board said in their statement. 'The Board stands committed to continuing in this endeavor.'
Here are the indictments the Mercer Grand Jury handed up last week in relation to the case:
• Gabriella A. Follmer, 53, of 2595 Oregon Road, Salvisa, was charged with 1st degree possession of methamphetamine and torture of a dog, both class D felonies, and 30 class A misdemeanors: one count of possession of drug paraphernalia and 29 counts of 2nd degree animal cruelty. Follmer's bail was set at $10,000 with drug-related conditions: reporting to pretrial services, submitting to random drug testing and no new arrests involving alcohol, illegal substances or pain medications with or without a prescription. In addition Follmer is restricted from having animals in her possession.
• Amanda G. Coontz, 31, of 2595 Oregon Road, Salvisa, was charged with 1st degree trafficking in methamphetamine, a class C felony; torture of a dog, a class D felony; and 30 class A misdemeanors: one count of possession of drug paraphernalia and 29 counts of 2nd degree animal cruelty. Coontz's bail was set at $20,000 with drug-related conditions, and she is also restricted from having animals in her possession.
• Karen Aubrey, 71, of 2595 Oregon Road, Salvisa, was charged with 29 class A misdemeanor counts of 2nd degree animal cruelty. Aubrey's bail was set at $2,000, and she is also restricted from having animals in her possession.
• Kenneth Brawner, 48, of 2595 Oregon Road, Salvisa, was charged with 1st degree trafficking in methamphetamine, a class B felony, and possession of drug paraphernalia, a class A misdemeanor. Brawner has previously been convicted of similar offenses in Mercer Boyle and Bullitt counties, according to the indictment. His bail was set at $20,000 with drug-related conditions.
Cpl. Chase Hale (Harrodsburg Police Department) testified. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Sayre Edges Lady Bulldogs In Basketball Season Opener
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenBurgin senior Jemma Jenkins
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Burgin senior Jemma Jenkins passed the ball around the press during the Lady Bulldogs' loss to Sayre on Monday, Dec. 2.
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs basketball team began their season in dramatic fashion on Monday, Dec. 2, when the Sayre Lady Spartans traveled to Jack Coleman Sr. Gymnasium.
Burgin led 9-8 midway through the first quarter, but turnover trouble gave Sayre an opportunity to take the lead, and forced an early timeout from Bulldog Coach Keith Monson. Gabby Thompson blocked a Sayre 3-pointer and drew a foul in transition. The senior kept Burgin within one-point after making four shots at the charity stripe in the final minute of the first quarter.
Sayre is a nightmare matchup for this year's Burgin team. Rebounding was a weakness leading into the season, and it showed early in the game. Sayre had a substantial length advantage over the Lady Bulldogs, and Burgin was outrebounded heavily in the first quarter; combined with their six first quarter turnovers, it was impressive Burgin was still within one-point, and is a testament to their shooting ability.
The second quarter was a completely different story. Juniors Haley Hurst and Ashton Lester started fighting for rebounds and the offensive end was taking care of itself. Thompson played a perfect pass below to Hurst, who spun toward the basket and laid it in off of the glass. Lester grabbed the next missed Sayre shot and threw it forward to Thompson for an easy basket. Freshman Bristol Keith fought for a tie-up, and forced a turnover on the following possession. Lester took advantage and kissed a floater off of the glass to give Burgin a six-point lead. One possession later, Lester connected with Hurst under the basket and she made a great move before finishing off of the glass. Burgin led by eight as both teams went into the locker room. title: Lady Titans struggle with Western Hills' defense
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County Lady Titans (1-2) won their first 12th Region game of the season on Thursday, Dec. 5, when they took down Somerset 63-42…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Lady Titans (1-2) won their first 12th Region game of the season on Thursday, Dec. 5, when they took down Somerset 63-42 behind 22 points and 11 rebounds from sophomore star forward Izzie Carlton. Mercer hit the road again one day later, with the Lady Wolverines of Western Hills (2-1) waiting on the other side.
Izzie Carlton went up strong for two of her 20 points during the Lady Titans 59-47 loss to Western Hills. Carlton also led the team in rebounds (6). (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren)
Freshman forward Malia Campbell gave the Lady Titans trouble in the post early on, but Mercer stayed on top for most of the first quarter. The game developed quickly and it became scrappy. Mercer made five foul shots, but Western Hills closed the opening quarter on an 8-0 run.
The Lady Wolverines made two 3-pointers early in the second, but Annie Releford fought for an offensive rebound and went back up to tie the game at 19. Soon after, Western Hills started to press higher up the court. The Lady Titans struggled with the press, and several turnovers allowed Western Hills to build a double-digit lead. Mercer too often left their teammates alone in the back-court which made trapping far too easy.
'Western Hills has a nice team but we had a really bad stretch in the second quarter when we let the game get away from us. We had some really bad turnovers that led to easy baskets. Our youth showed at that point, and we panicked,' said Head Basketball Coach Chris Souder.
After two quarters, the Lady Titans trailed 34-19.
Eighth grader Cardin Sickles fought hard for an offensive rebound and went straight back up for the first basket of the second half. Mercer's second basket came in identical fashion, but they couldn't slow down Western Hills offense. Freshman Olive Frisby played a brilliant pass to I. Carlton down low for an easy basket, but Mercer still trailed 42-25 with 3:49 remaining in the third. Sickles forced a turnover and I. Carlton found her way to the charity stripe for two of her 10 made free throws. Freshman guard Alexa Wade drained a 3-pointer one possession later, and Souder called a timeout. Mercer had built some momentum in the late stages of the third, but a freak accident forced Sickles to leave the court with a knee injury. Luckily for Sickles and t he Lady Titans, the injury was not severe, and she won't miss any significant time with the team according to Souder. title: Harlan Bears Break Mercer's Momentum For The Win
description: The Mercer County Senior High Titans boys basketball team (8-4) traveled to South Laurel High on Friday, Jan. 3, for the Raymond Reed Classic. The Titans faced their toughest test yet this season when…
content:
The Mercer County Senior High Titans boys basketball team (8-4) traveled to South Laurel High on Friday, Jan. 3, for the Raymond Reed Classic. The Titans faced their toughest test yet this season when they faced off against the Harlan County Bears (10-4), one of the favorites of the 13th region, and last season's KHSAA State Tournament runners-up. Mercer led going into the second quarter, but while their 3-point shots fell flat, Harlan was hot from behind the arc, and eventually claimed a 70-58 victory.
Senior Trevor Ellis went in for the shot in Mercer's loss to Harlan County on Friday, Jan. 5, in the Raymond Reed Classic in Laurel County. (Image: The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis).
Harlan hit 11 three-point shots during the game and two in the opening minutes to take a six-point lead. Mercer fought back by using Ellis but not by crashing the basket. When Ellis received the pass, and the defenders doubled and tripled down on him, he would hit the guards, cutting through the lane or back out to the key for the uncontested shot. Juniors Jackson Doughty and Kaleb Murray hit 3-point shots off the play, and Doughty added another jumper to tie it up, 8-8, with 3:30 left in the quarter.
Mercer allowed Harlan only one more 3-point shot during the quarter, and senior Hagan Preston found a way to work through the Bears' traffic to drive to the basket. Mercer led 19-13, until Harlan hit a long 3-point shot at the buzzer to make the score 19-16.
Ellis opened the second quarter with a trey, but Harlan answered back with a 3-point shot. Ellis hit a jumper to give the Titans a three-point lead, 24-21. The Bears took over the boards and snagged both offensive and defensive rebounds and went on a nine-point scoring run.
Preston was able to move through the Bears' defense once again for a basket, and good ball movement opened the lane for Murray on a drive to cut the lead to three points, 31-28. However, each time Mercer started to make headway, Harlan would hit a couple of long-range shots to shut down Mercer's momentum. This was the case again, at the end of the second quarter, when the Bears hit another 3-point shot at the buzzer, and took a 39-30 lead into the locker room. title: Kaelin Drakeford Lands In Chattanooga
description: Former Mercer County Titan standout football player Kaelin Drakeford entered the NCAA Transfer Portal shortly after the Eastern Illinois Panthers' season-ending loss to Tennessee Tech. Drakeford was a…
content:
Former Mercer County Titan standout football player Kaelin Drakeford entered the NCAA Transfer Portal shortly after the Eastern Illinois Panthers' season-ending loss to Tennessee Tech.
Drakeford was a key piece in the Panther's defensive setup from the moment he stepped on campus and started all six games during his freshman season. Drakeford featured in 37 more games for the Panthers from 2021-2024, tallying 180 career tackles, 8.5 tackles for a loss, 13 passes defended, four forced fumbles, and two interceptions. Drakeford is most proud to have achieved the 2,000-play milestone.
'There were a ton of ups and downs through my career, but just being out there each season through the tough times, whether it was injuries or losing streaks, I am proud that I was still out there battling with my teammates,' said Drakeford.
Drakeford began college amid the COVID pandemic and was redshirted in 2022 due to an injury in the season opener. He thoroughly enjoyed his time in Charleston, but as most of his classmates had graduated from the program, Drakeford felt it best to find a new home in his sixth and final season of Division-I football.
'Many of the guys I came in with were done after this past season. Coming off a good individual year, I just felt like this would be a good time to try and find a good spot and experience for my last year,' said Drakeford.
Kaelin Drakeford was ecstatic after making an important tackle late in a 16-13 overtime win over Charleston Southern on senior day. (Image: The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren.)
Drakeford finished this past season with a career-high 63 tackles and added a sack, two forced fumbles and an interception. The veteran defensive back was receiving offers as soon as he entered the portal, including from the University of Akron, where Drakeford's younger brother Ashton received his first Division-I offer last spring. Within the week, Drakeford received another enticing offer from the University of Maine. He seriously considered the Black Bears for several weeks until the University of Tennessee-Chattanooga reached out and offered a scholarship the day after Christmas.
'[I] really liked Maine a lot; it just was going to be more complicated,' said Drakeford. Apart from Chatt's proximity to home and the equator, Drakeford was pleased with the city, the coaching staff's charisma and their dedication to winning.
Drakeford committed to the Mocs officially on Saturday, Jan. 4. The Mocs finished the 2024 season with a 7-5 overall record and barely missed out on a spot in the FCS playoffs due to two conference losses against Western Carolina and Samford late in the season. In 2025, the Mocs will face Memphis in week one. The Tigers went 11-2 this past season. A week later, the Mocs will face a program no one is more familiar with than Drakeford. He and the Panthers have faced Tennessee Tech four times in the last four seasons. The Mocs conference schedule picks up as the season goes along, and Chatt faces its three most formidable conference opponents, Samford, Western Carolina and Mercer, over four weeks from Oct. 25 through Nov. 15. The former two-time All-State selection at safety for the Mercer County Titans is expecting to face perhaps his most difficult challenge in his final year of collegiate football.
'I'm very excited. It's a refreshing feeling to play a new schedule against new opponents. I'm also excited to see how my game evolves,' said Drakeford.
The Southern Conference has not announced full broadcasting schedules for the 2025 season, but all nine UTC home games will air on ESPN+, if not selected for national or regional broadcast. title: Mercer County Firefighter Saves Child From Ice
description: Broken ice on Holma Millpond at Holma säteri, Lysekil Municipality, Sweden. Image: W.carter via Wikimedia Commons.
content:
Broken ice on Holma Millpond at Holma säteri, Lysekil Municipality, Sweden. Image: W.carter via Wikimedia Commons.
Quick thinking by a local firefighter helped save one child from the ice last week.
At approximately 10:20 a.m. on Friday, Jan. 17, the Mercer County Fire Protection District received a call. According to WKYT, two-year-old Thaddeus Baer was stuck on ice in the middle of a local pond after sledding too far.
Dressed in his regular clothes, Firefighter Justin Railey crawled to the middle of the pond to reach the child.
'As soon as I stepped out, I immediately fell through,' Railey told WKYT. On his belly, the firefighter crawled out to the child and used an oar to pull him out.
'It was the bravest thing that I've ever seen in my 41 year career,' Mercer County Fire Chief Glen Phillips told WKYT.
Baer was back home with mom and ready for the ice to melt, according to WKYT.
Pond ice rescues are fairly rare in Kentucky. With temperatures plunging below freezing, there have been several of them across the Commonwealth. In Florence, a woman had to be rescued on Jan. 13 after falling through a frozen lake while trying to get her dogs off the ice, WKYT reported.
Chief Phillips at the Mercer County Fire Protection District told WKYT it was important to stay calm and to call for help if you find yourself in a similar situation.
Temperatures are expected to finally rise above freezing later this week, according to Weather.com. But that means iced over waterways can become even more dangerous until they completely thaw. Experts say no ice is to be considered 100 percent safe, but any ice that's less than four inches in thickness should be steered clear of. Here are some tips on keeping yourself safe on the ice courtesy of popsci.com.
• Don't go onto the ice alone.
• Remain calm if you fall through.
• Don't undress. You won't be able to swim any better without your coat and pants. You'll need to keep your winter clothing on for insulation. The air trapped inside your clothing can also help you stay afloat.
• Don't try a new route back to shore. You'll be safer by retracing your solid path across the ice. If you try a new route, you could fall through another thin spot on your way back to shore.
• Consider wearing a personal flotation device (PFD) under your coat when you walk out onto the ice. The main exception to this would be wearing a PFD while driving across ice in a vehicle. The extra bulk could prevent you from crawling out through a window to escape a sinking vehicle.
• Control your breathing. The shock of the cold water will often cause people to gasp, taking water into the lungs. The cold water can also lead to hyperventilation, which increases your chances of drowning.
• Stay horizontal to get away from the thin ice. Once you're out, stay horizontal to keep your weight dispersed on the ice. You could crawl on your belly, but a faster way to move is by rolling across the ice. Do this until you are on thick ice again and you feel certain that you can stand.
• Warm up immediately. Once the victim is out of the freezing water, monitor them for shock and seek professional medical care to get their body temperature back to normal. If it's not possible to reach definitive medical care, get the victim into dry clothing. Place warm water bottles throughout the clothing, especially under armpits, and in the groin and neck areas. title: Black History Presentation At Library And Gala On Feb. 8
description: Image: Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society (Composite image). Two events are coming up to celebrate Black History Month.
content:
Image: Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society (Composite image).
Two events are coming up to celebrate Black History Month.
Almetra Taylor
On Saturday, Feb. 8, Almetra Taylor of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society will present 'A Teacher's Story: The Life And Times of Ms. Clara B. Clelland' at the Mercer County Public Library (109 West Lexington Street) starting at 1 p.m. The program is free and open to the public.
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society will also host the Black History Gala on Saturday, Feb. 8, at the Stable at the Mercer County Fairgrounds (560 Linden Avenue). The Black History Gala starts at 6 p.m. with a dinner catered by Jerrica Spencer. Lucian Yates III will be the keynote speaker. There will also be entertainment, including light jazz during dinner and music after Yates' speech by DJ Michael Hughes. Tickets are $35 for couples, $20 for singles and $10 for 12 and under. The theme of the night is glancing back at our past and focusing on a positive future.
'We've been planning this for months,' said Phil Yates of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society. 'It will be a real night out.'
Lucian Yates III
The featured speaker is Lucian Yates III, Phil Yates' brother, who graduated from Harrodsburg High School before earning his bachelor's degree in history and political science and master's degree in history and education from Morehead State University. He earned his doctorate in curriculum, instruction and supervision from Ohio University. In his career, he has served as a professor at Prairie View A&M University, as professor and dean of graduate studies and research at Tennessee State University and as provost and vice president for academic affairs at Kentucky State University. Yates currently serves as the endowed chair and distinguished professor of education at Simmons College of Kentucky in Louisville.
The mission of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County African American Historical Society is to illuminate the origins of Harrodsburg, which celebrated its 250th anniversary last year. The society was begun with a $10,000 grant from the Kentucky Historical Society.
'It made it all possible,' Phil Yates said.

title: Sparrow, Pioneers preparing for postseason play
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com On Saturday, Nov. 23, the Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg men's basketball team picked up a position boosting second win over top-5 ranked…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
On Saturday, Nov. 23, the Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg men's basketball team picked up a position boosting second win over top-5 ranked NCCAA Division-I standout Ohio Christian University. At the time, the Pioneers were 6-1, coming off of their third win against a top 10 NCCAA opponent and excited about their potential for the rest of the season. Later that night, the campus and community were rocked with the news of a dangerous car accident that stalled the Pioneers return to Harrodsburg.
The team van was heading through a green light off Ohio State Route 56 when another vehicle entered the intersection unexpectedly. Both Head Coach Austin Sparrow and senior point guard Nakyir Joyce were taken to a local hospital with injuries. Sparrow was trapped in the vehicle for over an hour while first responders worked to free his leg. Luckily, Joyce was diagnosed with only a minor concussion. Sparrow on the other hand, suffered three fractures in his left femur. Soon after the accident, the University released a statement via Facebook announcing that both Sparrow and Joyce had received non life threatening injuries.
Today, both player and coach have returned to the court, but the road to recovery has been arduous. Sparrow's injuries required two surgeries, four screws and a metal rod, but the inability to walk didn't slow Sparrow down, and he attended practices in a rolling chair.
'Traveling to games that were 3 and 4 hours away has been difficult as well, but my coaching staff and players have done a great job in helping me make it work,' Sparrow said.
Joyce missed only one game, and made his return in a scrimmage with EKU on Friday, Dec. 6. Remarkably, the injury kept Sparrow off his feet for less than a month. After three weeks, Sparrow was able to walk again, and he is steadily working back to full mobility.
'[I] definitely appreciate being able to walk more now than ever,' said Sparrow, '[I] definitely appreciate the first responders and staff at Grant Medical Center, the nurses and doctors were great. The first responders who helped me while I was trapped in the car for an hour and half (while my leg was pinched) did a fantastic job of taking care of me and all of our players,' added Sparrow.
The wreck happened right as the Pioneers entered a crucial part of their season, with an EKU scrimmage, two NCCAA top-5 matchups and a rematch with Alice Lloyd College directly ahead. Sparrow took some inspiration from former players during his recovery.
'Well… I've had six players in six seasons tear their ACLs, and each time I've thought to myself, these guys are the toughest individuals I know… Basketball gets taken away and your mobility gets taken away and you still find a way to show up and be supportive for your teammates and coaches. I just thought back to how awesome those guys were during their struggles and took some inspiration from them,' said Sparrow, who added that program legends Tyron and Tyrese Duncan, who each tore their ACL while a Pioneer, have reached out numerous times to check in on their former coach. Tyron Duncan and Tyrese Duncan have checked on me a lot over these past few weeks,' said Sparrow.
During the last two months, the Pioneers have lost three games by two points or less; including losses to number three ranked Miami University-Hamilton and number two ranked Champion Christian College by a combined three points. More recently, CUH dropped a regional matchup with Simmons College, 68-55. In the last month of the season, the Pioneers will face two Mideast Region matchups with Welch College and no. 9 ranked Boyce College.
The Pioneers have proved time and time again they can compete with the best teams the NCCAA has to offer, and they've led at some point in each of their eight losses this season. Sparrow knows his team is capable of making another run this postseason if they can learn how to execute better in the game's final moments.
'We just have to finish games and learn to execute down the stretch of games. Our main focus is being ready to put our best performances of the season out on the court at the regional tournament hosted here in Harrodsburg,' said Sparrow.
The NCCAA D-II Mideast Regional tournament will be held at the CU-Harrodsburg Athletic Complex, beginning on Friday, Feb. 28. The Pioneers will be back in action in Harrodsburg on Saturday, Feb. 8, when they face Welch College for the second time this season.
