title: Mercer EMS Will Terminate Service April 27; County Reassures Public Ambulance Service Will Continue
description: File image. Mercer County Emergency Medical Services is still operating and providing ambulance service. The privately owned service will still be answering calls until noon on Saturday, April 27,…
content:
File image.
File image. Mercer County Emergency Medical Services is still operating and providing ambulance service. The privately owned service will still be answering calls until noon on Saturday, April 27, according to a statement released on Facebook and employees at Mercer EMS.
In their statement, Raintree Health, which operates Mercer EMS, said they had 'dramatically increased overall coverage, hiring, and staff wages to make them more competitive with surrounding markets.'
They said the decision to terminate services was made 'after discussions with Mercer County about the staffing levels and low wages and Mercer County's relatively small stipend contribution compared to other surrounding counties.'
County officials said local residents will still be able to rely on ambulance service after Mercer EMS terminates service.
'The Mercer County Fiscal Court, the City of Harrodsburg and the City of Burgin are committed to ensuring the best quality emergency services are provided to citizens and those visiting our community,' officials said in a Facebook post.
'We have a plan of action to make sure there is no interruption of Ambulance Services within our county. We have been working with surrounding agencies, which have been providing mutual aid services for months. We are working diligently on new provider agreements. We are collaborating with the Office of Inspector General and Kentucky Board of Medical Services to ensure a smooth transition between service providers in our community. Please rest assured that you will have around the clock coverage within our community.'
'We have a plan of action to make sure there is no interruption of Ambulance Services within our county. We have been working with surrounding agencies, which have been providing mutual aid services for months. We are working diligently on new provider agreements. We are collaborating with the Office of Inspector General and Kentucky Board of Medical Services to ensure a smooth transition between service providers in our community. Please rest assured that you will have around the clock coverage within our community.' In a comment on the original Facebook post, the Mercer County Fiscal Court said, 'EMS will be responding from within our county/stationed within our fire departments—not coming from outside of county. More details to come soon.'
Mercer County and the City of Harrodsburg pay 47.5 percent of the bill for Mercer County EMS while Burgin pays five percent. The dispute between the county and Mercer EMS predate the ambulance service's purchase by Raintree Health.
In June of last year, Roxann Parks, deputy director at Mercer County EMS, asked the county to increase their yearly contribution to $200,000. Park they had been forced to cut back on some services—such as bringing Mercer County patients back home from Danville—because of staffing shortages. Parks said they were unable to run two ambulances because of lack of staffing.
Mercer County EMS made 2,960 runs in 2022, averaging eight runs per day.
Park said Mercer County EMS also faced write-offs because of medical insurance billing and nonbillable calls—including falls and car wrecks—where the victim declined ambulance transport.
Ultimately, the fiscal court opted to renew the contract with Mercer EMs at $150,000 a year, the same as the year before.
In October, a former of Mercer EMS employee complained about the company to both the Harrodsburg City Commission and to the Mercer County Fiscal Court.
'Something's got to be changed,' said Paul Gray, who formerly worked for Mercer EMS, which officially changed hands at the beginning of October. 'There are a number of issues.'
Gray, who was born and raised in Mercer County but no longer lives in Mercer County, said local hospitals were irate at the situation at Mercer EMS, which he said was one of the only privately owned EMS providers in the state. Gray said the city or county could take over 911 operations. However, at that time, both city and county officials said it was not as simple as pushing a switch.
Paul Parks, who owned Mercer County EMS for 33 years, sold the company to Patrick Meko, who took over at the beginning of October.
At that time, Gray said he had no problem with the past administration or with the new owner, but Gray objected to the continued presence of one employee who remains with Mercer County EMS after the sale.
'You've got to change things,' Gray said. 'If you get rid of one person who's been leading the pack, you need to get rid of the other person who's been leading the pack.'
At the time, officials said Meko, the owner of Raintree Health, which operates Mercer EMS, has been meeting with all the stakeholders.
'I see him trying to get things in place to make a change,' Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said. Steele noted this was the first EMS company Meko has run, although he was in health care before purchasing Mercer EMS. 'That gives me a lot of hope.'
However, in January 2024, the fiscal court voted to file an application for a certificate of need with the Kentucky Office of the Inspector General for ground ambulance service, including the $1,000 application fee. County officials said there had been service outages.
'We've had some complaints related to EMS services,' Judge Steele said. 'We've recognized that we've had a lapse in service over many days in February.'
Steele also said the county was not currently under contract with Mercer EMS.
'We're still over two months in advancement on EMS services,' Steele said. She said the county would not continue financial contributions until the company showed they could provide service.
'We have to have quality ambulance care in Mercer County,' the judge said. 'What's going on right now is not working.'
The judge said applying for a certificate of need was the first step in giving the county a choice in ambulance service. Currently, the certificate of need is held by Mercer EMS, she said.
'We can't contract with anyone else because we don't have a certificate,' said Steele.
The certificate allows the county to make a decision on whether to proceed with another ambulance service, she said.
In their Facebook statement, Raintree Health, said they had 'worked tirelessly to find a resolution with Mercer County local government officials with very little reciprocated interest.'
Raintree also noted that, in Kentucky and other states, EMS services are considered non-essential.
'It is critical moving forward that citizens continue to write to their state legislature representatives to get these policies changed,' Raintree said. 'The challenges continue to mount for EMS services with high operating costs and low insurance reimbursement rates. Generally, it is not feasible for private ambulance services to operate without governmental assistance or stipends.'
Raintree Health intends to provide e1nergency coverage until Saturday, April 27, at noon.
On Facebook, the county reassured the public. 'Please rest assured that you will have around the clock coverage within our community,' they said.

title: County Enters Agreement With New Ambulance Service Provider
description: File image. The Mercer County Fiscal Court has entered into a new agreement with AmeriPro Health to provide local ambulance service. AmeriPro will receive $62,917 a month to provide two ambulances…
content:
File image.
File image. The Mercer County Fiscal Court has entered into a new agreement with AmeriPro Health to provide local ambulance service. AmeriPro will receive $62,917 a month to provide two ambulances staffed with a paramedic and EMT or advanced EMT.
At a special-called meeting on Friday, April 19, the magistrates voted unanimously to enter the three year agreement with AmeriPro, which will go into effect when the previous provider, Raintree Health—which was operating as Mercer EMS—closes. In a Facebook post, Raintree announced they would cease service at noon on Saturday, April 27.
According to Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, the county filed to receive a certificate of need—which would allow the county to either negotiate with a new ambulance service provider or to start providing ambulance service themselves—on Jan. 30.
According to Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, the county filed to receive a certificate of need—which would allow the county to either negotiate with a new ambulance service provider or to start providing ambulance service themselves—on Jan. 30. 'We've been working on this for months,' Steele said.
She said the county began to explore other options due to concerns with the current status of the provider, delays in coverage and relying on other agencies to provide service. The judge said an investigation is still ongoing at the state inspector general's office, with the earliest possible hearing in August.
Normally, obtaining a certificate of need can take up to eight months, Steele said, and the final hearing for that is scheduled for June. However, Steele said the county has applied for emergency hardship licensure under state law, and they have received notice that the county will get the certificate of need when Raintree closes.
The fiscal court also voted unanimously to enter into an agreement with AmeriPro Health. In a press release, AmeriPro calls itself 'a leading provider of patient logistics and last-mile healthcare delivery services.' The company began in the Metro Atlanta area in 2018 with 10 ambulances and has grown to have more than 800 employees with operations across six states, including Indiana and Kentucky.
Joe Rose, director of operations at AmeriPro Health, was at Friday's meeting.
'We're excited to be working with Mercer County,' Rose said. 'We've already started ramping up operations on our end.' Rose said AmeriPro can begin as soon as the county receives the certificate of need from the state.
The current plan is for AmeriPro to operate from an open bay at the Harrodsburg Fire Department. Steele said the long term plan is to house operations within the community.
'We will work out those details when they arrive,' Steele said.
At Friday's meeting, Steele thanked Boyle and Anderson counties for providing assistance. She said Boyle County will station two trucks locally in Mercer for 24 hours during the transition.
'We are 100 percent covered in our community,' Steele said.

title: ‘Anastasia' Takes The Stage At Mercer County Senior High School
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/April EllisKylie Mobley, center, plays Anya in 'Anastasia' which will hit the Mercer County Senior High Stage this weekend.
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Kylie Mobley, center, plays Anya in 'Anastasia' which will hit the Mercer County Senior High Stage this weekend.
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Kylie Mobley, center, plays Anya in 'Anastasia' which will hit the Mercer County Senior High Stage this weekend. April Ellis
Herald Staff
April Ellis
Herald Staff For many children, princess movies like 'Beauty and the Beast' and 'The Little Mermaid' were the best entertainment. Joyful songs, beautiful dresses and magical kingdoms in faraway lands never failed to enchant.
However, little kids aren't the only ones who enjoy a good princess story. The 1997 movie 'Anastasia' has entertained children and adults with its engaging plot and classic songs for years and, in 2017, inspired a musical adaptation on Broadway, which will now grace the stages at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road). 'Anastasia' runs this weekend with shows on Friday, April 26 at 7 p.m., Saturday, April 27 at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. and Sunday at 2 p.m.
'Anastasia' is a magical princess story that appeals to audiences of all ages. The elegant music, engaging characters, and beautiful costumes make it feel like the viewers are experiencing a fairy tale on stage right before their eyes.
It follows the legend of the Russian princess, Anastasia, whose family was killed by communist revolutionaries in 1918 when she was still young. In the story, Anastasia escaped her family's murder but hit her head while running away, causing her to lose all her memories of being a princess.
Grown up, she goes by Anya. Two clever con men, Dmitry and Vlad, set out on a quest, looking for a girl willing to pretend to be the lost princess. When they see Anya, they notice her resemblance to Anastasia and believe they can convince her to take the role. They offer to take her to Paris to meet her grandmother, where they would receive a substantial reward for recovering a long-lost royal family member.
T he Harrodsburg Herald/ April Ellis
Carter Wilson and Bray­don Branham play conmen Dmitry and Vlad Popov in'Anastasia' at Mercer County Senior High School.
T he Harrodsburg Herald/ April Ellis
Carter Wilson and Bray­don Branham play conmen Dmitry and Vlad Popov in'Anastasia' at Mercer County Senior High School. Along the way, Anya must learn how to be a princess while avoiding Russia's new leader, who wants to prevent any kind of royalty from coming back into power. Through the journey, Anya slowly starts to regain her memory on her quest to discover that she is Princess Anastasia.
Emilee Givens will direct Mercer's production. The last several productions have been musicals, in part because of the talent available to Givens.
Performances will be held on Friday, April 26, at 7 p.m., Saturday, April 27, at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m., and Sunday at 2 p.m. Tickets can be purchased at the door with cash or credit card or online at https://gofan.co/app/school/KY2789.

content:

Photo Submitted
AmeriPro has been hired to provide ambulance service in Mercer County. The company is accepting applications for staff at their website. Last week, the Mercer County Fiscal Court terminated its agreement with Mercer County Emergency Medical Service and entered into a new agreement with AmeriPro Health to provide ambulance service. The new ambulance provider is looking to add staff and is accepting application at their website.
AmeriPro will receive $62,917 a month to provide ambulance service, including two ambulances staffed with a paramedic and an EMT or advanced EMT. At a special-called meeting on Friday, April 19, the magistrates voted unanimously to enter the three year agreement with AmeriPro, which will go into effect when the previous provider, Raintree Health—which was operating as Mercer EMS—closes. In a Facebook post, Raintree announced they would cease service at noon on Saturday, April 27.
According to Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, the county filed to receive a certificate of need—which would allow the county to either negotiate with a new ambulance service provider or to start providing ambulance service themselves—on Jan. 30.
'We've been working on this for months,' Steele said.
She said the county began to explore other options due to concerns with the current status of the provider, delays in coverage and relying on other agencies to provide service. The judge said an investigation is still ongoing at the state inspector general's office, with the earliest possible hearing in August. Normally, obtaining a certificate of need can take up to eight months, Steele said, and the final hearing for that is scheduled for June.
However, Steele said the county has applied for emergency hardship licensure under state law, and they have received notice that the county will get the certificate of need when Raintree closes.
The fiscal court also voted unanimously to enter into an agreement with AmeriPro Health. In a press release, AmeriPro calls itself 'a leading provider of patient logistics and last-mile healthcare delivery services.' The company began in the Metro Atlanta area in 2018 with 10 ambulances and has grown to have more than 800 employees with operations across six states, including Indiana and Kentucky.
Joe Rose, the director of operations at AmeriPro Health, was at Friday's meeting. 'We're excited to be working with Mercer County,' Rose said. 'We've already started ramping up operations on our end.' Rose said AmeriPro can begin as soon as the county receives the certificate of need from the state.
Rose told WLEX that AmeriPro in Mercer County is hiring EMTs or paramedics. Anyone interested can visit ameriprohealth.com/ems-and-medical-transportation-careers for an application. The current plan is for AmeriPro to operate from an open bay at the Harrodsburg Fire Department.
Steele said the long term plan is to house operations within the community.
'We will work out those details when they arrive,' Steele said.
At Friday's meeting, Steele thanked Boyle and Anderson counties for providing assistance. She said Boyle County will station two trucks locally in Mercer for 24 hours during the transition.
'We are 100 percent covered in our community,' Steele said.
While the service territory includes Burgin and Harrodsburg, the agreement is with the fiscal court. Previously, Mercer County and the City of Harrodsburg paid 47.5 percent of the bill, while Burgin paid five percent. Steele said the City of Harrodsburg is unable to enter into the agreement at present.
Harrodsburg Mayor Bob Williams and Burgin Mayor Joe Monroe were both at the special-called meeting Friday.
'We'll be in talks over the next week or so to determine our role in this other than the space we're providing,' Williams said.
'We're going to continue our obligation as we have been and go forward with it,' Monroe said.
'Raintree Health's staff and management have worked extremely hard for the citizens of Mercer County, putting in countless hours to provide the best quality of care possible,' the ambulance provider said in a Facebook statement. 'We would like to sincerely thank the community for allowing our dedicated staff the opportunity to serve and take care of your needs.'

title: Mercer Schools Hires Healthy Kids Clinic To Provide Medical Services
description: File image. The Mercer County Board of Education voted last week to hire Cumberland Family Medical Center—operating as the Healthy Kids Clinic—to operate a school based satellite clinic serving…
content:
File image.
File image. The Mercer County Board of Education voted last week to hire Cumberland Family Medical Center—operating as the Healthy Kids Clinic—to operate a school based satellite clinic serving approximately 2,700 Mercer students. While school officials say the contract will allow the district to save a minimum of $170,000 every year with the potential to save $260,000 in the future, some local mental and dental health care providers expressed doubts about the company's ability to provide quality care. After a debate, the board proceeded with the contract, but removed mental and dental health care.
Cumberland already operates on-site health clinics in more than 20 counties, including Anderson, Boyle, Lincoln, Washington and Woodford. They offer increased services, including physical examinations, care and treatment of illnesses and injuries and the ability to prescribe and administer medications which are beyond the scope of practice of a registered nurse. According to the agreement, the clinics also have the capability to, upon request, provide training and supervision of district staff for the provision of health services to students and serve as a source of health care information to students and staff.
Some local providers objected to Cumberland offering dental services such as preventative and restorative oral health care, including but not limited to screening, cleaning, comprehensive exams, fluoride treatment, x-rays and the application of sealants. Cumberland also offers preventative oral health education and information to preschool through twelfth grade with parental permission.
They also objected to Cumberland offering behavioral health services in the form of treatment of depression and/or anxiety, adjustment difficulties, stress induced problems, exposure to trauma,interpersonal grief and loss, separation anxiety, other disorders of infancy, childhood or adolescence.
Dr. Renee Kilty, who practices at Harrodsburg Kids Dentistry, said she had to provide repairs to children who received dental treatment at school. few weeks ago.
Dr. Jaimie Rector, also of Harrodsburg Kids Dentistry, said she was worried about the continuity of care.
'I don't know if that can be done with the Healthy Kids Program,' Rector said.
She said she receives calls all the time from parents of children who were treated on a mobile unit without parents' consent.
'Parents don't understand what's going on,' Rector said. 'It's very good to have parents involved.'
School officials noted the mental and dental services were optional, although Superintendent Jason Booher noted the school district already contracted with a mobile clinic to provide dental services, including screening, which are required under state law before a child can be enrolled in a public school.
'We want parents to have a choice,' Booher said. 'Parents have a choice in schools too.' Booher noted that not having staff in school is a disadvantage when compared to other schools. He also said some people don't have the resources, including transportation, time and money, to make sure their children receive medical treatment.
'It is nice to have it,' Booher said.
The superintendent said being able to offer services at the schools would help minimize lost instructional time. Booher said parents who take kids out for medical treatment rarely bring them back.
'It's a great thing for the taxpayers of Mercer County,' Booher said.
Board members said their main concern was the medical service. Chairman Randy Phillips said they could revisit the decision later and add mental and dental health services.
'Our greatest need is the nurse practitioner,' Phillips said. He said there are options for the other services.
Finance Officer Amber Minor said she received a four page document to consent to service received by her children.
'We can say we only want cleanings and screenings to happen,' Minor said. 'Unfortunately, we know there are parents who are not getting their kids to screenings or cleanings at all.'
She said the district hoped to work with Healthy Kids and local providers.
'If we're already doing the same thing with a company from Jessamine County,' Booher mused, 'Why not take a free one?'
'Certainly, the intent is not to take anything from our local providers,' said board member Amy Hart. 'We do have that need within the system. I cannot go against my conscience and potentially limit the services they get.'
'We've never heard any concern from local providers before,' Phillips said, referring to services the district already offered.
'What is the solution for children who cannot attend school because they cannot get their teeth screened?' Hart asked.
'I've seen poor quality work, and I've cleaned up the messes,' Dr. Kilty said.
'I've got a dog home,' joked board member Billy G. Montgomery after an extensive debate. 'My view on it right now is we need to get this solved for tonight at least.'
Montgomery moved to proceed with the contract, removing items for mental and dental health. Board member Cliff Prewitt seconded. The motion passed unanimously.

title: Mercer Boys Fall In Close Call With Woodford
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenCarter Devine readied himself for a big swing dur­ing Mercer County's ga
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Carter Devine readied himself for a big swing dur­ing Mercer County's game with West Jessamine on Thursday, May 19.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Carter Devine readied himself for a big swing dur­ing Mercer County's game with West Jessamine on Thursday, May 19. The Mercer County Titans baseball team (15-17) traveled to Versailles on Saturday, May 11, to face the Woodford County Yellow Jackets for the second time this season. The Titans were stung in the second game of the season when Woodford rolled to an 18-3 win in Harrodsburg, but they displayed just how much they've improved throughout the season last Saturday.
Andrew Tatum got off the bus ready to dominate, and after singling on the opening at bat, the junior eventually took advantage of a ground out from Carter Devine, speeding around third base and scoring the Titans opening run. Next, Will Johnson grounded out to second base, giving Ayden Stephens plenty of time to score the second run. Both teams took advantage of some sloppy infield play in the first inning. Two errors and two walks allowed Woodford to take a 3-2 lead at the end of one inning.
Brayden Campbell was hit by a pitch, and sophomore Brayden McGuffy was subbed on to take his place. Eventually, Tatum singled to the Yellow Jacket right fielder, who struggled to control it and gave McGuffey and Evann White time to score from third and second, giving Mercer a 4-3 lead.
The Titans errored three times in the bottom of the second, allowing Woodford to open up a 6-4 lead. The lead off hitter for the Yellow Jackets was walked, and the second batter followed before Nolan Asher singled, loading the bases. Woodford managed two more singles before the Titans could grab the third out and bring in three more runs to make the score 9-4.
Jackson Doughty was subbed onto the mound and struck out the first batter he faced. The sophomore kept the Yellow Jackets at bay for three innings until the Titans offense sprung to life in the top of the sixth.

title: Fiscal Court Approves $14 Million County Budget
description: File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. The Mercer County Fiscal Court gave first reading to a budget of more than $41 million for the 2025 fiscal year. At…
content:
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. The Mercer County Fiscal Court gave first reading to a budget of more than $41 million for the 2025 fiscal year.
At their regular meeting on Tuesday, May 14, Judge-Executive Sarah Steele called it a significant increase in the budget. The county's budget was $22 million in 2023.
At their regular meeting on Tuesday, May 14, Judge-Executive Sarah Steele called it a significant increase in the budget. The county's budget was $22 million in 2023. 'We have a lot of projects coming,' Steele said.
The budget includes $12 million in reserves and $29 million in allocations, with $17 million coming from grants and state funding and $12 million in general expenses.
'That is huge,' Steele said. She said having so much in reserves is 'a good thing for a budget.'
'If turmoil happens, we can still operate for over a year,' Steele said.
The budget also includes a $161,000 increase in salary for payroll, retirement and insurance. The county is also adding another half-time position for animal control.
Magistrate Jackie Claycomb moved to approve the budget, seconded by Magistrate Dennis Holiday. The motion passed unanimously. The budget gets submitted to the state before the fiscal court gives it second reading.
The fiscal court also gave first reading to the animal control ordinance.
'This has been a long journey, said Steele, noting county officials had been working on it for over the last six to eight months. She said they'd met monthly, reviewed ordinances from other areas and met with local stakeholders. The public can review the ordinance when the fiscal court gives it second reading at their next meeting on Tuesday, May 28.
They also approved updates to the animal control center policies and procedures manual.

title: District Breaks Ground On New Home Of Mercer County Elementary School
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Mercer County Board of Education members Billy G. Montgomery, Amber Franceschi, Amy Hart, Cliff Prewitt, Board Chair Randy Phillips, Superintendent Jason Booher, Mercer County Elementary Principal Nekita Johnson, Director of Facilities Will Carlton and Finance Officer Amber Minor break ground on the site of the new Mercer County Elementary School. Last week, school officials broke ground on the new Mercer County Elementary School on Industry Road. On Tuesday, May 14, members of the Mercer County Board of Education and school and construction administrators gathered at the site to officially open construction. The total cost of the project is $33.6 million, which officials say is more than $2.5 million lower than initial estimates. While the submitted cost is $34.6 million, the district hopes to save approximately $1 million from the estimated costs because of interest earned on the funds during the construction. They also hope to receive a $1.5 million rebate for using geo-thermal heating. The estimated total construction cost for the project is $29.7 million, with a $1.4 million contingency, as well as $1.59 million in architect and engineering fees and other expenses. RossTarrant Architects is serving as architects on the project, while Structural Design Group Inc., CMTA Inc. and Joby Smith and Associates Inc. are serving as consultants. Trace Creek Construction is the construction manager On Tuesday, Booher said it would take approximately two years to complete construction on the new 77,182 square foot building, which will have the capacity to house 625 students from pre-school through second grade. Officials hope the 20-acre site will allow plenty of space for outdoor adventure and learning, with a courtyard classroom. If everything goes according to plan, students will begin attending classes at the new school in August 2026.

On Tuesday, Booher said it would take approximately two years to complete construction on the new 77,182 square foot building, which will have the capacity to house 625 students from pre-school through second grade. Officials hope the 20-acre site will allow plenty of space for outdoor adventure and learning, with a courtyard classroom.
If everything goes according to plan, students will begin attending classes at the new school in August 2026.

title: Mercer County Schools, First Responders Prepare For The Worst In Mock Bus Crash
description: Photo: Mercer County Emergency ManagementLocal first responders took part in a special training exercise organized by the Mercer County School District to prepare school staff and emergency
content:
Photo: Mercer County Emergency Management
Local first responders took part in a special training exercise organized by the Mercer County School District to prepare school staff and emergency personnel for a school bus disaster with injured students on Monday, May 20. The exercise included a flipped over school bus at the Mercer County Fairgrounds.
Photo: Mercer County Emergency Management
Local first responders took part in a special training exercise organized by the Mercer County School District to prepare school staff and emergency personnel for a school bus disaster with injured students on Monday, May 20. The exercise included a flipped over school bus at the Mercer County Fairgrounds. Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com Local first responders as well as officials and staff from Mercer County Schools prepared for a worst case scenario on Monday, May 20, when they participated in a first-of-its kind mock bus accident drill at the Mercer County Fairgrounds. The school district provided two buses for the training exercise, including a decommissioned bus that was flipped over and filled with smoke.
The drill was announced on the anniversary of one of the deadliest drunk-driving accidents in American history. On May 14, 1988, a driver crashed into a church bus, killing 27 people. Mercer Superintendent Jason Booher survived that crash.
Booher told Phil Pendleton of WKYT that drills like the one held Monday can help prevent future tragedies.
Booher told Phil Pendleton of WKYT that drills like the one held Monday can help prevent future tragedies. 'This is one of the positive things,' Booher told WKYT. 'That is the educational piece I call it. We are able to educate everyone to be more efficient if something like this occurs again.'
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, a former school employee, took part in a drill for drivers, in which they secured students in a smoke-filled bus.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, a former school employee, took part in a drill for drivers, in which they secured students in a smoke-filled bus. In one drill, first responders transported volunteers portraying victims from a smoke-filled bus to receive medical treatment. In another drill, bus drivers had to account for and secure students after an accident.
'Originally, this was just a training exercise for the school bus drivers,' said Mercer County Emergency Management Director Brad Cox. 'We were able to incorporate the first responders and do a county-wide drill. It lets us work together and gives us a chance to fortify our real-world capabilities.'
The drills were designed to be deliberately confusing, to closely reflect what could happen when something went wrong. Adding to the confusion, the Harrodsburg Fire Department had to leave the drill to respond to a real call.
'It was a unique training opportunity for our fire crew,' said Harrodsburg Fire Chief Michael Cox.
Photo: Mercer County Emergency Management
First responders transport a volunteer portraying an accident victim from a smoke-filled bus for medical treatment during an emergency drill held at Mercer County Fairgrounds on Monday, May 20.
Photo: Mercer County Emergency Management
First responders transport a volunteer portraying an accident victim from a smoke-filled bus for medical treatment during an emergency drill held at Mercer County Fairgrounds on Monday, May 20. Other agencies that participated included the Harrodsburg Police Department, AmeriPro EMS and the Mercer County Sheriff's Office.
'I enjoy doing these things,' said Dep. Wes Gaddis. ''It gives everybody an opportunity to see what their jobs are. It's a valuable training experience.'

title: Storm Kills One Mercer County Woman, Causes Extensive Damage
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com One woman is dead after a storm rampaged through Mercer County and Central Kentucky early Monday. On Monda
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com One woman is dead after a storm rampaged through Mercer County and Central Kentucky early Monday.
On Monday, May 27 at 12:53 a.m., first responders were dispatched to a residence for a tree on a house with a possible unresponsive person inside, Mercer County Emergency Management Director Brad Cox said. Units arrived on scene and transported one patient to the hospital with non-life threatening injuries.
The woman, who has been identified in media reports as Julie Sterling, 67, was pronounced dead at the scene.
Sterling's spouse was transported to the hospital, but he's expected to be okay, Cox said.
Including the fatility here in Mercer County, at least five people died in Monday's storm, according to media reports.
Cox was out Tuesday with officials from the National Weather Service Emergency assessing damage.
At Tuesday's fiscal court meeting, Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said the county road department will not be mowing this week and will instead focus on cleaning up roadsides. Both county and state road departments were out cleaning roads Monday.
The storms, which began with one on Sunday noon with 70 mile per hour winds that knocked down trees and power lines and left nearly 300 homes without power. The second came around later that night and left approximately 2,000 homes without power.
The National Weather Service has confirmed three tornadoes: an EF-1 tornado in Meade County, an EF-1 tornado that crossed through Butler and Warren counties and an EF-3 tornado whose path crossed over 35 miles through Lyon, Caldwell and Hopkins counties. Straight-line wind damage was confirmed in Grayson, Mercer, Garrard, Logan and Simpson counties. Surveys continue in Barren, Metcalfe, Monroe, Cumberland and Clinton counties where at least one additional EF1 tornado has been identified with wind speeds peaking at 105 mph in Cumberland County.
According to the state government, there are currently 9,903 power outages, down from over 215,144 earlier this week. Twenty-six counties and 12 cities have declared a state of emergency. Currently, Pennyrile State Park is sheltering 11 households and the state has provided five travel trailer units to Clay County for families who were displaced.
The Civil Air Patrol is piloting aerial surveys to capture images of the damage in the affected areas. Those who have experienced storm damage should take photographs before cleaning up and report the damages to local county emergency management officials.

title: Dancing Lady Dances Again In New Film Celebrating Harrodsburg's Past
description: Photo SubmittedThe Dancing Lady of Harrodsburg (played by Jan Pearce) and her dancing partner (played by Kelly Sikorski) both from Lexington Vintage Dance appear in
content:
Photo Submitted
The Dancing Lady of Harrodsburg (played by Jan Pearce) and her dancing partner (played by Kelly Sikorski) both from Lexington Vintage Dance appear in the new movie 'The Harrodsburg Legacy: 250 Years in the Making,' which premieres Tuesday, June 11, at Mercer County Senior High School.
Photo Submitted
The Dancing Lady of Harrodsburg (played by Jan Pearce) and her dancing partner (played by Kelly Sikorski) both from Lexington Vintage Dance appear in the new movie 'The Harrodsburg Legacy: 250 Years in the Making,' which premieres Tuesday, June 11, at Mercer County Senior High School. A film celebrating Harrodsburg's 250th birthday will premiere at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road) on Tuesday, June 11, starting at 7 p.m.
With the help of six dancers from Lexington Vintage Dance of Lexington, filmmakers hope to resurrect the legend of the lady who danced herself to death at Graham Springs Hotel in Michael Breeding's new film, 'The Harrodsburg Legacy, 250 Years in the Making.'
In Harrodsburg and Mercer County, history is everywhere. Around every corner is a mystery to unravel. An event or place to discover. A personality to meet or see in new light.
'Fortunately, it's all been saved due to Mercer County's early preservation efforts. The collection of saved structures and archival records is truly amazing,' Breeding said. 'The film honors this preservation tradition as well.'
With the help of 55 re-enactors who descended on Beaumont Inn on Feb. 18 along with second graders and youth from local schools, the story of Harrodsburg and Mercer County comes to life in a fascinating way. Rare and sometimes never before seen photos from the Harrodsburg Historical Society and Mercer County Public Library help to visually support the film's narrative. Special recognition is given to the Armstrong Archives as well. Original art by Sid Webb of Lexington and Marilyn Peters of Springfield are also featured.
Narrated by Robert Clotworthy, voice of 'Ancient Aliens' and 'The Curse of Oak Island' on the History Channel, this film is a fascinating journey through historic Hogtown.
'You can't watch this film and not want to move to Harrodsburg,' Breeding said.
'In only one hour, viewers will have a real feel for this community,' he said.
As part the film premiere, nearly 30 re-enactors will be appear to help celebrate the Harrodsburg milestone. Doors open at 6 p.m. and admission is free and open to the public. No tickets are required. Attendees are encouraged to dress in a costume representing any character from the past 250 years.
Film premiere: 'The Harrodsburg Legacy, 250 Years in the Making' at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road) on Tuesday, June 11. Doors open at 6 p.m. Film begins at 7 p.m. The event is free and open to the public. No tickets required.

(Composite image).
Dillon Carmichael performs Thursday, June 13, as part of Harrodsburg's 250th Celebration; the Settlement and Raid at Old Fort Harrod State Park runs four days from Thursday through Sunday, June 16; the Heart of Kentucky Juneteenth Festival runs two days from Friday, June 14, to Saturday, June 15. (Composite image). Harrodsburg's 250th birthday celebration continues this week with three nights of music and the Fort Harrod Settlement and Raid, which begins Thursday, June 13. Everything culminates with the cutting of Hogtown's 250th birthday cake on Sunday, June 16, which is scheduled for 4:45 p.m.
While the sestercentennial is the biggest event happening this weekend, it's hardly the only thing. The PlayThink Festival returns to Terrapin Hill Farms starting Wednesday, June 12, and continues until Sunday, June 16. The festival includes transformational workshops, fire and flow performances, yoga and meditation, healing arts, food and craft vendors, permaculture and sustainability.
The Heart of Kentucky Juneteenth Festival at West Lane Park kicks off two days of fun Friday, June 14, at 6 p.m. The first annual Miss Juneteenth Pageant starts 6:30 p.m. while Michael Fly and the Sounds are scheduled to perform starting at 8:30 p.m. There is a full slate of events on Saturday, June 15, with a car show, cornhole tournament, music, speakers and more.
Father's Day is Sunday, June 16. Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill has scheduled a whole day of Vintage Dad's Day fun on Saturday, with a car and tractor show, cigar lounge, vintage tool displays, bourbon tasting and vintage baseball featuring the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings and the Bluegrass Barons.
Happy 250th birthday, everyone! You don't look a day over 249.

title: Pool May Open July 1, Officials Say
description: Anderson-Dean Community Park announced via Facebook that 160 yards of concrete was poured earlier this week with more coming to finish the rest of the pool deck pad by the end
content:
Anderson-Dean Community Park announced via Facebook that 160 yards of concrete was poured earlier this week with more coming to finish the rest of the pool deck pad by the end of the week. According to park officials, the pool floor is currently being prepped for the liner, a heavy duty 60 millimeter thick liner almost like PVC. It will be installed by the middle of next week and then water will start being added to the pool around next Friday. Image: Anderson Dean Community Park.
Anderson-Dean Community Park announced via Facebook that 160 yards of concrete was poured earlier this week with more coming to finish the rest of the pool deck pad by the end of the week. According to park officials, the pool floor is currently being prepped for the liner, a heavy duty 60 millimeter thick liner almost like PVC. It will be installed by the middle of next week and then water will start being added to the pool around next Friday. Image: Anderson Dean Community Park. Officials at Anderson-Dean Community Park are hoping to get the pool open by July 1. That was the news from Anderson-Dean Park Manager Stephen Ransdell. On Tuesday, June 11, Ransdell gave the Mercer County Fiscal Court an update on the pool and other projects at the park. The fiscal court approved disbursing $436,000 to Anderson-Dean to pay bills. So far, the county has paid $762,280 towards the project to repair the pool, which has cost $1,247,480. Expenses for the park are supposed to be split evenly between the county and the City of Harrodsburg. The city is obligated to pay $485,200, but has not contributed to the new liner or the return system.
On Tuesday, Ransdell said the contractor, American Leak Detection of Mount Washington, is currently pouring concrete and hopes to have the liner installed this week. They will begin pouring water next week, Ransdell said. They want to test the pool for two weeks before opening it to the public, he said.
The original opening date for the pool was Memorial Day weekend. Officials say they have been hampered by delays in mandated state inspections. On Tuesday, Ransdell said UV filters may be needed to be installed to disinfect water.
'They're rather expensive,' Ransdell said. He said the contractors were working on getting an extension.
'It doesn't affect the pool being open, but it does affect the feature,' Ransdell said. He said other municipal pools have not had to install them. Ransdell said American Leak Detection is trying to find out if it has to be done now.
The Independence Day fireworks happen Wednesday, July 3, at Anderson-Dean. Ransdell told the magistrates he was still arranging food trucks.
The fiscal court gave second reading to $41 million budget for the 2025 fiscal year.
For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: First Miss Juneteenth Pageant Happens Friday, June 14
description: Contestants from the Miss Kentucky Heart of the Bluegrass Juneteenth Festival pageant took part in the 250th Celebration Parade on Saturday. The pageant is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Friday, June…
content:
Contestants from the Miss Kentucky Heart of the Bluegrass Juneteenth Festival pageant took part in the 250th Celebration Parade on Saturday. The pageant is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Friday, June 14, at West Lane Park (File image).
Contestants from the Miss Kentucky Heart of the Bluegrass Juneteenth Festival pageant took part in the 250th Celebration Parade on Saturday. The pageant is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Friday, June 14, at West Lane Park (File image). On Friday, June 14, the Kentucky Heart of the Bluegrass Juneteenth Festival will be holding its first ever Miss Juneteenth Pageant at West Lane Park (345 West Lane). The pageant and the festival are scheduled to begin at 6 p.m.
Juneteenth, officially Juneteenth National Independence Day, was named a U.S. federal holiday in 2021. It is celebrated annually on June 19 to commemorate the ending of slavery in the United States.
'We hope that the pageant will look past typical beauty standards and celebrate not only the contestants' beauty but also their contributions and impact in the community as well,' said pageant organizer Samantha Mays.
'Miss Juneteenth will exemplify dignity, strength and unity. She will be an example of the beauty, poise, and rich culture that so many African American women have enriched this country with.'
Contestants for the 2024 Miss Juneteenth Pageant (Image Submitted).
Contestants for the 2024 Miss Juneteenth Pageant (Image Submitted). The goal of the pageant is to promote youth empowerment and educate the youth about the rich African-American culture and history in Mercer County. There will also be live music from Michael Fly and the Sounds and various food trucks at the event.
This has been a joint effort, with the Juneteenth committee working to put the event together. Current members are: Travis and Phil Vandyke; Patricia Johnson; B.J. Stokes; Carley Scruggs; Samantha Mays; Sindicat Dunn; and Ruth Ann Bryant, who will presented with a Freedom Award at 11:30 a.m.on Saturday, June 15.
'We look forward to the community's support,' said Mays.
The Heart of Kentucky Juneteenth Festival at West Lane Park is a two-day celebration happening on Friday, June 14, and Saturday, June 15. The event is free to the public. Bringing a lawn chair is suggested since lim­ited seating is provided. For more information, visit juneteenthky.com or Facebook @Heart of KY Juneteenth.

content:
Ronald Hugh Reed, 84, husband, of Martha Shellenberger Reed died Wednesday, June 12, 2024, in Lexington. He was born in Harrodsburg, on July 3, 1939, to the late Hugh and Lois Reed. Ronald retired from Square D Schneider Electric after a 40 year career as a mechanical engineer. He was a former scoutmaster of Boy Scout Troop 43 in Versailles. A history buff, he was active with the James Harrod Trust in Harrodsburg where he served as treasurer for a period of time. He was a voracious reader, enjoyed music, and spending time on Herrington Lake. Survivors, in addition to his wife Martha, include: his daughter, Carrie (Jason) Rudzik of Lexington; one son, Thomas (Meredith) Reed of Lexington; three grandchildren, Jacob Rudzik, Lexington, Matthew Rudzik, and Adrienne Reed, all of Lexington. He is preceded in death by his brother, Bill Reed and sister-in-law, Bennie Kay Reed. A celebration gathering of family and friends was held Monday, June 17, 2024, at Clark Legacy Center, 3000 Versailles Rd. Frankfort, KY. title: Edward Orville Swanson
description: Orville Swanson Edward Orville Swanson, age 89, known to family and friends as Orville, passed into the arms of his Savior in Christ on Monday, June 17, 2024, at his home. He was born on November 21,…
content:
Orville Swanson
Edward Orville Swanson, age 89, known to family and friends as Orville, passed into the arms of his Savior in Christ on Monday, June 17, 2024, at his home.
He was born on November 21, 1934, to Cora Lulu (Seffrood) and Orlo Edwin Swanson on the home farm near South Wayne, Wisconsin and was a member of the West Wiota Lutheran Church. He was a 1952 graduate of South Wayne High School, then worked in the local area. On September 8, 1954, Orville married Dorothy Kay Collins at the Wiota Parsonage near Woodford, Wisconsin. They started their farming career on the E.A. Chapman Farm by South Wayne on February 16, 1955, and later moved to the Sunnyslope Home Farm where they raised their son, Edward, Jr., born October of 1955 and daughter Julie, born in May of 1959.
In July of 1973, Orville and family relocated to Wickenburg, Arizona where he was employed by the city. Later, in Flagstaff, he and his wife were managers of the Colony Estates, a large mobile home park. Extremes in weather encouraged them to settle in Kentucky where Orville worked in Pipeline Construction awhile and later as a bulldozer operator and manager of the Mercer County Landfill and Transfer Station in Harrodsburg for several years, He retired from there to Murray, Kentucky in late 2002.
Orville enjoyed old-time music and was an excellent dancer and had danced with two different square-dance clubs. He also drummed in several bands over the years and especially enjoyed 'The Country Drifters' country music and the great friends he made there. He enjoyed woodworking in his shop and donated to several dog houses. He also had an elaborate set-up of 'O' Steamers and Electric Trains with endless creations to make it more fun. Orv like playing Euchre. His many varied experiences was fuel for his favorite story telling among family and friends.
Surviving are his wife of 69 years, Dorothy; his son, Edward Jr. of Murray, Kentucky; daughter, Julie (J.Panke) Swanson of Flagstaff, Arizona; grandsons,, Adrian Rea and Ethan (Casie) Rea both of Arizona; great-grandchildren, Rowen, Evie, and Kinsey Rea all of Arizona. Also surviving Orville are many nephews and nieces and their families.
Orville was preceded in death by his parents; brothers, Lyle and Robert Swanson; sisters, Marie Krebs-Jorgenson and Dorothy Montgomery; sisters-in-law, Lilly and Tillie Swanson; brothers-in-law, Robert Krebs, Art Jorgenson, and Jr. Montgomery; as well as his infant great granddaughter, Harper Rea.
Orville had attended Martin's Chapel Methodist Church until he was home-bound with Alzheimer's. Graveside services will be held at 10:30 a.m., Friday, June 21, 2024, in Martin's Chapel Cemetery with Rev. Kerry Lambert officiating.
Expressions of sympathy can be made to the Humane Society of Calloway County, 607 Poplar Street # A, Murray, Kentucky 42071 or to the Martin's Chapel Cemetery Fund, 1619 Martin Chapel Road, Murray, Kentucky 42071.
Online condolences can be made at, www.jhchurchill.com

title: Desirae Huff Named New Coach Of CU-Harrodsburg Pioneer Women's Volleyball
description: Photo SubmittedNew Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Head Women's Volleyball Coach Desirae Huff pictured after leading her former team, Payson High School, dur­ing a game last season. Samuel Wa
content:
Photo Submitted
New Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Head Women's Volleyball Coach Desirae Huff pictured after leading her former team, Payson High School, dur­ing a game last season.
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sp****@ha***************.com
Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg announced a new athletic opportunity for students in May, appointing Desirae Huff as the head coach of the new Pioneer women's volleyball program.
'Volleyball is one of the fastest growing and most popular sports among high school females today so it goes without saying that we are thrilled to be adding women's volleyball to CU-Harrodsburg Athletics. This will provide yet another great opportunity for female athletes to compete at the collegiate level right here in Harrodsburg at Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg' said Jason Travis, Pioneer athletic director.
Huff was born and raised in the mountains of Arizona, but fell in love with the south during her two years with South Florida State College and later with Cumberland University, in Tennessee. She obtained her Master's degree in Education Administration and even began coaching volleyball while she was still a collegiate athlete. Huff has spent the last 10 years coaching at various levels, with the exception being 2019-20, when she set her career aside to take care of her children. Huff started a beach volleyball program at Payson High School in Arizona as well and has been leading it for the last three years. She has been a teacher for the last 10 years as well, and enjoys teaching English more than anything, but will be solely focusing on volleyball for the time being.
Huff is searching for players who are motivated to improve day in and day out. She says she prefers to focus on teaching and facilitating, and her goal is to recruit players who don't need additional motivation, because they're already working towards their own goals. Huff feels a successful program can be built through like-mindedness, structure and high expectations.
'I think if I can get eight we can definitely compete but if we have less than eight I think it's going to be more of a training year, and that's okay too. The goal is obviously to compete, but realistically I've been here a month, and couldn't start recruiting really until I was here in Kentucky,' said Huff. Want to read more great stories? title: Isaac Colvin
description: Isaac Colvin, 84, of Harrodsburg, widower of Barbara Jean Sanders, died Saturday, July 20, 2024, at the Harrodsburg Health and Rehabilitation Center. Born June 10, 1940, in Des Arc, Ariz., he was the…
content: Isaac Colvin, 84, of Harrodsburg, widower of Barbara Jean Sanders, died Saturday, July 20, 2024, at the Harrodsburg Health and Rehabilitation Center. Born June 10, 1940, in Des Arc, Ariz., he was the son of the late Lawrence and Ada (DeLozier) Colvin. He was a U.S. Army, after receiving his GED attended Crowley's Ridge Christian College, was a grocery clerk at the Air Force Base Commissary and later became a Lexington Herald newspaper carrier and was a member of the Harrodsburg Church of Christ. Survivors include: two sisters-in-law, Gale Hall and Diane Tuggle; special niece and nephew, Jeanette Evans of Grove, Okla. and Robert Colvin of Jacksonville, Ark. and several other nieces and nephews. He was preceded in death by one sister, Maddie Jane Chadwick and one brother, Otis Colvin.

title: After 33 Years, Robin Ison Is Checking Out Of The Library
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreRobin Ison, who has worked at the Mercer County Public Library for 33 years—the last 28 as the libraryȁ
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Robin Ison, who has worked at the Mercer County Public Library for 33 years—the last 28 as the library's director—is retiring.
The Mercer County Public Library (109 West Lexington Street) is hosting a celebration on Thurs­day, July 25, from 4 to 7 p.m. Robin Ison is checking out after 33 years at the library.
'I've only been director at the library for 28 years,' Ison said.
Ison's time at the library has been a transformative era, for the Mercer County Public Library, which has greatly expanded physically; for libraries as a whole, which have greatly expanded the services they provide for the public; and for Harrodsburg.
Mercer County has had library services for over 200 years. Ison said it was originally a subscription library located at the courthouse.
'You paid a fee and you checked out books,' Ison said. It became more like a public library when it relocated to Poplar Street.
'It became a demonstration library,' she said. Voters subsequently approved a small tax per $100 of assessed property, allowing the library to move from Poplar Street to Chiles Street. The children of the community 'loaded their wagons with library books,' Ison said, and hauled the library to its new home.
'I thought that was a neat community thing to do something like that,' Ison said.
Community, and the library's role in the community, is important to Ison.
'I love the people,' she said. 'I see this as one of the most wonderful services we have in our town.'
Ison joined the Mercer County Public Library 33 years ago on a part-time basis. Her first job was to update the library's card catalog, which operated on the Dewey Decimal system.
'Pretty soon they needed someone to do interlibrary loans,' Ison said, referring to the system that enables patrons to borrow materials from other libraries. 'So I became full-time.'
Just before Ison became the director, the library installed its first computer system, Polaris, which allowed patrons to search online for what they wanted to read and scan cards to check out books. Not long after becoming director, the library installed three public computers.
'It was pretty busy,' Ison said.
Today, the library operates two digital databases, including Hoopla, which allows patrons to access the library from home.
'It's still pretty busy,' Ison said.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
The Mercer County Public Library is looking for a new director, but they'll be hard pressed to find someone who takes a better picture than Robin Ison, seen here in 2019 with Kylo Ren and some Stormtroopers demonstrating the power of the force.
Then there is the expansion of the library's physical home. Relocating to Lexington Street, the library bought up shuttered businesses—the old A&P and old Western Auto, the old Fort Harrod Pharmacy and 'Thriftys'—using the space to expand the building and parking lot. In 2016, they bought the building next door at 114 North Main which they spent a year and nearly $1.4 million to transform into the History Research Center. Few have done more to revitalize downtown Harrodsburg than the Mercer County Public Library during Ison's time as director.
One of Ison's favorite parts of the library is the fireplace in the reading room, where she points out the mantel was carved by Calvin Shewmaker while the stonework was done by the late Stanley Kelly, using stone quarried from near Shakertown using techniques similar to those used by the Shakers. Ison also points out the quilt behind the circulation desk that was made by Mary Alexander, the painting of downtown Harrodsburg by Laura Sullivan and the big globe donated by Danville dentist Dr. Jack Hankla. Then there is the sculpture by Erika Strecker and the tile entryway by Zoe Strecker.
'There is just so much community,' Ison said as she ran her hand along the mantel. Want to read the rest of the story? Click to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Kentuckians In Paris: A Preview Of Olympic Athletes With Kentucky Ties
content:
UK Athletics
Former University of Kentucky track and field starlet Sydney Mclaughlin­Levrone (center) will be defending her gold medal in the 400-meter hurdles at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The state of Kentucky will be well represented at the 2024 Olympic Games. More than 30 competitors who were born, raised in or educated in Kentucky will be chasing a gold medal in Paris, France, which is hosting the games for the first time since 1924.
The most notable competitors are, of course, for­mer University of Kentucky track and field athletes Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone and Jasmine Camacho-Quinn, who will be expected to win the 400 and 100 meter hurdles, respectively. McLaughlin-Levrone holds the world record of 50.65 seconds in the 400 hurdles and is expected to win; Camacho-Quinn will be working to catch up to Tobi Amusan of Nigeria, who currently holds the 12.12″ record. Joining Camacho-Quinn is former Wildcat Masai Russell, who won multiple SEC championships and broke two collegiate records during her time as a Wildcat. Want to read the rest of the story? title: From NCCAA to NCAA: Former Pioneer Athletic Director Joins Transylvania
description: Photo SubmittedFormer Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Athletic Director Dalton Christopher has accepted a new position with Transylvania University. Dalton Christopher, a gradu
content:
Photo Submitted
Former Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg Athletic Director Dalton Christopher has accepted a new position with Transylvania University.
Dalton Christopher, a graduate of Mercer County High School, was an integral piece to starting the Campbellsville University—Harrodsburg campus athletic department and served the school as the athletic director for seven years before step­ping down earlier this year. While a Pioneer, Christopher oversaw the beginning of nine athletic programs: men's basketball, women's basketball, men's soccer, women's soccer, bowling, cheerleading, golf, esports and cross country. He also named fellow Harrodsburg native Austin Sparrow head coach of the Pioneers men's basketball team. Since then the program has experienced a great deal of success, most notably a NCCAA Division-II national championship in 2022.
On Sunday, Aug. 4, Christopher announced he has taken a new position as associate director of athletics (communications) with Transylvania University in Lexington. Want to read the rest of the story? title: Lady Titans Have High Hopes For 2024 Soccer Season
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenFront row: Stephanie Noort, Emma Tatum, Brelee Cox, Layldn Irvin, Isabelle Devensky, Addisyn Bartleson, Averi Adkins. Middle row: Xatzirit
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Front row: Stephanie Noort, Emma Tatum, Brelee Cox, Layldn Irvin, Isabelle Devensky, Addisyn Bartleson, Averi Adkins. Middle row: Xatzirit Hernandez, Hannah Hightower, Rosie Hernandez, Carty Sanders, Cheyenne Pickett, Allison Osoy, Aliyah Ison, Amonni Mccann, Addyson Foster. Top row: Coach Kim Ramirez, Avery Harrod, Kiley Waldridge, Emerson Daniels, Cayden Adkins, Olivia Rogers, Kylie Mobley, Saylee Sims, Adison Wilham, Skylar Webb, Hayden Nations, Alexis Barker, Coach Joshua Culver.
The Mercer County Lady Titan soccer team played two scrimmages on Saturday, Aug. 3, in preparation for the 2024 season. In the first of two games, Mercer County defeated Harrison County easily, 5-1. In their second game of the day, absent players and tired legs made the difference in a 3-0 finish with the Bryan Station Lady Defenders.
Two scrimmages in one day is a great test of endurance, and Head Coach Joshua Culver says one of the main focuses of this off-season has been to get the girls in better shape. Culver, along with his staff of Michael Grubbs and Kim Ramirez, have created a fitness test for each of the Lady Titans to work toward ahead of the season, and when they're not sweating on the field or weight room, they're testing their knowledge in the classroom.
'We have been in the classroom reviewing positions and roles so they have a deeper understanding when they get on the field,' said Culver.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Coach Joshua Culver hopes senior Laykin Irvin can get some offensive help from players including Adison Wilham. Senior Skylar Webb will be returning between the goalposts for the second consecutive season after tallying 156 saves and three clean sheets last fall.
Five games into the 2023 season, the Lady Titans had two wins, two losses and a draw. At that point, then junior Laykin Irvin had seven goals. As the season progressed, Mercer's opponents became increasingly aware of just how dominant Irvin's play in the final third is. Irvin went on to score a goal or two in every remaining Lady Titan win and finished the season with 20 goals and two assists.
Culver hopes his team's hard work this offseason, coupled with some slight tactical changes to the line-up, will take some pressure off Irvin in transition and spread out opposing defenses. Culver has high expectations for Baylee Sims, Adison Wilham, Cayden Adkins, Kylie Mobley, Kiley Waldridge, Hayden Nations and Emerson Daniels, and says they each can contribute with shots on goal and assists.
'We had multiple scorers and assists in the first game, which was awesome to see. I know they are all more than capable,' said Culver.
While one senior leads the team from the top of the formation, another will be directing play from the back. Skylar Webb will be returning between the goalposts for the second consecutive season after tallying 156 saves and three clean sheets last fall. She says she feels stronger and more confident ahead of her second season starting. Want to read the rest of the story? title: Overdose Awareness Day On Aug. 31 At Olde Town Park
description: Overdose Awareness Day 2024-8-22 screenshot. Mercer County ASAP (Agency for Substance Abuse Policy) and Mercer Transformation are hosting International Overdos
content:
Overdose Awareness Day 2024-8-22 screenshot.
Mercer County ASAP (Agency for Substance Abuse Policy) and Mercer Transformation are hosting International Overdose Awareness Day on Saturday, Aug. 31, at Olde Town Park (126 South Main Street). The event features music, speakers, free food and vendors. It will run from noon to 5 p.m. The theme for this year is 'Together we can.'
International Overdose Awareness Day is held on Aug. 31 every year. It is the world's largest annual campaign to end overdose as well as remember without stigma those who have died and acknowledge the grief of family and friends left behind. It was initiated in 2001 by Sally J. Finn at the Salvation Army in Melbourne, Australia. Each year, there are more than 1,000 events held around the world to support bringing an end to overdose. International Overdose Awareness Day is by the not-for-profit Australian public health organization, the Penington Institute.
'It will take all of us together to make a change in our local community,' said Tobie Reeser-Sherrow, chair of Mercer ASAP. 'We have a great list of guest speakers, including people who work in treatment, people who are in recovery, and some who have lost family or friends to overdose.'
Kentucky is one of the worst states in America for overdose fatalities, with a death rate of 53.2 per 100,000 total population in 2022, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In that year, 2,271 died from a drug overdose.
There is good news, though. Overdose deaths have been declining in Kentucky for the last few years. According to figures compiled by the Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center, fatalities declined 2.5 percent in 2022 from the year before. It was the first year Kentucky saw a decrease in overdose deaths since 2018. In 2023, there were 1,984 overdose deaths, a decrease of 9.8 percent from 2022. In that year, six Mercer County residents died from a drug overdose, according to the Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center.
The state's Narcan van will be at the event on Saturday, Reeser-Sherrow said, providing overdose education as well as free Narcan.
'We will have free burgers and hot dogs for everyone that attends,' Reeser-Sherrow said. 'If anyone wants to set up or contact me about the event, they can reach me at tlrees2@uky.edu.'
Overdose Awareness Day happens Saturday, Aug. 31, at Olde Town Park (126 South Main Street). The event will run from noon to 5 p.m. Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Friday Night Lights: Titan football is back in action
description: Mercer County Titan football made history in a number of different ways last fall. The 10-win Titans were the first team to achieve double digit wins since 2006, and only the third group to achieve…
content:
Mercer County Titan football made history in a number of different ways last fall. The 10-win Titans were the first team to achieve double digit wins since 2006, and only the third group to achieve the feat this century. They also achieved the program's third district title since 2005, knocked off Lincoln County for the first time in four meetings and 14 years, and earned a win against a Class-6A school (Dunbar) for the first time since 2016.
Ashton Drakeford followed Denim Griffieth into the endzone during Mercer County's win over Dunbar last year. Drakeford scored eight touchdowns in nine games last fall.
Titans are back and loaded with talent ahead of Head Coach Craig Yeast's third season at the helm. While the talent is there, depth is not, and the biggest adversity Yeast is expecting to face this season is keeping his players healthy.
'Our goal is to keep them healthy. If we can keep them healthy, all of our players, then we're going to have a chance to have a decent season,' said Yeast.
One massive change to the Titans' starting lineup will go a long way in determining the magnitude of success Mercer County can achieve this season. New quarterback, Cornelius Mapp, will be starting in his first ever varsity game when the Titans suit up to face Bullitt East next Saturday, Aug. 24, at Alvis Johnson Field.
'He's very, very intelligent and understands the offense really well. He throws a really good ball. The one thing we need to work on with him and continue to work on is a sense of urgency. He just needs to speed up a little bit, he's a junior and most of the other guys have plenty of varsity experience and he doesn't have it,' said Yeast. title: Burgin School Board Approves Tax Rate Increase After Public Hearing
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Board of Education voted to increase the property tax rate from 73.5 cents per $100 in accessed value to
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Board of Education voted to increase the property tax rate from 73.5 cents per $100 in accessed value to 79.5 cents per $100. The board voted to increase the tax at a special-called meeting on Thursday, Aug. 22.
Before they voted, the board conducted a public hearing as required under state law to allow the constituents to 'speak their piece,' Superintendent Will Begley said. Before the hearing, Begley provided the attendees with the rules. Speakers had to sign in to speak, were given three minutes to address the board, and were only allowed to speak once. The superintendent asked everyone to identify themselves as either renters or owners. Seven people signed up to speak. The first was Stacy Sellers, who said she loved her 'friendly little city.'
'I am opposed to these increases,' Sellers said, due to what she called the 'sky-high' assessment. She said she saw no proposed benefits for the children. Sellers said the district's tax base had increased $9.9 million in one year, from $41.8 million in 2023 to $51.7 million in 2024.
'There needs to be a tightening of the belt and less wasteful spending,' Sellers said. 'If you raise taxes too high, people will move away because they cannot afford to live here.'
'I am for the tax increase,' said Ed Stanley, the next speaker.
'School's pretty tight,' Stanley said, noting the school provides no transportation for sports.
'There is a lot of fundraising going on,' Stanley said. He said people 'move to Burgin because of the school.'
'If we don't fund the school, we're going to lose the school,' Stanley said. Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: City Terminates Investigation Into Chief Hurt At Kazimer's Request
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Harrodsburg
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Harrodsburg City Commission has voted to withdraw the investigation into a complaint against Chief Tim Hurt at the request of the citizen who made the original complaint. The commission voted to withdraw the investigation at their regular meeting on Monday, Aug. 26. They initially authorized the investigation in May based on a complaint filed by Jennifer Kazimer against Hurt.
Kazimer—who, with her husband, owns the Vault Ciders, Suds and Spirits on South Main Street—accused the police chief of violating the HPD code of ethics. Kazimer, who also served a partial term on the city commission and ran for election as mayor, complained about Hurt's actions during last year's Oktoberfest as well as the handling of the bodycam footage from a visit Hurt made to the Vault.
Hurt, citing the ethics code, has declined making a public comment on the complaint. On Monday, he referred the Harrodsburg Herald to his attorney, Thomas Clay.
'This has been a long and protracted ordeal for the chief,' Clay said. These defamatory statements are very troubling to me.'
'There are going to be negotiations over this settlement agreement,' Clay said. 'He was simply doing his job.'
Reached Tuesday morning, Kazimer referred the Harrodsburg Herald to a letter by her attorney sent to the city. An open records request was filed to obtain a copy of that letter, but it was not received before press time.
Trevor Short, executive director of the Harrodsburg Community Center by Mercer Area Family and Education and Wellness (MAFEW), said the organization had come to terms on a new lease agreement with the city for the National Guard Armory on College Street. The city terminated the lease agreement in April and has been negotiating a new agreement.
On Monday, City Attorney Norrie Currens said the city was looking for a 'nominal payment' of $200 a month for two years. Payments would increase gradually over the last three years of the agreement. Currens said she would create an amortization schedule and send it to MAFEW. MAFEW will also take over utilities at the armory starting Sept. 1.
'I want you all to review it and get back to us,' Currens said. Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: It's college football time in the Bluegrass
description: Austin Cocanougher Contributing Writer This upcoming Saturday, Aug. 31, Mark Stoops officially opens his 12th season as the head coach of the University of Kentucky Wildcat Football team. After…
content:
Austin Cocanougher
Contributing Writer
This upcoming Saturday, Aug. 31, Mark Stoops officially opens his 12th season as the head coach of the University of Kentucky Wildcat Football team. After finishing last year with a mildly disappointing 7-6 record, Stoops and company look to respond with a statement in 2024. With a bevy of fresh recruits, a haul of new transfers, and the return of experienced and accomplished veterans, the Wildcats bolster the roster to do just that. The question is, does the gauntlet of a schedule pose enough of an obstacle to keep Kentucky from taking substantial steps forward?
Former North Carolina State running-back Demie Sumo-Karngbaye transfered to Kentucky with teammate Devin Leary last summer. The senior is listed as the number one running back on the Wildcats' 2024 depth chart (UK Athletics/Caleb Bowlin).
As the 2024 college football season begins, Kentucky is set to face the top-10 toughest schedule in the country. Simply put, with this year's lineup of opponents, just getting bowl-eligible is no small feat. Although Kentucky's roster is the best it has been in years on paper, stacking wins in a loaded SEC is something only elite teams are able to do with consistency. title: Joe Hood
description: Ollie Joseph 'Joe' Hood, 81, of Harrodsburg, passed away at home surrounded by his family on Aug. 22, 2024. Born Sept. 16, 1942, in Harrodsburg, he was the son of the late Everett and Dorothy…
content:
Ollie Joseph 'Joe' Hood, 81, of Harrodsburg, passed away at home surrounded by his family on Aug. 22, 2024.
Born Sept. 16, 1942, in Harrodsburg, he was the son of the late Everett and Dorothy (Buchanan) Hood.
He enjoyed playing tennis, studying American history, visiting historic sites, and old cars.
He was a 1960 graduate of Harrodsburg High School, a 1963 graduate of Carson-Newman College, a 1967 graduate of Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, and a 1975 graduate of University of Kentucky Law School where he was the first law student to win both the Excellence in Brief Writing as well as Excellence in Oral Advocacy awards. He was Counsel to the Kentucky State Legislature with LRC (Legislative Research Commission) for over 30 years, a Harrodsburg City Commissioner for over 20 years, and a Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) Pastor for 30 years. He recently celebrated his 12th year Pastoring Perryville Christian Church, Perryville, Kentucky. He enjoyed traveling, particularly to Ontario, Canada, the Smoky Mountains and southwest Florida.
Joe was preceded in death by one brother, David Glenn 'Mickey' Hood.
Survivors include: his wife of 33 years, Wendy Hood; two sons, Joseph Mason Hood of Harrodsburg and Everett Lee Hood of Bowling Green; one future daughter-in-law, Alissa Leigh Woods of Bowling Green; one daughter, Jeannie Buchanan Randolph of Harrodsburg; one son-in-law, Stephen Chase Randolph of Harrodsburg and two grandchildren, Margaret Elizabeth Hood and Joseph Lee Hood both of Harrodsburg.
Memorial gifts may be sent to Perryville Christian Church, P.O. Box 86, Perryville, Kentucky 40468.
A Celebration of Life was held at Harrodsburg Christian Church on Aug. 27.
Sims Funeral Services was in charge of arrangements.

r Jones as Ethel Thayer, Larry Kendrick as Charlie Martin and Steve Sleeper as Norman Thayer. 'On Golden Pond' is directed by Darell Rickmers and stage managed by Tim White. Tickets are $12 and are available online at raggededgetheatre.org. Elf Jr. Auditions
Auditions for 'Elf Jr., The Musical' will be held Saturday, Sept. 7, at 10 a.m. at Ragged Edge Community Theatre (111 South Main Street). Callbacks will be Sunday, Sept. 8, at 2 p.m.

Ragged Edge's production of this YouthStage musical will be directed by Managing Director Allan Barlow with musical direction by Lori Patterson, choreography by Ami Wilcox, costumes by Judy Machal Barlow and stage management by Molly Pryse.
Being a YouthStage musical, auditions are open to actors between the ages of 6 to 18 and roles are available for all ages. Auditioners are asked to be prepared to sing a 16-bar cut of any song of their choosing. They should bring recorded accompaniment music on their phone or other device. No acapella auditions will be accepted. There is no need for a prepared monologue because auditioners will be asked to read scenes and cuttings from the script of 'Elf Jr., The Musical.'
