Public performances are scheduled for Nov. 15-17 and 22-24. In addition, there will be school matinees on Nov. 19, 20, 21 and 22. Audition forms need to be completed online at raggededgetheatre.org. title: Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival Returns Friday, Sept. 20: Special Concerts On Sept. 15 And Sept. 19
description: Adrian Crutchfield portrays at the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival in 2023.
content:
Adrian Crutchfield portrays at the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival in 2023.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Adrian Crutchfield, seen here performing at last year's Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival, will headline again this year.
The Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival returns with three days of jazz, food, and fun at Old Fort Harrod State Park (100 South College Street). The free festival will showcase 17 regional and national jazz ensembles from Friday, Sept. 20, to Sunday, Sept. 22. In addition, there will be special concerts at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill on Sunday, Sept. 15, and at Beaumont Inn on Thursday, Sept. 19.
'We are excited to be back at Fort Harrod, where the Jazz Festival first started in 2014,' said Sam Carr, who's been the guiding force behind the festival since its inception. 'It is very fitting for the festival to be at the Fort as we continue the Harrodsburg 250 Celebration.'
Carr said the jazz ensembles range from quartets to 17-piece big bands hailing from Kentucky, Indiana, Ohio and North Carolina. He said the acts showcase the diversity of jazz, from fusion to smooth, swing, modern and more.
Friday's headliner is saxophonist Adrian Crutchfield, hailed as the last horn man to play with Prince. In 2024, Crutchfiel toured with smooth jazz heavyweights Dave Koz and Brian Culbertson.
Saturday's headliner is the K-Jam Collective, an all-star band led by Dr. Keith McCutchen from Kentucky State University. Harrodsburg native Larry Griffin will be performing as a vocalist.
'I'm honored to write and create music with some of the most wonderful artists in the state and our region,' McCutchen said. 'Harrodsburg is a beautiful place with rich history and culture. The combination creates a great night of music.'
Sunday is the 'Collegiate Big Band Blast,' a Jazz Festival tradition.
In addition to the music, artisans will be set up on Saturday showcasing arts and crafts. There will also be food trucks and a beer garden. Old Fort Harrod is also offering free admission on Saturday and Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. for all attendees.
Here's the lineup.
Sunday, Sept. 15
Blue Groove Jazz at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill (3501 Lexington Road) at 4 p.m. The preliminary concert kicks off with Blue Groove Jazz Quartet, which consists of Sam Carr (alto and tenor sax), Eben Henson (drums), Pete McCaffrey (bass) and Mark Gardner (keyboards). The quartet has a loyal following in central Kentucky, performing at the Norton Center for the Arts at Centre College and Talon Winery's annual Jazz on the Porch Series.
Led by saxophonist Sam Carr, Blue Groove Jazz—and guests—perform at the 2023 Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival.
Thursday, Sept. 19
Gotcha Covered with Mark Gardner at Beaumont Inn (638 Beaumont Inn Drive) at 5 p.m.
Friday, Sept. 20
• RPM Fusion Quartet at 6:30 p.m. RPM—Ryan McGillicuddy (bass guitar), Glenn Ginn (guitar), Nick Deidrichsen (drums) and Gabe Evans (keyboards)—mines the bedrock of funk groups like James Brown, the Funky Meters and the Isley Brothers.
• Adrian Crutchfield at 8:30 p.m. Friday's headliner is famous as the last sax player to play with Prince. Crutchfield is known for his neo-soul sound and has played for Lionel Richie, Bette Midler, CeeLo Green, Anthony Hamilton, Fantasia Barrino, K-Ci and JoJo, the Gap Band featuring Charlie Wilson and hip-hop superstar Young Jeezy. Crutchfield has been featured by jazz artists including Kim Waters, Mike Phillips, Alex Bugnon, Jeff Lorber and Branford Marsalis.
The Campbellsville University Faculty Jazz Band—with bassist Saulo Moura—perform at the 2023 Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival.
Saturday, Sept. 21
• Blue Groove Jazz Quartet at 11 a.m.
• Campbellsville University Faculty Band at 12:15 p.m. A crowd favorite, the ensemble features Saulo Mouro (piano and bass), Denis Santos (sax and flute) and Chad Ford (percussion).
• Jamey Aebersold Quartet at 3:15 p.m. A renowned jazz educator and saxophonist, Aebersold's quartet includes Doug Elmore (upright bass), Jonathan Higgins (drums) and Wade Honey (piano). The recipient of the 2014 A.B. Spellman NEA Jazz Masters Award for Jazz Advocacy, Aebersold has led summer jazz workshops in seven countries. His company, Jazzbooks.com, has produced 133 book/audio jazz Play-A-Longs.
• Spherical Agenda at 5 p.m. The jazz-rock fusion band—Matt Wiles (bass), Brandon Coleman (guitar), Ben Tweedt (keyboards) and Devon Leigh (drums)—hails from Cincinnati, Ohio. They draw from the cutting edge of today's fusion as well as groups like Tony Williams Lifetime, Mahavishnu Orchestra, and Return to Forever.
• Ron Jones Contemporary Jazz Quartet at 5:45 p.m. A high energy group featuring Jones (alto saxophone), Winton Reynolds (piano), Tom Covello (bass) and Jerry Harshaw (drums) will present a versatile mixture of music from artists like Grover Washington Jr., Stevie Wonder, Chaka Kahn, Spyro Gyro, Anita Baker, Earth Wind and Fire, Bill Withers and other well-known artists.
Photo Submitted
The all-star K-Jam Collective will headline Saturday night at the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival.
• K-Jam Collective at 8:30 p.m. Saturday's headliners are directed by Dr. Keith Mccutchen from Kentucky State University. They will present 'Old and New Dreams: An American Review.' The band includes some of the finest jazz musicians and educators from Kentucky and beyond.
'We don't have all the great Kentucky artists in this group, but the ones we have are great,' Mccutchen said.
Mccutchen is a keyboardist and an associate professor of music at Kentucky State who has shared the stage with artists, including Mel Torme, Diane Schurr, Stanley Turrentine, and Richard Davis. The all-star K-Jam Collective includes Miles Osland (flute), the director of jazz studies and professor of saxophone at the University of Kentucky; Dalton Stanton (alto sax), a Down Beat magazine student award-winning saxophonist; Hunt Butler (tenor sax); Marlin McKay (trumpet), assistant professor of music at the University of Louisville; Brenda Flowers (trombone and vocals); Natalie Boeyink (bass), music educator at Indiana University; Mike Hyman (drums), music educator at the University of Louisville; and Larry Griffin (vocals), a native of Harrodsburg and the musical director and conductor of Capriccio Columbus, an award-winning family adult and youth choirs in Columbus, Ohio.
Harrodsburg native Larry Griffin will be the vocalist with the K-Jam Collective.
Sunday, Sept. 22
• David Hall at 11 a.m. Hall, who plays saxophone, clarinet, flute, flugelhorn, trumpet, steel pan drum, harmonica and keyboards. He has performed with artists including the Temptations, the Four Tops, the Drifters, the Lexington Philharmonic and the Lexington Swing Society. He plays regularly at Giuseppe's Ristorante Italiano.
The UK Jazz Ensemble perform at the 2023 Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival.
• The University of Kentucky Jazz Ensemble at noon. The ensemble has twice been awarded the Outstanding Jazz Ensemble certificate at the Notre Dame Collegiate Jazz Festival and at the Elmhurst Jazz Festival. They have been featured with many national touring artists, including Doc Severinsen, Mel Torme and Diane Schuur.
• Kentucky State University Choir at 1 p.m. The choir begins its 57th year under the direction of McCutchen. They have been first-place winners at choral competitions, including the national Spiritual competition in Cincinnati and a two time winner of the annual historically Black colleges and universities choral festival, in Las Vegas.
• Transylvania University Jazz Ensemble at 1:50 p.m.
• Asbury University Jazz Band at 2:40 p.m. Under the direction of Dr. Glen Flanigan, the 17-piece big band includes student musicians from Asbury as well as community members. They perform at numerous functions, including the High Bridge Film Festival, as well as annual touring ministry mission trips throughout the United States.
• Eastern Kentucky University at 3:30 p.m.
Morehead State perform at the 2023 Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival.
• Morehead State University Jazz Ensemble at 4:20 p.m. The jazz big band makes regular appearances at the Marshall Jazz Festival, the UK 'Battle of the Bands,' Morehead State Jazz Clinic, the Elmhurst Jazz Festival and more.
Organizers are stressing that the free event is kid- and pet-friendly. Pop-up tents are welcome. Spectators are advised to bring lawn chairs. For more information, visit kyheritagejazzfest.org. title: Local Golf Teams Prepare For Region Play
description: Burgin Independent senior Bryson Lacy chipped a shot from the rough during a tournament at Bright Leaf golf course on Thursday, Sept. 12. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren) Both the Burgin…
content:
Burgin Independent senior Bryson Lacy chipped a shot from the rough during a tournament at Bright Leaf golf course on Thursday, Sept. 12. ( The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren)
Both the Burgin Independent and Mercer County High School girls golf teams competed at Bright Leaf golf course on Thursday, Sept. 12. Over nine holes of par three, Mercer County was led by seniors Kate Carlton (43) and Lily Leitenberger (47), and Paisley King (46). Class of 2025 graduates Carlton and Leitenberger were recognized with their families before teeing off. Head Coach Leewood Goodlett is sad to see the seniors leave the program, but she believes their personal best performances could come in the Regional meet scheduled for Tuesday, Sept. 24.
'I'm very proud of the improvement I've seen this season. We are sad to lose our two seniors, but we also have a few young girls who continue to make progress,' said Goodlett.
The Burgin Independent Lady Bulldogs claimed the 12th Region All-A championship in August as they were the only Class-A school with enough members to field a team. While they didn't have to outplay any opponents to win, Head Coach Matt Grimes believes having such an interest in golf despite this being the Bulldog's first year with a full team, is encouraging and should lead to future success.
'It's an accomplishment that we can put together a team in just our second year, and everyone else who's been established and has had a program, can't,' said Grimes.
Burgin girls golf was led by senior Jemma Jenkins (43), Kate Hatfield (44) and Taylor Isaacs (44).
'We're in the infancy of the program. It was really exciting as the season progressed to see the improvement from each individual,' said Grimes.
The Lady Bulldogs will compete in the regional tournament at Wild Turkey Trace Golf Course in Lawrenceburg on Wednesday, Sept. 25, and the boys will compete one day prior at Peninsula Golf Resort in Garrard County.
The Bulldogs program graduates Jenkins, Alli Crawley-Stewart and Bryson Lacy.
'I am proud of each and everyone who came out to help give our two-year young program some momentum. Those who participated last year are the anchors of the team and I'm equally as pleased with our first year players who stepped outside of the box and tried something new this fall,' said Grimes.
The Mercer County Titan boys team is preparing for their regional tournament and the team and Head Coach Jay Anderson have found success on big stages lately.
The team of Tanner Robinson, Will Armstrong, Noah Nichols, Carson Whitenack and Collier Sexton finished runner up at the Central Kentucky Bluegrass Conference Tournament on Saturday, Sept. 7, and fifth at the 2A state tournament. They combined to shoot 34 over par in Owensboro. Christian Academy of Louisville, the winner, and one of the best programs in the state in recent years, shot eight over par.
Anderson said some mental miscues down the stretch got the best of the Titans at the 2A state tournament in Owensboro on Thursday, Sept. 9.
'But we couldn't be in any better position heading into the region. Our guys are confident, we know we have a chance,' said Anderson.
A chance to become the first Mercer County boys golf team to ever qualify for state. If each of the five individuals play to their potential the boys are likely to make history at Peninsula Golf Resort on Tuesday, Sept. 24.
'It wouldn't surprise me if any of our guys make it individually. We're right there knocking on the door. It's been a challenge just to get them to understand how good they are as individuals and as a team,' said Anderson.
The Titans entered the tournament hoping to reach second place, but still improved on their sixth place position last year. Whitenack, Sexton and Nichols had never golfed in a state tournament atmosphere, and Anderson believes the experience will help them control their nerves at the regional meet.
Mercer County golf will be graduating one senior, Ben Chapman.
'Ben is an exceptional teammate. He's understood that while he may not be the best golfer on the team, he is still a valuable part of the team. For a lot of guys, golf is an avenue for bonding, employment and many other things. You're teaching a game that parallels a lot of life's journeys and it's a game you can enjoy for the rest of your life. He's another example of the great kids I've been blessed to coach; they don't cause any problems, show up to practice and work hard, they take care of themselves in the classroom and have high moral fiber. I hope I've blessed him as much as he's blessed me,' said Anderson. title: Racing Community Mourns Loss Of Harrodsburg Crew Chief
description: Jeff Gullett photographed with his granddaughters Briley and Baylin Phillips after being inducted into the Ponderosa Speedway Hall of Fame last year.
content:
Jeff Gullett photographed with his granddaughters Briley and Baylin Phillips after being inducted into the Ponderosa Speedway Hall of Fame last year.
The Central Kentucky racing community and Harrodsburg alike are mourning the loss of a crew chief of legend, and a friend to many in Jeff Gullett. Gullett began his career in racing as a teenager, but only competed behind the wheel once according to his daughter Callie Phillips. He made his main impact building and preparing vehicles for others to race in, and began working for D&D Motorsports when he dedicated himself to racing full-time in the '90s.
Since 2005, Gullett has worked as the crew chief for Justin Rattliff Racing in Campbellsville and has helped several great drivers compete across the country. Gullett was an inductee into the South-Central Kentucky Dirt Racing Hall of Fame and was also honored as a past Battle of the Bluegrass Series Crew Chief of the Year. He helped drivers like Daulton Wilson, Justin Rattliff and Jason Jameson to several Lucas Oil Late Model Dirt Series victories during his tenure at JRR Motorsports, but the resounding message from his crew and everyone he worked with is he was much more than a great mechanic, but a great friend to everyone.
'Jeff Gullett honestly meant the world to me,' said Wilson in a JRR Motorsports press release. 'He was like a second dad. He always wanted the best for me no matter what. He picked a random kid out of North Carolina to mentor and give an opportunity of a lifetime to, and I'll always cherish it. I'll miss seeing his name pop up on my phone daily, whether it was to talk about business or just life in general. They don't make them like Gullett anymore, and thankfully I was blessed that our paths crossed,' said Wilson.
Tim Tungate was Gullett's right hand man with JRR Motorsports, and saw more than most, just how special of a person Gullett was.
'He was a great mentor, he knew a lot about racing, he knew a lot about life, he was a great friend,' said Tungate. With Gullett gone, it has become more evident than ever all of the work behind the scenes and extra effort he put into being the JRR crew chief. 'It's been kind of hectic this week trying to get stuff lined up, but 'you know what to do, just do it,' that's what he would say, 'don't be crying about it, just do it,'' said Tungate.
Gullett first began working with JRR Motorsports initial driver, Justin Rattliff, when Rattliff was only 15. They experienced the highs and lows of racing and life together for nearly two decades.
'Jeff was like a father figure to me when we started racing,' Rattliff was quoted in the JRR press release. 'He was with me for all of my modified and late model wins. When we transitioned to late models, he told me he would cut his hair if I won a Lucas Oil Series race. Well we did that back in 2007 at LaSalle, and off came the hair. As far as I know, he only missed one race and that was for his daughter's graduation. Jeff loved his family and grandkids more than anything and he will be deeply missed by all,' said Rattliff.
Gullett's only daughter, Phillips, is amazed at the reaction of the racing community from across the country since her father's passing.
'It was unreal,' Phillips said of the turnout at her father's visitation, and the outreach to her family after Gullett's passing. 'I knew that so many people loved him but the amount of outpouring from this, I can't even explain, it's truly been humbling,' said Phillips.
Phillips says her whole life has been racing, and if she wanted to spend time with her father growing up, it was at the racetrack, because he was typically busy working.
'Until my kids were born. Once my kids were born he slowed down a little, he didn't miss anything for my babies that's for sure,' said Phillips.
Gullett loved his family more than anything according to many that knew him. One way he connected with his granddaughters was by gifting them each a dollar scratch off ticket each night. Phillips said two members of the racing community set aside donations to her family to keep the tradition going.
'That was something they and their papaw did every night,' said Phillips. 'My girls got an insane amount of time with their papaw, and I'm so grateful for that.'
Phillips said it is a bit overwhelming for her to spend time at the race track nowadays, but her daughters' connection to their grandfather is special, and similarly to how she was raised, if they need to be at the racetrack to reconnect with their papaw, so be it.
'If it's something that's important to my girls, then I'll do it.' For more stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Titans Tower Over The Admirals
description: Mercer County football star Braidin Baughman sped around the edge during one of his two touchdown runs against Danville. (Samuel Warren) Mercer County High School Football (2-2) returned to Alvis…
content:
Mercer County football star Braidin Baughman sped around the edge during one of his two touchdown runs against Danville. (Samuel Warren)
Mercer County High School Football (2-2) returned to Alvis Johnson Field after two weeks on the road on Friday, Sept. 13, and faced the struggling Danville Admirals (0-4). Danville had only scored two touchdowns through their first three games, and the Mercer County defense had no problems holding the Admirals scoreless.
On the Admirals' first play, defensive end Trenton Berry dipped his shoulder under a block and tracked down the Danville runner from behind for a five-yard loss. Two plays later, Berry shot in between blockers and slung the Admiral quarterback down for a loss of 14.
It only took former Danville Admiral Braidin Baughman one play to leave his mark on the game. The senior took the handoff on the Titans' initial offensive play and made one cut outside into open space. Baughman had so much space he jogged down the sideline for the opening score.
Danville's offensive line pulled tackles and zone blocked often, which left Berry unblocked on many occasions. The senior was faster than anyone on the field Friday, and tracked down Jutayvion Beasley for a loss of three-yards on the Admirals' next offensive possession. On third and 15, Beasley had his eyes glued on the pitch from Nathan Doyle when Cohen Sanford met him in the backfield for a loss of seven yards.
'I was happy with the defense's effort, from the start of the game all the way to the last play. They clearly played with effort, we were very sound fundamentally, we ran hard to the football, and even our young guys got in and closed the game out,' said Head Football Coach Craig Yeast. title: School Board Approves Repairs For Sinkhole At Elementary School Site
description: File image. The Mercer County Board of Education agreed to pay up to $150,000 to fix a sinkhole at the site of the new home of the Mercer County Elementary Sc
content:
File image.
The Mercer County Board of Education agreed to pay up to $150,000 to fix a sinkhole at the site of the new home of the Mercer County Elementary School.
David Milan, vice president of Trace Creek Construction, which is serving as the construction manager for the project, gave the school board the bad news at their meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 17. Milam asked the board to authorize Superintendent Jason Booher to sign an agreement with Rising Sun Developing to repair the sinkhole as long as it did not exceed $150,000.
'We do not need to wait another month,' Milam said.
Everyone was under the assumption the land under the construction site was solid rock, Milam said, and Rising Sun based their original bid on that documentation.
'They found it not to be solid at 3.5 feet,' Milam said. He said the sinkhole measured 40 feet by 80 feet long by 35 feet deep, which Milam said was the equivalent of 10 in-ground swimming pools. He said the hole is not under the building.
'It is in the corner of the parking lot,' Milam said. 'It has to be fixed.'
Milam said engineers have been looking for ways to bring the cost of repairing the sinkhole down. He said they have found shotrock from previous construction, including remnants of geotech cloth.
'It appears there has been some work in the area,' Milam said. He said it was solid bedrock all the way around the sinkhole.
'The number one thing is to make sure it's put in right and put in safe,' said board member Billy Montgomery, who moved to approve paying to repair the sinkhole.
In other business, the Mercer County Board of Education approved the working budget for 2024-2025 and approved participating in the Kentucky Checkpoints program. title: Oktoberfest Returns Friday, Oct. 4
description: Prost! Volunteers Beth Wall and Janine Goldie were serving them up nice at last year's Oktoberfest (File image).
content:
Prost! Volunteers Beth Wall and Janine Goldie were serving them up nice at last year's Oktoberfest (File image).
Jeannie B. Hood of the Knights of Columbus serves up sugar waffles at Oktoberfest in 2023 (File image).
Oktoberfest returns Friday, Oct. 4, with three days of beats, brats and brews.
There will be more than 20 beers on tap as well as more than 15 food vendors offering everything from barbecue to hibachi dinners to kettle corn. Enjoy the bratwursts from the Harrodsburg Lions Club and sugar waffles from the Knights of Columbus. There will also be more than 20 crafts vendors offering everything from high fashion to handcrafted art to homemade spoon rings. Downtown businesses will be open all weekend.
TOD Transport On Demand is taking reservations to reserve a time you would like scheduled so you won't drink and drive. They will be open until 12:30 a.m. on Friday and 2 a.m. Saturday night. Call or text 859-396-6459 for more information.

description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreProst ya'll! Dennis and Nancy Ginn toasted downtown Harrodsburg at Oktoberfest in 2022. The three-day free festival returns from Frid
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore
Prost ya'll! Dennis and Nancy Ginn toasted downtown Harrodsburg at Oktoberfest in 2022. The three-day free festival returns from Friday, Oct. 4, and runs through Sunday, Oct. 6.
The Patriot Grave Marking Service at New Providence Cemetery (490 Providence Road) that was supposed to happen last Saturday was canceled because of inclement weather. The Col. James Harrod Chapter of the National Society of the Sons of the American Revolution has moved the ceremony to Saturday, Oct. 11, at 2 p.m. with the muster at 1 p.m. For more information, email Jim Stinnett at jb.stinnett66@gmail.com or call 859-612-7363. Learn more at their Facebook page, Facebook @coloneljamesharrodchaptersar.
The big event this week is Oktoberfest, which kicks off Friday, Oct. 4, starting at 5 p.m. In addition to the live music, beer and food, the Studio G Thriller Dancers will perform twice on Friday and Saturday.
Both local pumpkin patches are open. Daynabrook Greenhouse and Pumpkin Patch (135 Dunn Lane) is open Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Fridays and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sundays from noon to 6 p.m. The cost is $15 per person age 3 and up, which includes a pumpkin to take home. Concessions, tower zipline, greenhouse plants, and additional pumpkins are available at additional cost. Ride bracelets are $5 for unlimited rides For more information, visit daynabrookfarm.com or call 859-734-7863.
Devine's Corn Maze and Pumpkin Patch (623 Talmage-Mayo Road) is open Fridays from 6 to 10 p.m., Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. and Sundays from 1 to 5 p.m. Admission is free for children two and under, $10 for children aged three to 12, and $12 for everyone 13 years old and up. Group discounts are available. Each paid admission includes a pumpkin of your choice from the pumpkin patch and the activities listed above at no additional charge. To learn more, visit devinescornmaze.com or call 859-613-5066.

title: Titans Take To The Air In 35-14 Dismantling Of Marion County
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenMercer County Head Coach Craig Yeast was applauding Cornelius Mapp after throwing his fifth touchdown of the game. Mercer County Senior High School football (2-4)…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Mercer County Head Coach Craig Yeast was applauding Cornelius Mapp after throwing his fifth touchdown of the game.
Mercer County Senior High School football (2-4) traveled to Lebanon on Friday, Oct. 4, with hopes to end a two-game losing skid in the season's first meeting of District 4 opponents. Marion County (3-3) came into the game looking for their fourth straight win after three wins of more than 29 points against Washington County, Thomas Nelson and Dayton propelled the Knights' to .500.
The Titans set the tone on the kickoff as Cameron Bottoms and Jayden Sailor combined for a big hit on the return man and put the Knights back at their 10-yard line. The momentum carried into the ensuing drive, and Mercer County forced a three-and-out behind intense and physical play from the front seven. Linebackers Landon Yates and Grant Bennett were meeting Knight runners at the line of scrimmage all game if JJ Goodman or Gavinn Rodriguez hadn't already wrapped up the runner.
Marion County did an excellent job of containing the Titan offense on their opening offensive drive. Still, Cohen Sanford lowered his shoulder and powered through two Knight defenders on fourth down to keep the drive alive. Cornelius Mapp looked like a completely new player. Every ball was a tight spiral, and the junior completed all four pass attempts on the Titans' opening drive. After a penalty, the Titans moved back to the Knight 11-yard line on fourth and goal. Mapp let it fly on his first read, and Jacob Sanford snagged his first touchdown of the season in the corner of the endzone.
The Knights' run game improved on their second drive, and the Titans struggled to bring down senior ball-carrier Jonathon Marples. Six straight runs from the Knights resulted in 50 yards of offense before the option pitch caught the Titans off guard and moved Marion County into the red zone. Seniors Yates and Rodriguez stepped up and made back-to-back stops at the line of scrimmage to force a third down. Yates intercepted the third down pass attempt that followed and returned it 70 yards for a touchdown, but the play was brought back for a roughing the passer penalty. Marion County was gifted a fresh set of downs, but the Titan defense held firm and finally ended the 17-play, 82-yard drive after Bennett flattened the Knight quarterback for a four-yard loss. title: General Election On Nov. 5: Who's Running And Where To Vote
description: Here's a look at what's on the ballot for the General Election on Tuesday, Nov. 5. As for the presidential race, unless you've just emerged from 500 years of suspended animation, everyone knows former…
content:
Here's a look at what's on the ballot for the General Election on Tuesday, Nov. 5.
As for the presidential race, unless you've just emerged from 500 years of suspended animation, everyone knows former Republican president Donald Trump and Ohio Sen. J.D. Vance are running against Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz to be the next President and Vice-President of the United States of America. Also on the presidential slate are candidates Jill Stein and Samson Kpadenou of the Kentucky Party; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Nicole Shanahan and Shiva Ayyadurai and Crystal Ellis, who are running as Independents; and Chase Oliver and Mike Ter Maat, who are running for the Libertarian Party.
In the race for the U.S. Representative for the 6th Congressional District, which includes Mercer County, the Republican incumbent, Rep. Andy Barr, is facing Democratic challenger Randy Cravens.
In the race for the 55th Representative District, which includes Mercer County, the Republican incumbent, Rep. Kim King, is facing Democratic challenger Katrina A. Sexton.
There are also two constitutional amendments. The first is asking if voters are in favor of amending Sections 145 and 155 of the state constitution to prohibit persons who are not citizens of the United States from voting in Kentucky. If amended, Section 145 would read: 'Every citizen of the United States of the age of eighteen years who has resided in the state one year, and in the county six months, and the precinct in which he or she offers to vote sixty days next preceding the election, shall be a voter in said precinct and not elsewhere. No person who is not a citizen of the United States shall be allowed to vote in this state. The following persons also shall not have the right to vote:
'1. Persons convicted in any court of competent jurisdiction of treason, or felony, or bribery in an election, or of such high misdemeanor as the General Assembly may declare shall operate as an exclusion from the right of suffrage, but persons hereby excluded may be restored to their civil rights by executive pardon.
'2. Persons who, at the time of the election, are in confinement under the judgment of a court for some penal offense.
'3. Idiots and insane persons.'
If amended, Section 155 of the constitution would read:
'The provisions of Sections 145​ to 154, inclusive, shall not apply to the election of school trustees and other common school district elections. Said elections shall be regulated by the General Assembly, except as otherwise provided in this Constitution. No person who is not a citizen of the United States shall be allowed to vote in said elections.'
The second constitutional amendment would enable the General Assembly to provide financial support for the education costs of students in kindergarten through 12th grade who are outside the system of public schools.
Local Races
Mercer County voters will also asked if they are in favor of the sale of medical cannabis at a local dispensary and the operation of other cannabis businesses in Mercer County.
Six people are vying for the four seats on the Harrodsburg City Commission. In addition to incumbents Missy Wilham Banks, Charlie Mattingly, Kerry Anness and Marvin 'Bubby' Isham, Brian D. Steele and Jack L. Coleman, a former city commissioner, are running.
Until recently, only five candidates were running for the six seats on the Burgin City Council: incumbents Melinda Wofford, Jamie Keebortz, Sindicat 'Sid' Dunn and Sarah Moran, who has not served on the council before. They have been joined by three write-in candidates, including two who are already familiar with Burgin voters: former mayor and city councilman George Hensley, who filed to run as a write-in candidate on Sept. 4, and former mayor and Burgin police chief Jim Caldwell, who who filed to run as a write-in candidate on Sept. 10. In addition, Timothy Dollar filed to run as a write-in candidate on Sept. 13.
Four members of the Mercer County Board of Education—Amber Franceschi, Amy Hart, Randy Phillips and Cliff Prewitt—are running unopposed.
In the Burgin Independent School District race, Kathryn Hendershot and Bryan Vandiviere are on the ballot with incumbents Ben Bradshaw and Keith Monson.
Candidate Forums
Find out more about the candidates at the two General Election Political Candidate Forums in October.
On Monday Oct. 21, at 7 p.m., candidates for Harrodsburg City Council and State Representative for the 55th District have been invited to the Mercer County Senior High School Auditorium (1124 Moberly Road) to introduce themselves and answer six questions from voters and senior students from Burgin and Mercer County.
On Tuesday Oct. 22, at 7 p.m., candidates for Burgin City Council and Burgin Independent School District will be invited to Burgin School (400 East Main Street) to do the same.
Citizens may attend in person or listen to Hometown Radio WHBN at 1420 AM or 99.5 FM, or on Facebook. You are encouraged to submit questions for consideration to the Mercer County Democrat Party Representative Peter Taylor at peter@qx.net or to the Republican Party Representative John Holiday at jwholiday@yahoo.com no later than Tuesday, Oct. 12.
Sponsors are the Mercer Democrat and Republican Parties, the Harrodsburg Herald and Hometown Radio WHBN 1420 AM and 99.5 FM.
File image of the ballot collection vote at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
Polling Locations
There is only one drop box for mail ballots. It's located at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse (207 West Lexington Street). The hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Excused in-person absentee ballots can be left at the drop box starting Wednesday, Oct. 23 through Wednesday, Oct. 30.
In-person no-excuse absentee ballots can be cast on Thursday, Oct. 31; Friday, Nov. 1; and Saturday, Nov. 2.

title: Harrodsburg City Commission Bans Employees From Using Medical Marijuana
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Ha
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Harrodsburg City Commission voted to bar city employees from using medical marijuana. At their meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 15, the board discussed creating a personnel policy for medical cannabis. The commission had already voted to not allow distribution and sale of medical marijuana within city limits. The Mercer County Fiscal Court approved a medical cannabis option to be submitted to local voters in the upcoming General Election on Tuesday, Nov. 5.
The state legislature legalized medical cannabis in 2023. The ballot initiative would prohibit sales of medical marijuana but would not prohibit use. At Tuesday's meeting, City Attorney Norrie Currens said Harrodsburg had three options—to prohibit the use by employees, to accommodate employee use or to accommodate the use of medical marijuana for all employees except police officers. Currens said there had been no recommendation by the Kentucky League of Cities and said there had been a 50-50 split among Kentucky cities.
Medical marijuana is prescribed for people suffering from cancer, chronic pain, multiple sclerosis, post traumatic stress disorder and epilepsy. Currens said city employees would need prescriptions, and the prescriptions would be sent to the state for approval. If approved, employees would receive a card. Employees would have to have their prescriptions renewed every year. Employees who violated the drug-free workplace rules and don't have a card would face punishment.
'It's not something we can't change,' Currens said. She said the city has been revising policy over the last several years.
Currens said some city employees are in safety sensitive situations—driving vehicles and operating machinery.
'We're in a little bit of an odd space,' she told the city commission. Earlier this year, the federal government took steps to shift marijuana from its current classification as a Schedule I drug like heroin and LSD to Schedule III, alongside ketamine and some anabolic steroids. While the move would recognize the medical use of cannabis, according to PBS.com, it would not legalize marijuana for recreational use.
'We're in very uncharted waters,' Currens said. 'We don't have a clear path.'
Commissioner Marvin 'Bubby' Isham moved to prohibit it. Isham said every city employee except those who work at city hall operated with equipment where people could get hurt. Mayor Bob Williams seconded, and the motion passed unanimously. Currens said she will draft the new policy, which will be enacted at a later meeting. title: Harrodsburg To Notify Residents About Lead Service Line Inventory
description: File image. The City of Harrodsburg will soon be sending out notices to residents about the city's efforts to inventory—and eventually eliminate
content:
File image.
The City of Harrodsburg will soon be sending out notices to residents about the city's efforts to inventory—and eventually eliminate—any lead service lines.
The Harrodsburg Board of Commissioners was apprised about the city's effort at their regular meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 28.
While there are a variety of ways lead may come in contact with drinking water in a home, the government is primarily concerned with the service line, the pipe that runs from the water main to your home.
Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard said Harrodsburg, like every other community in the United States, is under a federal mandate to look for lead service lines. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates there are more than 9.2 million lead service lines serving water to properties across the United States. President Joe Biden has set a goal of replacing all lead service lines.
'We literally have to look to every single connection to every single house,' Maynard said. 'We are confident there is zero lead line under the ground.'
City workers are currently mapping water meters. Maynard said they hope to have it finished by next year. She estimated 50 percent of lines on the city's side and 80 percent on the customer's side had been mapped, but the city was still waiting on information from the PVA's office.
Image: EPA.gov.
Lead has been used for plumbing for thousands of years. The Latin word for lead, 'plumbum,' is the root for the English word 'plumbing.' However, lead is a known neurotoxin that can cause behavior and learning problems, hyperactivity, slowed growth, hearing problems and anemia in children, according to the EPA. For pregnant women, it can cause reduced growth of the fetus and premature birth. For all adults, lead can cause cardiovascular effects, increased blood pressure and hypertension as well as decreased kidney function and reproductive problems in both men and women. The use of lead for most residential plumbing was phased out in 1988.
'If it's after 1988, we can automatically eliminate it,' Maynard told the commissioners Monday.
Once the inventory is completed, the city has 10 years to eliminate all lead lines. They would have to submit updates every year on their efforts.
Maynard said residents whose lines the city was not sure of would get a letter.
'We're just looking for service lines,' Maynard said. She directed residents to epa.gov, which has full details on the federal government's efforts to eliminate lead lines. She said the city will have a live map on the city website so people can search for their address.
Maynard also advised the public that the Mercer County Fiscal Court raised the 911 fee on meters from $1.75 to $3.50 a month. The increase will go into effect Nov. 1 but will not be included in this month's bill, she said. Residents can expect to see the increase on next month's bill. title: It's time to move on
description: Austin Cocanougher Contributing Writer Mark Stoops is the single most successful coach in the history of Kentucky football. He has accomplished more in Lexington than many ever thought possible.…
content:
Austin Cocanougher
Contributing Writer
Mark Stoops is the single most successful coach in the history of Kentucky football. He has accomplished more in Lexington than many ever thought possible. Beyond having multiple 10-win seasons, taking UK to eight straight bowl games, and creating a real talent pipeline from our program to the NFL, perhaps no feat of Stoop's is more impressive than his completely changing the culture around football in the Bluegrass State.
No longer is Wildcat football a distant afterthought to the basketball program. No longer is Wildcat football the laughingstock of the South Eastern Conference. And no longer does the football program have to beg for attendance, donations, or resources to compete. Thanks to Stoops, the University of Kentucky is now an actual SEC football environment- on and off the field. Whether it be from the relationships he built with fans and donors, the blue-collar culture of toughness he brought to the locker room, or the dynamic recruiting he was able to instill, almost no coach could have taken Kentucky from where they were to where they are now. For that, Wildcat fans owe Mark Stoops all the praise and thanks in the world.
However, with success comes expectations, and to put it simply, Stoops has raised the expectations for the football program. While that is generally a good thing, he may end up being a victim of his success after a multi-year decline in on-field output. When Stoops arrived in Lexington, fans would have been thrilled with five to seven-win seasons and winning a bowl game once every two or three years. However, now that we have tasted what it's like to be very good, most fans are no longer okay with mediocrity. Is that fair to Stoops? Probably not. Is it the reality of being an SEC program? Absolutely.
Furthermore, it is not just the case that we have plateaued as a program and failed to make the next big jump. In general, we are actually on a multi-year regression. Despite recruiting at a higher level than ever, our on-field output is decreasing. Stoops' team has failed to generate consistent offense under four different offensive coordinators (in the last five years), has reversed their win streaks over South Carolina, Florida and Vanderbilt, and has generally just played undisciplined football. The things that made Stoops' early teams special–physical team ball, tough blocking, blue-collar mentality, work ethic and discipline–have been tough to find in recent years.
Beyond this, Stoops still needs to improve in the areas he has committed to improving over the past four seasons. Our offensive line gets weaker every week. There is little progress among wide receivers in their skill development. Our pass rush is rarely aggressive or effective. We still need to hire a full-time special teams coach. Last but not least, we are consistently committing more severe penalties than our opponents. Not only are the Cats regressing on the things they used to do well, but they need to improve in the areas they still need to improve in the areas they had not.
For these reasons, in addition to an overall lack of 'fight' the team shows every week, it is time for Kentucky to move on. The best of Stoops' time is behind us. It is clear that Stoops no longer has the drive, hunger, and mental willpower it takes to do his job at a high level. While we can point fingers at NIL, the transfer portal, and all the other changes taking place in college athletics, at the end of the day, it comes down to coach Stoops. It is time for a new voice, decision maker, and leader in Kentucky football's big seat.
With all that being said, fans would be naive not to recognize and appreciate the greatness that would be exiting our program. The man is the winningest coach in our history. But beyond that, he truly built what our program is today: an SEC underdog with the resources, name brand, and foundation to compete at a high level. For years, Stoops punched above his weight, out-recruited teams with double our resources, and out-coached several future Hall-of-Famers. While we owe Stoops a statue in his honor and a spot in our hearts, it is probably time that both sides move on from what has been the best coaching relationship in our program's history.
After a majorly disappointing season, off the backs of multiple underwhelming years, it is time to move on from Coach Stoops as the head coach of the Kentucky Wildcats football team. While he may be a great man and a historically good coach, you must always know when to move on. Of all times now, when the fanbase is more united than ever, has embraced the turning of the page, and is embracing the feeling of change in all areas of their sports fandom, it would be the perfect time for just that: a change.

title: Mercer earns redemption in battle of the Titans
description: April Ellis Herald Staff The Mercer County Senior High boys basketball team is 3-0 after redeeming themselves with a victory over Collins High School. Last season, Collins defeated the Titans by four…
content:
April Ellis
Herald Staff
The Mercer County Senior High boys basketball team is 3-0 after redeeming themselves with a victory over Collins High School. Last season, Collins defeated the Titans by four on their own home court. This time, after several lead changes throughout the game, Mercer narrowly pulled out a 54-50 win.
Senior Trevor Ellis scored the first points of the game, hitting the front side of two free throws. The big man was sent to the line several times during the game, shooting 11 foul shots, but he could have been sent several more times.
Early on, both teams struggled with shooting but tried to overcompensate with defense pressure. Shooters were blocked and every post shot was a battle. As it became more apparent, whistles were few and far between, and defenders became more and more aggressive.
Junior Jackson Doughty took his first charge of the night, but Mercer could not convert it to points. Collins pulled down a couple of offensive rebounds and jumped ahead 4-1.
Junior Kaleb Murray kicked the ball out to the corner while being fouled during Mercer's 54-50 win over Collins on Saturday, Dec. 7. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Casey Roberts)
After Collins added another bucket, 6-1, with 3:35 left to play in the first quarter, Head Coach Keith Adkins called a time-out to express his displeasure with his team. It took the Titans a few minutes to respond, but they finally did when Doughty hit a 3-point shot and closed the gap 6-4. Neither team scored again, and the first quarter ended 6-4 in Collins' favor.
The second quarter started better for the Titans when senior Hagan Preston hit a 3-point shot just minutes into the game. Ellis grabbed a rebound, which Senior Jadon King converted to a basket, and Mercer finally retook the lead 9-6. Preston dropped another 3-point shot, 12-6, and forced Collins to take their first time out.
With 1:56 left in the second quarter, Cole Harbin hit a 3-point shot reclaiming the lead for Collins. Mercer fought back with under a minute to play and senior Andrew Tatum hit a 3-point shot from the right wing. Collins put in the front end of two shots from the foul line to tie the game at 15. As the remaining seconds ticked off the first half, Doughty missed a 3-point shot; Ellis got the rebound and missed the putback, but was fouled hard before the buzzer. Ellis went to the free throw line thinking he would shoot, but the referees walked off the court. The Titan faithful expressed their displeasure on the lack of call from the stands.
To start the third quarter, Ellis had two quick baskets off a put-back and a layup and the Titans were back on top, 19-15. The game was very physical, and both teams were frustrated. Each side struggled with turnovers and every shot under the basket was a battle. Preston swooped in to block a shot, but Collins maintained possession, hit the basket, and retook the lead after two foul shots, 20-19.
Tatum and Doughty combined for five points after Gaither hit a 3-pointer for Collins and the lead switched again halfway through the third quarter.
Doughty stepped up, hit a trey from the corner, and hustled down the court to draw the charge and give Mercer the ball back. Preston took it down the floor and found King under the basket, 29-15.
Mercer did not look their best in spots, but a few brilliant plays of unselfish passing showed why they are one of the 12th region favorites. Out on the wing, Tatum blocked a Collins 3-pointer out of bounds. After the inbounds play, he was pulled to the ground on a defensive rebound and lost the ball as Collins players piled on top. Sophomore Mijaia Dunn dove on the floor in the middle of the scramble and ended up with the ball. Dunn found Preston, who connected with Ellis, who somehow kept the ball inbound. Ellis, with the one-handed pass, hit King who cut through the lane for the layup.
Preston pulled down the offensive rebound and hit the put back shot. Mercer led 38-30, but Collins hit a long 3-pointer at the buzzer to end it 38-33 going into the fourth quarter.
The fourth quarter started with a couple of unforced turnovers, and Adkins called for a time-out to refocus his team. A questionable call on an out-of-bounds ball gave Collins possession, and they scored a layup and cut the Titans' lead to three points, 38-35.
Mercer moved the ball perfectly across the floor to find junior Kaleb Murray open for the uncontested shot. Murray had another basket on the next possession. Mercer has to find a way to stop the turnovers and repeat that kind of plays to be successful as they head into the more challenging part of their schedule.
With 3:38 left to play in the game, Mercer only led by one, 44-43. Tatum fought through for a bucket with an assist from Ellis. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Kentucky Owl, Whiskey Brand With Mercer Ties, Declares Bankruptcy
description: Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A legendary whiskey brand with deep connections to Mercer County has declared bankruptcy. Kentucky Owl Bourbon, a premium blended whiskey which…
content:
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
A legendary whiskey brand with deep connections to Mercer County has declared bankruptcy.
Kentucky Owl Bourbon, a premium blended whiskey which can retail for hundreds of dollars and sell for even more on the collectible market, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy along with Stoli Group USA, according to Reuters.com.
Both companies are U.S.-based subsidiaries of the Luxembourg-based Stoli Group, which is not filing for bankruptcy, according to Reuters.
The two companies are seeking bankruptcy protection from a Dallas, Texas-based court to deal with $84 million in debt, according to Reuters.
Kentucky Owl was founded by C.M. Dedman in 1879 and operated until 1916, when the distillery was closed due to Prohibition. In 2014, Dixon Dedman, C.M. Dedman's great-great-grandson, revived the brand, releasing the first 1,250 bottles of small-batch blended bourbon. Stoli Group, the distributor and manufacturer of Stolichnaya and other Stoli-branded products, purchased Kentucky Owl from Dedman in 2017. While the blended whiskeys—bourbon and rye—Dedman created at Kentucky Owl remain hot items on the collector's market, he left the company in 2021. In 2023, Dixon introduced another line of blended whiskeys, which are sold under the 2XO label in partnership with Prestige Beverage Group.
The 2017 sale of Kentucky Owl attracted considerable attention here in Mercer County, especially after Stoli announced plans to build Kentucky Owl Park, a $150 million state-of-the-art distillery and tourist destination in Bardstown. Stoli had ambitious plans, including pyramid-shaped distillery buildings, a luxury hotel and a train station. At the time, many local residents wondered why Stoli was not building the Kentucky Owl distillery here in Mercer County.
However, despite breaking ground in 2018, the project faced significant delays, with only limited progress made on the site, according to thebourbonflight.com.
Stoli has been embroiled in a decades-long legal battle with the Russian government, which is seeking to reclaim ownership of vodka brands that were privatized in the 1990s, according to Reuters.
Russia attempted to bring what Stoli's lawyers call 'politically motivated' criminal charges against Stoli Group's owner, Yuri Shefler, and seize Stoli's assets, according to Reuters.
Earlier this year, the Russian government took possession of Stoli's last two distilleries in that country, which are worth approximately $100 million, according to court documents. The company also suffered a data breach and ransomware attack in August that caused severe disruptions to its global business, forcing the company to rely on manual bookkeeping for critical business activities, according to Reuters.
Dixon Dedman's family owned and operated one of Mercer County's biggest attractions, the Beaumont Inn, for more than a century. In 2022, they sold the Beaumont to relatives. title: Lady Titans Dominate Second Half In Win Over Burgin
description: The Mercer County Lady Titans (2-4) and Burgin Lady Bulldogs (1-4) met for the first time this season on Monday, Dec. 16, on Chris Souder Court. Mercer County came into the game on a three game losing…
content:
The Mercer County Lady Titans (2-4) and Burgin Lady Bulldogs (1-4) met for the first time this season on Monday, Dec. 16, on Chris Souder Court. Mercer County came into the game on a three game losing streak, in which they never surpassed 50 points. Burgin on the other hand had picked up their first win, a 66-13 victory over Oneida Baptist, just two days prior.
Mercer jumped out to a quick 5-0 lead after a 3-pointer from eighth-grader Annie Releford and a tough basket at the rim from Reese Ransdell. Burgin struggled to find open shots early on and scored their first four points at the foul line. Mercer senior Kate Carlton grabbed an offensive rebound, and spun directly into a shot off of the glass to maintain Mercer's lead. Burgin began to take advantage of the Titans defense not getting back quickly and s enior Gabby Thompson finished a breakaway for her first two points.
Izzie Carlton made this basket during Mercer's 75-36 win over Burgin on Mon­day, Dec. 16. Carlton finished the game with 22 points, 10 rebounds and five steals. (Image: The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren).
Burgin seemed determined to win the game after one quarter of play, but the points weren't on the board, and they trailed 10-6 after one. Senior Jemma Jenkins made a shot at the close of the quarter, but the buzzer sounded just before she released.
Ashton Lester avoided Annie Releford at the top of the key. (Image: The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren).
During the last two minutes of the first quarter and in the second, the game became rather physical. Both teams were pressing in the halfcourt and jumping passes and every player on the court wanted to get involved in loose ball situations, it was ugly. It seemed Mercer's Alexa Wade spent more time on the floor than her feet. Burgin's Kynlee Sexton was able to find calm in all the madness, grab an offensive rebound, and go straight back up for two off of the glass. Wade retaliated with a strong finish at the rim and an and-one, but Thompson drained a long two and Lester nailed a 3-pointer from the top of the key to keep the Lady Bulldogs in contention. title: Citing Higher Costs, Fire Protection Board Increases Property Tax Rate
description: Members of the Mercer County Fire Protection District participated in a drill in 2022. (Image: Mercer County Fire Protection District Facebook page.) The Mercer County Fire Protection District is…
content:
Members of the Mercer County Fire Protection District participated in a drill in 2022. (Image: Mercer County Fire Protection District Facebook page.)
The Mercer County Fire Protection District is raising the tax rate on real estate and tangible property. Chief Glenn Phillips from the Mercer County Fire Protection District informed the Mercer County Fiscal Court at their meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 14.
Phillips said the fire district is raising their tax rate from 80 cents per thousand dollars in assessed value to to $1 per thousand dollars in assessed value. For a property valued at $100,000, Phillips said that will raise the property owner's tax bill fro $80 to $100. The tax increase will go into effect when tax bills go out later this year.
Phillips said the tax increase is due to increased costs. He said the district purchased a tanker in 2020 for $250,000. Phillips said the bid for a new truck came in at $470,000. He said the new admissions standards will add another $80,000 to cost. In addition, many other costs including air packs have doubled.
'This is a have-to case,' Phillips said. He said anything attached to the fire department is doubling in price.
'It's not something we want to do, it's something we have to do,' Phillips said.
Magistrate Tim Darland asked about a firetruck that had flipped.
'I know you are the scapegoat,' Darland said. He noted he had to buy a new truck for his personal business and asked if the district had made any cuts.
'The taxpayers are going to ask us,' Darland said.
Phillips said drivers are trained. He said the district has 10 stations with 100 people. Phillips said it takes a 'big chunk of change' to run the department.
The Mercer County Fire Protection District is a taxing district that was organized in 1986 and is governed by a seven-member board of trustees. County firefighters handle about 700 calls per year on average, not just firefighting services but also vehicle accidents, medical emergencies, rescues and hazardous materials spills. The board of directors meets on the second Monday of each month at 6 p.m. at McAfee Station (2805 Louisville Road).

title: Bulldogs battle with Taylor County
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Bulldogs boys basketball team (2-12) battled with the high flying Taylor County Cardinals (14-3) on Saturday, Jan. 18. The Cardinals…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Bulldogs boys basketball team (2-12) battled with the high flying Taylor County Cardinals (14-3) on Saturday, Jan. 18. The Cardinals entered Jack Coleman Sr. Gymnasium on a five game winning streak and ranked second in the 5th Region.
Burgin was able to fight for positioning and earn open shots early, but they just weren't falling according to Head Coach Todd Claunch. Taylor County on the other hand, played with tremendous speed, and attempted a remarkable 70 shots throughout the game. Multiple put backs gave the Cardinals an early advantage.
Micah Mayes drained a turnaround fadeaway, which seems to be becoming his signature move, but the Bulldogs trailed 29-13 with 5:20 remaining in the first half. After missed shots allowed Taylor County to take an early lead, Burgin became too eager to make up for the deficit. The Bulldogs attempt to play at the same pace as the Cardinals led to some turnovers in the back court, and some easy buckets for the opponents. Taylor County was strong in the back court and some of Burgin's turnovers stemmed just from physical play. Junior point guard Landen Sexton made a quick jump pass to Hudson Taylor for a three.
Both teams sprinted up and down the court missing threes for a couple minutes, but to close out the first half, Mayes forced a turnover at the top of the key and finished strong on the other end. After two quarters, Burgin trailed 46-18. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Richard Womack
description: Richard Muse Womack, 97, of Birmingham, Alabama, died Wednesday, Jan. 15, 2025. Dick was born in Memphis, Tennessee, and raised on the family farm in Harrodsburg. After his high school graduation, he…
content:
Richard Muse Womack, 97, of Birmingham, Alabama, died Wednesday, Jan. 15, 2025.
Dick was born in Memphis, Tennessee, and raised on the family farm in Harrodsburg.
After his high school graduation, he joined the Navy in July 1945 and served until July 1946. He then entered the University of Kentucky, where he was a member of SAE Fraternity. He graduated with a degree in Pre-Veterinary Science. He later went on to become a life member of the university's alumni association, and served as president of the alumni board. He married Nancy Carol Brewer of Mayfield and they returned to Harrodsburg to farm for a few years. Dick then went to work for the Rain and Hail Insurance Bureau. After a few years, he joined the Travelers Insurance Company as a property/casualty field representative, and the family moved to Louisville. In 1966, he was transferred to Birmingham, Alabama, as office manager. Another transfer came in 1968, this time as manager of the Nashville, Tennessee, office. The family moved back to Birmingham in 1972, when Dick was offered the position of President/COO of McGriff, Seibels & Williams Insurance Agency. He later became chairman, growing the company from 32 employees to 300.
After selling his ownership in McGriff Seibels, he took a position as a consultant with the St. Paul Insurance Companies. He retired, but continued working privately as a consultant to the insurance industry on the hiring and training of salespeople and agency succession planning.
Dick was active in many civic organizations, and accepted leadership roles in most: co-chair of United Way, chairman of the Heart Fund, past board member for the Better Business Bureau, Chamber of Commerce, Boy Scouts, Junior Achievement, the Tip-Off Club and Kirkwood by the River. He remained active in the Birmingham Rotary Club into his 90s. He was a long-time active member of Independent Presbyterian Church, serving in many leadership roles over the years.
Following Nancy's death in 1993 after 43 years of marriage, Dick was blessed to meet and marry Eleanor Robinson Cox, with whom he enjoyed 28 years of happiness. Dick and Eleanor attended both St. Luke's Episcopal Church and Independent Presbyterian after their marriage.
Dick was predeceased by his first wife, Nancy Carol Brewer, and his granddaughter, Caitlin Brewer Bowles.
He is survived by his wife, Eleanor; his son, Greg (Susan); and his daughter, Rebecca Bowles (Robert). He is also survived by his stepdaughters, Virginia Love (Bill), Eleanor Roberson (Darrell), and Laura Colebeck (Elliott), as well as his grandchildren, Anne Sanford (Will), Joshua Bowles, and Abby Nevins (Holder), and four great-grandchildren.
A celebration of life will be held Tuesday, Jan. 28, 2025, at Independent Presbyterian Church on Highland Avenue in Birmingham.
The family will greet friends at 10 a.m., followed by a service at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, donations to a favorite charity would be appreciated.

title: Burgin City Council Tables Wet Ordinance For Another Month
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin City Council tabled the wet ordinance until next month. At their first meeting of 2025, the city council—including new
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin City Council tabled the wet ordinance until next month.
At their first meeting of 2025, the city council—including newly elected members Sarah Moran and former mayor and city councilman George Hensley—held off on giving first reading to the alcohol ordinance. Burgin voters elected to go wet, 320 to 228, in the 2024 General Election.
'I have some concerns about it,' said Councilwoman Melinda Wofford at the meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 14.
Wofford said the language in the ordinance said sales and manufacturing.
'I didn't think what our citizens voted on,' Wofford said. 'Citizens didn't vote on manufacturing.'
Burgin City Attorney John Wood said he would look over the ordinance again.
'If it's not clear to the citizens I think it may become an issue,' said Councilwoman Moran.
On Tuesday night, Wood said he wasn't sure there was any manufacturing section in the ordinance. He said he could revise the ordinance.
Wofford said she was also concerned about the role of the ABC administrator, including the possibility for conflicts of interest. Councilman Jamie Keebortz said it would be impossible to pick someone who wouldn't have a conflict of interest in a small town like Burgin.
Councilmembers also expressed concerns about possible locations, with Hensley asking how close could alcohols sales be to a school or a church.
'We can't override state law.' Mayor Joe Monroe said. 'We have to go by state law.'
'I've got more offers for my lot over here in the middle of town than I ever had since the election,' Councilman Hensley said.
Wood said he agreed with the council on removing language about manufacturing.
'There may be exceptions even if the city isn't wet,' Wood said, noting brewpubs like Lemons Mill Brewery in Harrodsburg.
Wofford and Moran asked to wait until Wood had reworked the ordinance.
It will the be Kentucky Alcoholic Beverage Control, not the City of Burgin, that will issue liquor licenses. The Harrodsburg Herald reached out to Alcoholic Beverage Control for clarification back in December.
'Businesses can apply for a license starting 60 days after an election is certified,' said Kristin Voskuhl, executive director of communications and public outreach at the Public Protection Cabinet.
'A licensee can sell as soon as their license is issued,' Voskuhl said via email.
Once a territory is voted wet, prohibition ceases 60)days after the election is certified by the County Clerk, according to state law. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Greyson Evans Is New Director Of Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority
description: Greyson Evans has been named as the new executive director of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority. (Image submitted). The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Ind
content:
Greyson Evans has been named as the new executive director of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority. (Image submitted).
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority has hired Greyson Evans as its new executive director. At a special-called meeting on Friday, Jan. 24, the board voted unanimously to hire Evans, who currently works for Bluegrass Area Development District, effective Tuesday, Feb. 18, pending preemployment screening.
At the request of the Industrial Development Authority, the Mercer County Fiscal Court and the Harrodsburg City Commission voted to hire Evans at $120,000 per year plus benefits. The county and city will split Evans' salary and benefits. He will be a county employee who reports to the Industrial Development Authority. All three bodies will have to approve any raises Evans may earn.
John Trisler, chairman of the Industrial Development Authority board of directors, explained that Evans will be employed and paid through the county. Trisler congratulated Evans.
'We are excited about the opportunity to continue working with you,' Trisler said.
'I'm excited to get to know him,' said board member Jason Booher, who also moved to hire Evans. 'He's going to do a tremendous job for Mercer County.'
Evans thanked the board.
'Hopefully, we'll see some really exciting things happen,' Evans said.
Evans replaces Mike Willand, who resigned as executive-director of the Industrial Development Authority earlier this month. Willand, a former executive with Wausau Paper, had served as executive-director since 2018.
'We appreciate Mike Willand's service to our community,' Trisler told the Harroldsburg Herald. 'We wish him the very best in his future plans.'
Evans currently lives in Lexington with his wife and four-month-old daughter. The family is looking at relocating to Mercer County, he said.
Evans is a native of Stokesdale, North Carolina. He earned his bachelor's degree in politics at Centre College and a master's of public administration from the University of Kentucky Martin School. In August 2024, Evans earned the Certified Economic Developer designation from the International Economic Development Institute at the University of Oklahoma.
He began his professional career in 2017, working for the Federal Emergency Management Agency as a grants assistant with the UK Mitigation Grants Program in 2017. In 2019, he joined Bluegrass ADD as a community development specialist, working his way up to community planning manager, where he played a role in the development of the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park.
Last year, Evans was one of the federal, state and local officials who celebrated the allocation of $11.5 million in state funding for the development of the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park. The allocation is part of more than $22 million in funding to purchase a 958-acre site from with Louisville Gas and Electric Company and Kentucky Utilities Company and develop it into an industrial park.
'He's been there through all the hurdles we've had to go through the past few years,' Mercer County Jude-Executive Sarah Steele said at a fiscal court hearing on Tuesday. Steele told the Harrodsburg Herald they were waiting on a closing date for the site.
On Friday, Evans called the Wilkinson Farm 'a nationally competitive site.'
'I am honored to bring employer to provide opportunities for young Mercer County residents for generations,' he told the board. Evans also invited community residents for their input.
'The Industrial Development Authority's doors are open,' Evans said.
He will be expected to take the lead on the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park and other efforts by the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority to further economic development in Mercer County.
'Our focus is on creating additional good paying jobs and the revenue that comes into our city and county government,' Trisler said. 'Jobs first help our community from an economic standpoint.'
Trisler, a former Mercer County judge-executive, said Evans would be a good fit leading the Wilkinson Farm project as well as the authority's other objectives.
'He will provide leadership on any kind of activities related to this plus any other industry in the community,' Trisler said.
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority meets on the third Tuesday of the month at 11:30 a.m. Their next meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, Feb. 18, at 11:30 a.m. at the Diamond Point Welcome Center (488 Price Avenue).

title: Burgin Celebrates Homecoming With One Win, One Loss, Plenty Of Bulldog Spirit
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenBurgin's Gabby Thompson drives the ball to the net during the Bulldogs' homecoming
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Burgin's Gabby Thompson drives the ball to the net during the Bulldogs' homecoming victory over Shelby County.
Burgin Independent tipped off its 2025 Homecoming festivities on Saturday, Feb. 1, with a fantastic performance from the Lady Bulldogs basketball team (8-11). The Lady Bulldogs, led by Head Coach Keith Monson, built a strong lead early behind excellent defense and three-point shooting, and never looked back after gaining a double digit lead on the Head Coach Scott Elder's Shelby County Lady Rockets (4-16), eventually earning a 59-46 win.
Hayley Hurst dominated the opening moments of the game; the junior forced two Lady Rocket turnovers, grabbed three rebounds and drained the Lady Bulldogs' opening three-pointer to give them a 6-1 advantage. Junior Ashton Lester's physicality and willingness to initiate contact meant she got to the foul line with ease. She made one at the line to give the Bulldogs a 7-1 lead. Burgin was shining as a defensive unit and Jemma Jenkins and Kynlee Sexton forced turnovers on back-to-back possessions. Seconds later, freshman Jocelyn Stanley swished a corner three, and the Lady Rockets called a time-out, trailing 10-1. Burgin forced four straight turnovers to close out the opening quarter, and Gabby Thompson drained a three in the final moments, putting Burgin up 13-3 after one quarter.
Sexton kept the Lady Bulldogs' momentum going in the second quarter with two foul shots and a steal, and Thompson dropped a long range jumper, moving the score to 17-5. Shelby responded to the Lady Bulldogs' physicality and were fouling hard, not to mention delivering blows underneath the basket on the offensive end, where they were making some tough lay-ups, and slowly climbing back into the game. Burgin led 17-11 with 3:35 remaining in the first half. Just as the second quarter started, Sexton and Thompson made clutch shots to keep Burgin ahead. Thompson made two at the charity stripe and Sexton swished a long range two despite having a hand in her face. Hurst jumped in front of another pass in the final moments of the first half, and Stanley earned a trip to the stripe, making one in the closing moments of the first half. At halftime, the Lady Bulldogs led 24-13.
The Lady Bulldogs gradually allowed Shelby County to climb back into the game, until Thompson answered. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Titans thrash defending region champs
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County Titans (16-7) faced the reigning 12th Region champions, and the current third-ranked team in the region, Pulaski County (15…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Titans (16-7) faced the reigning 12th Region champions, and the current third-ranked team in the region, Pulaski County (15-7), on Saturday, Feb. 8, at the MCSHS Gymnasium. After a 50-48 overtime loss to West Jessamine on Monday, Feb. 3, The Titans got back on track with back-to-back wins over 12th Region opponents Burgin and Rockcastle County. The Maroons on the other hand, were on a seven game win-streak that included a win over Caverna, a 29-point thrashing of East Jessamine and a 79-45 win over Rockcastle County.
Mercer's matchup with Pulaski County is the first step into a gauntlet of a five game stretch. Over nine days, the Titans face the Maroons, Russell County, Madison Central, Region 10 favorite George Rogers Clark and Region 7 powerhouse Ballard.
The Titans got behind early after consecutive misses from point guard Hagan Preston. The pace proved to be the issue, as the Titans became more explosive, baskets came with ease. 12th Region Player of the Year favorite Trevor Ellis made two foul shots, and finished at the rim for his first basket on the following possession. Preston kept the offense moving at a fast pace, and drove under the basket before losing his defender with a fake pass and scoring his first basket. Seconds later, senior Andrew Tatum delivered a three that killed Pulaski's momentum and forced an early timeout from the Maroon bench. The Titans' offense got a bit sloppy with their ball movement and Pulaski made them pay in the closing moments of the first quarter, but Mercer led after one, 13-10.
The Titans' offense was a mix of sloppy passes, lazy dribbling and bad shots early in the second quarter, and the inconsistency led to a 3 minute or more scoring drought from Mercer. In contrast to the rest of the season, Ellis was golden from the charity stripe, and made two shots to give the Titans an 18-16 lead. The bank was open for Pulaski and they responded with a long range three, but Preston retook the lead in seconds with a nifty reverse layup. Seconds later Kaleb Murray stood his ground and drew a charge call that fired up the crowd. Pulaski attacked the rim in the final moments of the first half, reclaiming a 21-20 lead as both teams went to the locker room. title: Titan academic team excels at Governor's Cup
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County High School academic team recently achieved a success the school hasn't in nearly two decades. Winning A District Governor's…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County High School academic team recently achieved a success the school hasn't in nearly two decades. Winning A District Governor's Cup is a rare achievement, in fact, Mercer County has only won three other District competitions this century. The Scotties dominated the turn of the century, winning three times between 1998-2001, and again in 2004. The last group of Mercer County students to claim a District Governor's Cup came in 2007 when Cynthia Russell was leading the program. Alumni Andy Smith, Keita Uchida, John McMaine, Caleb Berger and Eli Edwards were some key members of the last Titan academic team to achieve a District Governor's Cup.
What sets the 2024-2025 Academic Team apart is the manner in which they won the competition. The Titan group of quick recall members: Kate Carlton, Grayson Guerra, Sage Markham, Will Dean, Sydney Putnam, Taylor Curtsinger, Cameron Roution, Daphne Mullins, Aiden Matthews and Henry Lanham recently completed the district tournament without losing a single match.
The Titans compete in a district with Anderson, Washington and Woodford County's and finished in second place each of the first two seasons of Dr. Ekambaram Elumalai's tenure as coach. Having been with the group through consecutive second place finishes, Dr. Eka knew this group of seniors was capable of lifting the trophy.
'I requested to be the district champs before they graduated. It was an exciting moment for me when they became district champs. It's all their effort, and all the credits go to my graduating senior group,' said Dr. Eka. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald.
