title: City Government Class On March 24
description: File image. A class on how local government is supposed to work has been moved to Monday, March 24. Representatives from the Kentucky League of Ci
content:
File image.
A class on how local government is supposed to work has been moved to Monday, March 24.
Representatives from the Kentucky League of Cities will present 'Government 101,' covering the basics of local city governance from 5 to 7 p.m. in the auditorium at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road).
KLC personnel services attorney Michael Simon and municipal law attorney Megan Griffith will give the presentation.
At the Harrodsburg City Commission's regular meeting on Monday, Feb 10, City Attorney Norrie Currens said the presentation had been moved.
The program is designed to ask questions which have been raised about the city government, and especially about the 2023 hiring of Stacey Maynard as the city's chief administrative officer. Currens said the commission, which consists of the commissioners and the mayor—are considered a legislative body under state law. She said the city previously employed a chief administrative officer which had gone vacant until the city commission voted to hire Maynard.
Anyone with questions is asked to reach out to members of the city commission, to Maynard or to any supervisors if they had questions.
The Kentucky League of Cities is a is a non-stock, nonprofit membership association serving more than 370 Kentucky cities and municipal agencies. According to its website, the league provides cities, leaders and employees with services including legislative advocacy, legal services, community consulting, training and online training, policy development and research, and more. The organization also provides enterprise services such as financing options for cities, and the Kentucky League of Cities Insurance Services insures more municipal clients than any other insurance carrier in Kentucky.
The commission meets on the second and fourth Mondays of the month at noon at Harrodsburg City Hall (208 South Main Street). The phone number is 859-734-2383. For more information, visit online at harrodsburgcity.org.
'Government 101' presented by the Kentucky League of Cities on Monday, March 24, from 5 to 7 p.m. in the auditorium at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road). title: Harrodsburg Refers Complaint Against HPD To State Police
content:
File image.
A citizen's complaint against the Harrodsburg Police Department has been referred to the Kentucky State Police.
Last week, the Harrodsburg City Commission voted to hire a law firm to handle a citizen's complaint against the Harrodsburg Police Department.
The Harrodsburg Herald filed an open records request for information pertaining to the complaint, and received a reply from Harrodsburg City Clerk Shavonna Huffman on Friday, Feb. 14.
In an email, Huffman said the requested record was not being produced pursuant to state law, citing Kentucky Revised Statutes 61.878(1)(h).
'The subject matter of the citizens complaint has just been referred to the Kentucky State Police,' Huffman wrote in the email. 'The Kentucky State Police has not yet had an opportunity to conduct interviews pertaining to the complaint. Premature release of the complaint would impede the state police investigation.'
The Harrodsburg Herald reached out to the Kentucky State Police, but has not received a response.
At their regular meeting on Monday, Feb. 10, the city commission voted unanimously to authorize Mayor Bob Williams to sign an agreement with the law firm.
HPD Chief Scott Elder had no comment. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Earth Breeze To Locate $5.9 Million Facility In Harrodsburg, Provide 226 New Jobs
description: Screenshot. Earth Breeze, a producer of environmentally friendly laundry detergent sheets, is locating a facility in Harrodsburg. The facility is valued at roughly $5.9 million and will create 226…
content:
Screenshot.
Earth Breeze, a producer of environmentally friendly laundry detergent sheets, is locating a facility in Harrodsburg. The facility is valued at roughly $5.9 million and will create 226 jobs.
Gov. Andy Beshear made the announcement earlier today.
'We're excited to welcome Earth Breeze to our New Kentucky Home,' Gov. Beshear said in a press release. 'This project will create quality jobs and opportunities for the Harrodsburg community, and I we can't wait to see this innovative company succeed.'
The new 81,250-square-foot facility will handle multiple aspects of the Earth Breeze production process, including the blending of its proprietary eco-friendly formulation, drying and processing, cutting and packaging, order fulfillment operations, quality control laboratory testing and research and development. The 226 new positions will span various skill levels and departments, from facility director and production operators to quality control specialists and planning/administrative associates and managers, according to the state.
'We are incredibly grateful to the state of Kentucky for their outstanding support and partnership throughout this journey,' said Ben Smith, Chief Operating Officer of Earth Breeze, in a press release. 'From the very beginning, the state has demonstrated a clear commitment to fostering growth and innovation, helping us navigate every step with care and efficiency. Kentucky's strong workforce, business-friendly environment and collaborative spirit have made it the perfect home for Earth Breeze. This investment is not just about expanding our operations—it's about building a sustainable future together with the Harrodsburg community. We are excited to bring new opportunities, create quality jobs and be part of Kentucky's continued economic success.'
Earth Breeze was founded in 2019, according to a state press release. The company offers clean laundry without harsh chemicals like optical brighteners, artificial dyes, parabens, phthalates or preservatives. Made with 100 percent concentrated cleaning ingredients in a sheet that quickly dissolves, Earth Breeze is available at many leading retailer locations and online at earthbreeze.com.
For every order, Earth Breeze donates laundry detergent to shelters and disaster relief organizations. The company has partnered with more than 800 shelters, community organizations and disaster relief groups to provide more than 300 million loads of detergent to those in need. Across the U.S. and around the world, Earth Breeze has also sponsored the cleanup of over 999,000 pounds of plastic.
Local leaders also expressed support for the development.
'We are thrilled to welcome a new company to our community and excited for the new job opportunities this brings to Mercer County,' said Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele in a press release. 'We are looking forward to this partnership.'
The property is located on Morgan Soaper Drive in Harrodsburg and was developed by Hilpp's Mercer County TM Properties LLC.
'We are pleased and delighted to have Earth Breeze locating their manufacturing facility in Harrodsburg,' said Harrodsburg Mayor Bob Williams. 'The product, the leadership and the potential employment are all extraordinary factors in welcoming them to our community. Freddie Hilpp has been a tremendous asset in this endeavor as well, and we thank him for his efforts.'
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Industrial Development Authority, also issued a statement.
'HMCIDA, on behalf of our entire community, is thrilled by Earth Breeze's decision to locate and do business in our community,' said Greyson Evans, executive-director of the HMCIDA. 'For several years now, Harrodsburg and Mercer County have made a concerted push for job growth and to tell the world we're open for business. Partnership from an environmentally friendly American manufacturer that complements our existing business landscape so well is a blessing—we're very excited to engage with Earth Breeze and support them in their effort to prosper in Kentucky.'
Earth Breeze's investment builds on what state officials are calling best five-year period for economic growth in Kentucky history.
To encourage investment and job growth in the community, the Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority has preliminarily approved a 10-year incentive agreement with Earth Breeze under the Kentucky Business Investment program. The performance-based agreement can provide up to $2.4 million in tax incentives based on the company's investment of $5.89 million and annual targets of:
• Creation and maintenance of 226 Kentucky-resident, full-time jobs across 10 years.
• Paying an average hourly wage of $30.96, including benefits, across those jobs.
By meeting its annual targets over the agreement term, the company can be eligible to keep a portion of the new tax revenue it generates, according to the state. The company may claim eligible incentives against its income tax liability and wage assessments.

title: Albert Mueller
description: Albert R. 'Al' Mueller, 85, husband of Linda Moore Mueller, died Tuesday, Feb. 25, 2025, at his home. Born June 8, 1939, in West Allis, Wisc., he was the son of the late Albert and Agnes Miller…
content:
Albert R. 'Al' Mueller, 85, husband of Linda Moore Mueller, died Tuesday, Feb. 25, 2025, at his home.
Born June 8, 1939, in West Allis, Wisc., he was the son of the late Albert and Agnes Miller Mueller.
He was a lithographer and a member of the Carpenter's Christian Church.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: two daughters, Dawn (Rick) Weber of Palmyra, Wisc., and Dawn (Phil) Cramer of Prosperity, SC; one son, Steve (Shae) Mueller of Eagle, Wisc.; one brother, Harvey (Frieda) Mueller of Haughton, Louis.; five grandchildren; two great-grandchildren, Brayden Irwin and Camden Irwin; and several horses, dogs and cats.
He was preceded in death by his first wife, Delores Jean Mueller and one sister, Lorraine Kirchner.
Funeral services will be held 5 p.m. Saturday, March 8, at the Carpenter's Christian Church with Greg Warren, Jacob Bryant and John Kesel officiating.
Pallbearers will be Steve Mueller, Brandon Boesel, Ryan Katcha, Rick Weber, Jeff Boesel and Phil Cramer. Honorary pallbearers will be Larry and Lisa Votaw, David and Laurie Johnson, Tony 'Stretch' and Mary Broyles, Larry and Sheppy Jude, Ricky Peyton and Maurice Baker.
Visitation 2 p.m. until the hour of service at the church.
Alexander & Royalty Funeral Home and Cremation Services in charge of arrangements.
Memorial contributions are suggested to the Carpenter's Christian Church, 1340 US 127 Bypass, Harrodsburg, KY 40330, and/or St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, 501 St. Jude Place, Memphis, TN 38105, and/or Wounded Warriors Project, P.O. Box 758516, Topeka, KS 66675-8516.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at alexanderandroyalty.com.

title: Tourist Commission Increases Contribution To Local Events
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Tabitha Horne gets ahead of the crowd to photograph a band at Oktoberfest in 2023.
EDITOR'S NOTE: Since publication, there have been two announcements concerning Oktoberfest. Here is the full statement from the Oktoberfest organizers:
'The organizers of Oktoberfest regret to announce that the 2025 event will not take place. After nearly a decade of dedication, the team behind this beloved community tradition has made the difficult decision to step away due to time and financial constraints. 'Oktoberfest has been a labor of love, built through countless volunteer hours by our small but dedicated team,' said event organizers Noel Turner, Allen Goldie, and Greg Souder. One of the biggest challenges has always been securing the necessary funding to execute the event at the level it deserves. Despite the team's continued efforts, the financial burden and lack of compensation have made it increasingly difficult to continue. 'We are immensely proud of what we've built and grateful for the support we've received over the years,' the organizers added. 'If the community sees value in keeping Oktoberfest alive, we hope new leadership will step up to carry it forward.' The organizers extend their heartfelt thanks to the businesses, volunteers, and attendees who have supported Oktoberfest Harrodsburg throughout the years.'
Here is the statement released by the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission:
'The Mercer County Tourist Commission is dedicated to ensuring that the beloved Oktoberfest tradition in downtown Harrodsburg continues, despite the decision by the previous Oktoberfest committee to discontinue the event. While we respect and appreciate the hard work and dedication the committee has shown over the years in making Oktoberfest a success, we are not willing to let this cherished tradition fade away. Oktoberfest has become a staple in our community, bringing people together to celebrate music, food, and culture. Understanding its importance, the Mercer County Tourist Commission is stepping in to take the reins and ensure that the festival remains a highlight of Harrodsburg's annual events. 'We are incredibly grateful to the Oktoberfest committee for the time, effort, and passion they have poured into this event over the years,' said Daarik Gray, Executive Director of the Mercer County Tourist Commission. 'While change is never easy, we believe in the future of Oktoberfest and are excited to continue its legacy. I have full confidence in our Events Coordinator, Kaitlyn Harder, who has played a vital role in planning the festival in recent years. Her dedication and vision will ensure that Oktoberfest not only continues but thrives.' The Mercer County Tourist Commission is actively working on plans to continue Oktoberfest in downtown Harrodsburg in a way that honors tradition while also introducing fresh ideas to enhance the experience. More details will be announced in the coming months. For more information, please contact: DaarikGray Executive Director, Mercer County Tourist Commission
tourismed@harrodsburgky.com.'
The two announcements do not change the details reported in this story.
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission voted to make increase sponsorships for eight local events. At a special-called meeting on Thursday, Feb. 27, the tourist commission also voted to no longer allow funding requests outside the funding window.
The tourist commission was also informed that Oktoberfest organizers had withdrawn a request for an addition $60,000 in funding before the end of this fiscal year.
On Thursday, John Holiday, a member of the board of directors, moved to give eight local events more funding this year. Based on the data, these events attract the most visitors. This represents an additional 50 percent on top of what the events have already been allocated. According to Holiday's motion, Oktoberfest would receive $30,000, Pioneer Days would get $13,800, the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival would get $20,000, A.T.O.M. (A Thing On Main) Fest would get $2,500, the Native Dawn Flute Gathering would get $3,350, the Mercer County Fair and Horse Show would get $18,000, the Heart of Kentucky Juneteenth Festival would get $4,125 and the Ol' Iron Rundown would get $2,750.
Holiday's motion passed unanimously, as did his motion to no longer allow out-of-budget funding discussion. He explained the motion doesn't prevent the board from looking at future events. Budget requests for the 2026 fiscal year were due March 1. The deadline was announced in January.
'What's the point in having a request window if we're not going to abide by it?' Holiday asked.
'I'm here asking for more money,' said Sindicat 'Sid' Dunn of the Heart of Kentucky Juneteenth Festival, who addressed the board after they voted.
'I've got good news for you,' said Daarik Gray, executive director of the tourist commission. Gray explained that the tourist commission had already allocated $8,250, and that, with the extra 50 percent allocation, they would $12,375.
'I'll write you a check next week,' Gray said.
Dunn said the Juneteenth festival was in its fifth year. Last year the festival drew 4,000 people, with many coming from Lexington and Louisville. Dunn said this year they are working with production company and bringing in a stage and sound system. Dunn said they are looking at utilizing more of West Lane Park to handle the crowd. In addition, they are seeking to sign a headliner. This year, they are also adding a Juneteenth Golf Scramble on Thursday, June 19, at Old Bridge Golf Club in Danville.
'You have really grown this festival,' said Joan Huffman, chairwoman of the tourist commission.
Dunn called the Juneteenth Festival 'another little feather to put in Harrodsburg's hat.' For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Burgin Softball Looks To Build On Last Spring
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Pictured is the Burgin Lady Bulldog softball team. Back row from left to right: Head Coach Russell Jenkins, Gracie Watkins, Kaydance Logue, Jocelyn Stan­ley, Demi Mullins, Cloey Henson, Hayley Hurst, Ally Stewart and coach Mark Os­bourn. Front row: Claire Pauley, Leah Jenkins, Jemma Jenkins and Ashton Lester. The Burgin Lady Bulldogs softball team have been working hard this off­-season as they prepare for the 2023-24 season. Russell Jenkins is entering his sec­ond season as the leader of the program and his biggest focus in practice the off­-season has been pitching. In addition to Jemma Jenkins and Gracie Watkins, the Lady Bulldogs have added some much needed depth to the mound. 'We have spent much of our time trying to develop our pitchers, that was our biggest struggle last sea­son. We've got a couple of girls who are pitching for the first time and should be able to help us,' Jenkins said. Jenkins was worried it would take a while for the girls to shake the rust off from a long off-season, but he was encouraged after the first week of outdoor prac­tices. 'I was very encouraged by our first couple of out­door practices, the girls seemed like they were pick­ing up where we left off last year,' said Jenkins. Cloey Henson 1s the team's lone senior and fills the leadership role to perfection for the Lady Bulldogs. Along with Henson, J. Jenkins provides vocal leadership that the younger players need. 'She (Jenkins) usually addresses things before I get a chance. Both of them have been playing al this level for a while so they lead by example very well,' said Jenkins. Coach Jenkins is expect­ing a big contribution from sophomores Hayley Hurst and Ashton Lester. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. title: Lady Titans Recover And Earn First Win
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warrenlzzie Carlton knocked this ball over the center field fence during the Lady Titans&#
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
lzzie Carlton knocked this ball over the center field fence during the Lady Titans' 10-9 victory over Pulaski County on Saturday. Carlton's first ever varsity hit was also a grand slam, and tied the game at 8-8 in the bottom of the fifth. The Mercer County Lady Titans softball team (1-1) faced their first 12th Region opponent of the season on a beautiful and sunny Saturday, March 16, when they faced Pulaski County (3-1). Sophomore Brooklyn Thomas doubled on a dropped ball by Mercer's outfield, and moments later Claire Hamilton got the Lady Maroons on the scoreboard first after her single brought Thomas home. Freshman Jaley Bowman hit a hard ground ball to center field in Mercer's first at bat, and one out later she scored the Lady Titans' first run of the season thanks to a bunt from Peyton Boyd and an error by the Lady Maroon first baseman. Boyd scored Mercer's second run moments later thanks to a passed ball. The Lady Maroon's starting pitcher, Thomas, carved up the plate early on and Mercer didn't add to their total again until the sixth inning. Ava Musick struck out two batters and held her own until the fourth inning when the Lady Maroons hit their stride. Musick earned two outs with ease, but then a single, double, walk and back-to-back errors in the outfield added three quick runs and sophomore Ella Davis took over on the mound. Sophomores Chloe Carroll and Shelbie Sellers hit back to back ground balls into left field before Davis earned her first walk and Pulaski loaded the bases. Next, eighth grader Maggie Gregory singled to center field and scored two runs. Davis got down 3-0 in the count but battled back and the Lady Titans infield finished the inning with a double play. Midway through the fifth inning, Mercer trailed Pulaski 8-2. Bowman had a perfect day on the offensive side, singling on each of her at bats while being walked once and successfully stealing bases on all three of her attempts. title: Georgia Man Charged With Attempted Murder After Police Standoff
description: AUSTIN EDWARDS (Image: Boyle County Detention Center). Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A Georgia man is in custody after allegedly firing at police officers on Monday. According…
content:
AUSTIN EDWARDS (Image: Boyle County Detention Center). Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A Georgia man is in custody after allegedly firing at police officers on Monday. According to the complaint warrant, officers from the Harrodsburg Police Department were dispatched to Quality Inn on Danville Road at 2:45 a.m. on Monday, March 25, after receiving a call about a 'suicidal male armed with a handgun.' The male, identified as Austin Blake Edwards, 30, of Douglasville, Georgia, was confirmed to be a convicted felon, and police 'treated the situation as a barricaded subject,' according to the complaint warrant, with Cpl. Chase Hale of the HPD and Dep. T.J. Wren of the Boyle County Sheriff's Office conducting surveillance on the room. At 3:42 a.m., police say a gunshot came from Edwards' room, which was directed at Cpl. Hale and Dep. Wren, according to the complaint warrant. Officers were not injured at the time of the shooting, according to the complaint warrant. The police pulled back, and the HPD called in the Kentucky State Negotiator and Tactical Team, according to a Facebook post by Mercer County Emergency Management Director Brad Cox. Edwards was taken into custody at 8:52 a.m. without incident. According to Cox's post, a nearby daycare facility and the Mercer County School System were notified of the incident. The daycare delayed opening, and school buses in the impacted area were delayed until the scene was safe, according to Cox. Edwards was arrested and charged with possession of a handgun by a convicted felon and two counts of attempted murder. He is being held at Boyle County Detention Center on a $2 million bond. Cpl. Jarrod Duncan (HPD) was the arresting officer. Edwards is due to be arraigned next week, according to the Mercer County Circuit Clerk's office. This is not the first time this year that local police have found themselves under fire. Last week, a Harrodsburg man was indicted on charges including criminal attempt to commit murder of a police officer. According to the complaint warrant, two officers from the Harrodsburg Police Department—Patrolman Dustin Mical and Cpl. Ridge Yeast—were dispatched on a domestic dispute complaint on Tuesday, Jan. 2. Carl Gregory Isham, 52, of 940 Mackville Road, is alleged to have fired five to six rounds 'from a firearm at both uniformed officers, according to a warrant. Last week, the Mercer County Grand Jury indicted Isham for criminal attempt to commit murder, a class B felony, for shooting at Cpl. Yeast. Isham was also indicted for 1st degree wanton endangerment, a class D felony, for creating 'substantial danger of death or serious physical injury' to Patrolman Mical. Isham was also indicted for possession of a handgun by a convicted felon, a class C felony. Isham's bond was set at $200,000. title: Kazimer Accuses Police Chief Of Violating ‘The Public Trust'
description: File image. A local business owner complained to the Harrodsburg City Commission about Police Chief Tim Hurt this week. 'Our police chief viol
content:
File image. A local business owner complained to the Harrodsburg City Commission about Police Chief Tim Hurt this week.
'Our police chief violated the public trust,' said Jennifer Kazimer, who, with her husband, owns the Vault Ciders, Suds and Spirits on South Main Street. Kazimer also served a partial term on the city commission. The Kazimers have been living on Main Street for 18 years. 'I honor and respect our police department,' Kazimer said after she presented the commissioners with packets of information which included except from the HPD's code of ethics and from text conversations which she received through requests under the Freedom of Information Act. 'This is just the tip of the iceberg,' Kazimer said. After the meeting, she accused Hurt of violating the HPD code of ethics. 'Our chief of police violated the public trust,' Kazimer told the Harrodsburg Herald. At issue is an event that happened during last year's Oktobefest. On Saturday, Sept. 30, 2023, Chief Hurt went to the Vault, apparently because of complaints about possible violations. But it wasn't just what happened that Saturday. It's also what happened afterwards. In one social media posting that Kazimer provided to the city council, but which the Harrodsburg Herald has been unable to authenticate, a social media account listed as the Harrodsburg Police Department denies calling the 'ABC,' presumably the Kentucky Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control. However, in a copy of a letter provided by Kazimer, Maggie Woods, the distilled spirits administrator at the Alcoholic Beverage Control, appeared to say, 'It was your Chief of Police that was concerned that the event had gotten out of hand.' The Harrodsburg Herald was unable to contact Hurt for a comment, as he was out on FMLA leave, according to Chief Administrative Officer Stacy Maynard. In addition, Larry Wesley, assistant chief with the Harrodsburg Police Department, resigned effective March 1. City Attorney Norrie Currens was on vacation, Maynard said. 'It's not just what happened to us,' Kazimer said after the meeting Monday. 'It's about what happened to the festival.' On Sunday, Oct. 1, at 1:30 p.m., Justin Kyle Reister, 32, of Nicholasville, was arrested and charged with attempted murder of a police officer, 1st degree fleeing or evading police, 1st degree wanton endangerment of a police officer and driving on a DUI-suspended license, among other charges. HPD officers had observed Reister on foot 'leaving the area or Oktoberfest,' according to a uniform citation. The HPD—including Chief Hurt—ended up pursuing a vehicle whose driver refused to stop. While Hurt was traveling beside the truck, 'the suspect utilized his vehicle as a deadly weapon and steered hard left in an attempt to strike Chief Hurt's vehicle,' according to the uniform citation. Kazimer also referred to a request from a local citizen for bodycam footage of Hurt's visit at the Vault during Oktoberfest. In a photocopy of another text exchange which the Harrodsburg Herald was unable to verify, Hurt apparently texted his staff not to 'release the body cam footage' and to tell the citizen who requested the footage through that 'you can't get to it.' After receiving a response that the Kentucky League of Cities (KLC)—which provides legal services and guidance for Harrodsburg and other cities—had informed the HPD they 'had no grounds not to give it,' Hurt apparently texted to wait until he got back to the office. 'You better listen to me,' Hurt apparently texted. 'Look what happened with HellCat that I wasn't crazy about and then the ABC debacle.' Hurt appears to be referring to the hugely unpopular decision by the Harrodsburg City Commission on Sept. 25 to buy a 2023 Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat Widebody for $100,430 using funds from the city's alcohol regulatory fee. The city commission officially rescinded the motion to buy the Hellcat at their regular meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 10. In the text conversation supplied by Kazimer, Hurt finally said, 'Take it up there! Just got off the phone with City Hall.' The bodycam footage subsequently became available online, Kazimer said. 'Our department deserves better than this,' Kazimer told the city commission Monday. Commissioner Charlie Mattingly questioned Kazimer about the possible violations, including people leaving establishments with alcoholic beverages. 'Was it being served correctly?' Mattingly asked. 'I am not going to address that,' said Kazimer, who insisted the ABC found no violations. 'We tried to stop it we were not able to,' Kazimer said. 'There were other establishments having issues with that.' 'They're supposed to drink it there in the establishment,' Mattingly said. 'This is not the time to debate this,' said Mayor Bob Williams. 'We don't need to get off in the weeds to debate something we have no control over.' Williams said he wanted to wait until City Attorney Norrie Currens returned so they could get advice. The city commission took no action. After the meeting, Kazimer insisted she would be filing an official complaint. 'It's horrible you have to do business here under threat of retaliation from the chief of police,' Kazimer said. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. content:
Missy Wilham Banks has been serving on the Harrodsburg City Commission since January 2023, but she has called Harrodsburg home for much of her life. When she's not serving the city commission as head of the police and fire departments, she is working with the highest educational opportunity Harrodsburg has to offer, Campbellsville University School of Chiropractic.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Harrodsburg City Commissioner Missy Wilham Banks posed with her certification of achievement from the Kentucky League of Cities training course.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Harrodsburg City Commissioner Missy Wilham Banks posed with her certification of achievement from the Kentucky League of Cities training course. Banks was raised in Harrodsburg and was a dedicated athlete growing up. She recalls spending time with her younger brother, watching cartoons, collecting trading cards and playing baseball with the neighborhood kids. Her sports fandom led her to compete in track and field, basketball and softball while at Harrodsburg High School. Banks was a basketball player from seventh grade until she graduated. She ran track as a sophomore, and when Harrodsburg started a softball program in 1985, she was first in line to join the team.
'It was one of my best times because people were very helpful,' Banks said of her time running for the Pioneers' track and field team. 'I know we were competitive, but we thought more as a team; we were always trying to get the most points and we went to state that year. I didn't win anything at state, but I'll always remember Coach (Alvis) Johnson hollering. I could hear him all the way across the field at UK hollering ‘go Missy go,' it's just something I'll never forget,' said Banks.
Banks was also a member of the Beta Club, the National Honor Society, and the Fellowship of Christian Athletes while at Harrodsburg and was voted 'most athletic' her senior year, as well as being voted FCA Female Athlete of the Year as a senior.
Banks was most successful at basketball, and after graduating from Harrodsburg in 1987, she moved on to Berea College, where she continued her basketball career while earning her bachelor's degree in secondary education. Banks spent two years interning with the Grayson County School District before returning to her hometown, where she spent time working in the Burgin Independent and Harrodsburg school districts.

description: Photo: National Weather ServiceStraightline win
content:
Photo: National Weather Service
Straightline winds damaged buildings like this one in Salvisa and overturned a truck on U.S. 127 last week. No lives were lost in the storm, officials say.
Photo: National Weather Service
Straightline winds damaged buildings like this one in Salvisa and overturned a truck on U.S. 127 last week. No lives were lost in the storm, officials say. No lives were lost in the storms that swept through Mercer County last week. On Tuesday April 2, a strong low pressure system moved through the region resulting in hail, wind damage and 10 tornadoes, including one reported in Nicholasville, according to the National Weather Service. Locally, the worst damage came from straight line winds, with gusts of up to 80 miles per hour being recorded by the NWS.
In Salvisa, a storm blew ripped the roof off JM Weld Co. Once inside, the wind.
'The trusses came down on me and my wife right there in the shop,' Joseph Moore, the owner of the welding shop, told WLEX-18. 'I mean it was kind of a harrowing life flash before you before your eyes experience. You don't really realize that it's happening, until it's come and gone. You hear this big rush and roar of the wind rushing into the structure and it fills the roof off and you just kind of brace yourself.'
The heavy winds also overturning a tractor trailer by Family Affair Restaurant on U.S. 127.
Sheriff Ernie Kelty said the Mercer County Sheriff's Office had to call in extra deputies to handle the high volume of storm calls, which included redirecting traffic on U.S. 127 until the overturned semi could be removed.
'We tried to get the traffic moving as soon as possible as we can,' Kelty said Tuesday at the Mercer County Fiscal Court meeting.
One issue they faced was figuring out what to do with other semis on the highway, which couldn't be rerouted onto county roads.
'You'd be amazed at how much semi traffic there is on 127,' Kelty said.
'It was a busy day,' said Emergency Management Director Brad Cox. Cox thanked crews for clearing debris even while the storm was still raging.
'They had their hands full,' Cox said. 'We were very fortunate.'
Cox invited anyone with questions about the alert systems to contact the emergency management office.
'Feel free to give me a call,' Cox said. 'We're always looking to update service.'
The Mercer County Emergency Management Agency is located at the fiscal courthouse (207 West Lexington Street). The email is mercercountyem​@gmail.com and the phone number is 859-734-6333.

title: Burgin Schools Remember Columbine Anniversary With Rachel's Challenge
description: Photo SubmittedBurgin students heard speakers from Rachel's Challenge, named after Rachel Scott a victim from the 1999 Columbine High School shooti
content:
Photo Submitted
Burgin students heard speakers from Rachel's Challenge, named after Rachel Scott a victim from the 1999 Columbine High School shooting, on how to use compassion to prevent school violence.
Photo Submitted
Burgin students heard speakers from Rachel's Challenge, named after Rachel Scott a victim from the 1999 Columbine High School shooting, on how to use compassion to prevent school violence. April Ellis
Herald Staff
April Ellis
Herald Staff Last week, the nation recognized the 25th anniversary of the Columbine High School shooting, where 12 students and one teacher were gunned down by two students. More than 370,000 students have experienced gun violence at school since Columbine, according statistics compiled by the Washington Post. Meaningful connections between students, faculty, and staff are critical. Last week, the organization Rachel's Challenge—named after Rachel Scott, the first fatality at Columbine—presented their program at Burgin Independent Schools to assist staff and students in developing an environment that leads to kindness and compassion instead of violence.
Rachel Scott was a 17 year old student when she was shot to death in Columbine, Colorado, in 1999. Her father, Darrell Scott, was asked to talk about his daughter so often that he and Rachel's stepmother, Sandy, realized her story could help change how students relate to each other and possibly prevent bullying and school violence. The family created a non-profit organization for school violence prevention known as Rachel's Challenge.
Erica Sexton became Burgin's Family Resource and Youth Service Center coordinator in November 2023. One of her main goals was to improve mental health at the school. Bringing in Rachel's Challenge is one step Sexton's taken which she said has impacted Burgin's staff and students positively.
'I was unaware of the significance of the date when I set the date for Rachel's Challenge. However, once we realized the anniversary was upon us, it really made a deeper impact on the staff and students. Rachel's Challenge is a non-political, non-religious nonprofit dedicated to preventing bullying in schools before it starts and preventing youth suicide and self-harm,' said Sexton.
Rachel's Challenge holds live assemblies at schools and provides digital programs and support materials for students and staff. The program is divided into age groups to better focus on issues unique to younger as well as older students.
'Grades K-5 had their program earlier in the morning, and it was geared towards their age group. The elementary kids were excited to get their chain of kindness started,' said Sexton. Students in grades 6-12 were allowed to sign up for a 90-minute training after their program. 'We had 70 students and several staff members who attended the training and gained resources to help create an atmosphere of kindness and compassion at Burgin Independent.'
Before she was killed, Rachel's writing expressed her compassion for people in need. She wrote about wanting to help people with special needs as well as students who were new to her school and students who were picked on or put down by others. Rachel's Challenge focuses on teaching students compassion and preventing the negative emotional situations that ultimately cost Rachel her life.
'I truly believe that each and every student and staff member walked away with positive thoughts from the Rachel's Challenge Program,' said Sexton. 'Many tears were shed by staff and students touched by Rachel's story. I believe that Burgin Independent will implement many strategies taught from Rachel's Challenge.'

title: $21 Million In State Funds To Support Industrial Park, 250th And Roads
description: File image. More than $21 million in state funding will be invested in Mercer County thanks to appropriations made during the Kentucky General Assembly's recently concluded leg
content:
File image.
File image. More than $21 million in state funding will be invested in Mercer County thanks to appropriations made during the Kentucky General Assembly's recently concluded legislative session. The funds will go to a planned industrial park, Harrodsburg's 250th anniversary and local road maintenance.
'House Bills 1 and 6 provide Mercer County with over $13 million in direct community investment,' Rep. Kim King said in a press release. 'These funds are being used to support the growth of our community and will have a lasting impact for years to come.'
That includes $11.5 million in Fiscal Year 2025 to the Mercer County Fiscal Court for the Wilkinson Farm industrial park. According to the press release, the funding comes from legislation that makes one-time investments towards paying down public pension liabilities, improving water infrastructure, and preparing rural areas for economic development opportunities.
There are also appropriations of $2.18 million in FY 2025 and $2.505 million in FY 2026 to the Sestercentennial Commission to support operations.
The community will also see improvements on local roads. The General Assembly passed the 294-page road appropriations bill, which includes nearly $10 million in appropriations for Mercer County through Fiscal Year 2026.
According to a press release from the Kentucky Press Association, here's what's in store for Mercer County in the 2024–2026 Biennial Highway Construction Plan.
• Improve safety on US 68 at the KY 127 intersection in Harrodsburg. Projected expenditures: $640,000 in FY2024, $1,410,000 in FY2025 and $2,690,000 in FY2026.
• Improve system mobility along Moberly Road from KY 390 to KY 1989 in northwest Harrodsburg. Projected expenditures: $540,000 in FY 2024 and $1,870,000 in FY 2025.
• Address the condition of Martha Layne Collins Bluegrass Parkway from milepoint 52.315 to milepoint 56.287. Projected expenditure: $1.5 million in FY2025.
• Improve the level of safety and access at and around the intersection of US 127 and KY 598 (Sparrow Lane). Projected expenditures: $200,000 in FY 2024, $195,000 in FY 2025 and $750,000 in FY 2026.
Total expenditures: $1,380,000 in FY 2024, $4,975,000 in FY 2025 and $3,440,000 in FY 2026.
Total expenditures: $1,380,000 in FY 2024, $4,975,000 in FY 2025 and $3,440,000 in FY 2026. Two other projects that will happen in other counties may impact traffic here in Mercer County.
• KY 4 in Fayette. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet will conduct a regional corridor feasibility study to evaluate east-west connectivity between US 127 and Interstate 75. The study region includes Anderson, Fayette, Franklin, Jessamine, Mercer, Scott and Woodford counties. Projected expenditure: $500,000 in FY 2024.
• Jessamine US 68. KYTC will conduct a safety improvement feasibility study to improve the safety and driver expectations on US 68 in Mercer and Jessamine counties near the Kentucky River, from milepoint 14.45 in Mercer County to milepoint 1.38 in Jessamine County. Projected expenditure: $250,000 in FY2024.
According to King, House Joint Resolution 92 also includes $51,000 in FY 2025 to resurface Southworth Road.
'If we are to grow as a region, it is important that we have high quality and safe roads,' King said in the press release. 'Jobs go where roads take them, and Mercer County, along with much of the surrounding region, is receiving targeted investment into our roadways to support the community and future investments.'
Lawmakers adjourned the 2024 Regular Session on Monday, April 15, after passing more than 200 pieces of legislation that include bills and resolutions aimed at strengthening educational opportunity, providing law enforcement with more tools, and investing in local communities to increase access to jobs. Lawmakers will not reconvene to act on legislation until January 2025, but they will conduct interim committee meetings throughout the year.
For further information on the 2024 Regular Session, visit legislature.ky.gov.

title: Malachi Davis Shows Strength In New Orleans
description: Photo SubmittedMercer County senior and former football player Malachi Davis (center) took advantage of a photo opportunity
content:
Photo Submitted
Mercer County senior and former football player Malachi Davis (center) took advantage of a photo opportunity while at the USPA high school nationals in New Orleans. Davis is accompanied by his coach Jeremy Carlson (left) and Braden Tabor (right).
Photo Submitted
Mercer County senior and former football player Malachi Davis (center) took advantage of a photo opportunity while at the USPA high school nationals in New Orleans. Davis is accompanied by his coach Jeremy Carlson (left) and Braden Tabor (right). Mercer County Senior High School senior Malachi Davis has been in the weight room pushing himself to new heights year after year since the age of 13. In his four years in high school, Davis watched himself grow tremendously and add on hundreds of pounds to his weight total in the gym.
As a junior, Davis was back-squatting 450 pounds but suffered a setback when he broke his collarbone during a football game. His dedication to perfecting himself has only strengthened since that moment, and Davis now squats over 500 pounds.
Head of Centre College Sports and Performance Jeremy Carlson invested in Davis' potential while he was head of strength and conditioning at Mercer County and continues to coach Davis on his power-lifting journey today.
Davis recently showcased his strength at the United States Powerlifting Association (USPA) high school nationals in New Orleans on April 13, the 'largest and most organized' meet he had ever attended.
The meet accepted high school students of all ages, but Davis competed specifically in the 75 kilogram (165 pound) weight class. His class was drug tested and was classified as raw, meaning Davis competed unassisted from belts, straps, braces or even squat shorts, which makes his 513-pound back squat all the more impressive. Davis' squat was heavier than three times his body weight and was more than enough to break the national USPA record for his weight and age (500 pounds) and the Kentucky record (474 pounds). Despite having such an amazing first performance on the national stage, Davis still didn't come close to the goals he had set before the meet.
'We were shooting for 315 bench, 550 squat and deadlift, but you know not everything works out,' said Davis.

title: Planning Commission Approves Amended Gas Station Plan
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreThe Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission approved an amended development plan f
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission approved an amended development plan for a gas station on US 127.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission approved an amended development plan for a gas station on US 127. The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission approved an amended development plan for a gas station on US 127 and voted to recommend the annexation and rezoning of property by the City of Harrodsburg.
At a special-called meeting on Friday, April 26, the planning and zoning commission approved a development plan amendment submitted by Cumberland Developers LLC to build a 3,500 square foot gas station/convenience store on the property located at 1401 Louisville Road. The zoning map indicates the property is zoned B-2 (general business).
Last October, the commission approved plans to build a 4,500 square foot convenience store at the location. Cumberland Developers LLC of Somerset bought 40 acres for the convenience store and a proposed residential development.
'They have decided that's not what they wanted to do,' said Douglas Gooch of AGE Engineering, who represented the owners.
Gooch said they were trying to reduce the initial costs without killing the possibility for the future. He noted they had dedicated almost an acre for stormwater retention. He said they will have to resubmit the plan, eliminating work on an entrance that would not have accessed the proposed C-store.
'We've gone back to a two lane entrance and exit,' Gooch said. 'It's a watered-down version of what we had before.'
Board member Jerry Catlett worried how the north entrance would look to anyone visiting Anderson-Dean Community Park, which sits nearby.
'We'll be looking at the back of the store,' Catlett said. 'What can we do to address that entryway that looks nice?'
Gooch noted the owners intend to install a facade on the back of the building.
'Everybody in the park's going to be looking at the back end,' Catlett said. 'I hate to see garbage and stuff out the back as it's coming out of town.'
Gooch said it was important to his clients as well.
'I understand it's their intention to look nice, but two years down the road, will it look nice?' Catlett asked.
Chairman Bobby Upchurch noted there would be dual entrances on the north and south sides of the building. Upchurch asked about screening for the dumpster pad in the rear. The commission voted to approve the plan with the condition the owners build a three-sided brick block shelter with a gate for screening around the dumpster. They also stipulated that a three foot tall hedge be installed to hide the parking lot and that the rear facade of the building be constructed similarly to the facade at the main entrance on the southern side. Gooch said they would add a landscaping sheet.
'I appreciate you working with our concerns,' Catlett said.
'I'd hate to see it turn out to be something we wouldn't be proud of,' Gooch said.
The commission also voted unanimously to recommend the annexation of 23.999 acres of land owned by Cary King, located at the southeast corner of the US 127 and US 68 intersection in Harrodsburg.

title: Jeremy Carlson Holds Centre College's First Strength Coaches Clinic
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/David CarpenterFormer strength and conditioning coach at Mercer County Senior High School, Jeremy Carlson, held a coaches clinic on Centre College's campus last week. Mercer…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ David Carpenter
Former strength and conditioning coach at Mercer County Senior High School, Jeremy Carlson, held a coaches clinic on Centre College's campus last week.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ David Carpenter
Former strength and conditioning coach at Mercer County Senior High School, Jeremy Carlson, held a coaches clinic on Centre College's campus last week. Mercer County resident Jeremy Carlson may have moved into the college coaching realm since his time as the strength and conditioning coach at Mercer County Senior High School, but his passion for helping athletes across multiple levels succeed has never been greater.
On Saturday, April 20, a packed room of coaches, educators and sport performance professionals gathered for the first Centre College Sport Performance, Strength Coaches Clinic. Attendees included those from as close as Mercer County but also from multiple states in the Ohio Valley. From high school coaches, to Division I strength and conditioning athletic directors, Centre welcomed some of the leading minds in athletic performance in the mid-south.
Last winter, as Carlson returned to lead the sports performance department at Centre, he returned with fresh vision and direction. 'I wanted to come back with a clear vision, mission and slogan to guide our department. This was formed with the help of my assistant, Levi Agee, while we were at another strength clinic outside of Cincinnati,' said Carlson.
His goals included helping Centre catapult to excellence and leading the way for NCAA Division III sports performance. In this plan, Carlson felt that providing education was crucial.
'We believed that part of this vision needed to include an educational component where we hosted camps, clinics, etc. We wrote it all down and then honestly forgot about it,' he said. 'I found the notebook when I was flying out to my honeymoon in December. I had a couple hours on the plane and planned out the whole thing. Who was going to speak, who we were going to invite, sponsors, etc. When I landed, I reached out to a handful of coaches and they really seemed to enjoy the idea, and we went from there.'

title: Mowing Operations Scheduled For Mercer County And Central Kentucky
content:
Oregon Transportation Maintenance Specialist David Womak mows the Interstate 5 Chemawa interchange in 2020. Image: Oregon Department of Transportation via Wikimedia Commons.
Oregon Transportation Maintenance Specialist David Womak mows the Interstate 5 Chemawa interchange in 2020. Image: Oregon Department of Transportation via Wikimedia Commons. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) advises the traveling public that mowing season begins for Mercer County and the rest of Central Kentucky on Monday, May 13. District 7 crews and contractors will be working to mow and trim grass along state roadsides.
Cycle 1 Operations will begin Monday, May 13, and continue through Tuesday, May 28, for Boyle, Clark, Fayette, Jessamine, Madison, Mercer, Montgomery and Scott counties.
Specific counties—Anderson, Bourbon, Garrard and Woodford—will provide their own mowing operations. Exact dates of work for each county will vary, and work is weather dependent.
Mowing operations do not typically cause lane closures or similar impacts. However, motorists should be aware of traffic changes—especially slowed traffic, or traffic backups along two-lane highways. The Transportation Cabinet asks motorists to help put safety first by slowing down, and using appropriate discretion where crews are working.
Residents are also reminded that Kentucky law prohibits political, or other advertising signs from being posted on state right of way. Signs can be a hazard to motorists and mowing crews — signage will be will be removed from state right of way. Owners of signs may retrieve them for a period of time after removal by visiting the state maintenance facility within their county.
All work/closures are subject to change depending on weather, emergencies and other factors beyond the control of the Department of Highways.
District 7 includes: Anderson, Bourbon, Boyle, Clark, Fayette, Garrard, Jessamine, Madison, Mercer, Montgomery, Scott and Woodford vounties. Navigate traffic with GoKY or via Waze on your smartphone.

title: Blood Drive On Wednesday, May 8
description: Image: Kentucky Blood Center. The Kentucky Blood Center is making it even easier to save local lives by hosting a community blood drive on Wednesday, May 8, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. at Lions Park…
content:
Image: Kentucky Blood Center. The Kentucky Blood Center is making it even easier to save local lives by hosting a community blood drive on Wednesday, May 8, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. at Lions Park Community Center (133 Factory Street). Donors who give blood at this drive will receive a Kentucky Blood Center 'throwback' item as a thank you for their time. Giving blood takes about 45 minutes to an hour from registration to refreshment and can save up to three local lives. The collection process only takes approximately 10 minutes. Donations at Kentucky Blood Center directly benefit local lives at more than 70 hospitals across the Commonwealth. Blood donors must be at least 17 years old (16 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, be in general good health, show a photo I.D. and meet additional requirements. Sixteen-year-old donors must have a signed parental permission slip, which can be found at kybloodcenter.org. The Kentucky Blood Center is the largest independent, full-service, nonprofit blood center in the Commonwealth, has been saving local lives since 1968. Licensed by the FDA, the Kentucky Blood Center's sole purpose is to collect, process and distribute blood for Kentucky patients. The Kentucky Blood Center provides services in 90 Kentucky counties and has donor centers in Lexington, Louisville, Frankfort, Pikeville, Somerset and the Tri-County area (Corbin). title: Tourist Commission Looks To Make Tough Budget Decisions
description: Diamond Point Welcome Center (file image). The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission is looking to make what may end up being some unpopular decisions as members seek a way to balance the…
content:
Diamond Point Welcome Center (file image).
Diamond Point Welcome Center (file image). The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission is looking to make what may end up being some unpopular decisions as members seek a way to balance the organization's budget going into the new fiscal year.
At the board of directors meeting held Wednesday, May 8, they learned that 10 months into the current fiscal year, the organization was in the hole a little over $69,000, according to treasurer Bob Gigliotti. Gigliotti said the organization was running a surplus last year at this time. He said income was down $180,000 compared to the year before, which he attributed to a lack of ARPA funding and a drop in the dining tax revenue.
Gigliotti said the tourist commission has received 66 percent of what they budgeted for total income for the full year, and they would have to 'take a hard look at some of our expenses.'
Several of the board members said they were seeing a decrease in business from the highs they saw after COVID-19 restrictions ended, but even then business was still better than before the pandemic struck. In previous years, the tourist commission—which has been accused of hoarding money in the past—went into new budget period with a rollover.
'This year we're not going to do that,' Gigliotti said. 'If something happens in the next two months, we're going to be in the hole.'
Gigliotti said the funding requests for local events is $100,000 more than last year, and Daarik Gray, executive director of the tourist commission, pointed out that's without the 250th celebration.
Gray said he is looking at cutting money the tourist commission has paid for photography, videography, billboards and signage. He brought up getting rid of Placer.ai, a location intelligence and foot traffic data software that the tourist commission subscribed to last year.
'It's caused us a lot of problems,' Gray said. While the company claims 92 to 96 percent accuracy, some have objected to the results, noting that the software does not count people who don't have cellphones. Some of the complaints have come from the tourist commission's board of directors.
'I like it,' said Tiffany Yeast, the chair of the board of directors. While the software has its challenges, Yeast said estimations based on garbage collection and license plates also have challenges. Some organizations—including Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill—have approached the tourist commission for information collected by Placer.ai.
'We have a job to do as far as in terms of making a budget,' Yeast said. She asked the board to make suggestions.
'People will be asking some questions,' said board member David Coleman, who suggested the budget committee create talking points.
The tourist commission's budget has to be finalized at their next meeting.

title: City To Repair Main Street Starting This Week
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreContractors will try to repair the intersection of Main and Office Streets on Thursday, May 16, depending on the we
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors will try to repair the intersection of Main and Office Streets on Thursday, May 16, depending on the weather.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors will try to repair the intersection of Main and Office Streets on Thursday, May 16, depending on the weather. Much needed repairs on several Harrodsburg streets—including Main Street—will begin Thursday, May 16. The Harrodsburg City Commission voted to repair the intersection of Office and Main Streets at a special-called meeting on Wednesday, May 15. The city commission voted to modify a change order for their 2023 agreement with Mago Construction for the maintenance and paving of city streets. According to Commissioner Charlie Mattingly, who oversees the public works department, repairs on Main Street will begin Thursday, with contractors working all day to mill, repave and stripe the intersection. As always with road construction, everything is weather dependent.
'It's going to be an all day job tomorrow,' said Mattingly. He said Mago had a major breakdown at their local plant and will be using asphalt from their plant in Lawrenceburg.
'I'll be glad to get this Main Street fixed,' Mattingly said.
The magistrates unanimously approved the change order, which also directs Mago to pave West Lexington from U.S. 127 to Fort Street and Franks Court.
According to Mattingly, the original agreement with Mago totaled $648,105, but Bellaire Drive was deleted from the list of streets to receive work. Mattingly said other streets came in under budget, leaving the city with $60,000 to use for other projects.
The intersection of South Main still bears the scars from a major waterline break in January. The break led to icy conditions on the road, and the city issued a precautionary boil water advisory. While crews managed to repair the main, the street took a real beating, and citizens have wondered what the city was going to do about it before the 250th celebration. Harrodsburg's 250th Parade is scheduled for Saturday, June 8.
The issue came up at the commission's regular meeting on Monday, May 13, when Mattingly, who oversees the public works department, moved to use the leftover funds in the 2023-2024 budget to pave Parkview Drive, Franks Court and Lexington Street.
Commissioner Marvin 'Bubby' Isham objected, saying there were other streets—including South Main—that needed to be fixed first.
'Main Street needs to be done awful bad,' Isham said. 'We got this 250th coming up, and Main Street looks like crap.'
'I'm very much like Commissioner Isham here,' Mayor Bob Williams said, referring to Main and Lexington Streets. 'I believe this money would be better used to complete these two projects.'
Mattingly said getting the contractors to submit bids and do the work in such a short time frame would be difficult.
'Call in whatever favors you may have with McGlone or Mego,' Williams said, listing the two main contractors the city uses for paving. 'This is a major priority to get done now.'
'Call in whatever favors you may have with McGlone or Mego,' Williams said, listing the two main contractors the city uses for paving. 'This is a major priority to get done now.' According to Mattingly, the work on Main Street will cost approximately $30,000, while the work on West Lexington will costs more than $16,018.67 and paving Franks Court will cost $5,696.56.

title: Former Mercer Standout Darrian Baker Excited For His Final Season With EKU
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Arpan DixitDarrian Baker pictured blocking an opposing defensive end during his senior season at Mercer County. Baker is now a fifth year senior and defensive leader for the…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Arpan Dixit
Darrian Baker pictured blocking an opposing defensive end during his senior season at Mercer County. Baker is now a fifth year senior and defensive leader for the Eastern Kentucky Colonels.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Arpan Dixit
Darrian Baker pictured blocking an opposing defensive end during his senior season at Mercer County. Baker is now a fifth year senior and defensive leader for the Eastern Kentucky Colonels. Former Mercer County football standout and 2020 graduate Darrian Baker was recently selected as a representative of Eastern Kentucky University football on the Community Trust Bank 2024 Kentucky Collegiate All-Commonwealth Team. The pre-season recognition honors a handful of the best players on each Kentucky football program's roster and includes elite talents like Barion Brown and Maxwell Hairston of the University of Kentucky, Devin Neal of the University of Louisville, Easton Messer of Western Kentucky University and several others.
Darrian Baker image: EKU.
Darrian Baker image: EKU. Last fall, in Baker's fourth season of NCAA eligibility, he tallied 25 tackles, six for a loss, and four sacks while forcing one fumble. He has been working hard this offseason to make his final year as a Colonel his best yet and has been putting an extra emphasis on his pass rushing technique this spring. Baker's four sacks as a redshirt junior are the most in a single season outside of his junior year of high school, when he led the Mercer County Titans defense with five sacks.
Baker has big expectations for himself and the Colonels defense this fall, but even bigger accomplishments are being made off the field. Baker recently graduated with a degree in sports management, making him the first member of his family to graduate from college.
'Being a first generation graduate is a huge accomplishment for me and makes me proud of myself. I am the youngest of seven children, and a few of them went to college but never finished, so it feels amazing to be the first one to finish college and get my degree. I truly owe it all to my parents for the support they have given me throughout college, and I want to thank them even more because I know it wasn't easy raising my siblings and me. My parents and family have been with me every step of the way, helping me when I need it and providing support in every way,' said Baker of his parents, Greg and Linda Baker. Baker is using his fifth year of eligibility to get a head start on his master's degree in business administration.

title: Lady Titans Advance To Next Round Of Playoffs
description: The Harro
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Mercer County Lady Titans softball senior Peyton Boyd regained her balance and looked to the infield after fielding the second out in the top of the seventh inning during Mercer's 1-0 win over Casey County on Tuesday, May 28. The Mercer County Lady Titans (15-9) faced the Casey County Lady Rebels (20-15) in the 12th Region softball tournament opening round on Tuesday, May 28, in Harrodsburg. Mercer, now the third-ranked team in the 12th Region according to KHSAA RPI, earned their second win of the season when they defeated Casey 4-3 on Mar. 19, and earned a second win over the Lady Rebels in much swifter fashion, 10-4, on Apr. 18. Neither team could manage any offensive threat in the opening inning. Senior Ashley Howard started in the circle for Mercer and walked the first batter of the second inning. She responded by striking out the following batter before Senior Hannah Beasley and the Lady Titan outfield combined for outs two and three. The game's first big play came when Howard launched a high fly ball off the center field wall, doubling. Peyton Boyd followed with a perfectly weighted and placed bunt that split the infield. Boyd's bunt scored sophomore Ella Davis from second base, but she was eventually thrown out, sliding into third base. The Lady Titans will be back in action tonight, Thursday, May 30, at 6 p.m., when they face the winner of Southwestern and Garrard County in the semi-finals of the 12th Region tournament in Harrodsburg. title: City Commission Votes To Allow Mercer Schools To Paint Logo On Tower
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreContractors are at work sandblasting and painting the water tower that overlooks Mercer County Senior High School. School officials were unable to say when the work…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors are at work sandblasting and painting the water tower that overlooks Mercer County Senior High School. School officials were unable to say when the work would be done.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors are at work sandblasting and painting the water tower that overlooks Mercer County Senior High School. School officials were unable to say when the work would be done. The Harrodsburg City Commission voted unanimously—after extensive debate—to allow Mercer County Schools to paint their logo on the Industry Road water tower. The cost to add the logo will be paid by Mercer Schools.
Commissioner Bubby Isham made the motion, but Mayor Bob Williams objected.
'I am not in favor of this,' said Williams, who said he doesn't believe the city should break with the consistency of other water towers. He called the logo 'advertising.'
'We don't allow advertising or campaign signs on city property, but we allow advertising on this tank?' Williams asked. 'What's going to keep Campbellsville from coming in and saying we want one? What's going to keep Corning from coming in and saying we want one?'
Noting the water tower had been installed to serve the factory that now houses Essity, he said, 'By all rights, maybe it should be Essity.'
Even though the school district will pay for the logo, Williams said, 'That's taxpayers' money.'
Commissioner Missy Bank noted the water tower, which is city property, sits on school property.
'They are the future of our community,' Banks said. 'It's not a business, it's part of us.'
City Attorney Norrie Currens said there would be no issue with allowing the logo on city property because it's a school.
'They're only wanting to do one side,' Commissioner Isham said.
'This is the 250th birthday,' Williams said.
'It's going to be over in two months,' Isham said. 'The school's going to be there a hundred years from now.'
'We're all entitled to our opinion,' Williams said. The mayor said other communities have decided against it.
'I think we need to maintain the consistency of the other towers,' Williams said.
Isham noted Anderson County had allowed the school to put their logo on their tower. He moved to allow the school district to put their logo on the tank. The logo will be visible from the ballfields, while the city logo will face the bypass. Isham's first motion failed. but after Currens suggested clarification, it passed unanimously.
The commission also authorized the mayor to sign a contract with Currens Construction and All Points Broadband to build infrastructure on the Industry Road water tower to accommodate All Points Broadband equipment. This will be fully funded by All Points Broadband.
Williams explained the company, which bought out local internet provider BlueZoom Inc. back in 2019, had antennas on the water tower. He said the internet infrastructure will be built or rebuilt to make it safer and more efficient.
The mayor was also authorized to sign a hold harmless agreement between the City of Harrodsburg, Currens Construction and All Points Broadband for the work being done on the Industry Road water tower. Williams said All Points could not remove the equipment without knocking out thousands of customers.
'If equipment is damaged, the City of Harrodsburg and Currens will not be held responsible,' Williams said.

title: Chris Souder Returns To Lead Lady Titans Basketball
description: Mercer County Lady Titan basketball coach Chris Souder is pictured holding the net after Mercer County's second state championship win in 2018. Souder will be entering his 20th season as head coach of…
content:
Mercer County Lady Titan basketball coach Chris Souder is pictured holding the net after Mercer County's second state championship win in 2018. Souder will be entering his 20th season as head coach of Mercer County this winter. (Image: Arpan Dixit/ The Harrodsburg Herald ).
Mercer County Lady Titan basketball coach Chris Souder is pictured holding the net after Mercer County's second state championship win in 2018. Souder will be entering his 20th season as head coach of Mercer County this winter. (Image: Arpan Dixit/ The Harrodsburg Herald ). Mercer County Senior High School Athletics presented their newest hire to the public in the auditorium on Wednesday, Mat 29. Former Head Coach of Lady Titan basketball, Chris Souder, who had been leading the South Laurel Lady Cardinals for the last six seasons, was reappointed to his former position, replacing Hayley Spivey, who will continue her teaching role with the school while pursuing a doctorate degree.
'We are excited. This is an amazing day for the community,' said Athletic Director Donald Wayne Smith.
Souder is known across the state as an elite coach and his resume is nearly unmatched. During his initial tenure, Souder accumulated an astounding 460 wins in 19 seasons, including four straight 12th Region championships from 2015-2018, and back-to-back Sweet Sixteen titles in 2017 and 2018.
'We started with the best out there, and he didn't even have to fill out a resume, because his resume is sitting right here in front of us,' Superintendent Jason Booher said, motioning to the two state championship trophies affixed beside the podium.
Souder originally left Mercer County soon after his second state championship win to pursue a collegiate coaching career with Indiana State University.
'It was an opportunity I just couldn't pass up,' Souder told the Harrodsburg Herald in 2018. Soon after his appointment as assistant coach of the Sycamores, Souder discovered the college game just wasn't ideal for him, and by the fall of 2018 he had landed in London, where he would lead the South Laurel Lady Cardinals to a 136-63 record over six seasons.
Souder earned two more region championship trophies while a Cardinal in 2020 and 2021, and even knocked off Sacred Heart in the opening round of the 2020 Sweet Sixteen tournament. Unfortunately for everyone involved, the 2020 tournament was canceled after the first round due to COVID, but the win makes Souder the only Kentucky coach to defeat Sacred Heart in the Sweet Sixteen since then, as they are currently reigning champions, for the fourth year in a row.
Mercer County Athletic Director Donald Wayne Smith said Wednesday he had spoken to Souder twice about the potentiality of a return to Harrodsburg, but was told no both times. Smith's words alone were not enough to convince Souder of a return to the program he built, but his son Connor's were. Souder's grandson, Gritton, was the 'secret weapon' needed to bring Souder home according to Smith.
'My son's like, ‘I don't mean to guilt you, but y'know I don't want Gritton to be 2-years-old and you come home and he cries because he doesn't know who you are,' and that really is funny but it hit home,' said Souder. 'We're in South Laurel, which is a great place, but we're really just here for basketball, and this (Harrodsburg) is home. The opportunity came, and once me and Donald got really into discussions it was a no-brainer.'

title: Anna Kate Drakeford Plays In Final High School Basketball Game
description: Image: T
content:
Image: Tanya Hill Photography
Recent Mercer County Senior High School gradu­ate Anna Kate Drakeford set her eyes on the basket and attempted a three pointer during the Kentucky Indiana All-Star game held this past weekend, June 6-7. Mercer County basketball star Anna Kate Drakeford rounded out a 12-woman roster of All-Stars, representing the state of Kentucky in the annual double-header matchup with the Indiana All-Stars on June 8 and 9. Drakeford's historic season in which she was named 12th Region Player of the Year, Rise Up Media 859 Player of the Year and a Miss Basketball finalist by the Kentucky Association of Basketball Coaches, prompt­ed her selection to what's billed as the most talented team in Kentucky each year. The Kentucky-Indiana All-Star game was first established in 1940, when the first boys game was played. The girls game was added in 1976, and each has featured the biggest names to come through Kentucky high school basketball. Historically, Indiana dominates the boys series and currently leads 103-47, but in each of the last six years, the girls teams have split the series. The series began at Lexington Catholic High School, and after one half of play, Indiana led 46-41. Drakeford, who is committed to play with Thomas More College this winter, didn't play much in the first of the two contests but did assist in one basket in her six and a half minutes of play. The Kentucky All-Stars dropped their home game, 90-79. One day later, the two teams met at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in downtown Indianapolis, and Kentucky hoped to continue their streak of splitting the series. Drakeford assisted three scores in the first half, and Kentucky led at half­time, 34-25. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.
