title: City Commission Approves Changes To Water Tower Logo Project, New Utility Rates
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreContractors are working on the water tower overlooking Mercer County Senior High School.</
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors are working on the water tower overlooking Mercer County Senior High School.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Contractors are working on the water tower overlooking Mercer County Senior High School. The Harrodsburg City Commission voted unanimously—after another extensive debate—to allow changes to the logos being painted on the Industry Road water tower.
Last month, the commission voted to allow Mercer County Schools to paint their logo on the tower. The cost to add the logo will be paid by Mercer Schools. At the city commission's regular meeting on Monday, June 10, Jay Anderson, district instructional technology coach and assistant athletic director with the Mercer County School District, told the board about a problem.
'There is a pipe in the way of the logo,' said Anderson, who brought pictures of what would be on the water tower.
'Instead of putting Harrodsburg on the tower, we would put the logo on the tower,' said Commissioner Marvin 'Bubby' Isham, who originally brought the proposal before the commission.
While the placement of the school district's logo on the water tower has been the subject of considerable conversation over the past few weeks, Anderson said it had been in discussion for years.
'It symbolizes a great sense of pride,' he said, noting that other school districts also had their logos painted on water towers. 'It also acts as a good marker for people trying to find the school.'
Anderson said they'd like the school logo to be at 3 to 9 o'clock.
After discussion with City Attorney Norrie Currens, the commission voted to rescind the prior vote and voted to readjust the school logo so that it would be visible on the Industry Road side.
'It would be interesting to be able to see an artist's rendition with the two logos,' Mayor Bob Williams said.
The mayor said the main thing he was thinking about, was making sure everyone could see the city logo, especially with the 250th celebrations ongoing.
'It's a once-in-a-lifetime thing. I would like to have all three tanks showing 250 years,' Williams said. 'Is there anyway to do that?'
'Honestly, I feel like it would be fine,' said Commissioner Missy Banks. 'There are so many 250th signs. I don't think anyone will miss one sign.'
'How much time do we have?' asked Commissioner Charlie Mattingly.
Currens said the contractor, Currens Construction Services, which is owned by Terry Currens, was on hold, waiting for their decision. The commission voted to put the Mercer logo on the tank so it's visible from Industry Road and the bypass, with Williams voting no and Mattingly abstaining.
'I just want to set the record straight. I don't want anybody to get the idea that the city commission is not behind the school,' Williams said.
'Civic pride is one of the things that's been severely lacking in a lot of communities around the country,' Williams said. 'I just want to make sure that when we do this, we're doing it for the right reasons and in the right way.'
The commission then discussed using the city logo's 'H' logo instead of the Harrodsburg name.
'What do you think would look better on the tank?' Isham asked.
Currens said the overflow pipe would distort the city's name. The H logo would not run into problems with the overflow pipe. It would be visible on the Moberly Road side because of the pipe.
Anderson showed them a picture of the logo painted on the tower near Corning. 'It just won't be as big,' he said.
'I like the 'H,'' Williams said. 'I can probably live with that.'
The commission voted unanimously to proceed with the H logo and Harrodsburg's establishment date, 1774.
In other business, the Harrodsburg City Commission:
• Gave first reading to ordinance 2024-04, outlining nonrecurring charges assessed by the city water department, raising the reconnection fee from $35 to $50 and the nonpayment for North Mercer Water District from $85 to $100. The water district charges the city $50. It also establishes a returned check fee of $0. If given second reading, the revisions will take effect July 1.
• Gave first reading to ordinance 2024–15, increasing sewer rates in accordance with the annual consumer price index for 2023. If approved, the minimum charge of $16.82 for the first 250 gallons would increase to $17.44. If given second reading, the revised rates will take effect July 1.
• Gave first reading to ordinance 2024-16, increasing water rates in accordance with the annual CPI. If approved, the minimum water bill for 250 gallons per month would increase from $13.97 to $14.44. If given second reading, the revised rates will take effect July 1.

title: Desmond Smock
description: Desmond Gayle Smock, 90, widower of Sadie Rae Smith Smock, died Tuesday, June 18th, 2024, at the VA Medical Center Hospice Cottage in Lexington. Born December 17, 1933, in Washington County, he was…
content: Desmond Gayle Smock, 90, widower of Sadie Rae Smith Smock, died Tuesday, June 18th, 2024, at the VA Medical Center Hospice Cottage in Lexington. Born December 17, 1933, in Washington County, he was the son of the late Effie Smock Hardin. He was a 1952 graduate of the Mackville High School, Veteran of the United States Army during the Cold War, lifelong member of the Deep Creek Baptist Church, a retired employee of North American Phillips, and a lifelong farmer. Survivors include: one son, Kenneth Eugene Smock, of Boyle County; one daughter, Sandra Lynne Smock, of Boyle County; one half-brother, Delaine (Patricia) Hardin; one half-sister, Mary Von Devine; two nieces, one nephew, two grandchildren, four great-grandchildren, three step-children, step-grandchildren, 15 step-great-grandchildren, 5 step-great-great-grandchildren, and several cousins.

title: Win A T-Shirt—While Supplies Last—By Donating Blood On July 10
description: All donors to the Kentucky Blood Center drive on Wednesday, July 10, will receive a limited-edition 'Donor Vibes' T-shirt (while supplies last) as a thank you for boosting the summer blood supply.…
content:
All donors to the Kentucky Blood Center drive on Wednesday, July 10, will receive a limited-edition 'Donor Vibes' T-shirt (while supplies last) as a thank you for boosting the summer blood supply. (Image submitted).
The Kentucky Blood Center will host a drive for the Mercer County Community on Wednesday, July 10 from 10:30 a.m.–5:30 p.m. at Lions Park Community Center (133 Factory Street). All donors will receive a limited-edition 'Donor Vibes' T-shirt (while supplies last) as a thank you for boosting the summer blood supply.
As fun as summer is, it's a tough time on the blood supply. Donors can ensure it's a safe and enjoyable season for everyone by donating blood. Between warm-weather activities, family vacations and no school, donations typically dwindle during the summer months, but the need for blood doesn't take a vacation. Summer activities often lead to an increase in accidents and traumas and a spike in transfusions. Blood collected at this drive will save the lives of patients in Kentucky who require products for surgeries, diseases like cancer, traumas, organ transplants, premature births and more.
Blood donors must be at least 17 years old (16 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, be in general good health, show a photo I.D. and meet additional requirements. Sixteen-year-old donors must have a signed parental permission slip, which can be found at kybloodcenter.org. Appointments are preferred but walk-ins are welcome. To schedule a donation, visit kybloodcenter.org or call 800.775.2522.
The Kentucky Blood Center is the largest independent, full-service, nonprofit blood center in the commonwealth. Saving local lives since 1968, the Kentucky Blood Center is icensed by the FDA. Their sole purpose is to collect, process and distribute blood for patients in Kentucky. The Kentucky Blood Center provides services in 90 Kentucky counties and has donor centers in Lexington, Louisville, Frankfort, Pikeville, Somerset and the Tri-County area (Corbin). title: Harrodsburg Man Indicted For Criminal Attempt To Commit Murder
description: Mercer County Judicial Center (File image). A Harrodsburg man has been indicted on charges including criminal attempt to commit murder after a road rage incident in May. On Sun
content:
Mercer County Judicial Center (File image).
A Harrodsburg man has been indicted on charges including criminal attempt to commit murder after a road rage incident in May.
On Sunday, May 12, at 8:11 p.m., police responded to a shots fired call at Anderson-Dean Community Park following 'a road rage incident,' according to the uniform citation. Upon arrival, police discovered Darren Douglas Goode, 33, of 454 North College Street, standing next to his vehicle and another man behind his vehicle. According to the uniform citation, Goode told police he was being tailgated by the other man and that he returned fire after the other man shot at him.
Police found shell casings in Goode's vehicle and 'a hole in the passenger side mirror that appeared to have come from inside of Mr. Goode's vehicle.' No bullet holes were found in Goode's vehicle, according to the uniform citation.
The other man told police he was driving behind Goode and went over to pass him. 'Goode then rolled down his window and started shouting racial slurs' at the victim, according to the uniform citation. Following the other man to the park, Goode 'then fired shots at him striking the vehicle at least seven times,' according to the uniform citation. Police searched the other man's vehicle and did not find 'a firearm or any shell casings,' according to the uniform citation.
A witness observed Goode fire the shots and hold the victim at gunpoint, according to the uniform citation.
Police found Goode's firearm in his vehicle, according to the uniform citation. While placing Goode under arrest, police noticed alcohol on his breath and located 'a shooter of an alcoholic beverage' in the vehicle, according to the uniform citation.
Goode subsequently blew a 0.12, according to the uniform citation.
Last week, Goode was indicted on four charges, including criminal attempt to commit murder, a class B felony; 1st degree wanton endangerment and impersonating a police officer, both class D felonies; and driving under the influence, a class B misdemeanor. Goode's bail was set at $200,000 with the following conditions: no use or possession of a firearm; no contact with alleged victims; reporting to pretrial services; submitting to random drug testing; and no new arrests involving alcohol, illegal substances or pain medications with or without a prescription. Det. Rob Oney of the Harrodsburg Police Department testified.

title: Mercer County Natives Burn Rubber At Rockcastle Speedway

content:

Clay Turner used the full width of the track around the corner during one of his hot laps to qualify for the pro late model feature at Rockcastle Speedway on Saturday, July 13.

Two Mercer County natives, Josh Vinyard and Clay Turner, were behind the wheel, as they have been most summer weekends for the last several years.

title: City Bids Out Streets For Repairs—Including Lexington Street
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Harrodsburg City Commission approved putting out a l
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Harrodsburg City Commission approved putting out a list of city streets for paving. They also addressed a resident's question about a local roadway and approved bidding out repairs for Lexington Street.
At their regular meeting on Monday, July 22, the city commission approved a list of streets to be bid out for paving this year. The list includes Bellaire Drive from U.S. 68 to the entrance of the subdivision, Fairview Court, Legion Drive from U.S. 127 to the second Kroger entrance, Commerce Drive from U.S. 127 to the back entrance of the Walmart shopping center, Boswell Street, Elizabeth Court, Magnolica Street from Moreland Avenue to the deadend and East Street from Factory Street to the 'private drive' sign.
Bellaire was deleted from the list of streets to be repaired last year. Mattingly said it will be widened as well.
'There have been some complaints there is not enough room,' the commissioner said.
At the suggestion of Commissioner Marvin 'Bubby' Isham, the commission also approved bidding out repairs for Lexington Street in front of the Mercer County Public Library. Commissioner Charlie Mattingly, who oversees the public works department, warned the commission that repairs to that section of Lexington, which has undergone utility work, could cost as much as $80,000.
'It took $30,000 to fix Main,' Mattingly said, referring to efforts by the city to repair Main Street before the city celebrated its 250th anniversary. 'It would be double to fix Lexington,' Mattingly said. The budget for street paving for the 2025 fiscal year is $155,100, according to city hall.
'It's a whole lot more digging,' Mattingly said.
Before voting, the city commission conducted a public hearing on the municipal aid road funds. They heard from a resident who said a section of Bohon Road was in desperate need of repairs.
'That is private property,' said Mayor Bob Williams.
'We feel it's kind of ridiculous,' said Jason Alford, who said there were seven people living on that section of road, and they were responsible for six-figure repairs. Alford said everyone would be willing to have the property annexed by the City of Harrodsburg.
'It's really hard on us to maintain,' said Alford, who said they had received letters from code enforcement.
Commissioner Isham said other parts of the city had experienced similar issues.
'It has to be brought to a certain spec for the city to take over,' Isham said. He said there wasn't anything the city could do until the road was brought up to standards. Isham said the city could provide the residents with information about the standards. There were no other comments heard during the public hearing. Want to read the rest of the story? title: Mercer County Fiscal Court Votes To Enter New Jail Contract With Woodford County, Inmates Remain At Boyle County Detention Center
description: File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. Mercer and Boyle Counties have still not quite parted ways when it comes to housing jail inmates. At a special…
content:
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
Mercer and Boyle Counties have still not quite parted ways when it comes to housing jail inmates. At a special-called meeting on Tuesday, July 23, the Mercer County Fiscal Court voted to end the interlocal agreement, which was ratified by both counties in 1996. At their regular meeting on Tuesday, July 30, the fiscal court approved an inmate housing contract with Woodford County, which will go into effect Thursday, Aug. 1.
However, Mercer County inmates will remain at Boyle County Detention Center until officials come up with a plan. The contract with Woodford County would cost Mercer $46 per inmate per day, plus medical costs, for a minimum of 20 inmates. Currently, Mercer pays Boyle $65 per day per inmate plus medical costs.
'We have a backup,' said Mercer Judge-Executive Sarah Steele.
It's 17 minutes from Harrodsburg to the Boyle County Detention Center in Danville, while it's 31 minutes from Harrodsburg to the Woodford County Detention Center in Versailles, according to Google Maps. While county officials noted it may cost some in travel time, they said they hope to save money not housing inmates in Boyle County. Officials said they have toured Woodford County's jail. The contract has a 30 day termination periods. Mercer County would make no payment unless there are inmates in Woodford.
Mercer County Jailer Bret 'Chambo' Chamberlain said he has a plan for transportation and has hired some additional staff. Chamberlain said he would have paperwork at the fiscal court's next meeting. Judge Steele said she needs to meet with the Harrodsburg Police Department, the Mercer County Sheriff's Office and County Attorney Ted Dean, as well as Chamberlain. Officials said the contract with Woodford does not have a date attached to it. Mercer inmates will still be housed in Boyle County until they make a plan.
'This doesn't have to necessarily start August 1,' Steele said. 'We've got time to make a good plan.' Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Holt, Wilson And Keller Inducted Into Hall Of Fame
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenThe Mercer County Fair and Horse Show Board of Directors inducted t
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
The Mercer County Fair and Horse Show Board of Directors inducted three members into their hall of fame. 'Woody' Holt, center, and the late 'Big Joe' Wilson and the late Ricky Keller were inducted for their years of service to the motor sports events. Wilson's widow, Cindy Wilson and family accepted in his memory and Keller's widow, Liz Keller and family accepted in his memory. All inductees were joined by their family members.
On Saturday, July 27, before the final night of the horse show at the 2024 Mer­cer County Fair and Horse Show, the fair board and the community took the time to honor the efforts of three men—Woody Holt, the late 'Big Joe' Wilson and the late Ricky Keller—whose work made motorsports events at the fair possible for many years.
'For 197 years, the Mer­cer County Fair and Horse Show has remained a constant. Over generations and generations, this fair has persevered while preserving history, and providing comfort in continuity to people across the county and state, because of the dedicated efforts of men who were willing to sacrifice their time and energy to achieve a common goal for their community,' said board member David Best at the presentation ceremony. title: Titans battle with 6A powerhouse in season opener
description: The Mercer County Titans football team began their season a day after most other programs around the state on Saturday, Aug. 24, in the second kickoff of the Fort Harrod Little Caesars Bowl at Alvis…
content:
The Mercer County Titans football team began their season a day after most other programs around the state on Saturday, Aug. 24, in the second kickoff of the Fort Harrod Little Caesars Bowl at Alvis Johnson Field. Moments before, the Woodford County Yellow Jackets completed a 54-14 rout of Taylor County. A year ago, Woodford County fell to Bullitt East in the Fort Harrod Little Caesars Bowl, 41-28. Two years ago, Bullitt East won 13 straight games before defeating Male in the 6A state finals, claiming the program's first ever state championship. Even two years removed from their pinnacle achievement, if Mercer County managed to win it would be the most prestigious victory in the Titans' history, outside of the 15-12 victory over Russell High School in 2006.
Titan wideouts, from left to right, Braidin Baughman, Jayden Sailor and Cameron Bottoms lined up in a bunch formation and watched for the snap during the first quarter of Mercer County's 28-14 loss to Bullitt East in the Fort Harrod Little Caesars Bowl on Saturday, Aug. 24 (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren).
Both teams took some time to readjust and shake off the dust from a long offseason. Within 60 seconds of the opening kickoff, Mercer County's Braidin Baughman delivered a crucial hit, forcing a fumble by the Chargers, and the Mercer County offense shot themselves in the foot with back-to-back penalties. The Titans rallied and proved early the Charg ers' prowess wasn't going to have an effect at the line of scrimmage. Ashton Drakeford started at quarterback for much of the game while Cornelius Mapp took select snaps throughout the contest. Drakeford connected with junior Jayden Sailor on a crossing route for a gain of 25 and put the Titans in a position to take an early lead. One play later, Baughman took the handoff out of shotgun and darted to the pylon. Daniel Butler's extra point attempt put the Titans up 7-0 with 9:30 remaining in the opening quarter.
Titan defensive end Juhon Goodman was just inches away from knocking the ball loose from quarterback Cole Cornell during Mercer's season opening game against Bullitt East on Saturday, Aug. 24. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren) Other photos of the game can be found at: https://theharrodsburgherald.shootproof.com/gallery/25301882 For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. title: Former Anderson County Band Director Gets 25 Years For Child Porn
description: File image. A former Anderson County High School band director and teacher has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for production of child pornography. Patrick Howard Brady, 38, was a teacher at…
content:
File image.
A former Anderson County High School band director and teacher has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for production of child pornography. Patrick Howard Brady, 38, was a teacher at Anderson County High School, where he served as the band director until May 15, 2023, ac
cording to a press release from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Kentucky. Brady joined Anderson County schools in 2009, according to an archived 2011 edition of the Anderson County News . In 2021, the marching band won a 4A State Championship, according to an article available at anderson.kyschools.us.
According to Brady's plea agreement, he used text messaging, FaceTime and a social media app (VSCO) to engage a minor into a romantic and sexual relationship. Specifically, beginning in the summer of 2022, Brady and the victim engaged in a sexually explicit relationship, starting via text, calls, and FaceTime, eventually occurring in person, multiple times, including at the high school.
Law enforcement began investigating the relationship between Brady and the victim in May 2023, according to the federal press release. When law enforcement arrested Brady and seized his cell phone, he had removed the VSCO application from his phone. Brady admitted that, on two or more occasions, he knowingly used a minor victim to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of transmitting live visual depictions of that conduct.
Brady was sentenced to 25 years in prison by U.S. District Judge Karen Caldwell on Thursday, Aug. 22. Under federal law, Brady must serve 85 percent of his prison sentence. Upon release from prison, he will be under the supervision of the U.S. Probation Office for life. Want to read the rest of the story? title: Creating Family Memories At Devine's

content:
Visitors enjoying the ziplines at Devine's. (Image from Devine's website).
(Editor's Note: Find­ing Fun in Your Hometown is a new series exploring fun opportunities in Mercer County.)
In discussing the various avenues for local and afforda­ble family fun in our commu­nity, one won't go far without hearing the name Devine's—a local family farm that has become a community staple. Conveniently located a mile down US 127 at 623 Tal­mage Mayo Road on the his­toric James McAfee grounds, Devine's has been part of the local landscape for 17 years. It has become a popular gath­ering for families, youth and community groups during that time, pru1icularly during the fall and winter months.
Owners Glenn and Martina Devine, with son Jason also helping run operations, work each year to provide the
community with three season­al themes: the summer farm market in July and August, the Corn Maze and Pumpkin Patch from September to November, and Winter Fest from December to Feb­ruary.
Overhead view of Devine's. (Image from Devine's website).

title: City Commission Gives First Reading To Ordinance Increasing Property Tax
content:
File image.
The Harrodsburg City Commission gave first reading to an ordinance increasing taxes for all taxable property excluding motor vehicles. Under the ordinance, the tax rate will increase to .067 per $100 in assessed value, up from the current rate of .061 per $100. That is a four percent increase. The ordinance must be advertised and the city commission must hold a public hearing before they can give the ordinance a second reading.
City officials said the increase would cost property owners $2 per $100,000 of home value annually. The commission gave the ordinance its first reading at a special-called meeting on Wednesday, Sept. 4, at 11 a.m.
'Do we have to raise this tax?' Commissioner Charlie Mattingly asked.
'We've fallen way behind everybody else on our property assessment,' said Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard. .
'We can't afford to update the city itself,' said Commissioner Missy Banks. 'I think we need it in our budget.'
'I don't like to do it, but it's something we need to do,' Banks said. Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Bluegrass United shocks Lady Titans in 5-0 loss
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com Mercer County Lady Titans soccer (6-4-1) played their second game without captain and top scorer Laykin Irvin leading the front line on Monday,…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
Mercer County Lady Titans soccer (6-4-1) played their second game without captain and top scorer Laykin Irvin leading the front line on Monday, Sept. 9, when Bluegrass United (homeschool) traveled to Harrodsburg.
Both teams took their time settling in, and the opening 10 minutes were a continuous battle for possession. The Mercer County back line wasn't tested until a through ball forced Skylar Webb to leave the goalline. The senior made contact with the ball but couldn't hold on; a sloppy clearance left Webb in a bad spot and unable to reach the far post before a United forward (17').
Five minutes later, a United cross slipped through Webb's fingers and fell to a teammate. After 22 minutes, Mercer trailed 2-0, and Head Coach Josh Culver let the team know their effort wasn't at the level he wanted.
United had several other chances in the first half, but Mercer did just enough to keep them at bay. The Lady Titans looked exhausted after playing Somerset just two days prior.
Freshman Alexis Barker replaced Webb in between the posts to start the second half, but a similar situation to the first United goal cost the Lady Titans again. Barker was caught out and couldn't get back in time before United capitalized (45'). The Lady Titans were tired and United started to pick up intensity and dominated possession in the second half. In the end, Mercer fell 5-0. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: County Considers Options After Running Deficit On 911 Calls
description: File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County
content:
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Fiscal Court is considering their options on paying for 911 services after running a $107,000 deficit for the past year.
In May 2023, the fiscal court set a $1.75 per month service fee on residential and commercial water meters. The revenue was to pay Bluegrass 911 Communications, except for three percent, which was withheld by collecting entities.
At the fiscal court's regular meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 10, they revisited the issue after Judge-Executive Sarah Steele announced the county had run a $107,000 deficit, which she attributed in part to a major increase in call volume. Mercer is one of four counties that use Bluegrass 911, and she said Mercer's percentage of 911 calls had increased from 23 percent to 25 percent, which she said accounted for approximately $60,000 of the deficit. Steele also attributed the deficit in part because the fee wasn't added to bills until August. Before that, she said 911 services were still being collected on landlines, which, as a share of the market, have been in steady decline for decades.
'Most people don't have landlines anymore,' Steele said. She said the deficit was originally worse because the City of Harrodsburg was behind on their contribution. The county also lost out on another $12,000 because the initial report on the number of taps was inflated.
Magistrate Tim Darland said there was another contributing factor: 200 customers of the North Mercer Water District who were deducting their 911 fees.
'Is there anything we can do for that?' Darland asked Tuesday. 'That's ridiculous, in my opinion.'
'I don't have the wherewithal to file civil suits,' said County Attorney Ted Dean. Dean suggested contracting with a collection agency.
'If you don't have to pay it, nobody has to pay it,' Dean said.
'It's $1.75,' Darland said. 'I don't understand what people's thinking.'
'We've got to have 911,' Darland said.
Steele noted the $107,000 deficit is above what taxpayers are already paying.
'We're not the only county that has a deficit,' Steele said. She said they'd discussed the issue with the City of Harrodsburg.
'A lot of the run volume is happening in the city,' Steele said.
The rise in 911 calls is caused, in part, by an increase in multiple services getting called out, she said.
'It makes our call volume increase,' Steele said.
'Sometimes they have to have more people there because the call volume is so high,' she said. 'We're seeing a need for more dispatchers being in a room at a time.'
How to pay for 911 operations in a time of declining land lines is not a new problem. Back in 2019, both Harrodsburg and Burgin voted to institute a $40 parcel to pay for 911 operations, which subsequently failed to pass for lack of a motion at a special-called hearing of the fiscal court. That left the county to use carryover funds to pay for the federally-mandated service. In 2021, both the city and the county voted to merge services with Bluegrass 911.
Steele said Garrard and Lincoln are charging $4 tap fees. She said she would prepare some 'possibilities'—including possibly raising the fee—the magistrates could take action on at the next meeting. title: Titan Football Drops To 2-4
description: The Mercer County Titan football team (2-4) played their final regular season game before a three-game slate of district opponents beginning next week with Marion County. Madison Southern (2-4), whom…
content:
The Mercer County Titan football team (2-4) played their final regular season game before a three-game slate of district opponents beginning next week with Marion County. Madison Southern (2-4), whom the Titans defeated 42-6 last season in the two schools' first ever meeting on a football field, made the trip to Alvis Johnson Field searching for their second straight win after a 30-0 rout of Henry Clay on Sept. 20. While many teams across the state rescheduled games to Thursday night, Mercer County decided to play through the steady rain and wind gusts of up to 20 mph, and it resulted in some sloppy and inconsistent play.
Mercer's offense was at its best on the opening play of the game. Landon Yates ran a flat from the H-back position, and Cornelius Mapp connected with the senior, who turned up field and picked up 35 yards before being forced out of bounds. On the next play, Cohen Sanford bounced outside and made five Eagle defenders miss before finally being tackled from behind on the five-yard line. On fourth and goal from the Eagle three-yard line, Sanford found a hole and dove forward for the opening score of the game. Daniel Butler's extra point traveled just wide of the post.
Senior defensive tackle Gavin Rodriguez checked his alignment before a snap in the first quarter of Mercer County's game with Madison Southern on Friday, Sept. 27. Rodriguez finished the game with a team-leading eight tackles. (Samuel Warren/ Harrodsburg Herald ).
Braeden Kelley set the Eagles up with great field position after returning Butler's kickoff all the way to the Mercer County 30-yard line. The Titan defense did well, initially meeting the Eagles at the line of scrimmage on each play, but two offside calls and a personal foul call kept the Madison Southern drive alive. A second dropped snap by MadSouth quarterback Ethan Moore put the Titans in a great position to end the Eagles' hopes, but Moore scooped the loose ball, slipped one tackler and jogged into the endzone.
After going three and out on their next offensive drive, Sanford made a spectacular play, plucking the ball out of the air after a screen pass to Moore was bobbled. The interception set the Titans up on the Eagle 25-yard line. Each of the Titans' next four plays resulted in a loss, outside of a dropped snap turned into a dump to Sanford in the flat, which gained four yards.
A six-yard tackle for loss by Trenton Berry and a great open field tackle by Yates ended the Eagles' next drive in just three plays.
Sanford picked up 30 yards on the ground over the next four Titan plays but was forced to leave the game with an ankle injury, and the Titans' drive stalled. Sanford had done a great job replacing the efforts of Braidin Baughman while the senior's recovering from injury, and the Titans' run game struggled to do anything after the junior's departure.
The Titans were only able to pick up 42 yards over 19 carries in the remainder of the game. The drive eventually ended with a missed 43-yard field goal attempt.
Trenton Berry made back-to-back tackles in the backfield, including a sack for a seven-yard loss to end the Eagles' next drive, but Mercer didn't have enough time on the clock and went into the locker room trailing 7-6.
A great return by Jayden Sailor set the Titans up on the Eagles' 37-yard line on their opening drive of the second half. The Titan offensive line was blown up and Mapp was brought down, forcing a third down and 17. Cox was subbed in, and an Eagle penalty earned Mercer County a first down. One play later, the game's fifth fumbled snap stalled the drive, and it eventually ended with a shanked field goal attempt, this time from 50 yards out.
'Daniel's got a tremendous leg. It was a great snap, but it was not a great hold; I don't think the ball ever got on the tee. We had a little bit of wind behind us, and Daniel can make them easy from 45, he's got a great leg, a tremendous leg, and yes, I'll run him right back out there in that kind of situation,' said Head Coach Craig Yeast. title: Lady Titans battle hard but fall to Lady Rebels in straight sets
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County Lady Titans (8-8) traveled to Boyle County High School (21-8) with a chance to bolster their 8-4 record in the 12th Region…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Lady Titans (8-8) traveled to Boyle County High School (21-8) with a chance to bolster their 8-4 record in the 12th Region against one of the regions' best programs.
The Lady Titans took an early lead in each set and earned a 7-6 lead in the first period after a blistering hit from Ralasia Piazza landed just inside the corner. A block by Izzie Carlton earned Mercer a 10-6 advantage moments later.
Just like that, a flip switched, and Boyle County went on a six-point run before Coach Lynn Flach called a time-out. The Lady Rebels were firing hit after hit, and Mercer County couldn't catch a break for the remainder of the first period, eventually dropping it after a foul serve earned Boyle their 25th point, completing a 19-5 run.
Carlton made two blocks early in the second, and back-to-back kills from Piazza, much like the first half, gave Mercer an early 6-5 lead. Piazza's fifth kill of the game tied the score at seven, and it stayed tied for most of the remaining set. Sophomore Anne Whitenack rose high up for a hit to tie the game at 11, and Austin Dean did the same on the next rally to give Mercer a one point advantage.
A killer ace from Lady Rebel Charli Grubbs couldn't be returned and opened up a 17-13 lead for Boyle, but the efforts of Piazza and Whitenack earned Mercer several points in quick succession to tie the set at 24. Eventually, Grubbs' hit was smacked in Piazza's direction and the junior couldn't get out of its path before it eventually landed out of bounds. The second set ended 26-24.
Mercer jumped out to an early 5-0 lead in the final set, but Boyle battled back behind strong play from seniors Gracee Teague and Kendra Christopher, cutting Mercer's lead to 7-5. Carlton stayed active around the net and earned another block For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Harrodsburg Named One Of Most Scenic Towns In Kentucky
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreHarrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic cities in Kentucky and everyone will get a chance to see old Hogtown in all
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Harrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic cities in Kentucky and everyone will get a chance to see old Hogtown in all her glory when Oktoberfest returns Friday, Oct. 4.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Harrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic towns in Kentucky. That's according to WorldAtlas.com, a website that launched in 1994 and bills itself as one of the largest publishing resources in geography and other topics it covers, including sociology, demography, environment, economics, politics and travel. Other Kentucky cities named were Cave City, Slade, Cumberland, Clermont, Carrollton, Richmond, Cambellsville and Corbin.
According to WorldAtlas.com, one of the reasons Harrodsburg is so scenic is because of Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill. The website invites readers to 'visit the beautiful natural landscape of the shakers at the 3,000 acre Shaker Village,' which has '36 miles of trails which are ideal for hikers, horseback riders, and even classic carriages.'
While Kentucky's state parks are not as well known as the Grand Canyon or Yellowstone Park, WorldAtlas.com insists they shouldn't be overlooked. 'Kentucky is the only place in the world you can see the largest cave system and a moonbow in a single state.'
One of the most unique state parks in the Commonwealth is right here in Harrodsburg. Old Fort Harrod State Park offers more than a full-scale replica of the fort built by James Harrod in 1774. It's also home to the historic Mansion Museum, the George Rogers Clark Federal Monument, the Lincoln Marriage Temple and the oldest cemetery west of the Alleghenies. And don't forget the Osage Orange tree at Old Fort Harrod, which is both taller and broader than the National Champion but remains the Unofficial National Champion due to its split trunk.
Mercer County is also home to 22 streams, 15 creeks and three rivers as well as Herrington Lake, the deepest in Kentucky. For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Campbellsville Man Faces Kidnapping Charges After High Speed Chase
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A Campbellsville man is facing charges of kidnapping, resisting arrest and driving under the influence after an incident on Sunday,…
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
A Campbellsville man is facing charges of kidnapping, resisting arrest and driving under the influence after an incident on Sunday, Oct. 6.
At approximately 3:30 a.m., Bluegrass 911 received a phone call from a woman who complained that the male driver would not let her out of the vehicle. Officers with the Harrodsburg Police Department were dispatched to the area of Perryville Road and Mooreland Avenue, where they located a black 2013 Ford F150. According to the uniform citation, the truck sped off when police arrived, heading south on College Street at 'a high rate of speed.'
The truck ran the red light on Danville Road and the U.S. 127 Bypass and sped into Boyle County. According to the uniform citation, the woman continued to yell for the driver, subsequently identified as Christiaan S. Cato, 49, of Campbellsville, to stop.
Cato ran another red light at the intersection of the U.S. 2168 Bypass and U.S. 127, according to the uniform citation, before finally coming to a stop at Davco Drive in Boyle County.
Cato did not comply with officers' commands to get out of the truck, according to the uniform citation. Police tased Cato, who was then taken to Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center for treatment.
According to the uniform citation, the woman said she had been on a date with Cato in Marion County when he began drinking. She told police the only reason he stopped 'was because the truck ran out of gas.'
Police say they found 'two tall cans of peach-flavored alcohol,' according to the uniform citation. Inside the door handle police located a plastic bag containing a 'crystal-like substance' which they believe to be 'consistent with methamphetamine.'
Cato was arrested and charged with kidnapping an adult, reckless driving, 1st degree fleeing or evading police, resisting arrest, 3rd degree assault of a police or probation officer, 1st degree wanton endangerment, disregarding a traffic light, driving under the influence and 1st degree possession of methamphetamine. He is being held at Boyle County Detention Center on a $10,000 bond. title: Harrodsburg Named One Of Nine Slow-Paced Southern Towns
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreVolunteer Linda Honnold was at the sweetest spot in Harrodsburg in 2023: she was running the dessert table at the Christmas Tea Room at the Harrodsburg Historical…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore
Volunteer Linda Honnold was at the sweetest spot in Harrodsburg in 2023: she was running the dessert table at the Christmas Tea Room at the Harrodsburg Historical Society. This year's tea room happens on Friday, Dec. 6, and Saturday, Dec. 7.
Harrodsburg has been named one of nine slow-paced towns to visit in the southern United States.
'These towns are slow-paced but that doesn't mean they are boring,'editor Bradley Cooper wrote in the article. 'In fact, with the many museums, Civil War sites and beautiful national parks, visitors will find plenty of hidden gems in these slow-paced towns.'
Among the historic spots highlighted by Cooper include Old Fort Harrod State Park (100 South College Street).
'Visitors can explore a militia blockhouse, the Mansion Museum, which houses artifacts from the Civil War and the Lincoln Marriage Temple, a small log cabin where Abraham Lincoln's parents were wed,' Cooper wrote. Visitors can also enjoy the Christmas Tree Forest, sponsored by the Mercer County Chamber of Commerce and Auto Kustoms, which will remain open until Jan. 6, 2025.
World Atlas also highlighted Shaker Village at Pleasant Hill, which is lighting up for an 18th century style Christmas with Candlelight Tours Fridays on Dec. 6, 13 and 20, with tours at 5:30 and 7 p.m. Illuminated Evenings happen Saturdays on Dec. 7, 14 and 21, starting at 4 p.m. Hop on the Jingle Bell Shuttle, write a letter to Santa, sip hot chocolate, enjoy music performances, make a craft in the Elf Shop and sing carols while the staff light up the tree.
Shaker Village is also hosting Children's Tea Time with Mrs. Claus every Saturday through Christmas, with tea times at 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Dec. 7, 14 and 21. To learn more, or to make a reservation, call 859-734-5411 or visit online at shakervillageky.org. title: Strong Defense Carries The Titans Past Somerset
description: The Mercer County Titans boys basketball team (1-0) opened the season with a solid 14-point home win over the Somerset Briar Jumpers (0-1) on Monday, Dec. 2. With impressive defense and solid offense,…
content:
The Mercer County Titans boys basketball team (1-0) opened the season with a solid 14-point home win over the Somerset Briar Jumpers (0-1) on Monday, Dec. 2. With impressive defense and solid offense, the Titans were able to pull away for the win.
Mercer County came into the game ranked third in the 12th region, which is the highest they've been ranked since 2018 graduate Trevon Faulkner. Many players shined in this game such as senior Trevor Ellis, who scored 15 points and grabbed several rebounds. Other players who showed up and showed out were junior forward Kaleb Murray, who's energy and intense gameplay earned him 11 points and two steals. Senior guard and Lexington Christian Academy transfer Hagan Preston showed he can make an impact on both the defensive and offensive end of the floor, he ended the game with 10 points and multiple steals.
Senior forward Trevor Ellis dominated the paint in Monday's win. Here he delivers a big slam for two of his 15 points. (Imago Dei Media).
Overall the first quarter was all Titans, especially on the defensive side. Mercer earned an impressive six steals and two blocks in the first quarter alone. Ellis scored his first basket of the night seconds after tip-off. Murray came away with two steals on the next two possessions and was able to finish one on the other end. The overall intensity picked up for Mercer and Preston knocked down two 3-pointers. A couple blocks from Ellis kept the Briar Jumper's offense at bay. The Titans found themselves in a great position to start out the game after Murray drained two free throws, and they led 20-10 at the end of the opening quarter.
The second quarter started just like the first, with the menacing defense of the Titans thwarting the Briar Jumpers, but 6 '7 Briar Jumper big man Landen Lonesky started to give Mercer's defense a problem. Even though Lonesky had one of, if not the best, defender in the 12th region guarding him (Ellis), he was still able to complete multiple dropstep layups for easy buckets. Halfway through the second quarter, the Titans' offense slowed down and the Briar Jumpers' offense picked up the pace. The mix of layups from Lonesky and the two 3-pointers from guard Bryson Stevens closed the lead to four points at one point. With two minutes left in the first half, the Titans picked up their slack and ended the quarter leading, 30-25.
After halftime, the Titans came out confident as if they didn't struggle at all. This confidence ultimately led to the Titans turning the ball over three times within the first few minutes of the third quarter.
The third quarter was slow for the Titans, their only points coming from a layup and a mid-range jumper by sophomore guard Mijaia Dunn and Murray respectively. The second half of the quarter didn't go any better, and a 3-pointer by Jackson Doughty was the only other basket the Titans could manage. The Briar Jumpers' offensive struggles continued though, and the Titans held on to a 37-30 lead after three quarters.
In the fourth quarter, it became clear the Titans struggled in the half-court game. Their style of play wasn't working like it was in the first quarter. After a very slow first two minutes, the Titans needed something to keep them calm and ahead in the game. A timeout called by second year coach Keith Adkins was exactly what the Titans needed.
'The concern lies on the offensive end of the floor,' said Adkins. 'We just can't continue turning the ball over at the rate that we do.'
No points were scored in the next minute, and with constant free throw struggles holding the Titans back, it didn't matter, because the Titans pulled away after a huge late game dunk by Ellis. The Titans ended up finding a groove and had multiple defensive stops with numerous made baskets. With 40 seconds left in the game, Preston dribbled out the clock and the Titans ended up pulling off a 51-37 win.
'I thought the effort and communication was solid. We did a decent job of keeping the ball in front of us and I thought we contested shots really well. We do still need some work on guarding the ball screens, but that is something that will change a little from one game to the next,' said Adkins.
Mercer's next game will be at Jack Coleman Sr. Gymnasium in Burgin on Thursday, Dec. 5, at 7:30 p.m.
Scoring: Ellis 15, Murray 11, Preston 10, Doughty 5, Dunn 4, Tatum 2, King 2, Sparrow 2. For continued Mercer County boys basketball coverage, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Tourist Commission Unveils New Logo And Website
description: Image: Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission. The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission has unveiled a new logo and a new website.
content:
Image: Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission.
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission has unveiled a new logo and a new website.
Kinetic Strategic Design of Somerset created both the logo and the website, which was paid for using American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds. The website and logo together cost $26,000.
'We were fortunate to receive over $100,000 from the state ARPA Funds, and we were able to use some of the funds for this new design,' said Daarik Gray, executive-director of the tourist commission. 'We are grateful that those funds allowed us to accomplish this project, plus many others, to help showcase our wonderful community and all we have to offer.'
Back in September, Kirby Stephens, the creative director and president of KSD, took the board through the variations of the logo and the website. Stephens said the logo is about embracing the past as well as things happening today. Stephens said they chose the lowercase 'h' to represent the chairs at Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill. The two h's represent historic hospitality. They are surrounded by a circular field of stars that reflects on the history of the nation. Stephens said the two h's have an implied 'm' in historic red and blue. He presented the board with various configurations—different fonts and typefaces for advertising and the extended brand palette—including using the new tagline, 'historic hospitality since 1774.'
Alternative logo. Image: Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission.
'When creating the logo we thought it was important to embrace our history, while also trying to create a modern design,' Gray said. 'We feel like we were able to do that as we incorporated the Shaker-style chairs while also creating an H and M to represent both Harrodsburg and Mercer County. Additionally, the stars on the logo honor our role in Kentucky's foundation.'
The tourist commission also launched their brand-new website, www.visitharrodsburgky.com, which was also created by KSD Kinetic Strategic Design.
'When redesigning the website, it was important for us to have all the tools that visitors would need when planning their trip to Mercer County,' Gray said. 'Additionally, we wanted the website to be a tool for our local community to be able to use when trying to find events or things to do. We feel like we were able to accomplish all of those things plus more.'
'We are excited about the launch of both our new logo and website,' Gray said. 'It is a great way to move forward for our organization as we get ready for 2025.' For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Burgin Prepares To Go Wet
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin City Council took no action on an alcohol ordinance at their meeting on Tuesday, Dec. 10, which was the last regula
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin City Council took no action on an alcohol ordinance at their meeting on Tuesday, Dec. 10, which was the last regular called meeting on 2024.
'We're not going to do anything with it tonight,' said Mayor Joe Monroe, who said the ordinance was over 30 pages long. Monroe asked the council to read it over and they'd vote on it next month.
This year, Burgin voters elected to go allow alcohol sales, 320 to 228. City officials were asked when the city would officially go wet.
'That's a good question,' said City Attorney John Wood, who reviewed the state statute. He said the date is tentatively 60 days after the second reading, which would be in February 2025.
'The goal is to have the ordinance in place before they would be technically able to sell,' Woods said.
State law says businesses could begin applying for liquor licenses 60 days after the Mercer County Board of Elections certifies the 2024 election, Wood said, reading directly from the statute. The deadline for the county board of elections to issue the certificate of election was Monday, Nov. 18.
In any case, it will the be Kentucky Alcoholic Beverage Control, not the City of Burgin, that will issue liquor licenses. The Harrodsburg Herald reached out to Alcoholic Beverage Control for clarification.
'Businesses can apply for a license starting 60 days after an election is certified,' said Kristin Voskuhl, executive director of communications and public outreach at the Public Protection Cabinet.
'A licensee can sell as soon as their license is issued,' Voskuhl said via email.
Once a territory is voted wet, prohibition ceases 60)days after the election is certified by the County Clerk, according to state law.
The Burgin City Council is charged by ordinance to create an office of Alcoholic Beverage Administrator. According to a handout shared by Voskuhl, the requirements for the local ABC administrator are that no member of the board or member of his or her immediate family shall have any interest in any premises or business where alcoholic beverages are manufactured, stored, or sold. Nor shall he or she receive any commission or profit from any person applying for or receiving any license or permit.
In addition, the ABC administrator must be at least 30 years old and must have been a citizen of the state and resident of Mercer County for at least two years preceding the date of appointment. Through the ordinance, the city council will establish ordinances and local fees as well as applications, training requirements, Sunday sales and Election Day sales.
Sixty days after the election is certified, interested parties may begin the application process. They can apply online at the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control's website, abc.ky.gov. Applicants are required to submit an advertisement in a local newspaper declaring intent to apply for a license. Approval of the local administrator must be obtained prior to submission to the state ABC office.
A license cannot be issued for at least 30days from the date of the advertisement. It takes approximately 45-60 days for the ABC to process a new application due to premises inspections and various other tasks performed by the ABC Licensing and Enforcement personnel.
There are different processes for applying for quota licenses as opposed to applying for non-quota licenses. Non-quota applications will be accepted by ABC after the initial 60 days. New quota applications will not be accepted until ABC has placed an advertisement one time in the local newspaper informing the public of the availability of quota licenses and the number available, according to the ABC.
An applicant for a quota license cannot apply for a license after the 60 day wait period.
ABC will accept applications for 30 days following the advertisement in the newspaper. The number of quota retail package licenses issued by ABC in any county shall not exceed a number equal to one for every 2,300 residents, according to state law. title: Former Lady Titan Star Timberlynn Yeast Shines With The Thundering Herd
description: Former Mercer County Lady Titan star basketball player Timberlynn Yeast has spent most of the last two seasons forced to watch the game she loves from the sidelines. Yeast was the leading scorer for…
content:
Former Mercer County Lady Titan star basketball player Timberlynn Yeast has spent most of the last two seasons forced to watch the game she loves from the sidelines. Yeast was the leading scorer for the Lady Titans from her eighth grade year until she was a junior. Her 20.9 points and 8.4 rebounds per game in the 2021-2022 season earned her a second-team all-state selection. Unfortunately, just weeks before her senior season, Yeast suffered a knee injury that damaged her ACL and meniscus. She was forced to watch from the bench, but did all she could for her team, and was eventually named the Co-12th Region Player of the Year as the Lady Titans went on to claim their first 12th Region championship in five years.
By that point, Yeast had already committed to the University of Buffalo, but due to some unforeseen circumstances she, and four other former commitments, were released from their NLI. Within two weeks Yeast had found a new home, in Huntington, WV. After starring for the West Virginia Thunder in the Under Armour Association circuit, Yeast had made a second home of West Virginia, and decided to continue her career with the Thundering Herd. Yeast was back on the court for the first time in a long time, but it was short lived. Only a month had passed before the exact same injury that ended her senior season recurred. Repeating any injury can be disheartening, especially an injury as detrimental as a complex knee ligament injury, but Yeast knew it could be done.
Timberlynn Yeast squeezed past two Anderson County defenders during her Freshman season at Mercer County. (Image: Arpan Dixit/ the Harrodsburg Herald .)
'I just told myself I've done it before, I can do it again, and that kept me going,' said Yeast.
Yeast knew it had to be done, and if possible, done better. She has taken advantage of several types of therapy provided by Marshall, including underwater PT, and dedicated herself to the weight room, which she says has made a massive difference.
After not playing competitive basketball for nearly two years, Yeast was full of nerves before the Thundering Herd's season opener against Northern Kentucky, the program that gave Yeast her first D-I offer four years ago, but the fear of getting hurt paled in comparison to her excitement to play the game she loves, or the gratitude for her family cheering from the stands.
On Nov. 10, Yeast took advantage of limited minutes and shot 3-3 from the field while grabbing two boards, a steal and an assist in just 11 minutes of action. Now a redshirt freshman, Yeast averages about 10 minutes a game, but takes advantage of every moment. Yeast dominated in the month of December, averaging six points per game. Against Davis & Elkins, Yeast scored eight points while grabbing three steals and assisting one basket. Her .586 shooting percentage is the second best on the team. Now that the Thundering Herd are getting to a critical point of conference play, Yeast approaches each opportunity differently.
'Now it's pretty calming, just getting my mind right before the game and making sure I'm prepared– knowing that I've been working to get back and taking advantage of every opportunity– [and] trusting God through it all,' said Yeast.
Now that she is living her student-athlete lifestyle to the fullest, Yeast says she is happy to be at this stage in her journey.
'I've enjoyed it, especially being in Huntington, a small college town that loves Marshall athletics,' said Yeast.
When she's not going to each Thundering Herd sporting event and bonding with her teammates, Yeast is hard at work on the court, working to regain complete trust in her body.
'I hope to get back to attacking the basket at a high level with no fear; trusting my knee, and staying confident in my shot knowing that I have put the work in,' said Yeast.
Yeast and the Thundering Herd play next on Saturday, Jan. 18, against the traveling Appalachian State Mountaineers. Tip off is scheduled for 1p.m. Nearly all of Marshall's remaining Sun Belt Conference games this season will be viewable on ESPN+. Burgin Senior Gabby Thompson fires off a pass during the Lady Bulldogs' 64-29 thumping of the Frankfort on Mondav. Jan. 27. (Image: Sam Warren/T he Harrodsburg Herald .)
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs (6-10) had an all-around great performance in a 64-29 thumping of the Frankfort Lady Panthers (1-14) on Monday, Jan. 27, in the Jack Coleman Sr. Gymnasium.
Burgin was electric. Their speed and confidence showed in each possession, and their ball movement was so well executed, at times it seemed like they were playing against air. Sophomore Kynlee Sexton gave the Lady Bulldogs a 5-0 lead after she swished a trey on the left shoulder. A little over a minute later Sexton was fouled while shooting from the same spot, and made all three free throws. Next it was Senior Jemma Jenkins who drained a three from the same spot and gave Burgin a commanding 13-0 lead. Ashton Lester forced two turnovers in the first quarter that led to baskets, one of which, a swift pass forward to Gabby Thompson in transition for an easy bucket. Freshman Jocelyn Stanley missed a three off the side of the backboard, but grabbed her own missed shot and stepped inside the perimeter before swishing a mid range jumper. At the end of the first quarter, Burgin was firing on all cylinders and led 23-3. The Bulldogs had several second chance opportunities to thank for their tremendous offensive display in the first quarter.
'I was very pleased with the effort we gave last night boxing out. We have been working on that phase all year to try to make up for some height disadvantages we face about every game. [I] thought all the girls did a pretty decent job of sealing and then going to get the ball,' said Coach Keith Monson.
Seconds after Lester drained a three to reclaim the momentum early in the second quarter, Thompson jumped a pass and dribbled through the whole Frankfort lineup before passing to Leah Jenkins in the corner for another Lady Bulldog three-pointer. title: William Springate
description: William 'Bruce' Springate, 87, of Harrodsburg, husband of Patricia Willhite Springate, died Wednesday, Jan. 29, 2025, at the Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center in Danville. Born June 10, 1937,…
content:
William 'Bruce' Springate, 87, of Harrodsburg, husband of Patricia Willhite Springate, died Wednesday, Jan. 29, 2025, at the Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center in Danville.
Born June 10, 1937, in Sinai, he was the son of the late Clinton and the late Rebecca Gillis Springate. He was the owner and operator of Aggie Sale Sport Shop, was a graduate of Western High School and Eastern Kentucky University where he played basketball, was a basketball coach, a U.S. Army veteran; served on the Danville Country Club board, Harrodsburg Industrial Board, the Athletic Dealers of America board and was a member of the Fairview Christian Church.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: one daughter, Sharon (Joe) Bunch of Landrum, South Carolina; special family and friends, Mariano, Celia Flores and family; and several nieces and nephews.
He was preceded in death by three brothers, J.W. Springate, Bobby Springate and Clinton Ray Springate, and one sister, Bonnie Ackley.
Funeral services were held Saturday, Feb. 1, at the Harrodsburg Christian Church, with Micki McHugh officiating. Burial was in the Spring Hill Cemetery.
Pallbearers were Marino Flores, Joe Bunch, Mack Kersey, Tony Springate, Paul Lewis, Jay Bruce Springate, David Ackley, Brent Sallee and Bobby Gene Sallee. Honorary pallbearers were Bobby Springate, Larry Springate, Jerry Springate, Mickey Springate, Fred Rice, Bill Wickliffe and all of his golfing buddies.
Memorial contributions are suggested to the Heritage Hospice, P.O. 1213, Danville, KY 40423.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.ransdellfuneralchapel.com.

title: Learn How City Government Works On Feb. 17
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com Learn how your l
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Learn how your local government is supposed to work on Monday, Feb. 17.
Representatives from the Kentucky League of Cities will present 'Government 101,' covering the basics of local city governance from 5 to 7 p.m. in the auditorium at Mercer County Senior High School (1124 Moberly Road).
At the Harrodsburg City Commission's regular meeting on Monday, Jan. 27, City Attorney Norrie Currens said questions have been raised about the city government, and especially about the 2023 hiring of Stacey Maynard as the city's chief administrative officer.
'We follow what the law says,' Currens explained Monday. She said the commission, which consists of the commissioners and the mayor—are considered a legislative body under state law. Currens said the city previously employed a chief administrative officer. The position was last held by Ed Music. She said the city opted not to fill the position after it went vacant.
Currens also noted that the city commission voted to hire Maynard.
'We didn't change our form of government,' Currens said. 'We just filled a position that had been open for some time.'
She said some cities employ a city manager.
'We do not have a city manager form of government,' Currens said.
She invited the public to reach out to members of the city commission, to Maynard or to any supervisors if they had questions.
The Kentucky League of Cities is a is a non-stock, nonprofit membership association serving more than 370 Kentucky cities and municipal agencies.
According to its website, the league provides cities, leaders and employees with services including legislative advocacy, legal services, community consulting, training and online training, policy development and research, and more. The organization also provides enterprise services such as financing options for cities, and the Kentucky League of Cities Insurance Services insures more municipal clients than any other insurance carrier in Kentucky.
On Feb. 17 from 5 to 7 p.m., two attorneys from the Kentucky League of Cities will do a presentation outlining how the city is supposed to work.
Currens said they are offering it so everybody can understand the government.
Mayor Bob Williams said he would 'highly recommend' everyone who is able to attend the session.
Williams recommends city employees attend training sessions hosted by the league as well.
'There's a lot of information there,' the mayor said. 'It's a great networking opportunity.'
Maynard also addressed confusion about water cut-offs for nonpayment. She said cut-offs start on the 21st of the month. If that falls on a weekend or holiday, the cut-off will be on the next business day after the 20th.
'It's on the back of every waterbill,' Maynard said. She said she was working on creating a calendar which would be posted online.
Harrodsburg City Hall is located at 208 South Main Street. The phone number is 859-734-2383. For more information, visit online at harrodsburgcity.org.

title: Bulldogs bite back in win over Berea
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin Lady Bulldogs (10-13) redeemed themselves of an early season loss to Berea (11-12) in a fantastic display of effort on Monday, Feb.…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin Lady Bulldogs (10-13) redeemed themselves of an early season loss to Berea (11-12) in a fantastic display of effort on Monday, Feb. 10.
Everything was going wrong for the Lady Bulldogs soon after tipoff. Berea struck first through center Kadence Stepp. Lady Bulldog senior Jemma Jenkins had a layup touch every part of the rim before rolling out, and one possession later, fired a three that bounced on the rim three times before falling out. Next it was junior Hayley Hurst who's jumpshot rattled in and out. Kynlee Sexton tried to rally the Bulldogs, jumping in front of three Berea passes in just over a minute, but the Lady Bulldogs were still scoreless with 2:27 to go in the first quarter, trailing 6-0. Former Burgin player Kelsey Slone delivered a dagger from deep that gave Berea a 9-0 lead. The Lady Pirates excitement led to a disorganized press, and Leah Jenkins split the defense with a cross court pass to a wide-open Sexton, who scored Burgin's first basket. Ashton Lester earned a trip to the charity stripe and made one shot, but Burgin trailed 14-3 after one quarter.
The effort was there, and the shot selection wasn't bad, but Burgin's shooting struggles continued into the second quarter. The Lady Bulldogs first basket of the second quarter didn't come for over 3 minutes. Sexton drifted away and Hurst delivered a long pass forward to the sophomore for her second bucket. Senior Gabby Thompson wasn't finding her normal looks early in the game, but eventually started drifting into space and was always on the backside of a shot. She grabbed an offensive rebound and drained a floater to jumpstart Burgin's offense. Thompson repeated the process moments later and cut Burgin's deficit to 9. After seeing that only a couple baskets could change the game, the Lady Bulldogs were flying across the court. J. Jenkins dove on the floor and earned a jump ball. Lester scored three points from the charity stripe in the closing moments, but Burgin still trailed at the half, 25-15.
Gabby Thompson dribbled around Kelsey Slone during Burgin's comeback win over Berea on Monday, Feb. 10. Thompson finished with 11 points. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel Warren)
After the restart, J. Jenkins led Burgin's comeback. The senior burst into the lane and swiftly laid the ball off the glass. Lester went next and dropped a long range jumper. Sexton's sharpshooting put five points on the board in two possessions. The Lady Bulldogs made plays in the defensive end as well. Lester stripped the ball away and earned a foul in transition, making one free throw. Seconds later, J. Jenkins swatted a Berea shot and Sexton recovered the ball, and found Thompson who finished at the rim and cut the Lady Pirate's lead to two. J. Jenkins assisted another Thompson drive, and one possession later took advantage of a distracted Berea defense and drove straight to the rim for a layup that tied the game. Berea scored soon after, but Sexton forced her fifth turnover of the game and finished off the glass to keep the game tied. Burgin began to pull away midway through the fourth quarter. Lester made two clutch free throws, and moments later she fought for an offensive rebound, went straight back up and completed an and one. Burgin led 41-37 with 4:43 remaining.
Burgin Senior Jemma Jenkins scored two of her twelve points on a crucial possession in the fourth quarter. (The Harrodsburg Herald/Sam Warren)
Berea subbed their biggest players in and used their advantage in the paint to retake the lead. Ashton Lester was sent to the free throw line four times in the fourth quarter, and made three in two trips to tie the game at 47. J. Jenkins followed and made one to give the Lady Bulldogs a one-point lead. Hurst was sent to the line twice and made two shots. Burgin was ahead 50-48 with 51 seconds remaining, but the clock ran only .6 seconds before they fouled Berea's Absady Baker, who tied the game. Sexton was the next Lady Bulldog to be sent to the line and she made one. Thompson pounced on the missed second shot and gave the ball to Lester, who was fouled and gave Burgin a two point advantage. Burgin's two seniors made big plays late in the game to seal their tenth win of the season. J. Jenkins locked in and knocked down two free throws to put the Lady Bulldogs up four with seconds to go. The Bulldogs won by a final score of 56-52.
'I was extremely pleased with the all out effort,' Burgin Head Coach Keith Monson said of the win. 'They decided at half time to do what it takes to win, and they went back out and did it. It was a great total team effort. I thought our two seniors showed a lot of poise and team leadership tonight,' said Monson.
The Lady Bulldogs will be in action again today, Thursday, Feb. 13, when they travel to face Eminence High School. Burgin girls basketball will play its final home game of the season, and honor its seniors, next Tuesday, Feb. 18, when they take on Somerset Christian School.
Scoring – Lester 18, Sexton 13, Jenkins 12, Thompson 11, Hurst 2. For more great stories, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Fiscal Court Recognizes Firefighter Justin Railey For Saving Child From Ice
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
David Baer and Thaddeus Baer present Firefighter Justin Railey of the Mercer County Fire Protection District with an oar. Railey used an oar to rescue two-year-old Thaddeus from a frozen pond in January.
The Mercer County Fiscal Court has recognized a local firefighter who helped save a child from the ice in January.
At their regular meeting on Tuesday, Feb. 11, the fiscal court recognized Firefighter Justin Railey of the Mercer County Fire Protection District for his quick thinking back in January, when two-year-old Thaddeus Baer was stuck on ice in the middle of a local pond after sledding too far.
Railey crawled to the middle of the pond and used an oar to pull him out.
On Tuesday, Railey was presented with a certificate of appreciation by Magistrate Susan Barrington. Railey was also presented with an oar by Davie Baer, the father of Thaddeus Baer, in case he needed it for another rescue.
It was a snowy day to recognize a winter rescue, with the area under a winter storm warning remains in effect until 7 a.m. Wednesday, according to the National Weather Service.
'We were a little bit busy this morning,' Mercer Sheriff Ernie Kelty told the fiscal court Tuesday, with numerous drivers slipping off the road. Kelty said he had to call in deputies to handle accidents, with about 15 incidents within one hour.
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said county road crews had been out plowing since 5 a.m. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Mercer Winterguard Brings Home Honors
description: Ben Sears Contributing Writer mercerwinterguard@gmail.com After a few weeks off to clean up their routine and strengthen their skills, the Mercer County High School Winterguard traveled this past…
content:
Ben Sears
Contributing Writer
mercerwinterguard@gmail.com
After a few weeks off to clean up their routine and strengthen their skills, the Mercer County High School Winterguard traveled this past Saturday to their second contest of the season, this time at the Floyd Central High School in Floyds Knobs Indiana. This was their first time competing in their new class. If most of you remember they placed first at their Clark County competition and were moved up to a new classification grou p. This meant stiffer competition. They performed their show, Heart Strings featuring music from Sia, Elastic Heart.
Guard Member Lauren Waters performing her routine at the opening of the show performed in Indiana on Saturday, Feb. 22. (Photo by Mike Sims)
The guard placed 2nd in the Scholastic Region A with a score of 61.09 behind the Floyd Central Junior Varsity squad. Director of Bands Erica Ashford said, 'Despite having a lot of snow days and illness the past few weeks, the guard members and their instructor, Alex Smith, have worked really hard and put in the time to get better.' She went on to say, 'They have stayed late, they have come in on their days off, and they have put in hours of work at home. Their success this weekend is due to their commitment to get better and their desire to succeed in this new classification.' It showed. They added another minute to their show and have a little bit more to add to finally complete the 3 minute show.
Their next competition is this coming Saturday at Lafayette High School in Lexington. Come out and support the Titans and the indoor color guard sport. Their performance time is 3:26pm.
For additional information on Mercer County Band or Mercer County Guard, follow us on our socials, on Facebook at Mercer County Band or on Instagram at mercercoband or mercercoguard.

title: Ava Horn

content:
Ava Jewell Horn, 101, widow of Willie B. Horn, of Harrodsburg, died Thursday, Feb. 20, 2025, at the Willows of Harrodsburg.
Born June 5, 1923, in Washington County, she was the daughter of the late Merrill and Lillie (Robinson) Long.
She was a homemaker, member and past secretary of Calvary Baptist Church, was a member of the Baptist Association, WMU and was a Christian.
Survivors include: one daughter, Brenda (Bill) Rogers of Harrodsburg; three grandchildren, Will (Stephanie) Rogers of Harrodsburg, Dana (John) Perkins of Versailles and Lynette (Michael) Lawson of London; six great-grandchildren, Kayla and Nick Grimard, William and Lily Rogers and Brynna and Braden Lawson; four great-great-grandchildren, Cason Lee Martin, Avery Lawson, Hagen Perkins and Anna Tuschi; and two special friends, David Baker and Jeanetta Devine.
She was preceded in death by one sister, Leoda L. Carter; one brother, Leon Long; and great-granddaughter, Jessica Bryn Lawson.
The funeral was held Monday, Feb. 24, at Ransdell Funeral Chapel, with Bro. Daniel Smith, Larry Camic, David Baker and Dr. Robert Defoor officiating. Burial was in Spring Hill Cemetery.
Pallbearers were William Lee Rogers, Nick Grimard, Braden Lawson, Adam Lawson, Brian Perkins and David Baker. Honorary pallbearers were Jeanetta Devine, Ava Jewell's Sunday School Class, the staff and her friends at the Willows of Harrodsburg.
Memorial contributions are suggested to Gideon International, P.O. 176, Harrodsburg KY, 40330 and Calvary Baptist Church, 2195 Cornishville Rd, Harrodsburg, KY 40330.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.ransdellfuneralchapel.com.
