title: Harrodsburg Community Center Has An Exciting Summer Ahead
description: File image. The Harrodsburg Community Center, formerly the YMCA, has been busy planning an exciting summer of opportunities for kids of all ages to stay active both physically and mentally. Lifelong…
content:
File image.
The Harrodsburg Community Center, formerly the YMCA, has been busy planning an exciting summer of opportunities for kids of all ages to stay active both physically and mentally. Lifelong Harrodsburg native Trevor Short officially began his work as executive director of the community center in February, and has been working to provide as many opportunities to the public as possible, while planning for some exciting future endeavors.
Getting some gym equipment back in the building is an important step in the wide array of physical activity available for members of the community according to Short. Eventually, Short plans to offer memberships, like the former Ephraim McDowell Wellness Center on the ground floor, and with several classes and potential athletic opportunities being held in the same space, Short believes it will be a significant advantage to membership holders that wasn't there in the past. Currently, the community center is hosting several classes, including:
• Yoga with instructor Sherman Fracher. Fracher, who has been instructing yoga classes since 2003 in Cincinnati, recently moved to Mercer County and plans to continue her classes for the foreseeable future. As of now, only one class is hosted each Monday from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m., but Fracher says she would open up more time slots if there's interest from the public. Those interested in signing up can do so at: https://form.jotform.com/241625189824160. ;
• A Basketball camp with Prototype Athletics. The camp will be held upstairs at the community center on Monday, July 8, and welcomes kids in Kindergarten through the fifth grade. It is free to the public but participants must register at https://form.jotform.com/241835333726155. ;
• Free preview dance classes by Precision Dance. Precision Dance will offer free preview dance classes on Saturday, July 20. The schedule is as follows:
– 10:00-10:30 a.m.: Jazz/Hip-Hop for ages 6-9;
– 10:45-11:15 a.m.: Ballet for ages 4-5;
– 11:30-12:00 p.m.: Creative Movement for ages 2.5-3;
For more information and sign up for these classes, visit precisiondanceky.com or text 859-363-6124. While the classes are free, registration is required due to limited space.
On top of offering classes and future plans for equipment and memberships, the community center also offers ample amounts of space for members of the community to take advantage. The mirror room on the second floor is the home of dance classes with Precision Dance, and is $25 an hour to rent. The space can be rented for nearly any type of event, including get togethers, birthday parties, devotionals, classes and more according to Short. Several members of the community are already taking advantage of the space, including Sheri Lewis of Physique Fitness Training and John Owens of D1 Academy, who have been leading exercise classes.
'I've had to do a lot of work just to make this presentable,' said Short.
The full rental policy can be found on the Harrodsburg Community Center Facebook page.
When Short was growing up in Harrodsburg, he took full advantage of all the YMCA had to offer, and it's important to him the community can use this space in the same way.
'It was kind of the center point of our community. Everybody used the Y for anything we could. So that's kind of the idea and the approach I have to it. Just having the connection and the experience of the Y,' said Short.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Trevor Short, executive director of the Harrodsburg Community Center, said the goal is to make the community center as important to local residents as the YMCA used to be. 'It was kind of the center point of our community. Everybody used the Y for anything we could. So that's kind of the idea and the approach I have to it. Just having the connection and the experience of the Y,' said Short.
This includes making the basketball gym open to the public once again, and restarting the youth basketball league that so many once enjoyed. With the backing of several new and different revenue streams, Short plans to keep growing the community center to provide important educational aspects.
The end goal is to earn enough income to afford an after school program that is staffed by educational professionals. The community center has six computers that will be available and ample classroom space, but the cost of running the program to its fullest is too much at the moment.
'I was born and raised in Harrodsburg, lived here my whole life, so to be here at 33-years-old and trying to do something to give back to the community, it means the world to me, to be in this position and provide these opportunities. The three main things we want to focus on are athletics, arts and education. I feel like those three things are the pillars to growing a community, from youth to adults,' said Short. title: Cincinnati Reds At The All-Star Break
description: Image: Cincinnati Reds, via InstagramShortstop Elly De La Cruz has taken Reds fandom by storm since joining the team la
content:
Image: Cincinnati Reds, via Instagram
Shortstop Elly De La Cruz has taken Reds fandom by storm since joining the team last season. De La Cruz is the only All-Star selection for the Reds in 2024.
Austin Cocanougher
Herald Staff
As the MLB season draws to its halfway point, the Cincinnati Reds sit just below the .500 mark. Underachieving pre-season expectations of being a playoff team, the Redlegs are just a few small pieces away from breaking through. Between injuries, sickness, non-baseball-related absenc­es and suspensions, almost every key player on David Bell's 2024 roster has already missed some time this year.
Despite this, the franchise stays afloat and operates just below the bulk of wildcard favorites. And, because there are only 80-some games left to be played and the top of the league only seems to be getting better, most are calling for the Reds to 'sell off' assets and play for next year. In the past couple of weeks, this potential decision has been the talking point of Reds Country—with many debat­ing whether the current roster is ready to make their first real push.
With the trade deadline drawing near, we will soon learn where higher-ups within the organization stand on the issue. Do the Reds push their chips all in, hoping to spark a rebirth of the Big Red Machine? Or do they fold their cards, playing for a future hand? Here is my argument for why they should be aggressive and go for it now.
Last season, the Reds finished 82-20, one game away from making the last wild­card berth in the playoffs. Overachieving all expert predictions, this previous itera­tion of the ballclub was as electric as they were streaky. However, as the fun season drew to a close, it became apparent that the management's inability to improve the pitching staff's depth (through trades) was going to shoot the team in the foot, and it did.
Despite having a slightly worse record at the break, this year's roster is just as, if not more, talented than last year's team. When healthy, the starting rotation is solid, the defense is above average and the bullpen has been good enough. Inconsistencies at the plate, mostly through injured players, have caused a major regression. The encouraging thing is that this will likely regress toward the mean once players get consistent reps with clean health. Want to read the rest of the story? title: Look Out For Bargain Hunters: 127 Yard Sale Returns August 1
description: The Smock family have been participating in the 127 Yard Sale for more than two decades, and their event has grown to be the second largest in Kentucky, drawing more than 100 vendors (File Image).…
content:
The Smock family have been participating in the 127 Yard Sale for more than two decades, and their event has grown to be the second largest in Kentucky, drawing more than 100 vendors (File Image).
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Look out for bargain hunters, the 127 Yard Sale is back. The event runs sun up to sundown from Thursday, Aug. 1, through Sunday, Aug. 4. While there will be sales practically everywhere in Mercer County, the biggest will be at the Smock Farm (3580 Louisville Road) where more than 100 vendors have their wares on display. The Smock family have been participating in the 127 Yard Sale for more than two decades, and their event has grown to be the second largest in Kentucky.
Billed as the longest yard sale in the world, the 127 Yard Sale spans 690 miles, beginning just north of Addison, Michigan, and ending in Gadsen, Alabama. The 127 Yard Sale began in 1987. According to the website, Mike Walker, for­mer Fentress County Execu­tive in Jamestown, Ten­nessee, planned the event to encourage travelers to bypass interstate highways in favor of scenic routes that would take them through rural communities and allow them to experience what small towns and cities had to offer. The event celebrated its 25th anniversary in 2022.
It is illegal under state law to park on the highway. Sheriff Ernie Kelty said they will be putting out signs reminding motorists about the parking restrictions and the speed limit later this week. Kelty said his deputies will also step up patrols during the sale, especially on the north end of the county.
'We want everyone to have a good time and be safe,' Kelty said.
According to the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, the laws ensure drivers have the proper amount of sight distance for intersections, driveway entrances and curves. Any encroachment on state right of way requires a permit from the cabinet.
Some other safety tips for bargain hunters:
• Watch for parked cars, slowed traffic and vehicles turning into or out of side streets and driveways.
• Park a safe distance from the highway, preferably outside a 22-foot 'recovery zone' extending from the white line on the pavement edge. This area gives motorists room in which to maneuver in case of trouble.
• Watch for pedestrians, and especially for children and pets in the area of yard sales.
• Use seat belts, obey posted speed limits and other traffic laws, and refrain from drinking and driving.
The 127 Yard Sale runs all day each day, Thursday, Aug. 1, through Sunday, Aug. 4, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. While there will be sales practically everywhere—and not necessarily on U.S. 127—four of the biggest events in Kentucky are located nearby.
Mercer County
• Smock Farm (3580 Louisville Road/U.S. Route 127). Located about eight miles north of Harrodsburg and operated by Louise Smock and family. More than 100 vendors are expected.
Anderson County
• Eagle Lake (1187 Alton Road, Lawrenceburg). More than 400 vendors expected.
Boyle County
• Vendors Village (1041 Ben Ali Drive, Danville). More than 65 vendors expected. Call 859-239-9333.
For more information, visit 127yardsale.com.

title: Catch The 10-Minute Play Festival At Ragged Edge Community Theatre
description: The playwrights contributing to Ragged Edge Community Theatre's 10 Minute Play Festival. Top row: Elizabeth Orndorff, Johnny Payne, William Rayens and Nancy Gall-Clayton. Bottom row: Bill McCann, Lu
content:
The playwrights contributing to Ragged Edge Community Theatre's 10 Minute Play Festival. Top row: Elizabeth Orndorff, Johnny Payne, William Rayens and Nancy Gall-Clayton. Bottom row: Bill McCann, Lucy Wang and Father Albert J. DeGiacomo. (Composite image).
Ragged Edge Community Theatre has a lot of activity coming up, beginning with the 10-Minute Play Fest, which happens Saturday, Aug. 3, and Sunday, Aug. 4. Ragged Edge gave aspiring writers, directors and performers two props to build a story on and one week to write and rehearse a 10-minute play. The audience will get to see the results and participate in a talk-back afterward.
The festival will feature works by:
• Elizabeth Orndorff, 'The Tour Guide.'
• Johnny Payne, 'Line of Duty.'
• William Rayens, 'Going Home.'
• Nancy Gall-Clayton, 'Sweet Potato Pies.'
• Bill McCann, 'Give My Regards to Broadway.'
• Lucy Wang, 'A Walkable Feast.'
• Father Albert J. DeGiacomo, 'Making Funny Girl.'
The curtain rises at 7 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 3, and 3 p.m. on Sunday, Aug. 4. Tickets are $12 each ane can be purchased online at raggededgetheatre.org.
Ragged Edge will also be hosting free screenings of Disney's 'Moana' at 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. on Saturday Aug. 10. Concessions are available.
The 2016 animated family film features the voices of Auli'i Cravalho and Dwayne 'the Rock' Johnson. In ancient Polynesia, when a terrible curse incurred by the demigod Maui reaches Moana's island, she answers the Ocean's call to seek out Maui to set things right.
Ragged Edge will be holding auditions for 'Elf Jr. The Musical' on Saturday, Sept. 7, at 10 a.m. and Sunday, Sept. 8, at 2 p.m. Auditions are open to actors between the ages of 6 to 18 and roles are available for all ages. Please be prepared to sing a 16-bar cut of any song of your choosing. Auditioners should bring recorded accompaniment music on their phone or other device. No a capella auditions will be accepted. There is no need for a prepared monologue, performer will be asked to read scenes and cuttings from the script of 'Elf Jr., The Musical.' Please wear comfortable shoes for dancing if needed.
Public performance dates are scheduled for November 15-17 and 22-24. In addition, there will be school matinees on Nov. 19, 20, 21, and 22, 2024. Audition forms need to be completed online at raggededgetheatre.org. The deadline for submitting an audition form will be Friday, Sept. 6, at 9 p.m.
Ragged Edge's next theatrical production will be 'On Golden Pond,' which will run Fridays through Sundays Sept. 20 to 22 and 27 to 29. The curtain rises at 7 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, with the Sunday matinee at 3 p.m.

title: Broadband Update: All Points, State, Still Working On Contract
description: Image
content:
Image: Infestor via Wikimedia Commons.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Fiscal Court received an update on the project to provide broadband internet service to unserved residents. The fiscal court voted in June 2022 to enter a partnership with All Points Broadband to expand internet service throughout the county. The plan is to provide fiber internet service to 3,300 locations not currently being served. It involves hanging more than 300 miles of fiber and is projected to cost more than $26 million, with $15 million coming from the state, $9.5 million from All Points and $1.5 million from the county. Officials say it could be a two year project when work finally begins.
In February of this year, the court learned that All Points had received a draft contract from the state. At their regular meeting on Tuesday, July 30, the fiscal court learned that All Points and the Commonwealth of Kentucky had still not come to terms. Phillip Brown, director of government affairs at All Points, said the company and the state had been exchanging drafts and talking through issues. Brown said All Points officials met last week with the Kentucky Department of Local Government.
'I think we were able to resolve the majority of the things All Points would have classified as important,' Brown said. He said there were important things they needed to discuss.
'What it says in the contract really, really matters,' Brown said. 'It can become a much bigger issue.'
He said All Points had begun issuing requests for proposals from contractors, so they could start work when the contract is finally finalized.
'I wish I could give you specifics,' Brown said. 'I think we're close.' Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: Harrodsburg Ranked Among Most Welcoming Cities In America
description: T
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Amelie Simpson, Laura Taylor, Emma Hibbitts, Kaiya Pohlman and Jacob Moossy squeeze together for a selfie during Oktoberfest last year. Oktoberfest returns for its eighth year in downtown Harrodsburg starting Oct. 4.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Harrodsburg—that's right, Hogtown—has been ranked among the most welcoming towns for newcomers in the country.
That's according to a survey of 3,700 seasoned travelers conducted by ElectricityPrices.com. According to a press release, the travelers were asked to name 'towns where warmth and friendliness are the cornerstones of the community,' where 'newcomers can expect to be embraced with open arms.'
The top five were: Stockbridge, a town of 2,018 people located in the Berkshires of Massachusetts; Winterset, Iowa, the birthplace of John Wayne; Elsah, Illinois, a village with a total population of 519 people; Fredericksburg, Texas, a city with a population of 10,875; and Bandon, Oregon, a coastal town with a population of 3,321.
According to the press release, Kentucky is home to three of the nation's 150 most welcoming locations for newcomers. Midway, the home of Midway University, was ranked at 39. Bardstown, the self-proclaimed 'Bourbon Capital of the World,' was ranked at 50. Harrodsburg, the oldest town in Kentucky, was ranked at 139. The website singled out events like Pioneer Days—the four-day festival kicks off Thursday, Aug. 15—and the Kentucky Heritage Jazz Festival—the three-day festival kicks off Friday, Sept. 20—which they said 'foster a lively and inclusive environment.' Both festivals happen at Old Fort Harrod State Park (100 South College Street).
Back in 2019, the City of Harrodsburg hired Terri Bradshaw to create an economic development report. Among the seven strategies Bradshaw identified in her plan was creating a more vibrant downtown, improving the quality of life and improving connectivity to the outside world.
Among the events created in the years since is Friday Night On Main at Olde Town Park (126 South Main Street). On Friday, Aug. 9, there will be live music by Eight Daze Sober as well as food and shopping from 5 to 10 p.m.
There is also Oktoberfest, which will celebrate its eighth anniversary when it returns on Friday, Oct. 4. The three day festival runs until Sunday, Oct. 6. Want to read more great stories? title: KSP Arrests Corrections Officer For Drug Trafficking
description: CHAD CAIRO. Image: Boyle County Detention Center. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A correctional officer at Northpoint Training Center near Burgin has been arrested and charged…
content:
CHAD CAIRO. Image: Boyle County Detention Center.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
A correctional officer at Northpoint Training Center near Burgin has been arrested and charged with bringing approximately 23.9 ounces of a liquid substance suspected to be methamphetamine into the medium-security prison.
According to a KSP press release, KSP Post 7 in Richmond received a call from Northpoint on Friday, Aug. 9, just before 8 A.M., requesting investigative assistance about a corrections officer was bringing methamphetamine into the facility.
Preliminary investigation revealed Correctional Officer Chad Cairo, 27, of Danville, entered the facility with a clear water bottle containing approximately 23.9 ounces of a liquid substance suspected to be methamphetamine, in exchange for money. Cairo had been employed at Northpoint for just over one year, according to the KSP.
The agency gives his name as Chiaro in the press release, but it is spelled as Cairo on the Boyle County Detention Center website, where Cairo is being held on charges of 1st degree trafficking in methamphetamine and 1st degree promoting contraband. He is being held on a $5,000 bond.
KSP Trooper Mariano Cordova was the investigating officer.
Northpoint Training Center is a medium security correctional facility that opened in ​1983 and has an inmate population of 1230, according to its website. Although Northpoint's mailing address is in Burgin, its physical address is in ​Danville.
All charges are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt in a court of law. For more stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year!

title: County Adopts Compensating Rate, Real Property Rate Drops To 12.1 Per $100
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Fiscal Court adopted a new tax rate for real estate for the 2025 fiscal year. At their regular meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 13, the fiscal court voted unanimously to adopt the compensating rate of 12.1 per $100 in accessed value. That is the compensating rate, which is calculated by the state to generate roughly the same revenue as last year's rate of 12.6. Due to increases in property valuations, the compensating rate will generate more than $2.1 million in gross revenue for the county, which is still an increase of nearly $100,000 more than last year's rate.
The rates of 18.31 for tangible personal property and inventory and 9.2 for vehicles and watercraft remain unchanged.
'I didn't want to go over,' said Judge-Executive Sarah Steele Tuesday. Magistrate Tim Darland moved to accept the new rate. Darland's motion was seconded by Magistrate Stephen 'Pete' Elliott and passed unanimously by the court. They also voted to approve the tax rates of the Mercer County Soil Conservation District—.010 per $100 in assessed value—and the Mercer County Extension District—4.2 per $100 in assessed value. Both tax rates are the same as last year.
Mercer County Clerk Chris Horn said he had not received notification from the other taxing districts, including the public library, the health department, the fire district as well as the county and Burgin Independent Schools. Taxing districts have until September to file the paperwork with the clerk's office. Tax bills for the 2025 fiscal year will be sent out on Oct. 1. Want to read the rest of the story? The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission is creating a payment plan for businesses that have fallen behind on tax payments. By law, the tourist commission is supported by the collection of the transient room tax and restaurant tax. At their regular meeting on Wednesday, Aug. 14, the commissioners discussed creating payment plans as a way to ensure compliance with the restaurant tax collection.
Daarik Gray, executive director of the tourist commission, said some events have had to turn down vendors that are not compliant. Gray said one vendor asked about a payment plan, and he asked the board for their thoughts. Gray told the board one vendor is two to three years behind.
'They got caught up on 2024 but still owe back taxes,' Gray said. He said he'd never been asked about a payment plan before.
The vendor, whom Gray said owed approximately $2,000, said they'd been misinformed about collecting the tax. All restaurants and food trucks in Mercer County have to collect the restaurant tax, which is paid by the diners. The county offers a payment plan.
Board member Nikki Elliott suggested a contract. Treasurer Bob Gigliotti recommended requesting a 30 percent deposit up front with payments made over six months. Gray said he would confer with the tourist commission's attorney and send drafts to board members.

title: Mercer XC is expecting another successful season
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff Sports@harrodsburgherald.com Mercer County Cross Country has been hard at work this summer working toward their goal of winning another Region 5 championship. Last fall, the…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
Sports@harrodsburgherald.com
Mercer County Cross Country has been hard at work this summer working toward their goal of winning another Region 5 championship. Last fall, the Titans did what many didn't think was possible when they qualified both boys and girls teams to compete at the KHSAA State Cross Country Championship at the Kentucky Horse Park. The Titans' Head Coach Derek McIntyre wasn't in disbelief, but overcome with pride.
'This group has worked so hard this season I couldn't be more proud,' McIntyre told the Harrodsburg Herald last October.
Now that they've tasted success, the Titan runners are hungry for more, and they have already set a goal of repeating as Region 5 champions.
'Both the girls and boys teams have the ability to win the region,' said McIntyre.
The Titans have several runners ready to take the next stride and help replace the efforts of last year's seniors. Katie and Sam Lewis' departure would leave a crater to fill in any program, but McIntyre is confident in a successful season and the emergence of several new elite runners.
No one has higher expectations than seniors Marshall Hart and Mason Sanders.
'I am excited about how I think that this team will shape up, because we have a good chance at region this year,' said Sanders, who McIntyre says 'has never looked better.'
Sanders was forced to sit out of competition last season with an injury, but had a successful spring with the track and field team and will play an important role in any success the boys have this fall.
Hart made magnificent strides throughout last season, cutting seconds off of his time nearly every meet. His performance at the 5th Region meet earned him second place overall with a time of 17:21.16. Just one week later, Hart had the performance of his life and finished ninth at the state meet with a time of 16:47.25. In his final season as a Titan, Hart has set a goal of winning at the regional meet and eclipsing the 16 minute mark.
Landon Bryant, Karson Kerr, Jayden Foster, Ashton Butler and Ted Gagnon finish out the boys' roster, and are all capable of contributing according to McIntyre.
The Lady Titan runners will be without their second fastest runner at last season's 5th Region meet, Adriana Polhemus, but runners like Julia Hart, Roxy Bogardus, Alexis Benham, Layla Nowlin, Lilly Hart and Daisy Nowlin are more than prepared to compete and excel.
Despite still being in middle school, Julia Hart is the Lady Titans' fastest runner after the departure of K. Lewis and Polhemus. Bogardus is coming off of a summer of hard work and a successful track and field season and is an essential piece to the puzzle. Aurea Dove, Tabitha Grant, Journee Humpert and Abby Woods finish out the roster.
'We are in one of the toughest 2A regions in the state year after year. If we can win that, we can make some noise at state,' said McIntyre.
The Titan runners will begin their season on Saturday, Aug. 24, when they travel to Mt. Sterling. Fans will have plenty of opportunities to see Titan runners compete in Harrodsburg this season as six meets are scheduled at Anderson-Dean Park.

content:
Trudy Gayle Sutherland, 81, died Saturday, Aug. 31, 2024, at the Ephraim McDowell Regional Medical Center in Danville.
Born May 28, 1943, in Harrodsburg, she was the daughter of the late Harold Thomas and Eudora (Dean) Sutherland.
She was a 1961 graduate of Harrodsburg High School, was owner/operator of Harrod Cleaners and was a member of the United Presbyterian Church.
Survivors include: two daughters, Susan (Mark) Haven and Anne-Hunter (Bill) Ley, one sister, Kathy White; one brother, Terry (Ann Hunter) Sutherland; eight grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.
She was preceded in death by one son, William Dudley Curry and one sister, Anne Boggs.
Funeral services are today, Thursday, Sept. 5, at 2 p.m., at the United Presbyterian Church.
Memorial contributions are suggested to the United Presbyterian Church, 326 S Main St., Harrodsburg, KY 40330.

title: Burgin Sets Tax Rates, Bills Go Out Oct. 1
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com The Burgin City Council approved tax rates for the fiscal year. At their meeting on Tuesday
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Burgin City Council approved tax rates for the fiscal year. At their meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 10, the council approved a tax rate of .142 per $100 in assessed value for real property and .159 per $100 in assessed value for personal property.
The council had to pass an emergency ordinance to meet the submission deadline with the county clerk.
The council chose the lower compensating rate, which is calculated by the state to generate approximately the same revenue as the year before. The compensating rate is lower because of the increase in property values.
'I'm okay with this,' said Councilman Sindicat 'Sid' Dunn. 'We don't have any projects where we need any revenue.'
Councilman Jamie Keebortz moved to take the compensating rate on real property and keep rate the same on personal property. Keebortz also moved to make Oct. 1 the mailout date. The motions passed unanimously.
In other business, the Burgin City Council approved paying $870,000 to Cumberland Pipeline of Columbia to replace Burgin's main waterline from where it taps into Harrodsburg's line all the way to the water tower. Cumberland's bid was the cheapest of the two submitted for the project. The other bid, from B&M Pipeline of Mount Vernon, was for $1.5 million.
Mayor Joe Monroe also informed the council that testing for Burgin's long-waited flooding alleviation project was supposed to start this week.
'They are going to call us and give us a couple of days heads up,' Monroe said.
Part of the testing is to drill two test wells and see if they hit water and check the flow, the mayor said, one at the sinkhole and the other side of the railroad tracks. He said they were checking the ground for caverns or caves, anything 'that could cause problems.' Monroe said the testing should be done by Dec. 20, and the city should receive the report by Jan. 5, 2025. title: Board Of Appeals Denies Conditional Use Permit For Proposed Retreat On AT Dean Road
description: AT Dean Road (file image). Robert Moore
content:
AT Dean Road (file image).
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Joint Board of Adjustments and Appeals has denied an application for a conditional use permit to build a spiritual retreat center on AT Dean Road. The board of adjustments conducted a public hearing on Thursday, Sept. 12, to consider a request for a conditional use permit for Hallelujah Acres, which would be located on property owned by Joey and Erica Svec at 225 AT Dean Road. The property is zoned A-2 (agricultural). The issue had been tabled at a July 16 meeting.
The development would be near Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill. In a letter to the editor published in last week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald , Bob Gigliotti, president and CEO of Shaker Village, wrote that 'commercial development on the boundaries of this unique property will damage the his­toric integrity of the site and threaten the peacefulness of the property that so many guests have come to enjoy.'
In the letter, Gigliotti invited anyone opposed to the development, which he said presented 'a detrimental impact to historic and agricultural properties' like Shaker Village, to attend Thursday's meeting. title: Harrodsburg Named One Of Most Scenic Towns In Kentucky
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreHarrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic cities in Kentucky and everyone will get a chance to see old Hogtown in all
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Harrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic cities in Kentucky and everyone will get a chance to see old Hogtown in all her glory when Oktoberfest returns Friday, Oct. 4.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Harrodsburg has been named one of the most scenic towns in Kentucky. That's according to WorldAtlas.com, a website that launched in 1994 and bills itself as one of the largest publishing resources in geography and other topics it covers, including sociology, demography, environment, economics, politics and travel. Other Kentucky cities named were Cave City, Slade, Cumberland, Clermont, Carrollton, Richmond, Cambellsville and Corbin.
According to WorldAtlas.com, one of the reasons Harrodsburg is so scenic is because of Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill. The website invites readers to 'visit the beautiful natural landscape of the shakers at the 3,000 acre Shaker Village,' which has '36 miles of trails which are ideal for hikers, horseback riders, and even classic carriages.'
While Kentucky's state parks are not as well known as the Grand Canyon or Yellowstone Park, WorldAtlas.com insists they shouldn't be overlooked. 'Kentucky is the only place in the world you can see the largest cave system and a moonbow in a single state.'
One of the most unique state parks in the Commonwealth is right here in Harrodsburg. Old Fort Harrod State Park offers more than a full-scale replica of the fort built by James Harrod in 1774. It's also home to the historic Mansion Museum, the George Rogers Clark Federal Monument, the Lincoln Marriage Temple and the oldest cemetery west of the Alleghenies. And don't forget the Osage Orange tree at Old Fort Harrod, which is both taller and broader than the National Champion but remains the Unofficial National Champion due to its split trunk.

title: Judge Jeff Dotson Leaves Behind A Legacy Of Hope
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreThe Mercer and Boyle County Drug Court celebrated its first graduation in F
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
The Mercer and Boyle County Drug Court celebrated its first graduation in February 2024. From left: graduate Stephanie Burton, Judge Jeff Dotson, graduate Hannah Lawson and Drug Court Coordinator Denise Gates.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Judge Jeffrey Dotson has died, but he leaves behind a legacy of hope for many in Mercer County. Dotson served as Circuit Judge for the 50th Judicial Circuit, Division 1, which is made up of Mercer and Boyle counties. Before that, he had served as District Court judge for Mercer and Boyle counties since 2003.
Dotson, 59, died Saturday, Sept. 28, at the University of Kentucky Medical Center in Lexington, according to his obituary.
Born March 27, 1965, in Jenkins, Dotson earned his undergraduate degree at East Tennessee State University before obtaining his Juris Doctorate from the University of Louisville Brandeis School of Law. He practiced law in Harrodsburg until his election to the District Court judgeship in 2003. In 2022, he was appointed by Gov. Andy Beshear to fill the Circuit Court judicial seat, which became vacant when Judge Darren W. Peckler resigned.
A retired judge, Dan Kelly, will handle the Circuit Court caseload until the governor appoints Dotson's replacement, according to the Mercer County Clerk's Office.
Circuit Court hears civil matters involving more than $5,000, capital offenses and felonies, divorces, adoptions, termination of parental rights, land dispute title cases and contested probate cases. Dotson's most lasting legacy on the bench will be the Mercer and Boyle County Drug Court, which begin locally shortly after his appointment in 2022. Drug Court celebrated its first graduation earlier this year with Dotson presenting diplomas to Stephanie Burton and Hannah Lawson.
'This is a very exciting day,' he said.
Drug Court is available to individuals charged with drug use or nonviolent drug-related crime. According to kycourts.gov, it combines close court supervision and treatment with other services to 'break the cycle of substance abuse and crime.'
The program uses a team approach that involves collaboration among local judges, court staff, prosecutors, defense counsel, treatment professionals, law enforcement officers and other community agencies. While there are a lot of people and agencies involved, Dotson said it was the commitment of participants like Stephanie Burton and Hannah Lawson who made the drug court 'a very successful program.'
Many of the people honoring Dotson's memory this weekend had stood before him in court. 'Thank God for Jeff Dotson,' wrote one commenter on the What's Happening Mercer County Facebook page. 'He saved my life and sent me to treatment. I am glad he got to see me sober and doing well for myself. Thank you, and you will be missed, Judge Dotson.'
According to his obituary, Dotson is survived by his wife, Chris Dotson, his parents, Roger and Barbara Dotson of Salvisa, and his son, Jack Dotson of Harrodsburg.
A gathering of family and friends will be held Monday, Oct. 7, from 4 to 7 p.m. at the Greystone House of Beaumont Inn (618 Beaumont Inn Drive).
Memorial contributions are suggested to Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates KODA, 10301 Linn Station Road, Louisville, KY 40223, or to a charity of one's choice.

title: Harrodsburg Man Receives Eight Year Sentence For Jan. 6 Capitol Breach
description: Stephen Chase Randolph Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A Harrodsburg man has been sentenced to eight years in prison for his actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, breach of the U.S.…
content:
Stephen Chase Randolph
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
A Harrodsburg man has been sentenced to eight years in prison for his actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, breach of the U.S. Capitol. Stephen Chase Randolph, 34, of Harrodsburg, was one of four men convicted of multiple felony and misdemeanor charges for their roles in disrupting a joint session of the U.S. Congress to count the electoral votes in the 2020 presidential election.
Randolph was sentenced to eight years in prison, 36 months of supervised release, and ordered to pay $2,000 in restitution. Randolph had been found guilty of assaulting an officer with a deadly or dangerous weapon and inflicting bodily injury (a metal crowd control barrier). He was also convicted of an additional felony charge of assaulting, resisting, or impeding and officer.
Randolph was arrested by FBI agents on April 20, 2021, and indicted later that month. According to the indictment, Randolph and another man, Paul Russell Johnson, 38, of Lanexa, Virginia, used a metal crowd control barrier to 'forcibly assault, resist, oppose, impede, intimidate, and interfere with' two officers from the U.S. Capitol Police, inflicting 'significant bodily injury' on one of the officers. According to a Justice Department press release, the officer lost consciousness and suffered a concussion.
Johnson was sentenced to five years of probation, including intermittent confinement on the weekends for the first year, followed by two years of home and ordered to pay a $25,000 fine and $2,000 in restitution.
Federal agents were able to track down Randolph because of his online history. On images of the Jan. 6 attack, agents described Randolph as wearing a grey Carhartt toboggan, a black jacket with a breast pocket on each side and stitching detail on each sleeve, a grey turtleneck, black gloves with a red stripe, and jeans. The FBI were able to match those images with images from an Instagram account that apparently belonged to Randolph's girlfriend, as well as other social media accounts.
When the FBI photographed Randolph standing outside his workplace on March 3, 2021, he was wearing the same hat he'd been wearing during the Capitol assault, according to the court documents.
According to a statement of facts filed by the FBI, undercover agents visited Chase at his place of work in 2021. 'I was in it,' Randolph is quoted as telling the agents. 'It was f*****g fun.'
In addition to Randolph and Russell, James Tate Grant, 31, of Cary, North Carolina; and Jason Benjamin Blythe, 28, of Fort Worth, Texas; were also sentenced on Sept. 19, 2024, by U.S. District Judge Jia M. Cobb. A fifth defendant, Ryan Samsel, 40, of Bristol, Pennsylvania, will be sentenced on February 4, 2025
According to evidence presented during the trial, the group participated in the first breach of the restricted Capitol grounds on Jan. 6, 2021, and led the initial attack on United States Capitol Police. Their attack paved the way for thousands of rioters to storm the Capitol grounds.
In the 44 months since Jan. 6, 2021, more than 1,504 individuals have been charged in nearly all 50 states for crimes related to the breach of the U.S. Capitol, including more than 560 individuals charged with assaulting or impeding law enforcement, a felony. Anyone with tips can call 1-800-CALL-FBI (800-225-5324) or visit tips.fbi.gov. title: Fiscal Court Approves Increasing 911 Tap Fee From $1.75 To $3.50
description: File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County
content:
File Photo: Kentucky State Seal in the courtroom at Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse.
The Mercer County Fiscal Court gave second reading and final approval to an ordinance increasing the tap fee on residential and commercial water meters from $1.75 per month to $3.50 a month. The increase goes into effect Nov. 1.
The tap fee pays for 911 services. Last month, the fiscal court had to make up a $107,000 shortfall for 911 operations. In the past, 911 operations were paid for by a fee collected on landline phones. But the number of land lines has been declining for decades. While there is a fee collected on some—but not all—cell phones, the revenue collected does not cover the expense of operations. Back in 2019, both Harrodsburg and Burgin voted to institute a $40 parcel to pay for 911 operations, which subsequently failed to pass for lack of a motion at a special-called hearing of the fiscal court. That left the county to use carryover funds to pay for the federally mandated service.
Last year, the fiscal court enacted the tap fee to handle 911 operations. The collecting entities withhold three percent to cover their expenses. At their regular meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 8, the fiscal court voted unanimously to increase the tap fee. There was no discussion. Magistrate Susan Barrington moved to give the ordinance a second reading. Barrington's motion was seconded by Magistrate Tim Darland, who has previously said the state needed to increase the 911 fee on cell phones.
'They got so many lobbyists in Frankfort that it ain't going to happen,' Darland said.
Other counties charge tap fees to pay for 911 call operations. Judge-Executive Sarah Steele previously said even with the fee hike, Mercer is still lower than surrounding counties. Steele said Garrard and Lincoln are charging $4 tap fees. For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren—Mercer County senior John Mason Hopkins chased down a pass during the Titans' 6-1 victory over Frankfort Christian on senior night.
The Mercer County Titan soccer team (1-11-1) celebrated the efforts of five seniors before picking up their second victory of the season on Tuesday, Oct. 1. Jordan Piazza, Luis Osoy, Hayden McGuire, John Mason Hopkins and Krish Patel were each honored before kickoff for their dedication to Titan soccer.
'The energy it gives those kids, knowing that the end of their season is close. It's always good to get that win and see them have fun,'said Head Coach Mark Dunn.
In Mercer's second to last game of the regular season, Frankfort Christian (2-11-2) traveled to Harrodsburg and were immediately put under pressure by the Titans.
Sophomore Ian Alcorn recently made the move forward from his fullback position and played an important role in the Titans offensive game plan Tuesday. Mijaia Dunn, Alcorn and Piazza were in sync in the opening 20 minutes of the game and were firing shot after shot, but nothing could get past Royals' keeper Max Ruwett, who tallied eight saves in the first half. It took Mercer just under 30 minutes to net their first goal. Alcorn scored his second varsity goal after a pass from Mi. Dunn found the sophomore uncovered just inside the 18-yard box, and Alcorn fired the ball just inside the far post.
The Titans earned chance after chance with corner kicks, and sophomore Tanner Ison's delivery was on point nearly every attempt. Soon after the second half started Alcorn rose high up above his defender and used his head for his second goal. Alcorn found his third goal after a great forward pass from Grayson Guerra left Alcorn all alone in the opponent's third, and he completed his first ever hat trick with confidence.
'I've always wanted to play him up top,' said Ma. Dunn after the game. Alcorn had been forced to play back much of the season due to players missing games and a lack of depth in defense, but the sophomore is destined to be a forward according to Dunn. title: Guy Simmons
description: Dr. Guy Held Simmons Jr., 87, husband of Patricia 'Pat' (Roth) Simmons, of Harrodsburg, died Friday, October 4, 2024 at the Willows of Harrodsburg. Born Oct. 9, 1936, in Macon, Tenn., he was the son…
content:
Dr. Guy Held Simmons Jr., 87, husband of Patricia 'Pat' (Roth) Simmons, of Harrodsburg, died Friday, October 4, 2024 at the Willows of Harrodsburg.
Born Oct. 9, 1936, in Macon, Tenn., he was the son of the late Guy Held and Bertha Mae (nee Glover) Simmons Sr.
He was a pioneer of nuclear medicine physics who started his professional career in Cincinnati, went on to develop the first bachelor's degree program in Nuclear Medicine technology, was recruited by the University of Kentucky to serve under dual appointment to the College of Medicine, served as president of Ohio River Valley Chapter (ORVC) of the American Association of Physicists in Medicine and the national organization. Retired from the United States Public Health Service and the VA, he continued to serve the region for 25 years.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: two daughters, Sarah (Tom) Rougeux and Lydia Simmons; two sons, Scott Simmons and David (Jennifer) Simmons; one stepson, Steven Poppas; nine grandchildren; four great-grandchildren; and several nieces and nephews.
He was preceded in death by one daughter, Tracy Simmons; one stepson, Eric Scott Poppas; two daughters-in-law, Angel and Shirley Poppas; and one sister, Mary Ellen Simmons Bewley.
Private funeral services will be held at a later date.
Arrangements by Ransdell Funeral Chapel
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.ransdellfuneralchapel.com.

title: Lady Titans ease past Washington County
description: Alyssa Pittman Contributing Writer On Monday, Oct. 14, the Lady Titans Volleyball team (10-9) played the Washington County Lady Commanders (4-14) at Mercer County Senior High School. The Commanders…
content:
Alyssa Pittman
Contributing Writer
On Monday, Oct. 14, the Lady Titans Volleyball team (10-9) played the Washington County Lady Commanders (4-14) at Mercer County Senior High School.
The Commanders came up victorious in the freshman game, earning leads as high as eight points. The young Titans battled back several times in their sets, but came up just a little short. The JV team earned the first Lady Titan victory, winning their first set 21-18 and the second set 21-12. The Titans struggled to find their footing, but bounced back in the middle of the set to steal the set. The JV team dominated the second set to close out the Commanders.
The Lady Titans varsity team started their first set off amazingly. Jael Wooldridge was on a roll with block after block, as Washington struggled to communicate, letting balls drop all over the court. Madi Collier had several gorgeous serves racking up the points for the Lady Titans. After an Addisen Shepherd spike and recording two kills. With the Titans up 17-7, Washington County called a timeout to try and stop the momentum. After the timeout, the Titans scored two more immediately. The commanders went on a six-point streak making the score 19-13 before the Titans finally scored another point. The final point was awarded after a service error on Washington County, certifying the final score of set one, as 25-17. title: Jenni Link Takes Over As New Director Of The Mercer County Public Library
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreJenni Link took over as the new director of the Mercer County Public Library earlier this month. She said she
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Jenni Link took over as the new director of the Mercer County Public Library earlier this month. She said she hopes to continue the great service the library provides for the community. ' 'We have a great collection and resources,' Link said.
Meet Jenni Link, the new director of the Mercer County Public Library. Link started work on Oct. 7.
'It hasn't been quite two weeks yet,' Link told the Harrodsburg Herald during an interview last week. 'I'm still finding my feet.'
Link has decades of experience. Before taking the directorship in Mercer County, she served as the electronic records system manager at the Kentucky Community and Technical College System in Versailles. Before that, she served as assistant director at the Paris-Bourbon County Library in Paris. She also served as public services librarian at Bluegrass Community and Technical College in Lexington. She began her career as a librarian at the Lexington Public Library, starting as a library assistant.
'I've got lots of different library experience,' she said. Link admits it is daunting to take the job after Robin Ison, who retired earlier this year after serving as the library's director for 28 years.
'Robin Ison left big shoes to fill,' Link said. 'Everybody loved her so much.'
Link is originally from Mount Orab, a small village (population 4,347) in Brown County, Ohio. She said it was about an hour east of Cincinnati.
'It's right along 68, maybe three hours north of here,' she said.
She said she had always wanted to be a librarian.
'I used to take little white medical tape and put call numbers on my books,' Link recalled. She didn't have a library in her town, and Link recalled her parents driving her to the library at the county seat. 'It seemed like a natural thing to do,' she recalled.
Link earned her undergraduate degree in English and American Literature at Brown University, an Ivy League college in Providence, Rhode Island, and her master of library and information science degree at the University of Kentucky.
Link said she's lived in Lexington for about 20 years. She said her husband, a native of Lafayette, Louisiana, was not willing to move all that far north of the Mason-Dixon line.
'So we stayed,' Link said.
Link and her husband have two children. Their son is 22 and studying accounting at UK. Their daughter is 19 and taking the requisites to do ultrasound. Most of her family lives nearby. Link's mother and stepfather live right up Interstate 75 in West Harrison, Indiana. Link's sister and brother live in Cincinnati. She said her husband's family had relocated from Louisiana as well.
'They had enough of the hurricanes, so they live in Lexington now,' Link said.
Before applying for the directorship, she visited the Mercer County Public Library.
'I was curious about the library,' Link said. 'I came as a patron to look at it. It's so beautiful and spacious. I thought what a great opportunity.'
Mercer County has had library services for over 200 years. During Ison's time at the library was a transformational era, not just for the library but for the community it serves. The library bought up shuttered businesses—the old A&P and old Western Auto, the old Fort Harrod Pharmacy and 'Thriftys'—using the space to expand the building and parking lot. In 2016, they bought the building next door at 114 North Main Street, which they spent a year and nearly $1.4 million to transform into the History Research Center. Few have done more to revitalize downtown Harrodsburg than the Mercer County Public Library during Ison's time as director.
'The challenge for me is living up to Robin's example,' Link said. 'I've heard wonderful things about her.'
In addition to learning the systems and getting to know the staff, Link is getting to learn the community. She recently attended a breakfast hosted by the Mercer County Chamber of Commerce. And she looks to introduce herself to the mayor and the other elected officials.
'Folks can expect to see my face pretty soon,' Link said.
What's the biggest change in libraries?
'We don't shush people the way librarians did when I was a kid,' Link said. She said libraries have become more of a community center.
'People come for activities and to use the study room,' Link said. While other public institutions have fallen off in importance, she said, 'The library is still a place where everyone is welcome.'
Link said she enjoys reading about World War I.
'The world changed so much at that time,' Link said. 'That's what really fascinates me.'When pressed, Link struggled to name a favorite book. 'I have so many,' she said. 'It's like asking a car collector their favorite car.'
Link said she likes to garden, go camping with her family and take care of their backyard chickens.
'I read a lot, I walk my dog,' she said. 'I guess I'm a pretty quiet person.'
She also enjoys the commute from Lexington to Harrodsburg. Link drives down 68 by Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill.
'That's a beautiful drive,' she said. 'I enjoy seeing the baby lambs out in the pasture.'
Link said she's fascinated by the diverse terrain here in Mercer County, from the Palisades on the Kentucky River to Herrington Lake.
'You would not know you were in the same county,' she said. There are so many landscapes. Wants to see more of the county.
'I'm just really happy to be here,' Link said. 'I hope everyone will be patient with me while I learn the ropes.'
She said she is looking forward to meeting more people around town. Link said she wants to make Harrodsburg proud.
'I hope to continue the great service everybody's gotten here,' she said. 'We have a great collection and resources.'
She invites everyone to come and check out everything the Mercer County Public Library has to offer. The library is located at 109 West Lexington Street. The hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday, with special evening hours— 9 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.—on Tuesdays and Thursdays. To learn more, call 859-734-3680 or visit online at mcplib.info. title: Mike Sanford Elected Chair Of Bluegrass ADD
description: Photo SubmittedMike Sanford has been named chair of the Bluegrass Area Development District. Sanford, left, succeeds David West, right, judge-executive of Jessamine County, as chair. Mike Sanford has…
content:
Photo Submitted
Mike Sanford has been named chair of the Bluegrass Area Development District. Sanford, left, succeeds David West, right, judge-executive of Jessamine County, as chair.
Mike Sanford has been named chair of the Bluegrass Area Development District. Sanford, the general manager of the Mercer County Sanitation District and the executive director of the Lake Village Water Association, is the first citizen member to serve as chair.
Sanford is one of the new executive officers who was unanimously approved during the annual full board meeting held on Tuesday, Nov. 12.
'I'll do what I can for Mercer County while I'm there,' said Sanford.
He succeeds David West, judge-executive of Jessamine County, as chair. Sanford previously served as vice chair as well as treasurer and secretary.
'I knew it was coming,' Sanford said. 'It is my time.'
Nicholas County Judge-Executive Steve Hamilton will serve as vice chair, Boyle County Judge-Executive Trille Bottom will serve as treasurer and Winchester Mayor JoEllen Reed will serve as secretary.
Sanford is a Mercer County native who holds a bachelor's degree in environmental health science and a master's degree in public administration, both from Eastern Kentucky University. He has been with Lake Village and the conservation district since 2006.
The Bluegrass ADD serves as a regional planning and development organization that supports 17 counties in central Kentucky. The organization works on a broad range of initiatives, including economic development, workforce training, regional planning, and community services. Through its efforts, Bluegrass ADD strengthens local economies, promotes collaboration, and addresses the unique challenges facing the region's communities.
'We are excited to welcome these experienced public leaders into their new roles,' said Bluegrass ADD Executive Director David Duttlinger. 'Each brings a wealth of knowledge, a deep commitment to service, and a proven track record of leadership in their respective communities. Together, they will help steer the Bluegrass ADD toward a future of prosperity and collaboration for all our counties.' title: Clean Audit For Mercer School District
description: File image. The Mercer County School District has received a clean audit for the 2024 fiscal year. That's what the Mercer County Board of Education learned at their last regular meeting of the year,…
content:
File image.
The Mercer County School District has received a clean audit for the 2024 fiscal year. That's what the Mercer County Board of Education learned at their last regular meeting of the year, on Tuesday, Dec. 17, 2024.
Stephanie Abell, a CPA with White and Company PSC of Lebanon, told the board the auditors had issued an unmodified—or clean opinion. Abell said they reported finding no material weaknesses, significant deficiencies or instances of noncompliance in the district's financial statements.
'That's the opinion you want to have,' Abell told the board. The district had $44.6 million in revenue and $41.9 million in expenses for the fiscal year ear which ended June 30, 2024. According to the audit, the district increased the total amount due on bonds by $33.95 million with the addition of the new elementary school project bonding in fiscal year 2024. The District's total net position increased $4.65 million to $19.56 million, according to the audit, while current assets increased by $32.9 million, non-current assets increased by $1.8 million, and total liabilities increased by $26 million as compared to the prior year.
'That's a good thing,' Abell told the board. She said the district's general fund had seen an increase of more than $700,000.
'It's very important to see positive numbers there,' she said.
Abell also said the situation with OPEBs—other post-employment benefits, such as medical, dental, vision and hearing benefits for retired school employees—looked much better than in past years.
'The market has had a really good year,' Abell told the board. She said OPEBs were fully funded.
'Will it stay that way? The market will tell,' she said.
Abell also praised the job done by Nutrition and Food Service Director Chris Minor. She said the program's revenue went up when COVID funding for meal service went down.
Many government entities rushed to spend the last of the federal COVID funding before the end of the year. Abell noted the school district had used much of the federal funding for nonrecurring expenses, which meant they would not have to worry about taking a bigger hit in the future. Abell also praised the job done by Chief Financial Officer Amber Minor and her staff.
'There's a great team of folks here,' Abell said.
'You like a clean report,' said Board Chair Randy Phillip. For the rest of this story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Bulldogs Roll Over The Royals
description: The Burgin Bulldogs (2-6) picked up their second win of the season in a rout of Frankfort Christian Academy (2-8) on Thursday, Dec. 19, in the Jack Coleman Jr. Gymnasium. The Bulldogs started the game…
content:
The Burgin Bulldogs (2-6) picked up their second win of the season in a rout of Frankfort Christian Academy (2-8) on Thursday, Dec. 19, in the Jack Coleman Jr. Gymnasium.
The Bulldogs started the game with confidence and physicality and forced three turnovers soon after the jump. Burgin's first few baskets came in transition beginning with a corner three from sophomore Micah Mayes, who has shot 33% from behind the arc through six games. Freshman Hudson Taylor picked up a loose ball and finished through contact on the other end before completing the and one.
Casey Dodson played strong in the paint early, and Burgin was able to utilize his passing ability early. The junior kicked it out to Taylor for an open three, making the score 11-2 with 3:18 to go in the first quarter.
'Casey did a great job of distributing the ball and taking his shot when he should have. He is basically a first year varsity player after having to sit last season with an injury. He will only get better with every game,' said Head Coach Todd Claunch.
Burgin senior Casey Dodson dribbled at the top of the key and waited for play to develope during Burgin's win over FCA. Dodson finished the game with four points and several assists. ( The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren)
FCA finally got a few shots to fall, but the Bulldogs led 16-11 after one quarter.
Dodson finished a breakaway strong at the rim, but the Bulldog's offense struggled in the opening half of the second quarter. The Bulldogs were finding open looks and taking the right shots, but they weren't falling. Eventually Burgin's defensive play and quickness in transition led to a 7-0 run. Junior point guard Landen Sexton delivered a perfect pass to Mayes in a fast break situation for an easy basket. On the following possession, Sexton missed a floater, grabbed his own missed shot and put the Bulldogs up by nine. Burgin was playing far too fast for FCA and every look was an open one. Mayes knocked down two more treys in the final two minutes of the first half, and Burgin led 32-21. title: Check Out Harrodsburg Documentary At The Historical Society And On KET
description: Photo SubmittedThe Dancing Lady of Harrodsburg and her dancing partner—played by Jan Pearce and Kelly Sikorski from Lexington Vintage Dance—appear in
content:
Photo Submitted
The Dancing Lady of Harrodsburg and her dancing partner—played by Jan Pearce and Kelly Sikorski from Lexington Vintage Dance—appear in Michael Breeding's documentary 'The Harrodsburg Legacy: 250 Years in the Making.' You can watch the 30-minute movie at the Harrodsburg Historical Society at their monthly meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 14, or later this year at KET.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Harrodsburg Historical Society (220 South Chiles Street) will present the documentary, 'The Harrodsburg Legacy: 250 Years In The Making' during their monthly meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 14, at 7 p.m.
After the 30 minute film, documentarian Michael Breeding will make comments. A light supper of soup and crackers will also be served.
In 2025, Kentucky Educational Television (KET) will air 'the Harrodsburg Legacy,' which was made here in Harrodsburg to celebrate the area's 250th anniversary. Air dates have not been announced yet.
In an email, Breeding said it takes about three months to prepare a film for broadcast.
'We must have the film closed-captioned along with producing a few more materials and elements,' Breeding said.
Narrated by Robert Clotworthy, voice of 'Ancient Aliens' and 'The Curse of Oak Island' on the History Channel, the documentary is a journey through historic Hogtown. Filming took place in Mercer County in February 2024 with the participation of 55 re-enactors along with second graders and youth from local schools, who worked to resurrect the legend of the lady who danced herself to death at Graham Springs Hotel and other events from Harrodsburg's history. The movie utilizes rare and sometimes never before seen photos from the Harrodsburg Historical Society and Mercer County Public Library.
'The Harrodsburg Legacy' received its world premiere in June 2024 at Mercer County Senior High School during the celebration of Harrodsburg's 250th anniversary.
'The Harrodsburg Legacy: 250 Years In The Making' at the Harrodsburg Historical Society (220 South Chiles Street) on Tuesday, jan. 14, starting at 7 p.m. Filmmaker Michael Breeding presents his documentary about Harrodsburg and make comments afterwards. A light supper of soup and crackers will be served. Meeting starts 7 p.m. 859-325-9028 or harrodsburghistorical.org. title: Black Bears best the Titans
description: April Ellis Herald Staff The Mercer County Senior High Boys basketball team (11-5) made program history by advancing to the 2A State Tournament, but their first-round draw was against Harlan County,…
content:
April Ellis
Herald Staff
The Mercer County Senior High Boys basketball team (11-5) made program history by advancing to the 2A State Tournament, but their first-round draw was against Harlan County, who had beat them 70-58, just a couple of weeks before. The Titans stayed with the Black Bears in the first half, but poor shooting performance in the third quarter stalled their efforts and they lost, 53-36.
Mercer's defense kept them in the game, and junior Kaleb Murray kept Harlan's Maddox Huff, who averages over 30 points per game, to 20 points. When Mercer forced a turnover, their offense struggled to convert it to baskets.
At the start of the game, Harlan hit two quick baskets and Head Coach Keith Adkins called a time-out to settle his players. It took a few more minutes for Mercer to put points on the board when senior Trevor Ellis went down the middle for a bucket with an assist to senior Andrew Tatum.
Ellis and senior Hagan Preston pressured Harlan's shooters on the perimeter and in the paint. Preston saw success blocking 3-point shots and Ellis swatted away post shots. For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Titans Leave Colts In The Dust
description: The Mercer County Senior High boys basketball team (12-6) faced the West Jessamine Colts (7-8) on Friday, Jan. 24. It was a game high school basketball fans were anticipating after West beat Pulaski…
content:
The Mercer County Senior High boys basketball team (12-6) faced the West Jessamine Colts (7-8) on Friday, Jan. 24. It was a game high school basketball fans were anticipating after West beat Pulaski County early in the season, and Mercer was determined to hold onto their 46th district title. Mercer struggled their last couple of games offensively, but not Friday night, beating West 58-42.
This season, West's 6'8 transfer sophomore center Luk Tut was eligible for varsity play, and several thought it would make a difference, but the Titans adapted to Tut's height and handled it well.
The opening basket went to West Jessamine, but it didn't take long for Mercer to get on the board. Senior Trevor Ellis hit an open 3-point shot, and it was as if the Titan's curse of not shooting well was broken; from there on out, the game tied once, but Mercer never gave up the lead.
Junior Jackson Doughty was hot on both ends of the floor for the night. His first 3-point shot followed Ellis', and Doughty hit four on the night and totaled 16 points. Defensively, the guard snuck into the baseline and stripped Tut a few times before he had the opportunity to shoot.
Halfway through the first quarter, senior Hagan Preston made the full-court press look easy when he stole the ball on West's out-of-bounds play and finished with a layup. Preston also had a good night, scoring more since the start of the New Year in the Titan's first game against Harlan County.
Point guard Hagan Preston led the offense during the Titans win on Friday, Jan. 24. Preston finished with 13 points. (Image: April Ellis/ The Harrodsburg Herald .)
In the opening minutes, junior Kaleb Murray was tangled up in a rebound and took a brutal hit to the head after being knocked to the floor. Murray had to see stars and was taken out of the game. It set the tone for how physical the game was.
Senior Andrew Tatum added a 3-point shot, and Ellis tipped in a basket at the buzzer and Mercer ended the first quarter up 23-13.
Murray wasted no time in the second quarter, showing he wouldn't be pushed around and split defenders for a basket. Ellis found him open on his next trip down the floor and passed it out. When the defender closed in, Murray returned to Ellis for the layup. When their offense is on, it is fueled by smart passes and unselfish play.
For a couple of minutes, Mercer started to turn over the ball, and West cut their lead 27-20. This would lead to a bad quarter in previous games, but the team regrouped, settled back into their offense and retook the game.
Murray's defense has improved as the season has progressed and he has become a master of getting set under the basket and earning the charge call. He caused foul problems for West and sent Tut to the bench. Preston had a good spin move to the basket, followed by a drive on the next possession, and the Titans went into halftime up, 35-22. title: Lady Titans Earn Third District Win
description: Cardin Sickles of Mercer County takes the ball down the court during the Lady Titans' victory against Burgin (The Har
content:
Cardin Sickles of Mercer County takes the ball down the court during the Lady Titans' victory against Burgin ( The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren).
The Mercer County Lady Titans (7-15) returned to the court after consecutive losses to two elite programs in Spencer County (16-5) and District 46 foe West Jessamine (17-5) on Monday, Feb. 3, in a matchup with the Burgin Lady Bulldogs (8-11) in Jack Coleman Sr. Gymnasium.
Lady Bulldog sophomore Kynlee Sexton attacked the rim and drew a foul before scoring the game's opening point, but Mercer quickly responded with a basket from Cardin Sickles assisted by Olive Frisby. Burgin momentarily reclaimed the lead until Maddi Baker made a great move under the basket and finished off the glass while being fouled. The Lady Titans got into a rhythm behind Sickles attacking the basket. No Burgin player could keep up with Sickles off the dribble, and she can create an open shot out of any situation, but missed shots inside the paint cost Mercer early, and allowed Burgin to stay in the game.
Sexton was on fire early and scored six points through jump shots in the first few minutes. Two traveling calls didn't help the Lady Titans. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Sara Clarke
description: Sara 'Sallie' Wathen Montgomery Clarke, 88, widow of Augustine 'Gus' Edward Clarke II, of Harrodsburg, died Saturday, Oct. 12, 2024, at the Willows. Born June 19, 1936, in Lebanon, she was the…
content:
Sara 'Sallie' Wathen Montgomery Clarke, 88, widow of Augustine 'Gus' Edward Clarke II, of Harrodsburg, died Saturday, Oct. 12, 2024, at the Willows.
Born June 19, 1936, in Lebanon, she was the daughter of the late James Richard Montgomery and Sara Wathen Rubel Montgomery.
Survivors include: two daughters, Elizabeth Wathen Clarke of Atlanta, Georgia, and Margaret McKinivan Clarke (Dax) Carmickle of Lexington; two sons, Augustine 'Gus' Edward (Cheryl) Clarke III of Milton, Georgia, and Alexander Kenrick Hughes Clarke of Cham, Switzerland; one sister, Flaget Montgomery Nally of Saint Catherine; one brother, Thomas Alexander (Jill) Montgomery of LaGrange, Georgia; and three grandchildren.
She was a graduate of St. Catherine Academy High School for girls, received a bachelor's degree in sociology with a minor in English at Maryville University in St. Louis, Missouri, and was a social worker and served as a substitute teacher, a member of the Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR), the James Harrod Trust and the Harrodsburg Historical Society, and was a member of St. Andrew Catholic Church.
A memorial service will be held at 11 a.m., Saturday, March 1, 2025, at the St. Andrew Catholic Church. A private burial will be held at the Calvary Cemetery in Lexington.
Memorial contributions are suggested to the St. Andrew Catholic Church, 1125 Danville Road, Harrodsburg, KY 40330.
Arrangements by Ransdell Funeral Chapel.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at www.ransdellfuneralchapel.com.

title: Titans Take Two Of Three Against Tough Competition
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenMercer County junior Kaleb Murray looked for a pass during the Titans 54-38 loss to George Rogers Clark on Saturday, Feb. 15. The Mercer County Titans boys…
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Mercer County junior Kaleb Murray looked for a pass during the Titans 54-38 loss to George Rogers Clark on Saturday, Feb. 15.
The Mercer County Titans boys basketball team (18-8) tipped off their final week of regular season play with possibly their most prestigious this season, a 60-54 win over the Ballard Bruins (17-7) on Monday, Feb. 17, on the Chris Souder Court.
The Titans trailed by as many as 10 points before a fourth quarter rally and excellent free throw shooting clinched the win over Ballard. The Titans were down their senior guard, Andrew Tatum, after an ankle injury in Saturday's game against GRC, and sophomore Collier Sexton got the varsity start. While his nerves sometimes showed in the first half, he settled into his game in the second half and helped the Titans get the 'W' against an athletic and physical Ballard team.
Mercer's first points were from a wide open shot under the basket from Kaleb Murray with an assist from Jackson Doughty. Then Ballard answered with a 3-point shot. That scenario played out over and over throughout the game. Mercer would make a good play and start to gain momentum and Ballard would hit a 3-point shot to shift the advantage back to themselves. They hit eight 3-point shots during the game.
The Bruins started with a full court press, but it didn't phase Mercer, however, they intensified the pressure once Mercer crossed the half court line. It was a physical game and it didn't take long for both teams to rack up the fouls. Senior Hagan Preston went to the bench in the first quarter with two fouls and the Bruins went into the bonus. Of Mercer's 10 points in the first quarter, five were twos from Murray and a 3-point shot from Jackson Doughty and the rest were from the foul line. Ballard led at the end of the first quarter 14-10.
Just 30 seconds into the second quarter, Doughty drained another 3-point shot and cut Ballard's lead to one point, 14-13. Anytime Ballard had a semi-open three, they took it and quickly added five points. Preston hit a midrange jumper, but Ballard went on a six point scoring run, 25-15. Ellis struggled through traffic and missed a few shots, but once he got the foul call he hit both foul shots. The next possession he had a good put back and the Titans started to gain momentum, until Ballard hit another 3-point shot with 3 minutes left in the first half.
Ballard kept a constant attack on the ball and at times Mercer struggled, but as the game progressed they adapted and worked around the trap. Ellis was able to extend over the trap and found Doughty open for another trey. Murray was fouled, and hit the front end of his shots, but a lane violation gave him another opportunity and he redeemed the miss. Ballard fired another one up from behind the arc with only 25 seconds left in the quarter. In the next possession they trapped senior Jadon King and it looked like time was going to run out before Mercer could get a shot off, but Doughty shook his defender lose and King hit him on the cut. Doughty found Sexton on the baseline and with barely and inch to spare, he cut under the basket for a reverse layup and gave Mercer an extra boost going into half time, 31-26.
Mercer exploded out of the gate and went on a nine point scoring run and cut Ballard's lead to one, 35-34, but once again, the Bruins hit another 3-point shot. Murray connected with Ellis who plowed through the lane on a reverse. Doughty broke up a pass and the momentum definitely shifted Mercer's way, forcing a Ballard time out.
Out of the time-out, the Bruins hit yet another 3-point shot and then Mercer called a time-out. With 1:57 left in the quarter, Murray a hit a hesitation jumper to make it a 3-point game, 41-38. Doughty tied the ball up for a jump ball and Mercer regained possession. Ballard's coach was not happy with the call and ended up with a technical. Doughty hit both shots and it was one point game.
Preston was fouled and after hitting both shots, Mercer took the lead, 42-41. Ballard, of course, hit a 3-point shot. With an assist from Preston, Ellis hit another bucket for Mercer and they trailed at the end of the third quarter, 46-44.
Ellis pulled down a big defensive rebound and Preston converted it into a 3-point shot for a one point lead, 47-46. Mercer turned the ball over a few times and Ballard capitalized on their mistakes. Ellis had a strong power dribble, hit the basket and got the and one call. He hit is free throw and tied the game up 50-50. It was back and forth until Doughty hit both of his shots from the charity stripe and Mercer led by three, 57-54 with 53.1 seconds left in the game.
Out of Ballard's time-out, Ellis grabbed another big rebound and was fouled. He hit the first of two shots. Mercer's defense was stellar and did not allow Ballard to take an uncontested shot. Doughty grabbed a rebound and was fouled and put the nail in the coffin, hitting both foul shots, and Mercer walked away with the upset, 60-54.
