title: Flooding Causes Damage In Mercer And Across The State
description: Photo: Mercer County Fiscal Court Facebook pageThe Burgin Fire Department, the Mercer County Sheriff's Office and Mercer County Emergency Management hel
content:
Photo: Mercer County Fiscal Court Facebook page
The Burgin Fire Department, the Mercer County Sheriff's Office and Mercer County Emergency Management helped citizens in need during the recent flooding.
There have been 14 confirmed deaths across Kentucky and local residents had to be helped out of their homes during the first round of severe weather that hit the nation in the past week.
On Friday, Feb. 14, Gov. Andy Beshear declared a state of emergency. Even as work continued to help the most storm-damaged areas in the state, officials were warning residents about snow and below-zero wind chills are expected this week.
'If you can't turn your heat on by this afternoon, you need to call a family member or friend and go stay with them. If that option isn't available, please go to an emergency shelter,' said Gov. Beshear said at a press briefing Tuesday. 'The temperatures are dropping dangerously low, and we need to do everything possible to keep our neighbors safe.'
At that briefing, Beshear announced that the death toll in Kentucky has reached 14, with a male and female in Jefferson County were lost due to the weather.
Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele declared a state of emergency in Mercer County on Saturday, Feb. 16. Through the Mercer County Fiscal Court Facebook page, Steele also announced that roads throughout Mercer County were flooded, including East Water Street, Bondville Road, Bruner's Chapel, Old Dixville Road, Handy Pike, Dry Branch and Perryville Road/U.S. 68. On Monday, the Burgin School FRYSC Facebook account asked the public for a rental for a family of six who needed accommodations for a month or possibly longer depending on the damage to their home.
Across the commonwealth, Gov. Beshear said first responders from the Kentucky National Guard, the Kentucky State Police and Kentucky Emergency Management—alongside partners from the Indiana and Tennessee National Guards—had worked together on more than 800 response missions.
In Martin County, Beshear said the KSP sent out helicopters, and in a combined effort with the Kentucky and Indiana National Guards, successfully airlifted 296 Kentuckians who had been stranded due to the high water.
The second round of severe weather started Tuesday night, with the National Weather Service issuing a winter storm warning for Harrodsburg and other communities, with predicted accumulations of three to six inches of snow, followed by low temperatures Thursday through Friday.
The governor said all snowplow and salt truck crews are ready to keep state highways passable. The incoming extreme cold will make it difficult for crews to clear roads as salt and other anti-icing materials become less effective. Flooded roads will also impact snowplow routes.
Gov. Beshear launched the Team Kentucky Storm Relief Fund. If you would like to mail in a donation, make your check to Kentucky State Treasurer. In the memo line please note the donation is for the 'Team Kentucky Storm Relief Fund.' Send check to Public Protection Cabinet, 500 Mero Street, 218 NC, Frankfort, KY 40601.
As of Tuesday morning, the fund had raised over $50,000, which will help pay for each victim's funeral.
Donations can also be made online.
Safety Tips
• Watch your step. Floodwaters often hide sharp and dangerous debris, like broken glass and metal. Floodwater can also be contaminated with oil, gasoline or sewage.
• Wear the appropriate protective clothing and gear such as boots, gloves and safety glasses when moving debris.
• Stay away from electrical utility equipment after a storm, or if it is wet, to prevent being electrocuted. Report any utility issues to your local utility company.
• Flooded homes are hazards. Get a professional to check for loose wires, mold and hidden damage before re-entering.
• Use generators or other gas-powered machinery only outdoors and away from windows.
• Never drive into a road covered with flowing water. One foot of flowing water can sweep a car off the road; two feet will carry away an SUV or pickup. Even six inches of water can knock you off your feet. Never walk or drive through swift water. Turn around, don't drown.
• Respect barricades and posted signage. If you encounter a flooded road, turn around. You're not only putting your own life at risk, but also the lives of first responders.
• If you encounter a dark traffic signal, treat it as a four-way stop.
Drivers are urged to check traffic conditions before traveling at GoKy.ky.gov.

title: Tourist Commission Holds Off On Oktoberfest Decision
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreVolunteers at the ticket booth were kept very busy at the 2021 Oktoberfest. The annual event, which
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Volunteers at the ticket booth were kept very busy at the 2021 Oktoberfest. The annual event, which began in 2016, recorded its second highest profit 9n 2021. (File image).
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission has still not made a decision on request for more funding for Oktoberfest.
Oktoberfest organizers are asking for $60,000 before the end of this fiscal year and another $60,000 to be paid after the beginning of fiscal year 2026. That's on top of the $60,000 the tourist commission already dedicated to the festival in their 2024 budget.
The tourist commission held a special-called meeting on Thursday, Feb. 20, and discussed the request with local accountant Noel Turner, who formerly served as president of the Downtown Harrodsburg Main Street Program, which hosted Oktoberfest since its inception. Downtown Harrodsburg folded at the end of last year, and Turner currently serves on the committee that is organizing this year's event, which is scheduled to begin Friday, Sept. 26, and run through Saturday, Sept. 27.
On Thursday, Turner, who attended the meeting via Zoom, said the total budget for the 2025 Oktoberfest would be$328,200. That is an $88,000 increase over last year's event, which Turner attributed to increased entertainment and production costs.
Turner said the event has exploded over the past three years, from $160,000 to $233,000 for last year, which he said was over the budgeted amount. He was asked to email the actuals to the tourist commission. Turner said he would email the documentation after the meeting.
'I have a hard time figuring out how to email stuff,' Turner said. 'I'm ready for questions.'
Daarik Gray, executive director of the tourist commission, asked for the amount the tourist commission had contributed to Downtown Harrodsburg First before they dissolved.
'We don't know exactly because we're still paying expenses,' Turner said. 'I don't know the final number but I'm hoping it will be about $20,000.'
Turner said they were considering that income. He said much of the committee's money has been spent to get bands signed. He said they are planning to have two major acts this year, on Friday and Saturday.
'Those bands are going to cost us $20,000 each,' said Turner, who noted they had budgeted $42,000 on bands.
'If we do this, we'll be giving you $120,000 for one event,' Gray said. 'If that's what it takes to do it this year, what's it going to take next year?'
Last week, Greg Souder, who serves on the board that organizes Oktoberfest along with Turner and Allen Goldie, made an initial request for the funding. Souder had told the tourist commission that the committee's ultimate goal was for Oktoberfest to become self-sufficient.
'My opinion, as a financial guy, is a little bit different than Greg's,' Turner said Thursday. He asked if the tourist commission would not want to support Oktoberfest even if they were self-sufficient. Turner did say they hope to ask for half of what they're asking for this year.
He said the committee, which is still in the process of acquiring a nonprofit status, lost five months of opportunity to get sponsorships due to the dissolution of Downtown Harrodsburg.
'What matters is we have the appropriate amount of funding to get this event off this year,' Turner said. He said he has 'no expectation' they will ask for this much next year.
Gray asked if their goal is to have $60,000 in the bank account next year so they will always be a year ahead.
'We want to be ahead of that,' said Souder, who was also in attendance Thursday.
Gray noted they'd have to ask for $120,000 to get back to the same place. Turner said every dollar they raise is invested in the event.
Asked if the committee would open the Oktoberfest bank books for inspection by tourist commission employees, Turner said, 'We don't necessarily want to do that.'
Some of the board members questioned the need for more money.
'Do you really need to spend $20,000 for more national bands?' asked tourist commission board member Leigh Lopez. 'I know you don't want to go backwards, but at some point you've got to top out.'
'That's a decision we've got to make each year,' Turner said. 'This is an international event.'
'Some of us have been to every one of them,' said Joan Huffman the tourist commission chairwoman, 'And they've been wonderful.'
Turner called Oktoberfest a Hollywood style event, which he attributed to the production. Oktoberfest drew 24,000 visits in 2023, according to the tourist commission. Oktoberfest committee members insist the event's success is due to the production.
'People are not coming to Harrodsburg to drink beer,' Turner said.
'They're coming to see the entertainment,' he said. 'They can drink beer any where.'
He said the organizers negotiate with the productions companies and bands. Turner noted they were able to negotiate one band down from $15,000 to $10,000.
'If we start watering down the event or taking away things, that's going to be the nail in the coffin,' Turner said.
'This board will always support an event of this magnitude,' said tourist commission board member John Holiday said. 'Always.' For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Dorothy Henninger
description: It is with mixed feelings that we announce the passing of our mother, Dorothy Henninger, who died peacefully in her sleep and left us to go home to be with her Lord on Sunday, March 2, 2025, at the…
content:
It is with mixed feelings that we announce the passing of our mother, Dorothy Henninger, who died peacefully in her sleep and left us to go home to be with her Lord on Sunday, March 2, 2025, at the age of 88.
She was born on May 30, 1936 in Harrodsburg. She was kind, giving and accepting to everyone she knew and provided refuge to those who needed it over the years. She was much loved and will be sorely missed.
Dorothy was the first child of three to the late Richard Meredith Harris and Gertrude Quinn Harris Kober. Dorothy had a hard childhood, and her best memories were those years she spent with her father 'Pete.'
Dorothy was a member of the Bohon Road Baptist Church. She was a wife, mother, homemaker and caregiver for her father for many years. She went to work at Universal Button Fasteners and worked there for 33 years until retirement.
Other than her parents, she is preceded in death by her siblings, Mildred 'Jean' Gibson and Donald Kober; one son-in-law, Kenneth 'Butch' Harris, and several grandchildren, Mitzi and Jeremy Henninger, Andrea Song-Rodriguez, Zach Henninger, and many others.
Survivors include: her children, Beverly Harris, Terry (Tommy) Henninger, Robin Stewart, Evans (Angela) Stewart, Shawn Henninger, Chad Henninger, a special nephew, Harvey Bennett; 15 grandchildren, Cory and Toni (Todd) Piatt, Andrew and Eric (Monica) Perez, Shana (Chris) Kench, Haley, Scarlett, Sarah, Caleb, Cody, Mark, Kelli, Amy, Larry, and Stacy; great-grandchildren, Austin, Arron, Angel, Isabella, Eli, Abigail, Annika, Daxton, Jasmine, Alyssa, Zane, Isabel, Sophia and Charlie.
A remembrance of Dorothy's life was held Wednesday, March 5, at Alexander & Royalty Funeral Home with Justin Fulton officiating. Burial will be in Shawnee Run Baptist Church Cemetery.
Pallbearers were Evans Stewart, Chad Henninger, Eric Perez, Eli Perez, Caleb Young, Chris Kench, and Dakota Henninger serving as active pallbearers. Honorary pallbearers were Tommy, Shawn and Andrew Henninger.
Expressions of sympathy may take the form of donations to Bohon Road Baptist Church Missionary Fund, 510 Bohon Road, Harrodsburg, KY 40330.
May Dorothy's soul rest in the hands of her Savior, and may her memory be a blessing and bring smiles to all who knew and loved her.
paid obit.

title: Mercer's Laykin Irvin Signs With The Panthers
description: Soon to be Mercer County High School graduate Laykin Irvin has been a staple of the Lady Titans soccer team attack all four years of her high school career. Even as a freshman, Irvin was one of the…
content:
Soon to be Mercer County High School graduate Laykin Irvin has been a staple of the Lady Titans soccer team attack all four years of her high school career. Even as a freshman, Irvin was one of the most productive members on the team, but each year since she has put up simply astounding numbers. In each of her final three seasons Irvin averaged more than one goal or assist per game.
In that time, she made 54 appearances for the Lady Titans, scoring 73 goals and assisting five. Irvin was an All-District and All-Region selection each of her final three seasons, and was selected to the All 12th Region first team as a senior. Irvin finished her senior season ranked 23rd in the state in goals, with 35. She had back-to-back hat tricks in wins over Bourbon County and Harrison County, which certified the program's first ever 2A Sectional tournament win. Her seven hat tricks in 2024 is enough to put her second on the all-time list of Lady Titan soccer superstars.
Laykin Irvin passed up the final defender before scoring a goal against East Jessamine last year. (File image).
More recently, Irvin signed her letter of intent to continue her academic and athletic career at Kentucky Wesleyan College. It was an easy decision for Irvin, who likened the small community atmosphere of Wesleyan's campus to her hometown.
'Walking around campus in Owensboro felt natural; the campus was close together, small and everyone near was welcoming. It automatically felt like home,' said Irvin. Above all, the Panther's coaching staff ensured Irvin she was exactly the kind of player and person they wanted in their program.
'The coach showed interest in me first, when I went on campus they made that very clear. They expressed how badly they wanted me, and that was an awesome feeling,' said Irvin. 'I knew playing at this level was going to be a challenge with it being a division-II school, but I can proudly say. It is where I belong.'
Perhaps Irvin's most notable accomplishment is keeping a 3.5 GPA or higher throughout high school while dominating competition on the pitch. She plans to earn a degree in Exercise Science while a Panther. A degree that will aid her in her professional life, of which she says even four more years of soccer seems too little. Irvin has dreamt of being a college soccer player since first dribbling a ball, and she has dreams of playing on a much bigger stage.
'I'm excited to say, after college there's more to come, I'm not finished!' For more great stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Pulaski Ends Mercer's Season In Second Round Of 12th Region
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/April EllisSophomore Jackson Doughty hit a 3-point in front of the Mercer County bench during the Titans win over Southwestern on Mo
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
Sophomore Jackson Doughty hit a 3-point in front of the Mercer County bench during the Titans win over Southwestern on Monday, March 12. The Mercer County Titans (22-12) lost in the second round of 12th Region play to the Pulaski County Maroons (22-10) on Monday, March 11. It was a hard-fought game with the lead swinging in both direc­tions, and it was in the final minutes that Pulaski showed why they were the reigning 12th Region champions and pulled away for a six-point victory, 54-48. The Titans wrapped up a successful season and won games against opponents they hadn't beaten in some time. The direction under new coach Keith Adkins was a positive one. Last year, there were eight games the Titans led going into the fourth quarter that they ulti­mately lost. However, this year, they learned to finish games with a win. They won a district championship and advanced to the region's semi finals, a feat that has yet to be achieved since 2018. Losing seniors Jackson and John Lincoln Perry will hurt the Titans, but they return a talented sophomore class to build upon. In the opening minutes of the first quarter, junior Trevor Ellis was called for a foul and the Titan faithful drew a collective breath, hoping it wouldn't be a game with early foul trouble. The Titans had multiple turnovers and missed baskets that should have been easy points. John Lincoln Perry caught an elbow to the face and momentarily exited the game with a bro­ken nose. With three minutes left to play in the first quar­ter, the only points they had were foul shots hit by junior Andrew Tatum. 'I definitely think our guys came out a little nervous and tight. I even said after the game that the big­gest difference was that one program had been on this stage before and one had not. And that is part of the growth that we are going to experi­ence moving forward,' said Coach Adkins. 'Unless you win the state tournament, a season never ends the way you want it to. But, I truly believe that, as bad as this one hu1ts, it will help this group of return­ing players next year and in years to come.' The offense finally started to show signs of life when J. Perry hit a 3-point shot with an assist from Kaleb Murray. Ellis blocked a shot, recov­ered the ball and scored. Slowly, Mercer seemed to shake off their nerves and get into the game. Ellis ended the first quarter with a reverse to the basket, and Mercer trailed, 18-9. The Titans wasted little time getting on the board in the second quarter. Sophomore Jackson Doughty found Ellis cutting to the bas­ket for a basket and assist. John Lincoln Perry returned to the game and sparked the defense with back-to-back steals and a beautiful Euro-step to split the defenders for a layup. Tatum connected with Ellis down the lane for a basket. On the next posses­sion, Ellis pulled down the defensive rebound and fed it to Kaleb Murray for the layup. Mercer chipped away at Pulaski's lead, 20-17, with 4:23 left to play in the first half. Throughout the sea­son, Mercer improved their defense and it showed. Tatum forced another Pulaski turnover and converted it to a basket. Ellis hit the second half of his foul shots and the game was tied, 20-20. Pulaski had led by 11 at one point and with a jumper by J. Perry, the Titans took the lead for the first time, 22-20, with I :33 left in the sec­ond qua1ter. Pulaski's Gavin Cook tied the game up 22-22 at the half. For the rest of this story—including game statistics—check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Collier Signs With University Of The Cumberlands
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenByron Collier (center) pictured with his family from left to right: Curry (brother), Saralyn and Nick (par­ents) and Madi (sister) moments after signing t
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Byron Collier (center) pictured with his family from left to right: Curry (brother), Saralyn and Nick (par­ents) and Madi (sister) moments after signing to University of the Cumberlands.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Byron Collier (center) pictured with his family from left to right: Curry (brother), Saralyn and Nick (par­ents) and Madi (sister) moments after signing to University of the Cumberlands. Mercer County's Byron Collier signed to continue his student-athlete career at University of the Cumberlands on Wednesday, March 27. Collier was a standout for the Titan football team each of the last two seasons and always dreamed of one day playing a sport in college; he just always expected it to be football.
'I never thought I would do track in college,' said Collier.
Collier is one fourth of the winningest class of Titan football players ever and helped lead the offensive line last season and helped Mercer County to its first district championship since 2015.
'I really wanted to play football in college and just started doing track to get more in shape for football, but as soon as I joined the track team I instantly fell in love with the sport and how the track team was really a family,' said Collier.
Last season Collier threw a personal record of 139'5' in discus, which placed sixth at the 5th Region track and field meet, earning him an opportunity at the KHSAA Class-2A State Championship.
Cumberlands took note of Collier's impressive throws and boundless potential and reached out to him this past winter, inviting him to campus. One thing specifically stood out to Collier, the small community feel.
'I want to go somewhere that wherever I am on campus, I know someone, and that's how it seemed for the people there,' said Collier.
Collier also talked to another former Mercer County athlete currently on the Cumberlands football roster. Joziah Pennington played football with Collier for four years, and encouraged Collier to be a part of the Cumberland community.
For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: MAFEW Presses City Commission For Decision On Former Armory
description: File image. Officials from Mercer Area Family and Education and Wellness (MAFEW) pressed the Harrodsburg City Commission on their plans for the National Guard Armory on College Street. MAFEW formerly…
content:
File image.
File image. Officials from Mercer Area Family and Education and Wellness (MAFEW) pressed the Harrodsburg City Commission on their plans for the National Guard Armory on College Street. MAFEW formerly operated the facility as a daycare and have plans to run it as the Harrodsburg Community Center, in partnership with other agencies. However, that plan is on hold until MAFEW gets some indication from the city, which owns the building.
Last month, MAFEW officials led the commission on a tour of the facility during a special-called meeting, but the city commissioners made no decision. At their regular meeting on Monday, April 8, the commission was addressed by Donald Wayne Smith, president of the MAFEW board of directors, about their intentions for the building.
'It seems like we're still on the back burner,' said Smith, who said he had been forced to put people—including people wanting to make financial donations—on hold until the city commission makes their decision.
'It shouldn't take this long,' Smith said. 'I really just want you to give me an answer.'
Mayor Bob Williams deferred to City Attorney Norrie Currens, who said an appraisal of the facility requested by the city has not come back yet. Currens also asked MAFEW to update their financial information to reflect MAFEW's commitment to pay utilities at the building. Previously, the city had been paying utilities.
Others have expressed interest in the former armory. Last year, Jack Mattingly appeared before the city commission to discuss using the armory as a home for the Kentucky Veterans Hall of Fame.
On Monday, Smith said MAFEW has enough money to operate the building as a community center for a year and a half. Smith said outside of the roof—in January 2023, part of the outer roof of the building was ripped off during a storm— and the loan that's never been repaid, MAFEW has paid for all the improvements to the facility.
'We are getting an appraisal on the building,' Currens said. Once they had that, the city commission would decide whether to sell the building or hold onto it, she said. Currens said the future associated expenses with the building were concerning.
Commissioner Marvin 'Bubby' Isham said the city would probably receive the appraisal next week. They would hold an executive session and vote on it. Isham said the decision should be made by the end of this month.
The Harrodsburg Armory is one of eight armories built by the Works Progress Administration between 1941-1942, according to the Harrodsburg Historical Society's website. It is one of six poured concrete armories in the state, designed by Louisville architect Edd R. Gregg. The armory was used by the National Guard until 1977, when it was donated to the City of Harrodsburg. It served as the home of the Wilderness Trace YMCA until 2017, when MAFEW took it over.
On Monday, Smith stressed the potential value that could be offered by the community center.
'Stuff in there is going to be more valuable than daycare,' Smith said. He said a year and a half—two years—'will not kill this city.'
'We're going to get our appraisal,' Currens said. 'I think we're replowing old ground.'
For the rest of the story, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Harrodsburg City Commission To Make Changes in Public Participation Policies
description: File image. During last week's meeting, the Harrodsburg City Commission gave first reading to a new ordinance changing the procedure for participa
content:
File image.
File image. During last week's meeting, the Harrodsburg City Commission gave first reading to a new ordinance changing the procedure for participation in city meetings.
Reading from a draft of the new ordinance, Mayor Bob Williams said citizens are encouraged to bring matters of importance to department supervisors, Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard, or individually to any of the commissioners, the mayor or the city attorney. If the public wishes to address the city commission during a meeting, the ordinance establishes guidelines for doing so.
Anyone who wishes to discuss a topic on the commission's agenda should fill out a 'request to address the commission' form and submit it to the chief administrative officer at least 15 minutes before the beginning of the meeting. The form requires the speaker's name, the name of any agency the speaker may be representing, their address and phone number and the agenda item they wish to address.
According to a draft of the ordinance, speakers will be given three minutes to make their remarks. Any materials they would like to distribute to the commission should be provided to the chief administrative officer prior to the meeting.
Speakers who wish to address items not on the agenda should submit a request at least five business days before the meeting.
The speaker will also be asked to provide information and will be limited to three minutes to make their remarks.
In addition, the ordinance establishes comment guidelines concerning 'undue interruption or other interference with the orderly conduct of business. The mayor may terminate the speaker's participation if, after being called to order, the speaker persists in improper conduct or remarks.'
According to the draft ordinance, the mayor and commissioners will not enter into a dialogue with speakers. 'Questions from commissioners will be for clarification purposes only.'
The draft ordinance also disallows political endorsements, demonstrations in support or opposition—clapping, cheering or hissing—and threats of personal violence.
If approved, anyone who violates the guidelines will be cautioned by the presiding officer or asked to leave. Copies of the draft ordinance are available at city hall.
The next meeting of the Harrodsburg City Commission will be Monday, April 22, at noon.

title: Planning And Zoning Commission Approves ‘Bright Leaf Estates' Development Improvement Plan
description: File image. The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission approved an improvement plan for a residential development near Bright Leaf Golf Resort. The improve
content:
File image.
File image. The Harrodsburg-Mercer County Planning and Zoning Commission approved an improvement plan for a residential development near Bright Leaf Golf Resort. The improvement plan was submitted by Kimike Properties LLC to redesign Tyler Avenue in Brightleaf Estates and create eight lots. The property is located on Tyler Avenue in Mercer County and is zoned R-2 and R-3 (High Density Residential and Multifamily).
Kendal Wise of Vantage Engineering, who spoke on behalf of the applicant, said the property is located off Adams Lane next to Bright Leaf and consists of multi-story apartment buildings with up to eight units. Wise said the original intent was to create condominiums with amenities, but he said there had never been a formal condo association set up to administer common areas and roads. Wise said Campbellsville University in Harrodsburg tried to buy all the units over the last few years to create housing for students.
'They put them up for sale,' Wise said.
He said Mike Smith of Danville bought the units with the intent of renting them out.
'There are still four to five people who own condos out there,' Wise said. He said there were three in the building closest to Adams Lane. Wise said Smith owns nearly all the other buildings and the units.
Wise said the goal for other parties who are not willing to sell or participate in a condo association is to move them into one building. He said Smith is willing to trade. Wise said the owner wants to see if the commission would be willing to allow them to create a county road, which would allow the owner to divide the property.
'Right now it's a private road, a loop in really bad need of repair,' Wise said. He said the plat would need at least eight variances, because the buildings are situated closer to the road than setback requirements will allow.
'We were working on the plans, and then you all came out with new street regulations,' Wise said.
He said the proposed county road will have curbs and gutters in some places but not others. Nor will it have sidewalks. The road will be 20 feet wide, which will match minimum standards.
If the commission didn't approve the improvement plan, Wise said they'd go back to the drawing board.
'They're already making renovations to the buildings and the parking lots,' Wise said. 'It's just going to end up being a private development.' He said he could not speculate on how individual owners would pay for mowing and other services.
He said the plan for the road is to eliminate the loop and make the road wide enough to accommodate two lanes of traffic.
On approval, the applicant would have to file a bond with a 20 percent contingency, said Shawn Moore, executive director of planning and zoning. He said the applicant would have to maintain the road for three years before the county would take it over. Moore called the current road, which is 550 feet long, a 'glorified driveway.'
'What you're going to end up with is a county road where two cars can safely pass somewhere in the future,' Moore told the commission. 'It will make a really bad situation a whole lot better.'
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele, who was in attendance at the meeting, was asked her opinion.
Steele said the area would be improved.
Steele said the area would be improved. 'We have busing issues there already,' the judge said. She said she was worried about the width of what would become the entrance.
'That is super congested,' Steele said. 'Is that going to cause any issues?'
She said she thought the second entrance was better than the first entrance. 'I think, aesthetically, the county says yes,' Steele said.
The commission approved the improvement plan with variances as shown..

title: Mark Pope Is Back
description: Elliott Hess/UK AthleticsMark Pope greets the crowd at his first p
content:
Elliott Hess/UK Athletics
Mark Pope greets the crowd at his first press conference as the new head coach of the UK Wildcats. The Mark Pope Era has officially begun in Kentucky, and fans could not be more ecstatic. Signaled by the 25,000 fans who waited to be in Rupp Arena for a press conference, the Big Blue Nation was long overdue for a dose of medicine to make them healthy again. And by all indications, Coach Mark Pope is just that shot in the arm. Pope, a former player, team captain and national champion, joined the Wildcats as the first alumnus to lead the program since Joe B. Hall. Before signing on to replace John Calipari, Pope coached at Brigham Young University (BYU) and Utah Valley. While at these spots, Pope had an overall record of 187-108 (63.4 percent). However, despite his underwhelming overall record, Pope's teams improved in record almost every season. This theme has been consistent across his entire career. Although he has inherited very poor and barren programs, he has built them into consistent conference contenders. Since being named the Kentucky head coach, fans have gone through sev­eral phases of acceptance. lnitially, it seemed as though the most passionate and vocal of fans were displeased with the hire, citing a near-unlim­ited budget of money to hire a coach, claiming that Pope was a reflection of Mitch Barnhart 'settlino' for mediocrity. However, as the night turned into day and the day turned into the next evening, fans seemed to start buying in. Then, after a Barnhart radio interview and a Rick Pitino viral video, fans seemed to jump on the Pope bandwagon.

title: Man Wins $50,000; Misses $1.3 Billion Lottery Jackpot By One Number
description: Photo SubmittedA Harrodsburg man won $50,000 playing Powerball, missing the $1.3 billion jackpot by one number.
content:
Photo Submitted
A Harrodsburg man won $50,000 playing Powerball, missing the $1.3 billion jackpot by one number.
Photo Submitted
A Harrodsburg man won $50,000 playing Powerball, missing the $1.3 billion jackpot by one number. Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com A Harrodsburg man won $50,000 playing Powerball. According to a press release from the Kentucky Lottery, the man, who wishes to remain anonymous, was just one number off from winning the $1.3 billion jackpot.
'I usually only play when the jackpot is over a billion. You know, when it's worth it,' the man joked.
The April 6 drawing was the fourth-largest jackpot in Powerball history and the winner purchased ten Quick Pick Powerball plays at Kroger on South College Street. The supermarket will receive $500.
'The numbers were delayed so I checked them the next morning,' he said. 'I saw I had matched the numbers but then verified the amount on the app.'
That's when the man saw the $50,000 prize and was in disbelief.
'There was doubt,' he said. 'This can't be real!'
The player matched four of the white balls and the Powerball to win the game's third prize of $50,000.
'The only number I missed was 44, I had 48 so I was just off by four,' the man said.
After taxes, the winner walked away with a check for $36,000. He plans to use some of the winnings on an upcoming trip and to pay off bills.
In addition, two $150,000 winning tickets were purchased at a Quick Shop in Paducah.
The Kentucky Lottery advises winners to:
• Sign the back of their tickets.
• Keep them in a secure location.
• Claim their prize within 180 days from the date of the drawing.
Winners must claim their prizes at lottery headquarters located at 1011 West Main Street in Louisville.In 2023, the Kentucky Lottery paid out more than $1.4 billion in prizes. Since 1989, proceeds from Kentucky Lottery tickets have raised more than $6.8 billion for good causes. Since 1999, Kentucky Lottery proceeds have funded more than $5 billion in scholarships and grants for Kentucky college students.
In 2023, $7,815,854 in lottery tickets were sold in Mercer County, according to the Kentucky Lottery. In that same year, statewide sales totaled $1,839,372,974, according to Lexington Herald-Leader, versus $1.4 billion in prizes paid out. For more information, visit kylottery.com.

title: Mercer Track Standout Sam Lewis Signs With Georgetown College
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Samuel WarrenMercer County Senior High cross country and track and field standout Sam Lewis signed with George­town College on Monday, April 29. Pictured sea
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Mercer County Senior High cross country and track and field standout Sam Lewis signed with George­town College on Monday, April 29. Pictured seated from left to right are: Georgetown Coach Luke Gar­nett, Adam Lewis, Sam Lewis and Kim Lewis. Pictured standing are Lynn Flach, Derek McIntyre and Katie Lewis.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Samuel Warren
Mercer County Senior High cross country and track and field standout Sam Lewis signed with George­town College on Monday, April 29. Pictured seated from left to right are: Georgetown Coach Luke Gar­nett, Adam Lewis, Sam Lewis and Kim Lewis. Pictured standing are Lynn Flach, Derek McIntyre and Katie Lewis. For the last four years, Mercer County cross country and track and field standout Sam Lewis has been making a name for himself as a hard worker and a leader. He recently signed his letter of intent to continue his academic and athletic career at Georgetown College, where he will join both the cross country and track and field programs.
This past fall, Lewis boasted the second highest boys finish at the regional competition ever, helping lead the Titans to a third place finish while placing fourth overall with a time of 17:36.58. Soon after, Lewis placed 25 out of 260 competitors at the KHSAA Class-AA State Cross Country Championship, with a time of 17:45.03. Lewis' contributions, along with junior Marshall Hart's, guided Titan cross country to its highest team finish (12th) since 2006. In track and field Lewis placed in last spring's 5th Region meet in the open 3200 meter run and helped the 4×800 m relay team to a second place finish. Unfortunately, Lewis isn't cleared to participate with the Titans in his final season due to injury, but is expecting to return to training this summer.
Along with his talent on the course and track, Lewis' character and dedication to learning is what made his time with the Titans so impactful.
'Sam is a role model to all his teammates and a mentor to the younger kids. He leads by example and shows that the expectations of this program are training, hard work, positive mindset, encouragement to all and to be a family,' said Mercer County Track and Field Coach Lynn Flach.
Lewis wasn't a fan of running growing up. Sam's twin sister, Katie Lewis, who has been running cross country and track since the fifth grade, was his main motivation for giving it a try.
'I stayed away from running until the eighth grade when I was bribed into running for the cross country team by my twin sister Katie,' said Lewis.

The 2024 Kentucky Primary Election happens Tuesday, May 21, with polls open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. While the presidential primary has been pretty much decided already, there are still important races down the ballot. In the Republican primary, James Toller is challenging incumbent Kim King for the state representative nomination, while Justin Johnson and Sarah Bryant are vying for the nomiation for commonwealth attorney. In the Democratic primary, five candidates—Randy Cravens, Jonathan Richardson, Todd Kelly, Don B. Pratt and Shauna Budd—are competing to challenge Republican incumbent Andy Barr in the race for the 6th Congressional District, which includes Mercer County. Here's a handy guide to make your voice heard, with information taken from the websites of Mercer County Clerk Chris Horn and the state elections website. Absentee Voting By Mail
For voters who are eligible for an absentee ballot by mail, the ballot can be requested by visiting www.govote.ky.gov or calling the Mercer County Clerk's Office at 859-734-6310. Tuesday, May 7, was the last day for mail-in absentee ballot requests Voters should not request a mail-in ballot if they intend to vote in person. After the voter has completed their ballot, it can be returned two ways. Ballots can be returned either in-person in the drop box at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse (207 West Lexington Street, Harrodsburg) or through the mail. If returned by mail, the postage on the return envelope should total $1.63. Returned ballots will be processed at the clerk's office on the primary election day. In Person Voting Options Voters who have an eligible excuse may vote absentee in-person excused at the Mercer County Clerk's Office from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. starting Wednesday, May 8, and running through Wednesday, May 15. There will be no voting Saturday or Sunday. All voters eligible to vote in the May 21, primary election who have not requested to vote absentee, will be able to cast early in-person ballots on Thursday, May 16, through Saturday, May 18, from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. at the clerk's office.

Who's eligible for absentee voting?
Voters are eligible to receive an absentee ballot mailed to the residential address in the county in which they are registered if their completed application is received 14 days before an election and if the voter is: • Prevented from voting in person at the polls on election day and from casting an excused or no-excuse in-person absentee ballot on all days in-person absentee voting is conducted because he or she will be absent from the county of their residence all hours and all days excused or no-excuse in-person absentee voting is conducted.
• A participant in the Secretary of State's crime victim address confidentiality protection program as authorized by state law.
• Not able to appear at the polls on election day or the days excused or no-excuse in-person absentee voting is conducted on the account of age, disability, or illness, and who has not been declared mentally disabled by a court of competent jurisdiction.
Voters are eligible to receive an absentee ballot mailed to a mailing address different than their residential address if their completed application is received 14 days before an election and if the voter is a resident of Kentucky; a student who temporarily resides outside the county of their residence; people who have been incarcerated in jail and charged with a crime, but has not been convicted of the crime; are changing or has changed their place of residence to a different state while the registration books are closed in the new state of residence; or temporarily residing outside the state but still eligible to vote in the state.
Voters, or their spouse, experiencing a medical emergency within 14 days or less of an election, are eligible to receive an absentee ballot mailed to a mailing address different than their residential address if their completed application is received 14 days before an election
Voters otherwise eligible to vote on election day are eligible to vote an in-person absentee ballot during the six business days immediately before the last Thursday occurring before election day if they meet one (1) of the following requirements:
• Is a resident of Kentucky as defined by state law who will be absent from the county of their residence on the day of an election and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Has surgery, or whose spouse has surgery, scheduled that will require hospitalization on the day of an election and during the days of no-excuse in person absentee voting.
• Temporarily resides outside the state but is still eligible to vote in this state and will be absent from the county of their residence on the day of an election and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Is a resident of Kentucky who is a uniformed-service voter as defined in KRS 117A.101​ confined to a military base on election day and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Is in her last trimester of pregnancy.
• Has not been declared mentally disabled by a court of competent jurisdiction and, due to age, disability, or illness, is not able to appear at the polls on electi​on day and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Is a student who temporarily resides outside the county of their residence and will be absent from the county of their residence on the day of an election and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Any person employed in an occupation that is scheduled to work during all days and all hours, which shall include commute time, the polls are open on election day and during the days of no-excuse in-person absentee voting.
• Any election officer tasked with election administration for the current election cycle.
Any person prevented from voting in person at the polls on election day and from casting a no-excuse in-person absentee ballot on all days no-excuse in-person absentee voting is conducted because he or she will be absent from the county of their residence during all days and all hours no excuse in-person absentee voting is conducted.​
In case of a medical emergency within 14 days or less of an election, a registered voter and the registered voter's spouse may apply for an absentee ballot. The application shall state that the emergency condition occurred within the 14 day period. The application shall be notarized. The application form may be requested by and delivered by the voter or the spouse, parents, or children of the voter. If the voter has no spouse, parents, or children, the application form may be requested by and delivered by the brother, sister, niece, nephew, or designee of the voter. The application form shall be restricted to the use of the voter.
Upon receipt of the application and verification, the county clerk shall issue an absentee ballot.
For full details, visit elect.ky.gov or mercer.countyclerk.us.

title: Former Titan Seth Tatum Finds A New Home In Charleston, South Carolina
description: Photo SubmittedSeth Tatum, pictured above during his time as a manager for the University of Louisville, was recently named director of basketball operations at the College of Charleston, the oldest…
content:
Photo Submitted
Seth Tatum, pictured above during his time as a manager for the University of Louisville, was recently named director of basketball operations at the College of Charleston, the oldest university in South Carolina.
Photo Submitted
Seth Tatum, pictured above during his time as a manager for the University of Louisville, was recently named director of basketball operations at the College of Charleston, the oldest university in South Carolina. Former three sport athlete for Mercer County Senior High School, Seth Tatum, has adjusted well to his new work environment following his appointment as Director of Basketball Operations with the College of Charleston early in April. Tatum enters his first administrative position following seven straight seasons of working with the University of Louisville men's basketball program as a manager and graduate assistant. Former Cardinal Head Coach Chris Mack hired Tatum initially before the 2021-22 season, and now Tatum will be joining Mack and the Cougars, one of the most successful Division-I basketball programs over the last two seasons. The Cougars have amassed an impressive 58-12 record in the last two years while winning two consecutive Coastal Athletic Association tournament championships under former head coach Pat Kelsey, who joined the Louisville staff on March 28.
'I'm settling in well in Charleston. It's a beautiful place to live and an amazing program to work for. They give us great resources to be successful and I'm super excited to do everything I can to help Coach Mack continue the winning tradition that Charleston basketball has had recently. The role is what I expected, I have my hand in a lot of different fields,' said Tatum.
Tatum will be handling a very broad workload as director of basketball operations. Everything from scheduling to travel procedures and videography to opponent scouting, Tatum's position encompasses pretty much any behind the scenes task.
'It's a really wide umbrella. It deals kind of with everything,' said Tatum.
Basketball has always played a significant role for Tatum. He recalls attending his father Spencer Tatum's practices when he was the head coach at Harrodsburg High School in the early 2000's. While a Titan, Tatum played basketball under three separate head coaches and experienced the most successful season in Titan basketball history in 2016-17. He also had success with David Buchanan and Adam Shartzer on the football and baseball teams respectively. While a Cardinal, Tatum worked under Rick Pitino, David Padgett, Mack, Kenny Payne and two interim head coaches. Tatum is attacking the new job head on and knows his history of working under great coaches has prepared him well for all of the new responsibilities.
'The diversity of coaches that I've been around really helped me to see the game from a lot of different angles and I really feel like that's helped prepare me to be where I am today,' said Tatum. 'I'm super grateful for those guys because they were all good to me, and they treated me well, and they're a part of who I am today. The experiences that I have with them helped shape me and form me to who I am today.'

title: Man Charged With Attempted Murder After Shots Fired In ‘Road Rage Incident'
description: File image. A Harrodsburg man is being charged with attempted murder after a road rage incident with multiple shots fired, according to police. On Sunday, May 12, at 8:11 p.m., police responded to a…
content:
File image.
File image. A Harrodsburg man is being charged with attempted murder after a road rage incident with multiple shots fired, according to police.
On Sunday, May 12, at 8:11 p.m., police responded to a shots fired call at Anderson-Dean Community Park following 'a road rage incident,' according to the uniform citation.
Upon arrival, police discovered Darren Douglas Goode, 33, of Harrodsburg, standing next to his vehicle and another man behind his vehicle. According to the uniform citation, Goode told police he was being tailgated by the other man and that he returned fire after the other man shot at him.
Police found shell casings in Goode's vehicle and 'a hole in the passenger side mirror that appeared to have come from inside of Mr. Goode's vehicle.' No bullet holes were found in Goode's vehicle, according to the uniform citation.
The other man told police he was driving behind Goode and went over to pass him. 'Goode then rolled down his window and started shouting racial slurs' at the victim, according to the uniform citation. Following the other man to the park, Goode 'then fired shots at him striking the vehicle at least seven times,' according to the uniform citation.
Police searched the other man's vehicle and did not find 'a firearm or any shell casings,' according to the uniform citation.
A witness observed Goode fire the shots and hold the victim at gunpoint, according to the uniform citation.
A witness observed Goode fire the shots and hold the victim at gunpoint, according to the uniform citation. Police found Goode's firearm in his vehicle, according to the uniform citation. While placing Goode under arrest, police noticed alcohol on his breath and located 'a shooter of an alcoholic beverage' in the vehicle, according to the uniform citation.
Goode subsequently blew a 0.12, according to the uniform citation.
Goode was arraigned Monday, May 13, at district court, where he pleaded not guilty to charges of attempted murder and driving under the influence. He is due to return to court for a pretrial hearing on Thursday, May 23, at 1:30 p.m., according to court documents. Goode was released from the Boyle County Detention Center on a $100,000 bond on Dec. 14.
Patrolman Hunter Kelly of the Harrodsburg Police Department is the arresting officer.
All charges are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Stephens struck out two more batters in the top of the second inning.

title: Sara Dunn Finishes Mercer Tennis Career At KHSAA Singles Tournament
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Sara Dunn forehanded a return during her KHSAA state tournament round of 32 match with Ella Cason on Tuesday, May 28, at Berea College. Last week, Mercer County tennis star Sara Dunn achieved the highest recognition of her over 10-year career when she was awarded the regional trophy in Danville. Dunn has qualified for the state tournament each of the last three seasons but finished as runner-up in the regional tournament in both her sophomore and junior seasons. In each of her previous state tournament appearances, Dunn opened the tournament with a victory and fell in the second round. On Tuesday, May 28, Dunn defeated Briana Adams of Knott Central High School 6-2, 6-1 and advanced to the round of 32 in the KHSAA singles tournament at Berea College. Adams' last match ended in a loss in the semifinal of the 14th Region tournament, which is why she had to face a higher seed like Dunn in the first round. Dunn was in high spirits ahead of her round of 32 match with Ella Cason of Owensboro Catholic High School. A week ago, Cason swept the 3rd Region tournament, winning four straight matches, eighth straight sets, 6-0. She came into this match with the same attitude and immediately pressured Dunn. The first two games were close and narrowly lost by Dunn, but little by little, Cason's consistency began to wear Dunn down; it just wasn't meant to be. title: Harrodsburg Kicks Off 250th Birthday With Parade On Saturday, June 8
description: Members of the 2123rd Transportation Company of the Kentucky National Guard march in a 2018 parade. (File image). It's a birthday party 250 years in the making, and everything kicks off this weekend,…
content:
Members of the 2123rd Transportation Company of the Kentucky National Guard march in a 2018 parade. (File image).
Members of the 2123rd Transportation Company of the Kentucky National Guard march in a 2018 parade. (File image). It's a birthday party 250 years in the making, and everything kicks off this weekend, with the 250th Celebration Parade, which is scheduled to start at 11:30 a.m. on Saturday, June 8. The parade route starts at Old Fort Harrod State Park and proceeds down Lexington Street, turning left onto Main Street to Mooreland Avenue and up College Street back to the fort.
For Daarik Gray, chairman of the 250th Board of Directors, it's about time.
'We are excited about this momentous occasion for our community,' Gray said last week. 'As Kentucky's oldest city, we look forward to showcasing all of the things we've accomplished in the last 250 years, as well as looking forward to the many great things we have coming in the future.'
Gray already has a full-time job as the executive director of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Tourist Commission. He said the original board was formed in early 2019 by Mayor Art Freeman.
'There have been a lot of people over the last five years that have played a part in helping bring this event together, and I hope he'd be proud of what we've accomplished,' Gray said. 'There has been a lot of work behind the scenes to help get everything together. Representatives from numerous organizations have come together to make this event one to remember.'
He said Vice-Chair Jill Cutler and the Mercer County Chamber of Commerce have been working on the parade for well over a year.
'They formed a committee that has worked tirelessly on this, and we look forward to bringing a parade back downtown to help kick off the 250th festivities,' Gray said.
But the parade is only the beginning of the festivities. One big component of the 250th celebration will be the Settlement and Raid at Old Fort Harrod State Park, which begins Thursday, June 13, and runs through Sunday, June 16. In addition to the encampment featuring settlers, natives and traders at Fort Harrod, there will be demonstrations and activities each day, as well as the traditional raid on the fort scheduled for 3 p.m. on Saturday, June 15, and Sunday, June 16. Gray had nothing but praise for the park staff.
'David Coleman and his team at Old Fort Harrod State Park do an amazing job for the Fort Harrod Settlement and Raid each year, and this year they've got even more special things planned for the celebration,' Gray said.
He also praised the Harrodsburg Historical Society, led by President Nancy Hill, which has also planned activities, including Tea with Historical Characters on Thursday, June 13; Friday, June 14; and Saturday, June 15.
'The Harrodsburg Historical Society has a jam-packed lineup of events for people to enjoy,' Gray said. 'They are located right in the center of the festival, so we expect them to see a lot of visitors throughout the festival.'
For a full schedule, visit their website at harrodsburghistorical.org/harrodsburg-250th-calendar-of-events.
Dillon Carmichael will be co-headline the live music for Harrodsburg's 250th anniversary celebration on Thursday, June 13, starting at 8:30 p.m. (File image).
Dillon Carmichael will be co-headline the live music for Harrodsburg's 250th anniversary celebration on Thursday, June 13, starting at 8:30 p.m. (File image). Another big part of Hogtown's birthday party will be music. The Advocate Brass Band will perform Saturday, June 8, at Old Fort Harrod starting at 7 p.m. That's followed by three big days of music in downtown Harrodsburg on Thursday, June 13; Friday, June 14; and Saturday, June 15; starting with Hunter Flynn at 6 p.m. on Thursday. Dillon Carmichael will headline Thursday, starting at 8:30 p.m. For the full musical lineup, visit harrodsburg250th.com.
'When we were planning our musicians for the festival, we wanted to get those with ties to the state of Kentucky,' Gray said. 'Our first look, of course, was Mercer County's own Dillon Carmichael. Along with Dillon, several of the other musicians have ties directly to Harrodsburg or to the state of Kentucky.'
For kids activities, organizers have partnered with Party on Air Inflatables, who will set up on Chiles Street.
Everything leads up to the Founders Day Celebration on Sunday, June 16.
'The dates couldn't have lined up better for us than for June 16 to fall on a Sunday, as we can cap off our entire celebration on the actual day Harrodsburg was founded,' Gray said. 'The Harrodsburg Historical Society and Old Fort Harrod have teamed up to help round out the entire event. We will begin the day with a showing of a documentary that Michael Breeding has been working on for the past several years. As the event comes to a close, we are excited to have our Lt. Governor Jacqueline Coleman, State Sen. Amanda Mays Bledsoe, State Rep. Kim King, Harrodsburg Mayor Bob Williams and Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele speak.'
The whole community—contractors, city and county workers, board members and volunteers—has been working to prepare Harrodsburg for the big day, and Gray invites everyone to come take a look at what all their hard work has accomplished.
'We look forward to sharing in this experience with both our local community members as well as the thousands of visitors that we expect to visit our community,' Gray said. 'Planning for this event has been years in the making and has been a collaborative effort of so many people to help showcase the town we all love.'
For a full schedule of events, visit harrodsburg250th.com/events.

title: Mayes honored for service as coach and missionary

content:
Chad Mayes is pictured with the Paul and Carolyn Berry Award at the National Christian College Athletics Association (NCCAA) Hall of Fame banquet on June 5.
Harrodsburg native Chad Mayes was presented with the Paul and Carolyn Berry Award at the National Christian College Athletics Association (NCCAA) Hall of Fame banquet on June 5, 2024. According to the NCCAA, the inaugural award is intended to honor a coach who shows integrity through sports with a Christ-like approach to impact society, and uses sports to further the gospel of Christ and the development of life-long relationships.
Mayes has been coaching for most of his life and has spent significant time working with the Harrodsburg, Mercer County, and Boyle County girls' basketball teams, but that's not the passion he enjoys most. Mayes' calling is spreading the word of the gospel to as many souls as he can, and he and his wife, Chandi Mayes, have been traveling to Puerto Rico for missionary trips for more than 16 years. Mayes' extended time away in the summer doesn't affect his leading of the Asbury University women's basketball program, in fact it helps the Lady Eagles, as well as hundreds of other athletes across the country, through charitable deeds and sharing a love for athletics with those less fortunate. title: Harrodsburg Approves 2025 Budget
content:
File image.
The Harrodsburg City Commission has approved their new budget for the 2025 fiscal year. At their regular meeting on Monday, June 24, the commissioners okayed the new budget, which includes $11,001,884.94 for the general fund and $10,265,641.96 for the water and sewer revenue fund. According to Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard, the new budget includes the initial payment for the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park—all together, $2 million, with $1 million for the first bond payment as well as $1 million for the matching grant—as well as a 4-percent pay increase for city employees.
While Maynard worked with department heads on reducing expenses, the city took $1,392.888.55 from cash on hand at the bank to balance the general fund portion of the budget and another $659,273.26 to balance the water and sewer portion of the budget.
In last week's print edition, it was incorrectly reported that the city commission gave first reading to the budget at a special-called meeting on Monday, June 17. The commission only reviewed the budget at that time. They gave it first reading at another special-called meeting on Thursday, June 20. The budget goes into effect on Monday, July 1, the first day of the new fiscal year. Get the rest of the story. title: ‘James Harrod: The Battle For Kentucky' returns Friday, July 5
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Eric and Sarah Forman, with their daughter, Nora Forman, return as James Harrod and Ann McDonald in 'James Harrod: The Battle For Kentucky.' The outdoor drama returns for its ninth season on Friday, July 5.
Outdoor drama returns to Old Fort Harrod State Park when the ninth season of 'James Harrod: The Battle for Kentucky' begins its month-long run on Friday, July 5.
A co-production by the fort and Old and the Friends of Fort Harrod, the play brings to life the founders of the oldest town in Kentucky, including James Harrod and Ann Coburn McDaniel Harrod. Returning as Harrodsburg's first super couple are Eric and Sarah Forman.
It has been a busy year for the Formans. They served as grand marshals for the 250th Celebration Parade. Sarah also appeared as Ann Harrod in 'the Trial of James Bridges,' a fictional exploration of Harrod's disappearance in 1792, while Eric portrayed Harrod's son-in-law.
Then there is 'James Harrod: The Battle For Kentucky.' In addition to acting in the play, Sarah also serves as director. This year, she is overseeing a cast of 36 performers and two staffers. It helps that many of them have been with the play for years.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Members of the cast of 'James Harrod: The Battle For Kentucky' are getting ready for another season of outdoor drama.
The Formans have been involved with the play since it began. Their daughter Nora has been in the play since she was one week old in 2016. There are also Susan and Will McGinnis, who play Jane Coomes and William Pogue; Michael Schroeder, who serves as the play's gun master and performs as James Cowan, his wife Tamme Schroeder, who appears as Dark Star, and their daughter Isabella Schroeder, who appears as one of the Natives. The play's author, Lisa Botner Goodrich, appears as one of the settlers, while her daughter, Michelle Smith, serves as the light and sound technician. Michelle's husband Josh Smith appears as James Hamilton and their children Alexis Smith appears as Nellie Pogue, and Brendan Puckett appears as Jamie McDonald. Both Loretta Jones, who appears as Ann Pogue, and her son Javan Jones, who appears as Native leader Standing Bear, are big hits with the audience. Loretta Jones' granddaughter also appears in the play. Jonathan Brantley appears as Long Winter and also serves as assistant director and fight choreographer, while his father, David Brantley, will appear as the villainous Judge Henderson. Carol Kulling and her daughter, Jill Cutler, are handling the costumes, and Jill will appear as one of the settlers. Jill's son, Than Cutler—who has previously starred as James Harrod—will play George Rogers Clark and Gen. Lewis.
Those are only some of the multiple generations of family who are working on the play.
'We have some new teenagers that have been doing a very good job this year,' Sarah Forman said, listing Matthew Morris, who will play Abraham Chaplin, and Zaiden Barrow, who will play Shadow Wolf.
This is a momentous year for the drama about the founding of Harrodsburg. Not only is it Hogtown's 250th anniversary, but it is also the 100th anniversary of the Kentucky State Parks system. Back in 1924, the Kentucky General Assembly established a parks commission under the leadership of State Geological Surveyor Dr. Willard Rouse Jillson. Their mission was to identify park sites of exceptional natural or historical importance. In 1926, Fort Harrod, Pine Mountain, Natural Bridge and the now-closed Blue and Gray were recognized in the legislative record as the first four Kentucky State Parks.
On Monday, July 1, Gov. Andy Beshear joined state tourism and parks leaders at the Old State Capitol to commemorate the 100th anniversary of a historic speech Dr. Jillson delivered on July 1, 1924, to the General Assembly, underscoring the importance of acquiring and preserving natural parks under state custodianship for the enjoyment of future generations.
'Our state parks have provided unforgettable experiences for families for 100 years, from hiking the scenic hills of Appalachia to boating on the sparkling waters in Western Kentucky,' said Gov. Beshear. 'Kentucky tourism is a $13.8 billion industry, and our state parks play a significant role in offering unique opportunities to travelers. As we celebrate the centennial anniversary, I encourage everyone to support our state parks by exploring the wonderful experiences they provide.'
Today, Kentucky is home to 44 state parks, including 17 resort parks and 13 golf courses. Kentucky State Parks is planning a series of events and programs throughout 2024 to celebrate its 100th anniversary. For more information, visit parks.ky.gov.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Loretta Jones, who portrays Ann Pogue, shows off the cast T-shirt for the 2024 season of 'James Harrod' The Battle For Kentucky.'

Harrodsburg is one of seven towns in Kentucky that has been celebrated online for its thriving local businesses.
WorldAtlas.com recently named Harrodsburg and six other towns for their small businesses 'bursting with individuality.' The website invited readers to 'explore beyond huge franchises and discover a world of independent shops that capture the vibrant characteristics of the state.'
Noting Harrodsburg's status as the oldest town in Kentucky, WorldAtlas said old Hogtown 'continues to foster a thriving community speckled with one-of-a-kind outlets and indie cafes.'
Among the local businesses the website called out were Blush Boutique (106 S Main Street), which it called 'your one-stop shop for cute tops, trendy accessories and Kentucky souvenirs,' and J. Sampson Antiques & Books (107 South Main Street) for curious articles, rare books and appraisals.
WorldAtlas invited its readers to 'fill up with good food at Granny's Diner' (513 West Broadway Street) and order a Phoebe—a double espresso with a nice blend of caramel and white chocolate—at Harrod's Perk and Chill (540 North College Street).
Other Kentucky towns with thriving businesses listed by the website include Versailles, Murray, Frankfort, London, Elizabethtown and Hazard.
In the daily rush, it can be easy to overlook everything that Harrodsburg has to offer. Take a refresher course every Tuesday this summer at the Midweek Farmers Market at Olde Town Park (126 South Main Street). Vendors offer locally raised produce, meat, eggs, baked goods, canned goods, honey and homemade and handcrafted items from 4 to 7 p.m. In the event of inclement weather, the market will move to the Mercer County Fairgrounds (560 Linden Avenue). For more information, call 859-734-4378 or visit their Facebook page @Mercer County Farmers Market.

title: Kentucky's Favorite Son, Reed Sheppard, Drafted By Houston
description: UK Athletics Photo/Ethan Rand<
content:
UK Athletics Photo/Ethan Rand
Kentucky native and former Wildcat Reed Sheppard was drafted third overall by the Houston Rockets during the NBA draft on Wednesday, June 26.
The last day of the John Calipari era has officially come and gone for the University of Kentucky. Draft night, lovingly tabbed as 'graduation day' by UK's former commander and chief John Calipari, was a major success for several beloved Wildcats. But, perhaps the biggest moment for all of Big Blue Nation was when their home state hero, Reed Sheppard, the son of former Kentucky superstars Jeff Sheppard and Stacy Reed, was drafted third overall by the Houston Rockets.
When he committed to his childhood dream team in November of 2021, most experts predicted Sheppard to be a 3-4 year college project, and a role playing contributor to his freshman team. Very few actually considered the 13th region prodigy a legitimate SEC star in the making. Even fewer thought of him as a one-and-done, and absolutely nobody believed Reed Sheppard could be a top three pick in the NBA draft.
However, once Sheppard arrived on campus and began showing his true abilities against the other top ranked recruits in the 2023 recruiting class, it became obvious Reed was much more than the role player he was considered by most to be. This became even more apparent after his dominating performances in the GLOBL Jam event that the Wildcats participated in over the summer. Displaying crazy athleticism, great passing abilities, tremendous court vision, freaky instincts and a generational ability to knock down shots, Reed shocked everyone who watched him play, except his always confident mother, Stacy.
Throughout the college season, despite his team having an up and down roller coaster type year, Reed continued to impress even his firmest of believers and toughest critics. While coming off the bench for the Cats, Reed consistently recorded the team's top plus/minus (a stat reflecting score line changes when specific players are on the court) showing he almost always made the entire team better. Furthermore, as he began getting more playing time towards the back end of the season, Sheppard recorded team highs in several statistical areas, and even led the entire country in 3-point shooting percentage at a ridiculous 52 percent. title: Harrodsburg Named One Of The ‘Coziest Towns' In Kentucky

content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
Kellie and Cash Cocanougher get cozy at the Mercer County Fair and Horse Show last year. This year's carnival kicks off on Monday, July 22.
Harrodsburg has been named one of the six coziest towns to visit in Kentucky in 2024. That's according to WorldAtlas.com, which recently celebrated the coziness of Hogtown and five other towns in Kentucky, which the website called 'one of the most welcoming places to visit in the US.'
Small Kentucky towns like Harrodsburg 'offer unique opportunities to truly experience a slice of authentic Kentucky,' the website contended, offering visitors 'a blend of scenic beauty, cultural significance, and community spirit.'
Other towns named on the list include Bardstown, Berea, Danville, Paducah and Midway.
According to WorldAtlas.com, 'cozy little Harrodsburg offers a unique glimpse into the state's pioneer past.' The website noted that top attractions in Harrodsburg include Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill and Old Fort Harrod State Park, as well as geographic landmarks including the Kentucky River Palisades and Herrington Lake.
Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill's Craft Fair kicks off Aug. (Image: shakervillageky.org).
The website directed to upcoming events like Shakertown's Craft Fair, which kicks off Saturday, Aug. 3, and runs through Sunday, Aug. 4. For a cozier look at Shakertown, check out the Music on the Lawn series, which runs every Friday and Saturday into the fall. On Friday, July 12, Scott Collins is scheduled to start playing at 6:30 p.m. On Saturday, July 13, Dean Phelps will perform by the fire pit. title: Anderson-Dean Community Park Is Finally Headed In The Right Direction
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Robert MooreAfter a year of waiting, those in search of a
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Robert Moore
After a year of waiting, those in search of a sunny day by the pool can return to Anderson Dean Park Aquatic Center in the coming days.
Stephen Ransdell has been working hard to improve Anderson-Dean Community Park since taking over as park director in March of this year. Despite the park being behind in so many areas, according to Ransdell, most of his time as of late has been spent working to open the community pool. After months of waiting and adjusting to inopportune circumstances, the wait is nearly over for the many Mercer Countians desperate to enjoy a sunny day poolside.
As of Tuesday, July 9, the park is expecting a valve replacement for a key attraction at the pool. Replacing the valve, coating and buffing the slide and one more scrub of the new liner is all that stands in the way of state approval. The most likely scenario according to Ransdell involves state approval on Wednesday or Thursday, and the eventual opening of the pool to the public on Friday, July 12, if everything goes to plan that is, and that's not something Ransdell has come to expect during the pool's reconstruction.
If not Friday, then by next Monday, July 15, Anderson Dean pool should be open to the public. Those wanting to make sure they make the opening day should await updates from the park via Facebook at Anderson-Dean Community Park or their website, andersondeancommunitypark.com. title: Two Indicted For Making False Reports
description: Image: Robert Moore,
content:
Image: Robert Moore, the Harrodsburg Herald.
Two Mercer County residents have been indicted on multiple counts of filing false reports over the past year.
Dakota L. Milton, 21, and Anastasia M. Wellbaum, 23, both of 851 South College Street No. A12, Harrodsburg, were indicted by the Mercer County Grand Jury last week on multiple class D felony counts of filing false reports which generated an emergency response in 2024.
According to the indictment, Milton is alleged to have knowingly reported a false carbon monoxide alarm on Jan. 8, a false stove fire on April 5, a false smoke alarm on May 11—all of these calls were made to the Harrodsburg Fire Department—and a false bicycle hit and run accident to the Mercer County Fire Department on June 16. On May 9, in Mercer County, Wellbaum is alleged to have knowingly making a false report of a gas leak to the Harrodsburg Fire Department, according to the indictment. On June 18, Wellbaum also reported a false bicycle hit to the Mercer County Fire Department, according to the indictment. Bail for both Milton and Wellbaum was set at $5,000. Patrolwoman Erin Rice (HPD) testified.

title: Harrodsburg Historical Society Wants You To Be Another Brick In The Wall
description: A sample of the bricks being sold by the Harrodsburg Historical Society to raise funds for renovations at Morgan Row (Image Submitted). The Harrodsburg Historical Society wants you to be another bri
content:
A sample of the bricks being sold by the Harrodsburg Historical Society to raise funds for renovations at Morgan Row (Image Submitted).
The Harrodsburg Historical Society wants you to be another brick in the wall. They are holding a brick campaign to support—financially—Morgan Row, the historic headquarters of the Harrodsburg Historical Society.
By purchasing a commemorative brick, you can help support building repairs and maintenance projects at Morgan Row, which was built in the 1810s by Joseph Morgan and his son-in-law John Chiles. Morgan Row is credited as being the oldest row house in Kentucky.
The Harrodsburg Herald recently took a tour of the building. Nancy Hill, president of the Harrodsburg Historical Society, said they had finished work to stabilize the foundation for the kitchen using a grant from the Kentucky Colonels.
'It was a huge chunk of change,' Hill said. They are putting the finishing touches on renovating rooms upstairs, which was paid for through a bequest from the late Howard Gregory, who had served as president of the Harrodsburg Historical Society and as chairman of the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Landmarks Association before his passing. But there is still much work to be done to Morgan Row, including stabilizing the foundation of the office additions, work on the gutters and roof, painting the outside doors and windowsills, reglazing of the windows and the continuing problem with bats, or, as Hill calls them, 'critters.'
'We have a lot of issues, as you'd expect of any historical building,' she said.
The Harrodsburg Herald/ Robert Moore
Nancy Hill, president of the Harrodsburg Historical Society, stands in one of the newly remodeled rooms on the second floor of Morgan Row. They are selling memorial bricks to pay for more work at the historical building.
Bricks cost $75 each, with three lines of engraving and 20 characters maximum per line. No advertising is allowed. Hill said they haven't decided '100 percent' what they will do with the bricks. She said suggestions have included constructing a walkway, building planters or a memorial wall.
'We don't have enough bricks to even think about that yet,' Hill said. 'We need more.'
The Kentucky Historical Society recently recognized the Harrodsburg Historical Society's continuing efforts to 'preserve and share Kentucky stories.' One of those stories is Morgan Row, which was once a fashionable place for the well-to-do, according to the Harrodsburg Historical Society's website. In 1960, the historical society took part in a community effort to save the building, which was slated for demolition to make way for a parking lot, with Corning donating $10,000 towards purchasing the historic property. It took a lot of hard work by local volunteers to clean and restore the building. The Harrodsburg Historical Society is again asking for the public's help in restoring Morgan Row.
To order a brick online, visit fundraisingbrick.com/harrodsburg. To pay by check, send your order and a check to the Harrodsburg Historical Society, P.O. Box 316, Harrodsburg, KY 40330.
