title: County, City Create Joint Committee
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Fiscal Court is creating a joint committee with the Harrodsburg City Commission to discuss issues that impact both the county and the city.
At the fiscal court's regular meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 27, Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said they had invited the city commission to hold a joint working session, but the city preferred to form a committee made up of two city commissioners and two county magistrates. Magistrates Tim Darland and Stephen 'Pete' Elliott volunteered to serve on the committee, which is tentatively scheduled to meet next Wednesday, Sept. 4, at noon.
'I think the whole bunch ought to get together one time,' said Elliott.
'We can bring that up next week,' Darland said.
Other magistrates also felt that a joint meeting of both bodies would be better.
'I feel like the whole court needs to be involved in this,' said Magistrate Susan Barrington.
'You run into quorum issues,' said Harrodsburg Mayor Bob Williams, who was in attendance Tuesday.
'I think we need to get the ball rolling,' Judge Steele said. 'We have got to work together on a lot of items.'
Harrodsburg Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard and City Attorney Norrie Currens will also attend committee meetings. Want to read the rest of the story? Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Meet Harrodsburg's Pioneers At History Underfoot Tour On Sept. 14
description: Photo: Keith RightmyerJerry Sampson, president of the James Harrod Trust, takes part in the 2023 History Underfoot Tour at Spring Hill Cemetery. Sampson will
content:
Photo: Keith Rightmyer
Jerry Sampson, president of the James Harrod Trust, takes part in the 2023 History Underfoot Tour at Spring Hill Cemetery. Sampson will play pioneer and Revolutionary War hero Mark McGohon at this year's tour.
The 19th Annual James Harrod Trust History Underfoot Cemetery Tour happens Saturday, Sept. 14, at Spring Hill Cemetery (529 North Greenville Street). Tours happen every half hour, starting at 6 p.m. and running through 8 p.m. During the tour, guides will escort visitors to graves where cos­tumed interpreters explore the personal stories of the people who built Harrodsburg.
Jerry Sampson, president of the James Harrod Trust, which hosts the tours, said there will be four interpreters this year. None of the subjects are actually buried at Spring Hill, but Sampson said they were chosen because they were all pioneers.
'We did that in celebration of Harrodsburg's 250th birthday,' Sampson said.
Sampson will portray Mark McGohon (1755-1848), who immigrated from Ulster, Ireland. McGohon's mother and infant sibling died crossing the Atlantic, and McGohon and his little sister found themselves stranded in America, unable to contact their father, who'd immigrated earlier. McGohon would not reunite with his father until the Revolutionary War. After the war's conclusion, McGohon and his wife, Elizabeth Dunn, relocated to Fort Harrod. McGohon took part in a journey to recover their horses, which had been taken by the Shawnee. They found the horses tethered on the other side of the Ohio River, which was Shawnee territory. The resourceful McGohon climbed a Sycamore tree and called out to his wife's little white mare, Nell, who broke her tether and led the other horses across the river.
The family made their home on a farm off Shakertown Road, and McGohon died at his daughter's home near Mackville. In 1930, his family and the Jane McAfee Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution exhumed McGohon's body and reinterred him in Memorial Acre at Old Fort Harrod.
Other subjects at the History Underfoot Cemetery Tour include:
• Jane Coomes is portrayed by Lisa Botner Goodrich. Coomes and her husband, William Coomes, were the first Catholic immigrants to Kentucky, arriving at Fort Harrod in June 1775. Coomes became the first schoolteacher in Kentucky and is credited with manufacturing the first salt at Drennon Springs. In addition, she delivered babies and rendered medical care, using hot grease to cauterize wounds and seal them against infection. Her husband William was with the Ray brothers when they were attacked at Shawnee Spring. William Coomes saved himself by crouching silently behind a fallen tree. After living nine years at Fort Harrod, the family moved to Nelson County.
• Gen. George Rogers Clark (1752-1818) is portrayed by Than Cutler. Clark, the elder brother of William Clark of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, was born in Albemarle County, Virginia. By 1775 Clark was surveying Central Kentucky and is credited with laying out Leesburg, near present-day Frankfort. In 1776 Clark traveled to Williamsburg, then the state capitol of Virginia, to petition for the creation of Kentucky County. Clark also secured 500 pounds of gunpowder for the defense of the settlements. He went on to become the highest-ranking American military officer in the Northwest Territory, where, among other deeds, he ordered a flotilla to shoot the Falls of the Ohio during a solar eclipse. In January 1779, British Governor Henry Hamilton surrendered at Vincennes, Indiana.
• Ann Kennedy Wilson Pogue Lindsay McGinty (1735-1815) is portrayed by Amalie Preston. Ann Kennedy was a first generation American whose parents immigrated from Ireland. She outlived four husbands—John Wilson, William Pogue, Joseph Lindsey and James McGinty. A hard-nosed businesswoman, she received her own landgrant of 800 acres and ran the first licensed tavern at Fort Harrod and is credited with bringing the first spinning wheel into Kentucky. She even outlived the original Fort Harrod. Even after the fort had been dismantled, she continued to live in the blockhouse until her demise.
Sampson called the cemetery tour 'a wonderful dose of history.'
'It's nothing scary,' he said. 'It's all about our history and our culture.'
Sampson said the tour tends to attract many of the same people year after year. 'We want to get new people, too,' Sampson said.
The James Harrod Trust History has a mission to 'protect, encourage and continue the preservation of cultural and historical places in Mercer County,' according to their website. In addition to the cemetery tour, the trust also offers self-guided walking and driving tours of Harrodsburg and Mercer County.
The Mercer County Land Patents book is still available for sale at $95.00. Call Sampson at 859-734-7829 to buy a copy. The trust also offers one-year memberships at $25 for individuals and $50 for families.
The 19th Annual James Harrod Trust History Underfoot Cemetery Tour happens Saturday, Sept. 14. Tours happen every half hour, starting at 6 p.m. and running through 8 p.m. For more information, call Sampson at 859-734-7829 or visit online at jamesharrodtrust.org. The Mercer County Lady Titans (6-2) had an exciting and historic week of soccer beginning with the opening round of the Class 2A state sectional tournament. One week prior Mercer County dropped their first game of the season to the Lady Colonels of Bourbon County, 2-1.
'It felt like we should have had a much better game, we should have won, we just missed a lot of shots,' said Head Coach Josh Culver.
Culver and the team watched the film from their loss to Bourbon very closely, and made sure they were prepared for the two team's next matchup, on Monday, Aug. 26. The Lady Titans tallied their third clean sheet of the season when they took down the Lady Colonels 5-0, behind three goals and an assist from Laykin Irvin.
Two days later on Wednesday, Aug. 28, the Titans traveled to Bourbon County again, this time to face the Harrison County Fillies, who the Titans had already defeated convincingly during the preseason.
'Luckily, when I made the schedule at the beginning of the season, I didn't know they were in 2A,' said Culver. 'It kind of gave us an idea of where they were gonna be. We knew where we were and where they were.'
The Fillies took the lead in the first half after a well placed through ball caught the defense out of position, but the Lady Titans made adjustments at halftime and another Irvin hat trick carried Mercer County to its first Class 2A sectional tournament win in school history. No boys or girls team had ever won their sectional. The back-to-back victories set apart
the 2024 Lady Titans soccer team from any other squad to walk the halls of Mercer County Senior High School.
'It's a pretty surreal feeling. I told them that's something that can never be taken away, that trophy will sit in the trophy case in the high school. That's their legacy they're leaving behind and that's something that they get to do for the first time ever,' said Culver.
The Lady Titans wouldn't have been able to reach this pinnacle without the work of forward Laykin Irvin, who is well ahead of schedule to become the season-leading goalscorer in Mercer County soccer history. The senior has scored an absurd 17 goals through eight games, and is only 13 away from breaking Chelsea Moore's record of 30 goals in the fall of 2015.
'I had no clue I'd come out almost averaging a hat trick a game. I've impressed myself a lot, especially playing with knee problems. To be able to contribute to my team with two hat tricks during the two games at 2A state is definitely something that I won't forget. For us to have accomplished that for the first time ever, is one thing, but for me to have six goals within those two games, was just icing on the cake,' said Irvin.
On Saturday, Sept. 14, the Lady Titans will face Johnson Central at Rowan County High School at 10 a.m. in the first round of the 2A state championship.
The Lady Eagles have amassed an impressive record so far in 2024. Of their eight games this fall, six have been called short due to the mercy rule. Outside of their draws against Fleming County and Ashland Blazer, Johnson Central have defeated their other six opponents by a combined score of 58-0, including an impressive 18-0 win over Shelby Valley to begin the season. If the Lady Titans are to continue building the legend of their historic 2A tournament run they will need to knock off likely the best team in the 15th Region.
'If our girls play 100%, I truly believe they can get it done but it has to be from start to finish. It has to be a clean game,' said Culver.

Daynabrook Greenhouse and Pumpkin Patch and Devine's Corn Maze and Pumpkin Patch are both open for the fall season (Composite image).
Fall is almost here and that means it's pumpkin patch time. Fall Fest at Daynabrook Greenhouse and Pumpkin Patch (135 Dunn Lane) began Sunday, Sept. 1, and runs through November. In addition to the pumpkin patch, there's the corn maze, pedal cars, playground, inflatable, small zip line, wagon ride, petting zoo, covered pavilion and super slide. The cost is $15 per person ages 3 and up, which includes a pumpkin to take home. Concessions, tower zipline, greenhouse plants, and additional pumpkins are available at additional cost. Ride bracelets are $5 for unlimited rides on the tea cups, swing ride—48 inch height requirement, train (size restricted), dizzy disco, carousel and roller coaster.
Daynabrook Farm is open for the fall season (image from website).
Daynabrook is open Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Fridays and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sundays from noon to 6 p.m. For more information, visit daynabrookfarm.com or call 859-734-7863.
Devine's Corn Maze and Pumpkin Patch (623 Talmage-Mayo Road) open Friday, Sept. 13. They say they're pulling out all the stops for their seventeenth season. Devines Corn Maze is open for the fall season (image from Facebook page).

title: Fiscal Court Considers Increasing 911 Tap Fee From $1.75 To $3.50 A Month
content:
File image.
The Mercer County Fiscal Court gave first reading to an ordinance increasing the tap fee on residential and commercial water meters from $1.75 per month to $3.50 a month. The tap fee pays for 911 services. The fiscal court was forced to make the move after running a $107,000 deficit for the past year. If given second reading, the increase goes into effect Nov. 1.
At their regular meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 24, the fiscal court also approved shifting money from other line items to pay the shortfall once they receive from Bluegrass 911 Communications, which has handled 911 operations for the county since 2021.
In the past, 911 operations were paid for by a fee collected on landline phones. But the number of land lines has been declining for decades. While there is a fee collected on some—but not all—cell phones, the revenue collected does not cover the expense of operations. Back in 2019, both Harrodsburg and Burgin voted to institute a $40 parcel to pay for 911 operations, which subsequently failed to pass for lack of a motion at a special-called hearing of the fiscal court. That left the county to use carryover funds to pay for the federally mandated service.
Last year, the fiscal court enacted the tap fee to for handle 911 operations. The collecting entities withhold three percent to cover their expenses.
At Tuesday's meeting, Magistrate Tim Darland said the state needed to increase the 911 fee on cell phones.
'They got so many lobbyists in Frankfort that it ain't going to happen,' Darland said.
Judge-Executive Sarah Steele said even with the fee hike, Mercer is still lower than surrounding counties. Steele had previously said Garrard and Lincoln are charging $4 tap fees.
'I'm just trying to pay our bills,' Steele said Tuesday. 'It's not my goal to have a big, fat bank account.'
She said the county will address the homeowners who are refusing to pay the tap fee.
'Everybody needs 911,' Steele said. Find out the rest of this story. Click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Titan Soccer Battles With Garrard County In First Home Game Since August
description: The Mercer County Titan boys soccer team (1-10) were desperately searching for their first win of the season until they met to face the Anderson County Bearcats last Tuesday, Sept. 17. The win was no…
content:
The Mercer County Titan boys soccer team (1-10) were desperately searching for their first win of the season until they met to face the Anderson County Bearcats last Tuesday, Sept. 17. The win was no doubt spurred by the most promising performance of the Titans season thus far, when a week prior they played a physical and tactically sound 80 minutes against the Boyle County Rebels, holding them within a goal until the closing moments and eventually falling 2-0.
While all 11 Titan players played an important part in the win, it was senior forward Jordan Piazza who walked off of the field with his first ever hat trick. Piazza secured the opening goal on the first shot of the game with a long distance, floating, and curling shot that the Bearcat keeper gave up on and couldn't correct after realizing just how much the shot curved.
'It was probably one of the best experiences to have. Doing that and helping my team secure the lead, that just felt great to me,' said Piazza.
More recently, Mercer County faced the Garrard County Golden Lions (8-4) on Tuesday, Sept. 24, in the Titans' first home game since the season opener against Danville on Aug. 13.
The Titans had plenty of chances early on, and a one-two between Mijaia Dunn and Cannon Buchanan resulted in the Titans first breakaway, and shot. Moments later, a clever set-piece play ended in Piazza smacking a volley off of the crossbar. 12 minutes into the game, the Titans got onto the scoreboard after a perfectly crossed corner from Tanner Ison fell on the head of Ian Alcorn and into the goal.
The Golden Lions pulled one back moments later when a long ball forward to Zak Dailey resulted in a cross to freshman Lucas Wilson, who rocketed the ball into the ceiling of the net.
Freshman Liam Moffett battled for a loose ball during Mercer's 5-5 draw with Garrard County.
The Titans will be back in action in Harrodsburg, pending inclement weather, on Saturday, Sept. 28, when they face Western Hills with a noon kickoff.

title: James Shouse
description: James Keith Shouse, age 63, passed away Friday, Oct. 4, 2024. Keith was born May 27, 1961, in Harrodsburg, to Pat (Agee) Shouse and James Robert Shouse. Keith was of the Christian faith and a former…
content:
James Keith Shouse, age 63, passed away Friday, Oct. 4, 2024.
Keith was born May 27, 1961, in Harrodsburg, to Pat (Agee) Shouse and James Robert Shouse.
Keith was of the Christian faith and a former employee with Edwards Sawmill, retiring after 25 years of employment. Keith never met a stranger and was very outgoing, loving to talk to every person he met. He enjoyed fishing, hunting and bingo. Keith loved children, especially his numerous nieces and nephews.
Including his parents, Pat and James Shouse of Salvisa, Keith is survived by his brother, Gary Michael of Salvisa; two sisters, Regina Ann Coulter and her husband Jeff of Salvisa and Debbie Warner and her husband Joe of Harrodsburg; and several nieces, nephews, great nieces, great nephews and great-great nieces and nephews, whom he loved dearly.
Keith was preceded in death by his paternal grandparents, Sam and Mary Shouse, and his maternal grandparents, Celta Huff and Gilbert Agee.
Funeral service will be 7 p.m., Thursday, Oct. 10, 2024 at the Ritchie & Peach Funeral Home with Bro. Dallas Daniel officiating.
Visitation will be Thursday from 4 p.m., till time of service at 7 p.m.

title: Eugene Milburn
description: Eugene Beckham Milburn, 91, husband of Joann Terhune Milburn, died Thursday, Sept. 26, 2024, at UK Bluegrass Hospice Care. Born Jan. 20, 1933, in Boyle County, he was the son of the late Wesley Oscar…
content:
Eugene Beckham Milburn, 91, husband of Joann Terhune Milburn, died Thursday, Sept. 26, 2024, at UK Bluegrass Hospice Care.
Born Jan. 20, 1933, in Boyle County, he was the son of the late Wesley Oscar and Josephine Lou Key Milburn.
He was a United States Air Force veteran of the Korean War, retired from Philips Lighting as a production line supervisor, was a former member of the Danville Bowling League and was a member of Harrodsburg Baptist Church.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: three sons, M. Bradley (Tressa) Milburn, David (Julia) Milburn and Donnie Hampton; one daughter, Sandy Milburn; five grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.
He was preceded in death by one daughter, Lisa Milburn Breeze, four brothers and four sisters.
Funeral services were held Wednesday, Oct. 2, at Alexander & Royalty Funeral Home and Cremation Services with Dr. Robert DeFoor officiating. Burial was in Spring Hill Cemetery.
Pallbearers were Bradley Milburn, Donnie Hampton, Jordan Breeze and Beckham Milburn. Honorary pallbearers were Sydney Breeze and Johnny Breeze.
Expressions of sympathy may be sent to the family at alexanderandroyalty.com.

Edward N. 'Ed' Dials, 83, husband of Olene Chumbley Dials, died Monday, Oct. 1, 2024, in Danville.
Born Oct. 4, 1940, in Elliott County, he was the son of the late Lowell and Iva Ison Dials.
He was a retired IBM advisory engineer of mechanical design and attended New Life Baptist Church.
Survivors, in addition to his wife, include: one daughter, Angela (Jimmy) Ryan of Louisville; one stepdaughter, Angela Utterback of Florida; one brother-in-law, Robert Kesterson; three grandchildren; two great-grandchildren; one niece and one nephew.

title: Local And State Candidates Discuss Issues At Election Forum
description: Rep. Kim King and challenger Katrina Sexton at the election forum held earlier this week. Composite image. Local and state candidates answered questions at the Mercer County Political Candidate
content:
Rep. Kim King and challenger Katrina Sexton at the election forum held earlier this week. Composite image.
Local and state candidates answered questions at the Mercer County Political Candidate Forum on Monday, Oct. 21, at 7 p.m. at Mercer County Senior High School.
The forum featured the six candidates vying for the four seats on the Harrodsburg City Commission—Missy Wilham Banks, Charlie Mattingly, Kerry Anness, Brian Steele, Marvin 'Bubby' Isham, and Jack L. Coleman—and the two candidates for State Representative for the 55th District—Kim King and Katrina Sexton. The candidates were given a chance to give opening statements and then answer six questions from Burgin High School Junior Barron Bradshaw and Mercer County Senior Sage Markham. Earl Motzer served as the moderator.
Councilwoman Missy Wilham Banks, an incumbent who is completing her first term on the city council, was given first crack at a question about city ordinances. Banks said Harrodsburg needed to establish an ordinance board to deal with abandoned and neglected properties. The city currently goes through the court system, she said.
'Our hands are tied,' Banks said.
Councilman Kerry Anness said there needed to be more citizen involvement. 'We can't be everywhere at once,' Anness said.
'We have them all over town,' said Councilman Marvin 'Bubby' Isham. 'It's more than getting one ordinance done.'
Isham said there was also a need to upgrade city sidewalks, which are not owned by the city but by the property owners. 'A lot of them don't have the money to fix that stuff,' he said.
Brian Steele, the only candidate who has not served on the city commission before, said he wants the commission to hold itself more accountable, including changing the meeting time from noon to the evening.
Jack Coleman, who has served on the city commission and as a state representative, noted the city, under former Mayor Art Freemen, had formed a board to discuss the issue.
'The ordinances need to be a bit broader,' Coleman said.
'It was a lot simpler back then than it is now,' said Commissioner Charlie Mattingly. Mattingly noted that the city was able to demolish six abandoned buildings in one year.
'We're not doing what we should be doing,' Mattingly said.
The candidates were asked about homelessness. While they all seemed to agree that there needed to be more housing available in the city, but, in the words of Commission Anness, it was a 'complex issue.'
'I don't have a good answer,' Anness said.
'Harrodsburg, to me, is not that bad for homelessness,' Commission Isham said. Discussing efforts the city has taken in the past to address the issue, including opening warming shelters, Isham said of the unhoused, 'They don't want your help.'
Brian Steele said more effort needs to be directed to the issue but said, 'It's not going to ultimately solve the problem.'
Jack Coleman said city leaders recognized Harrodsburg had a huge homeless problem from 2016 to 2017. 'Everybody got together,' Coleman said.
'It's not as bad as it was,' Commissioner Mattingly said. 'It's still too bad.'
'I don't believe this is an economic problem,' Councilwoman Banks said. 'It's not just because they're homeless. They're broke. They're drug addicts.'
All six candidates agreed when asked about local corruption. 'I'm not factually aware of any,' Steele said. But he said many citizens felt disenfranchised, judging by Facebook comments. 'They just don't trust the government.'
'Citizens need to have their voices heard,' Mattingly said, before adding, 'They can put anything on social media.'
Anness said elected officials' phone numbers are listed on the city's website.
'Call us. Call the commissioners,' Anness said. 'I take calls any time of the day.'
The candidates were asked about economic development in Harrodsburg, compared to other communities such as Danville and Lawrenceburg.
'This community is on the cusp over the next few years of development,' said Steele, referring to the Wilkinson Farm Industrial Park. At the same time, he cautioned the audience, 'IT's nothing that's going to happen overnight.'
Coleman said he'd spoken to representatives of large corporations about opening businesses here in Harrodsburg.
'We do not have the population and the demographics,' Coleman said.
'We're not situated demographically to bring business in,' Mattingly said.
'Harrodsburg is Harrodsburg,' Banks said. 'A lot of people like going out of town and coming back home.'
She blamed the planning and zoning commission.
Anness noted the city was in the process of installing and repairing infrastructure, including a $2.2 million sewer project. He said a lot of the lines are 'ancient.'
'Harrodsburg is laying the groundwork,' he said.
Isham also noted the city had recently annexed property for future expansion.
'Planning and zoning is doing a great job,' Isham said. He said the planning and zoning commission except to approve recent Dollar General stores, which are being built on properties already zoned for business.
'You've got to let them do it or you're going to get sued,' Isham said.
The candidates were asked about the city's budget.
'People want services, and you've got to have revenue to provide those services,' said Mattingly, who added, 'I hate raising taxes.'
'This is a tough question,' Banks said. 'We are living on a 1990 budget wanting things in 2024.'
'I don't have the answer,' Banks said.
Discussing the recent decision by the Mercer County Fiscal Court to increase the tap fee on residential and commercial water meters from $1.75 per month to $3.50 a month, Isham said, 'That's a bill that every person in Mercer County needs to pay if they want 911.'
Steele said there are opportunities for federal grants to pay for services. 'I would be very reluctant to consider any kind of tax increase,' Steele said.
Kentucky State Rep. Kim King.
The two candidates for State Representative for the 55th District—Kim King, the Republican incumbent, and Katrina Sexton, the Democratic challenger—answered questions next.
Asked about overdose deaths, Rep. King said every challenge the state legislature faces has a connection to drugs. 'It affects everything,' King said.
Sexton said the issue does not impact only the users. 'It's their families and loved ones,' she said. 'It's their children.'
Both candidates discussed the second constitutional amendment on this year's ballot, which would enable the General Assembly to provide financial support for the education costs of students in kindergarten through 12th grade who are outside the system of public schools.
'I do not support that,' Sexton said. While she said she supports school choice, she said, 'It's not the way to do it.'
'It doesn't lay out a plan for what's going to happen to the funding,' Sexton said.
Katrina Sexton, candidate for the state representative's office.
King said opponents were 'griping' the amendment was too vague. 'They would be griping because it's too specific,' King said.
'I voted to put it on the ballot,' King said. 'We need the input from every single voting family.'
'I will be voting for it,' King said.
There is only one drop box for mail ballots. It's located at the Mercer County Fiscal Courthouse (207 West Lexington Street). The hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Excused in-person absentee ballots can be left at the drop box starting Wednesday, Oct. 23 through Wednesday, Oct. 30.
In-person no-excuse absentee ballots can be cast on Thursday, Oct. 31; Friday, Nov. 1; and Saturday, Nov. 2.

title: Georgetown honors Warren on senior day
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Georgetown College Tigers football team (6-2) went down 7-0 after the initial drive from MidSouth Conference rivals University of the…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Georgetown College Tigers football team (6-2) went down 7-0 after the initial drive from MidSouth Conference rivals University of the Cumberlands (5-4) on Saturday, Nov. 2, at Toyota Stadium in Georgetown. The Tigers have recently got back on track after dropping two of their first three games of the season. Both of the Tigers' losses were away games. On Sept. 14, the Tigers battled with Division-I FCS Alabama A&M and took the lead first, even tying the game in the third quarter, before eventually losing 24-16. The Tigers only other loss came in the season opener against the number ten ranked team in the most recent NAIA coaches poll, Montana Tech.
Now well into conference play, the Tigers have all but reclaimed their second consecutive MidSouth Conference champions title. After dominating in wins over conference rivals Bethel College and Cumberland University (TN), the Tigers still have three wins to claim if they're to solidify themselves as a number one seed in the NAIA Football Championship Series, starting with the Cumberlands Patriots.
Georgetown College wideout Dillon Warren looked up field for someone to block during the Tigers come from behind 19-16 victory over MidEast Region rivals University of the Cumberlands on Saturday, Nov. 2.
Before kickoff, Georgetown College honored its 24 football seniors, including former Mercer County High School graduate Dillon Warren, who returned for a fifth season of college in order to finish his second degree. Warren is the Tigers second leading receiver and so far, playing in four less games than last season, he has tallied 296 receiving yards compared to 291 last fall. Warren says the appointment of new wide receivers coach Dayne Keller has had a positive impact on his game.
'This coach came in and implemented some new things we haven't really done before and honestly, me working on some stuff that I wasn't necessarily super confident with last year, kind of helped put more confidence on my back this year,' said Warren after the game. Warren also expressed his gratitude to the program that gave him an opportunity to play the sport he loves while earning a college education. 'I'm going to graduate from here in December with a nice degree and I just appreciate the opportunity they gave me to come here and play football, and also to get a degree from a great institution like Georgetown,' said Warren.
The Patriots initial drive spanned 70 yards and drained nearly six minutes from the clock. Georgetown got off to a good start on their second offensive drive when junior quarterback Gehrig Slunaker connected with Warren for a gain of 12 yards, but the drive stalled, and even after the Tigers recovered a muffed punt, the offense was still warming up and couldn't gain another first down.
The Tigers offensive struggles continued for most of the first half, the defense scored first after bringing down Patriot runner Job Matossian in the endzone for a safety. The Tiger offense finally got on the scoreboard with 5:53 remaining in the first half, when Cumberlands failed to convert a short-yardage fourth down from their own 26-yard line. Darius Neal, former Frederick Douglas graduate, powered in his eighth touchdown of the season to give the Tigers their first lead. The Patriots marched 75 yards down the field and reclaimed all momentum just before halftime, finishing the drive with a 9-yard touchdown run with only 32 seconds remaining in the first half.
The Patriot secondary was locked in, and for the most part, shut down the Tigers passing game. Warren was targeted four times during the second and third quarter, but finished the game with one reception for 12 yards. He also tallied 62 yards on three kickoff returns.
The Tigers turned to Neal and the run game to complete the comeback. Neal ran for 51 yards over six straight carries to kickstart the Tigers' second scoring drive early in the third quarter, and burst through the line from two yards out to give the Tigers their first lead with just under two minutes to play.
In the end, the Tigers moved one win closer to claiming a MidSouth Conference Championship with a 19-16 win. The Campbellsville University Tigers (8-1) and Lindsey Wilson College Blue Raiders (6-2) still lie in the way of a number one seed in the tournament for Georgetown. The Tigers will face CU on Saturday, Nov. 9, in Campbellsville, and LWC on Saturday, Nov. 16, in Columbia.
'We started out with a loss to Montana Tech, a little rocky game, but we're hitting our stride right now, and I really feel confident about our team,' said Warren. For more stories like this one, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

Rita Lawhorn, Bonnie King and Cynthia Luttrell got started on their holiday shopping at last year's Christmas Bazaar at St. Andrew Catholic Church.
It's beginning to look a lot like Christmas around Harrodsburg and Mercer County as several events return to kick off the holiday season. title: Getting Ready For Holiday Road Trips
description: City road crews worked to clean Main Street of snow and ice. (File image). Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com With Thanksgiving and the Christmas holidays approaching, local and…
content:
City road crews worked to clean Main Street of snow and ice. (File image).
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
With Thanksgiving and the Christmas holidays approaching, local and state officials say they're prepared for winter driving.
'We're ready to roll,' said Harrodsburg Public Works Director Frank Lukitsch. His department handles city streets.
There hasn't been a whole lot of call for a lot of plowing over the last several years, with only two storms managing to accumulate more than an inch of snow last winter. Lukitsch couldn't estimate how much road salt he had on hand. He said the city has more road salt on order if it's needed. 'We don't even have room to store any more,' he said.
Mercer County Road Supervisor. Todd Palmer estimated he had 2,500 tons of road salt if they needed it to treat county-maintained roads.
'That's just what's on hand,' Palmer said. 'We've got room to hold a whole lot more.'
The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) maintains most roads, streets and bridges that are part of the State Highway System, including interstates, parkways and U.S. routes such as U.S. 127.
In a press release, KYTC said they have an inventory of snow fighting materials and equipment, including over 1 million gallons of brine (salt-water mixture), 1.1 million gallons of calcium chloride (added to salt) and 369,000 tons of salt. The state has more than 1,400 plow trucks across Kentucky, with more than 2,300 staff and crew members.
'Safety on our roadways is a team effort between state crews and the public,' said KYTC Secretary Jim Gray in a press release. 'Our road crews brave the elements to treat and clear roads, and motorists can do their part by slowing down and giving our folks plenty of room to operate.'
With the holidays bearing down upon us, there are two forecasts to look out for: the number of drivers who are projected to take to the roads and the weather. The American Automobile Association is projecting 79.9 million Americans will travel 50 miles or more from home over the seven-day Thanksgiving holiday travel period. This year's projection of nearly 80 million travelers is an increase of 1.7 million people compared to last year and 2 million more than pre-pandemic travel in 2019, according to the AAA.
Lori Weaver Hawkins, public affairs manager for AAA Blue Grass, said the majority of travelers will be going by personal vehicle, making for increased traffic congestion throughout the Thanksgiving travel period.
'Motorists are reminded to practice good driving behaviors, stay focused on the roadway and pack their patience to avoid aggressive driving behaviors,' said Weaver Hawkins in a press release. 'In addition, AAA reminds travelers going by personal vehicle to stay alert for those who are at the roadside. Slow down and move over for tow drivers and other first responders as well as stranded motorists at the roadside. It's not only the law, but it's the safe thing to do. We want to be sure everyone makes their way home for Thanksgiving dinner.'
The predicted high temperature on Thanksgiving Day is 44° with an overnight low of 30° and a 54 percent chance of precipitation, according to Weather.com. There is a chance of snow showers in the early morning on Friday, Nov. 29.
The winter solstice, the first day of winter, will be Saturday, Dec. 21. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is predicting warmer-than-average temperatures for the southern tier of the U.S. to the eastern Great Lakes. NOAA is also calling for wetter-than-average conditions this winter, with the strongest probabilities in Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky.
Here are some winter driving tips, courtesy of the AAA.
• Be prepared. Have your vehicle checked before hitting the road, especially for a long road trip.
• Check the weather. Check the weather along your route, and when possible, delay your trip if bad weather is expected.
• Stay connected. Before hitting the road, notify others and let them know your route, destination and estimated time of arrival.
If you get stuck in the snow, here are some more tips about what to do, courtesy of the AAA:
• Stay with your vehicle. Your vehicle provides temporary shelter and makes it easier for rescuers to locate you. Do not try to walk in a severe storm. It is easy to lose sight of your vehicle in blowing snow and become lost.
• Don't over exert yourself. When digging out your vehicle, listen to your body and stop if you become tired.
• Be visible. Tie a brightly colored cloth to the antenna of your vehicle or place a cloth at the top of a rolled up window to signal distress. At night, keep the dome light on if possible. It only uses a small amount of electricity and will make it easier for rescuers to find you.
• Clear the exhaust pipe. Make sure the exhaust pipe is not clogged with snow, ice or mud. A blocked exhaust pipe can cause deadly carbon monoxide gas to leak into the passenger compartment of the vehicle while the engine is running.
• Stay warm. Use whatever is available to insulate your body from the cold. This could include floor mats, newspapers or paper maps. Pre-pack blankets and heavy clothing to use in case of an emergency.
• Conserve fuel. If possible, only run the engine and heater long enough to remove the chill. This will help to conserve fuel.
KYTC is also advising travelers to prepare an emergency kit to keep in their vehicles with essentials to stay safe if stranded during a winter event.
For more information, visit aaa.com.

title: Burgin Independent High School Earns College Success Award
description: File image. Robert Moore Herald Staff rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com Burgin Independent High School is one of 31 Kentucky high schools to earn the College Success Award from GreatSchools.org, the…
content:
File image.
Robert Moore
Herald Staff
rmoore@harrodsburgherald.com
Burgin Independent High School is one of 31 Kentucky high schools to earn the College Success Award from GreatSchools.org, the nation's leading nonprofit school information site. Now in its sixth year, the recognition honors public high schools that excel at preparing students to enroll and succeed in college, as determined by available data in each state.
'It is a testament to our graduates for not just getting ready for post-secondary success but for our graduates to stay with it and finish the task with a degree,' said Burgin Superintendent Will Begley. 'Many students opt out after a tough semester. It takes determination to overcome some of the barriers that come your way when you are in college and that is what is so inspiring.'
Burgin Independent School also received an 8 out of 10 rating from GreatSchools.org, performing at the 71st percentile compared to other schools in Kentucky. Burgin also received a 6 out of 10 in the academic progress rating. According to Great Schools, Burgin is at the 54th percentile in Kentucky. In the college readiness rating, Burgin is rated at 10 out of 10, and performs in the 98th percentile in Kentucky. In the equity rating, Burgin was ranked at seven out of 10, and performs in the 64th percentile in Kentucky.
Burgin is one of 1,436 winners in 19 states that have demonstrated successful track records of graduating students who enroll in two- or four-year colleges, are ready for college-level coursework and persist on to their second year. College readiness is crucial for high school students' future success as companies still overwhelmingly hire candidates with a college degree, officials say.
In addition to Burgin, other Kentucky winners include Boyle County High School, DuPont Manual High School in Jefferson County and Western Hills High School in Franklin County. Mercer County Senior High School did not receive an award this year, but they earned a College Success Award in 2020.
'We want to provide vibrant learning experiences for all our students, which means we are 'All In' when it comes to making sure every student is equipped to succeed after high school,' Commissioner of Education Robbie Fletcher said in a Kentucky Department of Education press release. 'For many, that means pursuing a postsecondary education. Our College Success Award-winning schools are models of excellence both within the Commonwealth and across the nation, underscoring our commitment to keeping students at the forefront of what we do each day.'
State officials say the College Success Award is possible because Kentucky is leading the nation in both collecting and transparently sharing information on how students perform after high school, which is valuable information for families, educators and policymakers.
'We applaud Kentucky for prioritizing a high-quality public education that puts students on the path to bright futures,' said Jon Deane, CEO of GreatSchools. 'It's inspiring to see how entire school communities—students, teachers, and families—can work together in pursuit of a common goal: success for all. Congratulations to these 31 schools for receiving the College Success Award as proof of their hard work and dedication.'
Explore the College Success Award methodology and browse the full list of winners at GreatSchools.org. For more great stories, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Kaelin Drakeford And The Panthers Earn 16-13 Win On Senior Day
description: Both the Eastern Illinois Panthers (3-8) and Charleston Southern Buccaneers (1-10) have lost several games decided by less than a touchdown in 2024. Coming into the game, they each resided in the…
content:
Both the Eastern Illinois Panthers (3-8) and Charleston Southern Buccaneers (1-10) have lost several games decided by less than a touchdown in 2024. Coming into the game, they each resided in the bottom two spots of the Ohio Valley Conference power rankings. The Panthers recognized several graduates before kickoff, including former Mercer County standout athlete Kaelin Drakeford.
Drakeford had a significant role in the success of Titan football and basketball teams from 2017 to his graduation in 2020 and has since featured in every EIU game he has been healthy for. 2024 is Drakeford's most successful season to date; this fall the Panthers' safety has tallied 56 tackles, two forced fumbles, two tackles for loss and an interception. Drakeford says he has focused on playing to his strengths in 2024, and feels good about the level of physicality he brings to the Panthers' defense each given play.
On senior day, Drakeford led a defensive secondary that allowed only 85 passing yards on 11 receptions. The Panthers' offense scored on the final two drives of the first half to take a 13-6 lead into the locker room. On the first drive of the second half, the Panthers marched into Buccaneers territory, but their drive was cut short after quarterback Pierce Holley threw an interception. The turnover caused the momentum to switch, as the Panthers' next five offensive drives resulted in two turnovers and three punts.
Kaelin Drakeford shot forward from his safety spot and delivered a big hit on Charleston Southern tight end Landon Sauers during the fourth quarter of the Panthers' 16-13 overtime win. ( The Harrodsburg Herald /Sam Warren)
The Panthers defense, led by Drakeford and linebackers Anthony Shockey and Phoenix Porter, dominated in the second half. Over the course of six Buccaneer drives, the Panthers allowed only 65 total yards of offense after halftime. The Buccaneers were able to tie the game after a 47-yard punt return from Noah Jennings kickstarted a 15-yard scoring drive with 4:52 remaining, but the Panthers' defense held strong and didn't allow a single yard during the final defensive stand of regulation, sending the game to overtime. Panthers' Head Coach Chris Wilkerson had faith in his defensive unit and sent them on the field first after winning the coin toss. On fourth and one, Drakeford and Shockey met the Charleston Southern runner at the line of scrimmage and forced the turnover needed to give their offense a shot at winning the game.
After moving the ball to the eight-yard line, the Panthers set up to attempt a game-winning field goal. In a matter of seconds, Panther fans' hopes were drained as the snap went sailing over the holders hands and quickly rolled near midfield. One Buccaneer had a break on the ball, but he was so desperate to return the fumble for the game-winning score that he kicked the ball forward to create more space for himself, which immediately nullified the play. After deliberation amongst officials, the Panthers were awarded a fresh set of downs back inside their opponents five-yard line. Three plays later, Julian Patino put the final kick of the game through the uprights, earning the Panthers their third win in 2024.
'A lot of my games I've played here have ended like that, so I was just staying confident and staying ready 'til the very end,' Drakeford said after the game. 'It feels good. Not every game you're going to get every play, but I'm just glad to get a win for all the seniors, fifth and sixth year guys; it was a good win.'
Drakeford has spent the last four years earning a bachelor's degree in political science and is currently wrapping up a second degree in business. He is more than happy with his decision to spend his college career in Charleston, Illinois.
'It's amazing. I've met some great people here. It's been a blast; the best times of my life,' said Drakeford.

title: Rebuilding A Dynasty: With Chris Souder Back At The Helm, Mercer Plans To Rebuild Around Talented Youth
description: The Harrodsbur
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /April Ellis
The 2024-2025 Mercer County High School girls basketball team pictured from left to right; back row: manager Monica Ison, man­ager Brooke Baker, Cardin Sickles, lmperia Blacketer, Maddi Baker, Demi Mullins, Allie Fenwick, Emma Fenwick, London Yates, Reece Ransdell. Front row: Layken Johnson, Phoenix Yates, Lizzie Nichols, lzzie Carlton, Ralasia Piazza, Kate Carlton, Olive Frisby, Alexa Wade, Karis Wilham.
Lady Titan basketball is back after an eventful offseason, including the reintroduction of Head Coach Chris Souder. Souder had several questions about his 2024-2025 Lady Titan basketball squad after the loss of stellar senior duo Anna Kate Drakeford and Sara Dunn. The pair averaged just over 37 points per game a season ago, and the former led the program in scoring the last two seasons. Just over six points per game are being displaced through other players leaving the program, so it's truly a rebuilding year for the Lady Titans.
Even a year ago, the Lady Titans roster lacked depth, and featured several freshman and middle-schoolers. This year's squad will be no different. The five-player freshman class will be crucial to the program's development for years to come. Souder says Alexa Wade and Maddi Baker have stepped to the forefront, and the pair will both play key roles in the rotation. Allie Fenwick, Emma Fenwick and Olive Frisby round out the class.
Sophomores Phoenix Yates and Lizzie Nichols each featured more than 10 times last year, and could provide quality minutes. The sophomore class is led by Izzie Carlton, who will be the focal point of the offense this season. The 6'3 center averaged 11.1 points and 8.6 rebounds per game in her freshman season and the Lady Titans will be most successful offensively when they can rely on Carlton. title: George Shannon
description: George Thomas 'G.T.' or 'Tommy' Shannon, of Burgin, widower of Dolores Freeman Shannon, died Wednesday, Jan. 8, 2025, at his home in Burgin. Born Oct. 8, 1941, on Curdsville Road in Mercer County, he…
content:
George Thomas 'G.T.' or 'Tommy' Shannon, of Burgin, widower of Dolores Freeman Shannon, died Wednesday, Jan. 8, 2025, at his home in Burgin.
Born Oct. 8, 1941, on Curdsville Road in Mercer County, he was the son of the late Bessie Carrier Shannon and William (Bill) Shannon of Burgin.
Survivors include: one son, Tim (Sonya) Shannon; two daughters, Leia (Dwayne) Norman and Sherri Shannon; one sister, Patricia Phelps of Stanford; fiancée Wilma Yates Baker of Lexington; seven grand children; seven great-grand-children; and fur babies Gracie and Bandit.
He was preceded in death by two brothers, Bennie Michael and Lennie Patrick Shannon.
He was a 1960 graduate of Burgin High School, where he played football and basketball. He served six years in the U.S. Army and completed various courses, including, aviation technical, leadership, oral and written communications, faculty development, maintenance management and personnel management for executive courses. He served four years in the Kentucky National Guard. Along with being a Federal Civil Servant, he was also a Mercer County Civil Servant.
G.T. served the federal government 28.5 years before retiring Jan. 4, 1993. During his Federal Civil Service career, he was an aircraft technician, aircraft technical inspector, aircraft repair supervisor, aircraft inspector foreman, oil analysis management specialist, maintenance management specialist, and a supervisory oil analysis management specialist. At retirement, he was a supervisory oil analysis management specialist with the Department of Army, managing world-wide field operations of the Army Oil Analysis Program. G.T. was Fort Campbell's 1980 Civilian Employee of the Year, trades and craft category. Also he was a decorated US Army Vietnam era veteran, and DoD Civil Servant receiving the following: Department of the Army Achievement Medal (civilian award), Army Commendation Medal W/ Oak Leaf Cluster, National Defense Service Metal, two awards of the Good Conduct Medal, Aircraft Crewman Badge and Expert Rifle Badge. He also received the Commander's Award for Civilian Service for his contributions to Operation Desert Shield/Storm. After retiring from the federal government, he worked as an assistant manager at the Southern States Co-Op stores in the Danville and Harrodsburg and also was manager of Cane Run Fishing Camp.
He served five years as Mayor of Burgin, as well as serving about eight years on the Burgin City Council. During Judge-Executive Kenneth Kirkland's administration, G.T. served as Mercer County's Director of Services.
G.T. belonged to the Masonic Order, Mercer Lodge 777. He was a Kentucky Colonel, a charter member and president of the Rineyville Optimist Club and was Lt Governor, Zone 5, KY-WVA District of Optimist International.
Funeral services were held Sunday, Jan. 12, at the Ransdell Funeral Chapel. Private burial was held in the Camp Nelson National Cemetery in Nicholasville.

title: Lady Titans dominate CAL
description: Samuel Warren Herald Staff sports@harrodsburgherald.com The Mercer County Lady Titans basketball team (5-12) picked up their first win since Dec. 27 on Monday, Jan. 20, when they outclassed the…
content:
Samuel Warren
Herald Staff
sports@harrodsburgherald.com
The Mercer County Lady Titans basketball team (5-12) picked up their first win since Dec. 27 on Monday, Jan. 20, when they outclassed the Christian Academy of Louisville Lady Centurions (3-13). Lady Titan Head Coach Chris Souder should have no complaints about his team's intensity and effort in the opening moments of the game, but rather their execution. Sickles earned a foul under the basket and earned Mercer the first point of the game, but simple mistakes ruined the Lady Titans first quarter. A traveling call on Mercer, and a foul on the defensive end allowed CAL to take a lead, and they never looked back. As the Lady Centurions continued to make shots, Mercer was called for another travel, and then over and back. The Lady Titans turned the ball over eight times in the opening quarter, six of them were called travels. Despite the sloppy play, when Mercer held possession, they found good shots around the rim. CAL didn't have anyone physical or long enough to play effective defense on sophomore Izzie Carlton or eighth grader Cardin Sickles. Freshman Alexa Wade blew past the CAL defense and layed it off the glass with seemingly no contest, but she's just that fast. Carlton made three baskets at the rim and was a perfect 4-4 from the free throw line in the first quarter. In the final seconds of the first, Sickles fought for an offensive rebound and was fouled while going back up. She made one shot, but Mercer still trailed 17-13.
'I was pretty upset in the first quarter, but the girls did respond,' said Souder.
Eighth grader Annie Releford began the second quarter with a perfectly lofted pass over a CAL post player, which fell into hands of Carlton for an easy basket. Moments later, Wade slipped a pass to Carlton in the post and she made the shot while being fouled, cutting CAL's lead to one. With 3:30 left in the first half, Wade swished a long range three, and gave Mercer their first lead, 24-23. Sickles grabbed a rebound and sent a long pass forward to Wade for a layup, and seconds later Wade swatted the ball free and freshman Maddi Baker picked it up on the way to the rim, and finished off of the glass. Kate Carlton drew a foul and made one from the charity stripe. Then it was Emma Fenwick who forced a turnover and drew a foul before making both shots. The Lady Titans had taken over the game, and led 34-30 at halftime.
Sophomore Lizzie Nichols kept Mercer's momentum going in the second half and swished a corner three to open scoring. The Lady Titans scored on the next three straight possessions and took a commanding 43-30 lead, prompting a CAL timeout. Wade assisted another tough I. Carlton basket at the rim. One possession later, she drew a foul and made both shots. I. Carlton was fouled while shooting three times in the third quarter, and made five foul shots. Her 11-14 shooting from the charity stripe during the game led to a season-high 34 point performance. Next, Baker drew a foul at the rim and made both shots. Wade blew by the Lady Centurion defense for another layup to close out the third quarter, and Mercer led 54-40 after three quarters.
It seemed the Lady Titans had shored up their fifth win of the season, but Mercer stayed on the gas in the fourth quarter. After Nichols nailed her second three, Sickles and I. Carlton took advantage of the Lady Centurions weak post play, and attacked the rim time and time again. The pair combined for 19 points in the final period, and put a stamp on Mercer's 78-54 win, which is the most points the Lady Titans have scored so far this season.
'We also made an adjustment at halftime defensively that really got us going,' said Souder. 'We still have tons of room for improvement but it was great to get a win.'
Scoring: I. Carlton 34, Sickles 18, Wade 11, Nichols 6, E. Fenwick 3, Baker 2, K. Carlton 1. For more great stories, check out this week's edition of the Harrodsburg Herald. Click here to subscribe.

title: Ring Of History: Titan Wrestling Hosts First Home Dual
description: The Mercer County Titan wrestling program hosted their first ever meet on Wednesday, Jan. 22, in the Mercer County High School gymnasium. The night began by recognizing the program's eighth graders,…
content:
The Mercer County Titan wrestling program hosted their first ever meet on Wednesday, Jan. 22, in the Mercer County High School gymnasium. The night began by recognizing the program's eighth graders, and a middle school dual with Anderson County immediately followed. Just three days prior, the middle school program qualified Peyton Mankin for the state competition. Mankin will compete at state on Saturday, Feb. 1, at Freedom Hall at the Kentucky Exposition Center in Louisville. The youth wrestling program also took the mat Wednesday. Youth wrestler Janru Roos claimed the Region 3, 10U championship in the 93 lbs weight class. Jensen Layton claimed a spot at state with a 5th place finish, and Tristan Turner placed second in the 12U 135 lbs weight class. The Youth Wrestling State competition is scheduled this upcoming Sunday at Freedom Hall.
The momentum from a successful regional meet helped the middle school team claim a 49-12 team win over Anderson County. All but two eighth graders won their match. Eighth grader Kyler Bryant finished his middle school career with an emphatic win, which Coach Craig Hampton said was a huge performance. Perhaps the best performance of the night was that of eighth grader Evan Baker, who easily won his middle school match, and also helped the high school team by picking up a win in his match against Lexington Christian Academy.
'We were very happy with Evan Baker's performance,' said Hampton.
Seniors Gage Bennett, Ayden Snellen and Aiden Watson were honored for their impact on the program in its inaugural season. Unfortunately for the Titans, Snellen, Watson and some other key members of the team were not feeling well enough to wrestle. The weights often didn't align, and Mercer got the tougher matchup in most circumstances. Bennett was forced to wrestle an opponent who outweighed him by 40 lbs, but it was hard to tell because of the competitive nature of the match. Bennett had his opponent on his back momentarily, but eventually fell behind in the match.
'Gage has been a very bright side to our first year program. He shows up ready to work everyday at practice, great attitude, very coachable. [He] didn't know anything about the sport before this season and has kept a winning record so far,' said Hampton.
Freshman Cannon Buchanan slammed his opponent in the first period of his match, and went on to claim a win after two more hard fought rounds. Freshman Aaron Bricarello claimed a win in the 144 lbs weight class. Bryson Garcia slammed his opponent seconds after the first round began and eventually won his match. Junior Sammy Bragg was the fifth and final Titan to win their match and earn points for the Titans.
Bryson Garcia got himself out of this position and eventually won his match during the Titans dual with Lexington Christian Academy. (Image: Samuel Warren/ The Harrodsburg Herald .)
In the end, the Titans fell to LCA, 36-24. Mercer County fans came in droves to support the Titans in their only home meet of the season and created an electric environment.
'We were stoked with the community's response to our first ever home match. I've had a bunch of people come up and tell me how exciting it was to watch! Great crowd and atmosphere that night,' said Hampton.
More recently the boys team placed eighth at the Bourbon City Dual Clash on Saturday, Jan. 25. The Titans have one more dual scheduled this season before regional competition, and will travel to Green County today, Thursday Jan. 30, for a dual with the Dragons.
The girls program competes in Region 4, which will host its regional tournament at Taylor County on Saturday, Feb. 15. The KHSAA Region 6 wrestling tournament will be held on Saturday, Feb. 22, and hosted at the Corbin Arena. content:

All registered donors at the Kentucky Blood Center's drive on Friday, Feb. 14, will receive an 'I Love KY Blood Donors' long-sleeve shirt (while supplies last).
The Kentucky Blood Center will host a drive for Mercer County on Friday, Feb. 14, from 11:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. at Youngs Park (530 Linden Avenue). All registered donors at this upcoming drive will receive an 'I Love KY Blood Donors' long-sleeve shirt (while supplies last).
Starting in January, all blood drives will move to Youngs Park at 530 Linden Avenue, near Ephraim McDowell James B. Haggin Hospital, according to the Kentucky Blood Center.
Winter weather and illnesses have had an impact on the blood supply this year. The Kentucky Blood Center is the provider for more than 70 hospitals in across the Commonwealth, local patients rely on a healthy blood supply for everything from traumas to cancer treatments, surgeries, diseases, organ transplants and more.
The blood donation process is easy and has a major impact on the community. Whole blood donations take less than an hour from registration to refreshment. One donation can save up to three local lives.
Blood donors must be at least 17 years old (16 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, be in general good health, show a photo I.D. and meet additional requirements. Sixteen-year-old donors must have a signed parental permission slip, which can be found at kybloodcenter.org.
Appointments are preferred but walk-ins are welcome. To schedule a donation, visit kybloodcenter.org or call 800-775-2522.
The Kentucky Blood Center is the largest independent, full-service, nonprofit blood center in the Commonwealth. The nonprofit agency has been saving local lives since 1968. Licensed by the FDA, the Kentucky Blood Center's sole purpose is to collect, process and distribute blood for patients in Kentucky. KBC provides services in 90 Kentucky counties and has donor centers in Lexington, Louisville, Frankfort, Pikeville, Somerset and the Tri-County area (Corbin). title: Winterguard Shines In Winchester
description: Mercer County Winterguard members Lauryn Maddox, Tabitha Grant, and Joyce
content:
Mercer County Winterguard members Lauryn Maddox, Tabitha Grant, and Joyce Ritchie struck a pose during a performance of their 2025 show, 'Heart Strings,' in Winchester on Saturday, Feb. 1. (Image Submitted).
The Mercer County High School Winterguard team competed in their first competition of the 2025 season this past on Saturday, Feb 1, competing at Roger D. Campbell Middle School in Winchester. They performed the first half of their new 2025 show, Heart Strings.
Heart Strings was more or less, in its own way, a carry on of the back and forth pullings of relationships from what we saw in the fall marching show, My Hollow Heart. With music from SIA, Elastic Heart, the show is the beautiful and yet painful back and forth of love and how the heart strings can be tugged in such ways that affects the emotions of so many.
'The show is about the heart and the way it persists through hard times. To quote the song—a bigger blade might be too sharp, but I've got thick skin and an elastic heart,' said Alex Smith, the director of the Winterguard program. 'Like elastic, the heart, the emotions can stretch and withstand the things you would think it cannot.'
Alex went on to add: 'All the excitement of the 2024 Marching Program, going to state, the finals, all of that. I wasn't ready to see it end. So the story goes on in a special way.'
The Mercer County Winterguard formed in the fall of 2022 and only did exhibitions at home basketball games during its first year. The 2023-2024 season was the first show they competed in. The show Con Artist took them to finals at Northern Kentucky University. title: Mercer School Board Reviews $25.8 Million Draft Budget
description: Image: Tnemec. The Mercer County Board of Education reviewed the draft budget for the 2025-2026 school year. At their first meeting of the year, Finance Officer Amber Minor took them through the first…
content:
Image: Tnemec.
The Mercer County Board of Education reviewed the draft budget for the 2025-2026 school year. At their first meeting of the year, Finance Officer Amber Minor took them through the first step in the school district's yearlong budget cycle.
Among the key takeaways, the draft budget projects total revenues of $28.5 million, including a beginning balance of $6 million, with no change in local general fund revenue, which is raised from taxes.
The draft budget projects total expenses of $25.8 million, a $106,413 increase compared to the fiscal year 2025 working budget. The budget includes a contingency of 10.75 percent as well as a step increase for salary and fringe expenses.
Minor noted her office had received notification about a potential shortfall in the Support Education Excellence in Kentucky funding program. SEEK provides funds to local school districts for transportation and special needs education. Minor told the board she had not received final numbers for SEEK, but speculated the transportation allocation would be under the initial projections. Minor said it's happened numerous times over the eight years she's been with the school district. Minor told the board that she didn't use the highest number when crafting the district's current budget.
'What does it mean for next year? I don't know,' Minor said.
Minor said Kentucky​​​​​​​​​​Secretary of Education Jamie Link will ask the General Assembly to fund the shortfall. She said she included a little increase of SEEK revenue in the draft budget. She said it was still lower than what they were told what it would be last year.
'We can adjust that as we go through the budget cycle,' Minor said.
The school budget cycle is divided into three steps. The board reviews a draft budget in January. They must approve a tentative budget by May 30 and a working budget by Sept. 30. The tentative budget will include updated projected revenue and beginning balance.
January is school board appreciation month, and board members were presented with gifts and goodies—including cookies—and framed certificates of appreciation.
Superintendent Jason Booher also thanked Director of Facilities Will Carlton and the staff for their work during the recent cold weather. Booher said he'd also met with the mayor of Harrodsburg and the judge-executive to thank them for the jobs the city and county had done keeping local roads open.
Booher told the board the district had not used a non-traditional instruction— an NTI day—since he joined the school system.
'In person learning is what's best for kids,' Booher said. He said schools are currently allowed to take 10 NTI days a year and the state legislature may allow schools to take five more NTI days this session.

title: Three Nominees Selected To Replace Judge Jeff Dotson
description: The Judicial Nominating Commission has announced nominees to fill the Circuit Court judicial vacancy in Boyle and Mercer counties. The counties make up the 50th Judicial Circuit and the vacancy is in…
content:
The Judicial Nominating Commission has announced nominees to fill the Circuit Court judicial vacancy in Boyle and Mercer counties. The counties make up the 50th Judicial Circuit and the vacancy is in the circuit's Division 1.
Circuit Court Judge Jeff Dotson in file image.
The judicial seat became vacant when Judge Jeffrey L. Dotson passed away in September 2024.
The three nominees for the judgeship are attorneys Christopher Kala Herron of Danville, Whitney Zimmerman Johns of Harrodsburg and Christopher Joel Reed of Danville.
Chris Herron is in private law practice and is the Boyle County attorney. He received his juris doctor from the University of Louisville Louis D. Brandeis School of Law.
Whitney Johns is in private law practice and is an assistant county attorney for Mercer County. She received her juris doctor from the University of Kentucky College of Law (now the University of Kentucky J. David Rosenberg College of Law).
Joel Reed is in private law practice and serves as a special attorney for the Kentucky Department of Public Advocacy. He received his juris doctor from the Florida Coastal School of Law.
Circuit Court is the court of general jurisdiction that hears civil matters involving more than $5,000, capital offenses and felonies, divorces, adoptions, termination of parental rights, land dispute title cases and contested probate cases. In counties with a Family Court division of Circuit Court, Family Court judges have primary jurisdiction in cases involving family issues, including divorces, adoption, child support, domestic violence and juvenile status offenses.
A retired judge, Dan Kelly, will handle the Circuit Court caseload until the governor appoints Dotson's replacement from the list of nominees.
In 2022, Jeffrey Dotson was appointed by Gov. Andy Beshear to fill the Circuit Court judicial seat, which became vacant when Judge Darren W. Peckler resigned.
Dotson had served as District Court judge for Mercer and Boyle counties since 2003. Dotson's most lasting legacy on the bench will be the Mercer and Boyle County Drug Court, which begin locally shortly after Dotson's appointment to the Circuit Court bench. Drug Court celebrated its first graduation last year with Dotson presenting diplomas to Stephanie Burton and Hannah Lawson. title: Ordinance Allows City To Cut Off Water If Leaks Are Discovered
description: File image. The Harrodsburg City Commission gave first reading to an ordinance allowing the city to disconnect customers who have not repaired water leaks. At their regular meeting on Monday, Feb. 24,…
content:
File image.
The Harrodsburg City Commission gave first reading to an ordinance allowing the city to disconnect customers who have not repaired water leaks.
At their regular meeting on Monday, Feb. 24, the commissioners introduced ordinance 2025-01, which relates to water leak repairs. According to the ordinance, the Harrodsburg Water Department will identify customers who appear to have a leak by 'a computer generated leak report.' The Public Works Department will determine if that leak is on the city side—from the meter to the water line—or on the customer side—from the water meter to the home. It the leak is determined to be on the city's side, the city will repair the leak. If the leak is determined to be on the customer's side, it is the customer's responsibility to repair it, according to the ordinance.
The city will notify the customer of the leak—either in person, or be email, phone, door hanger 'or any other means available,' according to the ordinance. If the customer has not made repairs within 24 hours, the city 'may turn the water off,' according to the ordinance.
'When the water loss from a leak is substantial, or damage is likely to result from the leak,' the city 'reserves the right to turn the water off immediately upon notice to the customer,' according to the ordinance.
On Monday, City Attorney Norrie Currens explained the ordinance is intended to prevent water loss.
Commissioner Kerry Anness said it 'may not be possible' for customers to make repairs within 24 hours.
'I may not be able to get a plumber to fix it,' Anness said.
'It's not a 'shall,' it's a 'may,'' Currens said. She said the ordinance give the city the discretion to act.
'Within 24 hours we have the right to turn it off,' Currens said.
The ordinance will not go into effect until the city commission gives it second reading, which may be at their next meeting on Monday, March 10, at noon.
While they were discussing the water leak ordinance, Commissioner Cnarlie Mattingly asked for clarification on water leak adjustments. The city can adjust bills for customers who have suffered a water leak. The city can make bill adjustments once every two years per customer.
On Monday, Mattingly asked if sewer charges were figured in leak adjustments. He said he'd been asked by several residents.
'We adjust the water and the sewer,' explained Chief Administrative Officer Stacey Maynard. 'We don't have to but we do.'
It was explained that not including sewer charges would cost residents with water leaks more money. For the rest of the story, click here to subscribe to the Harrodsburg Herald online edition–just $2.99 for the week or $24.95 for the year.

title: Lady Titans Earn District Softball Championship
description: The Harrodsburg Herald/Myron EllisThe Mercer County Senior H
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Myron Ellis
The Mercer County Senior High School softball team posed for a picture with the 46th District trophy after their victory over East Jessamine on Tuesday, May 21. This is the Lady Titans first district championship win since 2021.
The Harrodsburg Herald /Myron Ellis
The Mercer County Senior High School softball team posed for a picture with the 46th District trophy after their victory over East Jessamine on Tuesday, May 21. This is the Lady Titans first district championship win since 2021. Both teams were strong in the circle for the district championship on Tuesday, May 21, but the Lady Titans defeated the East Jessamine Jaguars 1-0 for their first district championship since 2021.
Senior Ashley Howard was stellar from the circle for the tournament and recorded 24 outs. Mercer allowed only three hits, striking out nine and walking one. Jaguar pitcher Remie Smith may have taken the loss, but she pitched well for her team, holding Mercer to five hits, striking out eight and walking three.
The game went scoreless up until the extra inning, when freshman Lily Hart was able to get on base after being hit by a pitch, stealing her way to third and scoring the lone winning run on a passed ball.
Senior Hannah Beasley led Mercer with two hits in three at-bats. This will be Beasley's first trip to a region game in her high school career, along with senior teammates Peyton Boyd and Haylee Ransdell. This will be Howard's second trip, after she pitched in a regional game her freshman year.
Hart was first up to bat and was hit by the pitcher. While it might not be a favorable way to get on base, getting on base is what is important. J. Bowman singled, and after a few steals, Mercer had runners on second and third but failed to score with two strikeouts and a line out to right field.
Ashley Howard was stellar from the circle during the tournament and struck out the first two batters. Ava Musick connected with Izzie Cartlton on first base, and the Lady Titans sent the first three batters to the dugout, and the inning was 0-0.

title: Magistrate Jackie Claycomb: A Closer Look
description: Magistrate Jackie Claycomb takes pride in serv­ing Mercer County and in his free time enjoys clas­sic cars. (file image). Jackie Claycomb has represented Mercer County on the fiscal court for more…
content:
Magistrate Jackie Claycomb takes pride in serv­ing Mercer County and in his free time enjoys clas­sic cars. (file image).
Magistrate Jackie Claycomb takes pride in serv­ing Mercer County and in his free time enjoys clas­sic cars. (file image). Jackie Claycomb has represented Mercer County on the fiscal court for more than 10 years. As a resident of Talmage Mayo Road, Claycomb represents the third District, which encompasses much of the west central part of the county, including Talmage, McAfee, Ebenezer, and Jackson Pike to the railroad tracks.
Claycomb was raised in Campbellsville and graduated from Taylor County High School in 1971. Four days after graduating, Claycomb's bags were packed and he left for basic training with the National Guard in Fort Leonard Wood Missouri.
'I was not a person that would have made it in college anyway,' said Claycomb.
As young as 16, Claycomb was working in a Lee's Famous Recipe restaurant, and soon after returning from basic training, he moved to Harrodsburg to help run a new store as a member of the management team.
'I cooked the first piece of chicken ever served out of this store,' said Claycomb. 'I really liked Mercer County when I came here, I thought I was in heaven, compared to Campbellsville.'
Claycomb wasn't enjoying his experience in the National Guard, and after three years of service he signed a contract with the Army as a full time enlistee. He worked in Fort Knox for a year and a half and worked two and a half years in Fort Sill, Oklahoma. Despite the distance, Claycomb would return to Harrodsburg every weekend to help run the restaurant, and of course catch up with Ruth, who he later married. Claycomb hired Ruth to work at the Lee's in Harrodsburg when the store opened, and fell in love soon after. Claycomb spent his entire adult life with Ruth until her passing in January of this year, and he still has a connection with her through the pets they shared.
'My wife was a lover of animals. At one time, she had 21 cats and five dogs… I had to build her a cat house to get ‘em out of my sunroom and my garage,' joked Claycomb. The cat house has seven windows, perches and even a radio that plays country music all day. Today, Claycomb takes care of four cats and three dogs, including a Pomeranian puppy named Annie.
Claycomb helped open an additional three stores across the state while working for Holda systems in Campbellsville.
Twelve years ago, Claycomb decided to leave the stresses of the restaurant business behind, ending a 40 year career in management with Lee's Famous Recipe. He sold the business to his nephew Jeff Claycomb, who runs it today.

title: Lady Titans Beat Lady Cardinals, Snap Five Game Losing Streak
content:
The Harrodsburg Herald /Samuel Warren
Mercer County second baseman Ava Musick tagged out a South Laurel run­ner before throwing out another at first base during the Lady Titans win over South Laurel on Thursday, May 9. The Mercer County Lady Titans (11-8) snapped a five-game skid of losses on senior night Thursday, May 9, when they defeated the South Laurel Lady Cardinals (23-8) 5-2, thanks to three key runs in the bottom of the first inning. Not only had the Lady Titans not won a game since April 19, but the Lady Cardinals traveled to Harrodsburg as the top team in Region 13 and a team that won 12 of its last 15 games. Seniors Ashley Howard, Hanna Beasley, Peyton Boyd and Haylee Ransdell were recognized before the game for their contributions to Mercer County softball over the last four years. 'I am really proud of this senior class. They all have contributed in many ways to help this team succeed. They have left their mark on the Mercer County softball program. My only regret is not having another season with them on our team,' said Lady Titans Head Coach Darren Ransdell. Jayla Sanders set the tone on Mercer's second at bat. The sophomore delivered a bunt down the left field line and beat the throw to first base. Howard smacked a hard grounder on the next at-bat, and the Lady Cardinal shortstop couldn't control it. The Lady Titans had their game faces on and caught South Laurel off guard. Four errors over three at bats allowed Mercer to get three runs on the board before earning their second out. Ava Musick hit a line drive into the dirt in front of the Lady Cardinal center fielder, and the South Laurel third baseman fumbled the ball before overthrowing home. Boyd bunted and scored Musick from third base on the next at bat. Boyd was originally called out, but after some conferring between the referees, she was put back on first. It didn't matter, though, as South Laurel earned two outs quickly to keep the damage to a minimum.
